@how own mechanism: When the argument principle hands you ∑ᶠ w, divisor (fun u ↦ p.eval u) (closedBall c R) w for a polynomial p that is NOT monic, do not look for a packaged zero-count-equals-card lemma (the ones in sibling files require q.Monic); prove divisor = rootMultiplicity pointwise and convert the finsum to a multiset count by hand. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  When the argument principle hands you ∑ᶠ w, divisor (fun u ↦ p.eval u)
  (closedBall c R) w for a polynomial p that is NOT monic, do not look for a
  packaged zero-count-equals-card lemma (the ones in sibling files require
  q.Monic); prove divisor = rootMultiplicity pointwise and convert the
  finsum to a multiset count by hand.

  + IF: The goal identifies an analytic divisor finsum over a closed disk
    with (p.roots.filter (fun w ↦ ‖w - c‖ < R)).card, and p carries a
    leading coefficient you cannot normalise away (e.g. a cleared Laurent
    polynomial with arbitrary top coefficient).

  + HOWEVER: The only compiled bridges from zeroCountInClosedBall to a root
    count assume q.Monic, and there is no Mathlib lemma stating the divisor
    of a polynomial evaluation equals its root multiplicity.

  + THEN: (a) Pointwise, for p ≠ 0 and w ∈ U: factor p with
    exists_eq_pow_rootMultiplicity_mul_and_not_dvd, unfold with
    MeromorphicOn.divisor_apply, and certify the order with
    meromorphicOrderAt_eq_int_iff using the cofactor as the analytic unit.
    (b) Globally, rewrite the finsum with finsum_eq_sum_of_support_subset
    over (p.roots.filter …).toFinset, convert each summand with
    Polynomial.count_roots and Multiset.count_filter_of_pos, and close with
    Multiset.toFinset_sum_count_eq. Boundary nonvanishing upgrades ‖w‖ ≤ R
    on the support to ‖w‖ < R. (c) Cast ℤ → ℂ through
    (Int.castAddHom ℂ).map_finsum with the divisor's finiteSupport on the
    compact disk.
    + LEAN:
      api[Polynomial.exists_eq_pow_rootMultiplicity_mul_and_not_dvd]
      api[MeromorphicOn.divisor_apply] api[meromorphicOrderAt_eq_int_iff]
      api[finsum_eq_sum_of_support_subset] api[Polynomial.count_roots]
      api[Multiset.count_filter_of_pos] api[Multiset.toFinset_sum_count_eq]
      api[Function.locallyFinsuppWithin.apply_eq_zero_of_notMem]

  + BECAUSE: The divisor is defined through the meromorphic order, and the
    order of a polynomial evaluation at w is exactly its root multiplicity
    regardless of the leading coefficient; monicity only ever entered
    through the packaged lemma's proof, not through the mathematics.

@flexiarg math-formalization-CA/fourier-inversion-for-real-oscillatory-integrals
@title Close Real Oscillatory Integrals by Fourier Inversion, Not Residues
@keywords fourier, inversion, oscillatory-integral, residue, contour, cosine-transform, poisson-kernel, exp-decay, transform-pair
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [FA]
@why math-strategy/proof-architecture
@see-also math-formalization-CA/measure-integration-api math-informal/dualise-the-problem math-informal/failure-mode-characterization
@how own mechanism: When a real oscillatory integral (cosine/sine transform of a rational or exponentially decaying kernel) would classically be evaluated by residues and the library has no residue or contour-deformation machinery, dualise: compute the Fourier transform of the *symmetric decaying* kernel directly from the library's one-sided exponential lemmas, then apply Fourier inversion and take the real part. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  When a real oscillatory integral (cosine/sine transform of a rational or
  exponentially decaying kernel) would classically be evaluated by residues and
  the library has no residue or contour-deformation machinery, dualise: compute
  the Fourier transform of the *symmetric decaying* kernel directly from the
  library's one-sided exponential lemmas, then apply Fourier inversion and take
  the real part.

  + context: A target like ∫ cos(tx)/(x² + a²) dx over ℝ or a half-line, where
    the informal proof is a semicircle contour and the residue theorem, and
    searches for `residue`, `circleIntegral`-based deformation, or a packaged
    transform of 1/(x²+a²) come back empty.

  + IF:
      The kernel is even and absolutely integrable, then the transform pair
      runs through elementary API: 𝓕(e^{-c|x|}) is two one-sided complex
      exponential integrals (upper half-line for Re a < 0, lower for
      Re b > 0, stitched with `intervalIntegral.integral_Iic_add_Ioi`),
      and inversion `hf.fourierInv_fourier_eq` at the frequency of interest
      recovers the kernel value. The cosine integral is the real part of the
      inversion integral; the half-line integral folds out of the full-line
      one by evenness (`integral_comp_abs`).

  + HOWEVER:
      The seam is convention-heavy: Mathlib's Fourier transform is 2π-normalized
      (`Real.fourier_real_eq_integral_exp_smul`, `Real.fourierInv_eq'`), so the
      frequency must be rescaled (s / (2π)) and the phase identity verified at
      each point — plan a `field_simp`-heavy closing block. Inversion also
      demands integrability of the *transform* as an explicit hypothesis, and a
      continuity hypothesis at the evaluation point; both must be discharged by
      hand. Do not expect the ODE route as a cheaper alternative: the second
      derivative of the cosine kernel produces a ∫cos(tx) term that has no
      Bochner-integral meaning, so the ODE argument is structurally unavailable,
      not merely long.

  + THEN:
      Split the closure into named lemmas: (1) integrability of the kernel;
      (2) the explicit transform of the decaying kernel; (3) inversion to the
      full-line cosine integral; (4) the evenness fold to the half-line and a
      scaling lemma to move from the problem's kernel to the standard one.
      Each is independently checkable and reusable by sibling problems with the
      same bridge.

  + BECAUSE:
      The library's Fourier folder is deep enough to carry the whole argument,
      while its complex-analysis folder has no residue theorem at all; the
      honest cost comparison is "adapt Fourier API and conventions" versus
      "build contour integration from scratch", and it is not close. The
      informal route's difficulty is a property of pen-and-paper infrastructure,
      not of the statement.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[State the full-line integral first; the half-line is a corollary by evenness.]
    next[Compute 𝓕 of the symmetric decaying kernel from one-sided exp lemmas before touching inversion.]
    next[Rescale the frequency by 1/(2π) and verify the phase identity pointwise.]
    next[Discharge integrability of 𝓕 f and continuity at the point explicitly; inversion needs both.]
    next[Take real parts at the end, after the complex inversion equality is established.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CA/measure-integration-api
@title Find the Library's Measure-Theoretic Statement Before Rebuilding It
@keywords measure, integration, Bochner, lintegral, Haar, normalization, junk-value, instance-diamond, adapter, specialization
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [FA PR]
@why math-informal/reduce-to-known-result
@see-also math-formalization-CA/measure-restrict-simplify math-formalization-CA/lp-norm-comparison math-formalization/transport-across-an-instance-diamond
@how own mechanism: Measure-theoretic results usually exist in the library under a more general statement, a different normalization, or a restricted variant — so treat the work as locating and adapting that statement, and audit the totalized integral's premises before believing the result. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  Measure-theoretic results usually exist in the library under a more general
  statement, a different normalization, or a restricted variant — so treat the
  work as locating and adapting that statement, and audit the totalized
  integral's premises before believing the result.

  + context: A formalization whose remaining obligation is measure-theoretic —
    an integrability side condition, a convergence theorem, a change of
    coordinates, a norm comparison — and where writing the classical proof
    directly into the problem file looks like the shortest route.

  + IF:
      The library already contains the mathematical content, then the residual
      work is an adapter and should be named as one: specialize the general
      statement to the case at hand, compose with an explicit scaling to move
      between conventions, or select the restricted variant that matches the set
      being integrated over. A Fourier limit theorem under another phase
      convention becomes the target composed with a nonzero frequency scaling
      plus a separate character identity; a one-dimensional statement that looks
      absent is often the fixed-dimensional or Jacobian formulation at `n = 1`;
      the radial coefficient in dimension three is the general Haar coefficient
      normalized to `4π`.

  + HOWEVER:
      Three things make this harder than a search.

      The library's generality is where the instances hide. Chaining a
      specialization can expose a measurable-space diamond; the repair is to
      return to the general theorem and instantiate its measure and function
      explicitly at the use site rather than to fight the chain. Elaboration will
      also decline to synthesize witnesses that look obvious — a constant on
      `Icc` may need its finite-measure witness supplied by hand.

      Restricted and unrestricted variants are not interchangeable. When the
      comparison holds only on the set being integrated over, the `_on`
      monotonicity theorem is the correct one; strengthening a local bound into
      a global one to fit the unrestricted statement proves something you do not
      have. The same discrimination applies at the Bochner/`lintegral` seam and
      at the compact-support/full-support interface: concentration and tail
      decay do not discharge a compact-support hypothesis, and an approximate-
      identity instantiation that ignores the kernel-support interface is
      unsound rather than merely stuck.

      Most dangerous, the integral is *totalized*. A non-integrable integrand
      does not fail — it returns a junk value, and a missing integrability
      premise becomes a theorem that is false but elaborates. Jensen applied to
      `log ∘ g` without integrability of the transformed function is the standard
      instance; a transform theorem that omits measurability is another, and may
      genuinely need an integrable/non-integrable split rather than an inferred
      hypothesis.

  + THEN:
      Search the general form first — fixed-dimensional, Jacobian, Haar, another
      normalization — and specialize, before building the named classical proof.
      When you do adapt, isolate the adaptation: the scaling, the character
      identity, the parity-specific identity, each as its own lemma.

      Instantiate at the use site when a specialization chain produces a
      diamond, and supply concrete measure witnesses rather than waiting for
      elaboration to find them.

      Choose the restricted variant when the hypothesis is restricted, and check
      the support interface before instantiating anything that assumes compact
      support.

      Audit every integrability premise explicitly. Before applying a theorem
      through a totalized integral, state what must be integrable and prove it —
      a junk value will not tell you it was missing.

  + BECAUSE:
      Measure theory is the part of a formalization where the library is deepest
      and the local proof is longest, so the ratio between finding and rebuilding
      is at its most extreme here; and it is simultaneously the part where the
      type system's totality is most willing to accept a statement that means
      nothing. Both failures are invisible at the point of writing — the
      rebuilt proof looks like progress, and the junk-valued theorem looks like
      a result. Naming the adapter and auditing the premises is what makes them
      visible while they are still cheap.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Search the general/fixed-dimensional/Haar form and specialize before building.]
    next[Name the adapter — scaling, normalization, character identity — as its own lemma.]
    next[Instantiate the general theorem at the use site when a chain exposes an instance diamond.]
    next[Pick the restricted (`_on`) variant when the hypothesis is restricted.]
    next[Check the kernel-support interface before instantiating a compact-support theorem.]
    next[State and prove every integrability premise; the totalized integral will not.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CA/ode-gronwall-api
@title Prove ODE Flow Stability Through Mathlib's Grönwall APIs
@keywords Lean, Mathlib, ODE, Gronwall, flow, stability, Lipschitz, exponential-bound, reversed-time
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty intermediate
@cross-list [CA ODE]
@why math-informal/reduce-to-known-result
@see-also math-informal/local-to-global math-strategy/convention-bridge
@how own mechanism: For exponential stability of two ODE trajectories, first search Mathlib's Grönwall layer for a theorem matching either the norm of their difference or their distance; then isolate negative time by applying the same theorem to a reversed field and reversed trajectories. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  For exponential stability of two ODE trajectories, first search Mathlib's
  Grönwall layer for a theorem matching either the norm of their difference or
  their distance; then isolate negative time by applying the same theorem to a
  reversed field and reversed trajectories.

  + context: A Lean goal asks for a bound of the form
    `|phi t a - phi t b| <= exp (L * |t|) * |a - b|` from a state-Lipschitz
    vector field and a flow or trajectory predicate.

  + IF:
      The goal is already expressed as distance between two trajectories, use
      `dist_le_of_trajectories_ODE`. If it is expressed as the norm of their
      difference and derivative bounds are readily available, use
      `norm_le_gronwallBound_of_norm_deriv_right_le` and simplify the resulting
      zero-error bound with `gronwallBound_ε0`.

  + HOWEVER:
      These theorems are naturally forward-time statements. Applying them
      directly when `t < 0` creates endpoint-order and sign obligations that
      obscure the estimate. Rewriting absolute values alone does not turn a
      backward trajectory into the forward trajectory expected by the API.

  + THEN:
      Split on the sign of `t`. For nonnegative time, apply the matching
      Grönwall theorem to `s ↦ phi s a - phi s b`, or directly to the pair of
      trajectories. For negative time define the reversed field
      `(s,y) ↦ -f (-s) y` and reversed trajectories `s ↦ phi (-s) a` and
      `s ↦ phi (-s) b`; prove the same Lipschitz and derivative hypotheses, and
      apply the forward theorem at `-t`. Normalize distance, norm and absolute
      value only after the analytic estimate is obtained.

  + BECAUSE:
      Mathlib already contains both a trajectory-distance Grönwall theorem and
      a norm-of-function theorem. Choosing the interface closest to the local
      hypotheses removes most proof plumbing. Time reversal converts the other
      half-line into the same forward theorem instead of requiring a second
      inequality argument.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Choose the distance API or norm-difference API according to the goal's current representation.]
    next[Prove the forward estimate before normalizing norm, distance and absolute value.]
    next[Handle negative time with the reversed field and trajectories.]
    next[Simplify the zero-error Grönwall bound with gronwallBound_ε0.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CA/riemann-darboux-api
@title Bridge Darboux Sums to the Lebesgue Integral by Telescoping the Cells
@keywords Darboux, Riemann, Lebesgue, partition, cells, telescoping, bridge, bounded-measurable
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@why math-formalization-CA/measure-integration-api
@see-also math-formalization-CA/ae-integral-zero math-strategy/convention-bridge
@how own mechanism: The comparison between Darboux sums and the Lebesgue integral is not in the library as a single theorem: prove it cell by cell and telescope, keeping the lower and upper halves as separate statements. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  The comparison between Darboux sums and the Lebesgue integral is not in the
  library as a single theorem: prove it cell by cell and telescope, keeping the
  lower and upper halves as separate statements.

  + context: A bounded measurable function on a closed interval where the target
    relates the classical Riemann–Darboux integral to the Lebesgue integral —
    typically that the lower Darboux integral is at most the Lebesgue integral,
    which is at most the upper one.

  + IF:
      The comparison is made on a single partition cell, then it is elementary:
      on each cell the infimum bounds the function pointwise from below and the
      supremum from above, and the Lebesgue integral over that cell is between
      the two products with the cell's measure. Summing over the partition
      telescopes to the required inequality.

  + HOWEVER:
      The two halves are not one argument. The lower bound and the upper bound
      have different witnesses on each cell, and attempting them together
      produces a proof in which the direction of each inequality has to be
      tracked through the sum — which is where the sign errors are. Keep them as
      two statements.

      The cells themselves need attention rather than assumption. Their measures
      must sum to the interval's measure, and shared endpoints must be shown to
      be almost-everywhere disjoint rather than genuinely disjoint — closed cells
      overlap at endpoints, and a proof that assumes strict disjointness is
      proving something about a partition it does not have.

      Do not expect a packaged bridge. This is the seam between two definitions
      of integral, and libraries generally develop each side thoroughly and leave
      the comparison to the user.

  + THEN:
      State the lower and the upper comparison separately. Prove each on a single
      cell first, then sum, showing that the cell measures add up and that
      endpoint overlaps are null.

      Keep the bounded-measurable hypotheses explicit at the cell level, where
      they are used, rather than carrying them as ambient assumptions.

  + BECAUSE:
      This comparison is a convention bridge rather than a theorem about
      functions — it reconciles two constructions of the same quantity — and
      bridges of that kind are exactly what a library omits, because neither side
      needs it internally. Recognizing it as a bridge sets the right expectation:
      no search will find it, the work is elementary, and the only difficulty is
      the bookkeeping that the classical statement suppresses.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[State the lower and upper comparisons as two separate lemmas.]
    next[Prove each on one partition cell before summing.]
    next[Show the cell measures sum to the interval's measure.]
    next[Show shared endpoints are almost-everywhere disjoint rather than assuming strict disjointness.]
    next[Keep the boundedness and measurability hypotheses where they are used.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CA/series-evaluation-api
@title Evaluate a Series Through Ordered Partial Sums and a Boundary Limit
@keywords series, tsum, conditional-convergence, partial-sums, Abel, index-shift, uniform-continuity, boundary-limit
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty intermediate
@cross-list [NT]
@why math-strategy/proof-architecture
@see-also math-formalization-CA/measure-integration-api math-formalization-CA/rpow-exponent-limit
@how own mechanism: Evaluating a classical series formally means choosing the right notion of sum first — ordered partial sums for anything conditionally convergent — and then separating convergence, transport to the boundary, and evaluation into three independent obligations. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  Evaluating a classical series formally means choosing the right notion of sum
  first — ordered partial sums for anything conditionally convergent — and then
  separating convergence, transport to the boundary, and evaluation into three
  independent obligations.

  + context: A named series to be evaluated in closed form — a zeta value, a
    Leibniz-type alternating sum, a boundary value of a power series — where the
    textbook derivation is a few lines of manipulation.

  + IF:
      The series converges absolutely, then the library's unordered sum is the
      right object and the manipulations are direct: index shifts, term
      regrouping, and interchange all have API and none of them need an ordering
      argument.

  + HOWEVER:
      Unordered summation is not what a conditionally convergent series has. A
      classical alternating series is *not* summable in the unordered sense, so
      stating it with `∑'` either fails to elaborate or, worse, states something
      other than what was meant. Conditionally convergent series must be
      expressed as a limit of ordered partial sums, and every later step has to
      respect that ordering.

      The three jobs in a boundary evaluation are genuinely independent and get
      conflated. Establishing that the series converges at the boundary does not
      require knowing its value; Abel's theorem moves the unknown sum to a radial
      limit; evaluating that radial limit is an interior computation with a
      closed form. Attempting them together produces an argument that is circular
      in exactly one place and hard to see.

      Small mechanical steps have their own API and are worth locating rather
      than reproving: an index shift for a two-index zeta rearrangement,
      `integral_comp_add_right` for translating an interval integral, a uniform
      continuity statement for a series of functions. Each is a one-line lookup
      and a half-page reconstruction.

  + THEN:
      Decide the notion of sum before writing the statement, and use ordered
      partial sums whenever convergence is conditional.

      Split a boundary evaluation into three named lemmas — convergence at the
      boundary, Abel transport to a radial limit, evaluation of the interior
      closed form — and prove them separately.

      Look up the mechanical steps (index shift, integral translation, uniform
      series continuity) instead of rebuilding them, and reuse a template that
      already worked for a series of the same shape.

  + BECAUSE:
      The gap between the classical and the formal treatment of series is almost
      entirely about which sum is meant. Classical notation leaves the ordering
      implicit and lets rearrangement pass unremarked, while the library's
      default is the unordered sum precisely because it is the one that is
      rearrangement-invariant. A conditionally convergent series formalized with
      the default is not a harder proof of the same theorem — it is a different
      statement, and the divergence is silent until something will not close.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Decide absolute vs conditional convergence before writing the statement.]
    next[Use ordered partial sums for conditional convergence and keep the ordering through every step.]
    next[Prove boundary convergence without reference to the value.]
    next[Move the unknown sum to a radial limit by Abel, as its own lemma.]
    next[Evaluate the interior closed form separately.]
    next[Look up index shifts, integral translations and uniform series continuity rather than reproving them.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CA/uniform-continuity-boundedness
@title Bound the Image Before Controlling the Quotient
@keywords uniform-continuity, boundedness, image, quotient, denominator, api-chain
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty intermediate
@why math-informal-CA/estimate-by-bounding
@see-also math-formalization-CA/metric-cauchy-convergence math-strategy/proof-architecture
@how own mechanism: When an estimate involves a quotient of uniformly continuous functions, get the boundedness of the image first as its own lemma; the quotient control depends on it and cannot be obtained alongside it. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  When an estimate involves a quotient of uniformly continuous functions, get the
  boundedness of the image first as its own lemma; the quotient control depends
  on it and cannot be obtained alongside it.

  + context: An analysis obligation where a uniformly continuous function's
    values appear in a denominator or in a ratio, and the target estimate mixes
    the continuity modulus with the size of the values.

  + IF:
      The domain is bounded — or totally bounded — then uniform continuity gives
      a bounded image through a short chain of library steps, and that bound is
      the constant every subsequent quotient estimate needs.

  + HOWEVER:
      Attempting the quotient bound directly entangles two independent facts: how
      fast the function varies, and how large it gets. The modulus of continuity
      says nothing about the latter, so an argument that needs both and has
      proved neither separately will stall at a point where it is unclear which
      is missing. The order matters more than the difficulty: the boundedness
      step is short, and having it in hand makes the quotient step routine.

  + THEN:
      State and prove the boundedness of the image as its own lemma, via the
      uniform-continuity-to-bounded-image chain.

      Only then estimate the quotient, using that bound for the denominator and
      the modulus for the variation, keeping the two roles visibly distinct.

  + BECAUSE:
      Uniform continuity is a hypothesis about differences and boundedness is a
      conclusion about values, and the step between them is exactly where the
      domain's boundedness enters. Proving them in one motion hides that entry
      point, so a proof that fails gives no signal about whether the domain
      hypothesis was too weak or the estimate was arranged badly. Separated, the
      failure names itself.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Prove the image is bounded as a standalone lemma from uniform continuity.]
    next[Identify where the domain's boundedness enters and state it explicitly.]
    next[Estimate the quotient using the value bound for the denominator and the modulus for the variation.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CV/complex-liouville-periodicity
@title Reduce a Lattice-Periodic Entire Function to Its Fundamental Domain
@keywords Liouville, periodicity, lattice, fundamental-domain, compactness, entire, boundedness
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, complex-analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty intermediate
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-formalization-CV/entire-and-singularity-api
@see-also math-informal/quotient-by-irrelevance

! conclusion:
  An entire function periodic under a lattice is constant, and the formal proof
  is the reduction: restrict to a compact fundamental domain, get boundedness
  from continuity there, and hand the bound to Liouville.

  + context: An entire function invariant under a lattice of translations, where
    the classical conclusion — that it is constant — is immediate and the formal
    obligation is to produce the boundedness hypothesis Liouville wants.

  + IF:
      The periods generate a lattice, then the function's whole range is already
      attained on one fundamental domain, and a fundamental domain can be taken
      compact. Continuity on a compact set gives a bound, periodicity transports
      that bound to the plane, and `Liouville` in its bounded-entire-implies-
      constant form closes the goal.

  + HOWEVER:
      The reduction is the content, and it is easy to state as if it were free.
      Two obligations have to be discharged explicitly: that every point of the
      plane is a lattice translate of a point of the chosen domain, and that the
      chosen domain is compact. Neither follows from writing down a
      parallelogram; both are ordinary but real work, and the transport of the
      bound is a separate step from the bound itself.

  + THEN:
      Choose the fundamental domain and prove it compact. Prove that every point
      is a lattice translate of one of its points. Bound the function on the
      domain by continuity, transport the bound by periodicity, then apply the
      bounded-entire-implies-constant API.

  + BECAUSE:
      Liouville is stated as an implication whose hypothesis is global
      boundedness, and periodicity is a hypothesis about symmetry — the whole
      proof is the bridge between them. Writing that bridge as a compactness
      argument on a named domain turns "obviously bounded" into three checkable
      steps, which is exactly where a formal proof of this shape either closes or
      reveals that the domain was never shown to cover the plane.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Choose a fundamental domain and prove it compact.]
    next[Prove every point of the plane is a lattice translate of a point in it.]
    next[Bound the function on the domain by continuity on a compact set.]
    next[Transport the bound to the plane by periodicity, as its own step.]
    next[Apply the bounded-entire-implies-constant form of Liouville.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CV/derivative-bounds-api
@title Bound the Derivative, Then Integrate Back to the Function
@keywords derivative-bound, Schwarz, Cauchy-estimate, radial-integration, Lipschitz, domination, injectivity
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, complex-analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-strategy/isolate-computational-kernel-before-transport
@see-also math-formalization-CV/holomorphic-disk-api math-formalization-CV/entire-and-singularity-api

! conclusion:
  When a bound on a function is out of reach, apply the standard rigidity to its
  derivative instead and integrate back — and check first whether a plain
  Lipschitz estimate settles the question without any of the machinery.

  + context: A quantitative complex-analysis goal — a sharper Schwarz-type bound,
    a constancy result, an injectivity claim — where the direct estimate on the
    function does not follow from the hypotheses in hand.

  + IF:
      The hypotheses vanish to higher order than the standard theorem assumes,
      then the standard theorem applies to the derivative. A holomorphic function
      whose value and first derivative both vanish at the origin gets its
      second-order bound by applying first-order Schwarz rigidity to the
      derivative and recovering the function bound by radial integration. The
      same move converts sublinear polynomial growth, where bounded Liouville is
      unavailable, into Cauchy's derivative estimate at an expanding radius.

  + HOWEVER:
      The machinery is often unnecessary, and reaching for it first costs the most
      when it succeeds — because then nobody checks. For `az + h z` on a convex
      domain, injectivity follows from a Lipschitz constant for `h` strictly
      below `|a|`; testing that takes a line, while the argument principle or
      Rouché takes a page and yields the same conclusion under a stronger
      hypothesis than the problem needed.

      Integrating back is not free either. The radial integration that recovers
      the function bound from the derivative bound has to be set up over an
      explicit path with an explicit parameterization, and the sharpness of the
      final constant depends on that setup. A bound obtained by an unstated
      integration is a bound nobody can check for sharpness.

  + THEN:
      Before invoking global machinery, test the elementary domination: is there
      a Lipschitz constant, a linear term that dominates, a direct comparison?
      Record the test even when it fails, so the machinery is justified rather
      than assumed.

      When the function-level bound is unavailable, state the derivative-level
      theorem you intend to apply, apply it, and write the integration back to
      the function as an explicit step with its path and parameterization.

      Match the estimate to the growth: bounded to Liouville, sublinear to
      Cauchy's derivative estimate at an expanding radius, higher-order vanishing
      to Schwarz on the derivative.

  + BECAUSE:
      Derivative bounds are the currency of this subject because the library's
      rigidity theorems are stated at first order, while problems are routinely
      posed at second order or under growth conditions no first-order theorem
      accepts. Moving down to the derivative and integrating back is the standard
      adapter between the two, and it is cheap. What is expensive is skipping the
      elementary test on the way — the machinery will close the goal from a
      hypothesis stronger than the problem gave you, and the resulting proof is
      correct, opaque, and unnecessarily strong.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Test the elementary Lipschitz or domination bound first, and record the test.]
    next[If the function bound is unavailable, name the first-order theorem that applies to the derivative.]
    next[Write the radial integration back to the function as an explicit step with its parameterization.]
    next[Match the instrument to the growth: bounded, sublinear, or higher-order vanishing.]
    next[Check the resulting constant for sharpness against the integration you actually performed.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CV/entire-affine-by-divided-difference
@title Prove an Entire Function Is Affine by Making a Divided Difference Constant
@keywords Liouville, entire, affine, divided-difference, dslope, slope, cocompact, limit-at-infinity, one-point-compactification
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, complex-analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-formalization-CV/entire-and-singularity-api
@see-also math-formalization-CV/complex-liouville-periodicity

! conclusion:
  To prove an entire function equals `a₀ + a₁ * z`, do not classify the function:
  show the divided difference `(f z - f 0) / z` is entire (after filling z = 0)
  and tends to a finite limit as z → ∞, then apply the cocompact-limit form of
  Liouville to make the divided difference constant.

  + context: A rigidity goal stating that an entire function is affine —
    typically reached after a singularity-at-infinity normal form `f(z) - a`
    behaves like the reciprocal of a polynomial in `1/z` of degree exactly one —
    where the classical proof passes through polynomial classification or
    Picard-class theorems the library may lack.

  + IF:
      The behaviour at infinity can be stated as `Filter.Tendsto` along
      `cocompact ℂ` of the divided difference `dslope f 0` (Mathlib's
      `Complex.dslope`, i.e. `slope f 0` with the removable value at 0 filled),
      then the goal factors into two library-shaped obligations:
      differentiability of `dslope f 0` on all of ℂ via
      `Complex.differentiableOn_dslope`, and constancy via
      `Differentiable.apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact`, the Liouville form that
      only needs a finite limit at infinity — one point of the
      one-point compactification, not a global bound.

  + HOWEVER:
      `apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact` is easy to miss because Liouville is
      usually reached through its bounded-entire form; search for
      `tendsto_cocompact` rather than `Liouville` to find it. The limit along
      `cocompact ℂ` must be transported from a punctured-germ eventual
      equality at 0: compose with `tendsto_inv₀_cobounded'` (inversion maps
      cocompact ℂ into the punctured germ at 0) and rewrite
      `Metric.cobounded_eq_cocompact` to change filter vocabulary. Recovering
      `f z = f 0 + a₁ * z` from a constant divided difference needs an
      explicit `z ≠ 0` case split and multiplication by `z`; `dslope_of_ne`
      unfolds the filled value away from 0.

  + THEN:
      Establish the normal form at infinity (degree-one reciprocal pole of the
      inverted translate). Derive `Tendsto (dslope f 0) (cocompact ℂ) (𝓝 L)`
      from it by filter algebra: inverse along cocompact, continuity at the
      germ, `Tendsto.congr'` for the eventual-equality correction term
      `(a - f 0) * z⁻¹ → 0`. Prove `Differentiable ℂ (dslope f 0)` from
      entireness of `f`. Apply `apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact` pointwise to get
      `dslope f 0 = L` everywhere, split on `z = 0`, and multiply out.

  + BECAUSE:
      The divided difference converts a two-coefficient existential into a
      constancy statement, which is the shape Liouville-type lemmas discharge;
      every other route (polynomial classification, Picard, coefficient
      killing by Cauchy estimates) needs growth hypotheses or missing
      theorems, while this route needs only a first-order normal form at
      infinity that the earlier singularity work already provides.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[State the goal as constancy of the divided difference, not as a coefficient existential.]
    next[Get differentiability of the filled divided difference from Complex.differentiableOn_dslope.]
    next[Transport the limit along cocompact ℂ from the punctured germ via tendsto_inv₀_cobounded'.]
    next[Apply Differentiable.apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact pointwise.]
    next[Split on z = 0 and multiply the constant slope equation by z to finish.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CV/entire-and-singularity-api
@title Manufacture the Entire Function Whose Decay Contradicts
@keywords Liouville, entire, removable-singularity, puncture, reciprocal, Cauchy-estimate, growth, branch-locus, pole-classification
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, complex-analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-informal/argue-by-contradiction
@see-also math-formalization-CV/holomorphic-disk-api math-formalization-CV/complex-polynomial-bound

! conclusion:
  Liouville is not a lemma you look up but a shape you build toward: construct
  the entire function whose growth is contradictory — by inverting, zero-filling,
  dividing out, or removing singularities — and handle exceptional sets by filter
  algebra rather than induction.

  + context: A complex-analysis obligation about global behaviour — an entire
    function's rigidity, a singularity's removability, the non-existence of an
    entire extension — where the classical proof is a sentence and the formal
    proof is a construction.

  + IF:
      The growth hypothesis can be turned into decay of some derived entire
      function, then the argument closes by Liouville. The derivations are few and
      reusable: invert an omitted-value translate and zero-fill the reciprocal;
      divide by the escaping coordinate when eventual agreement at infinity is
      the hypothesis; take a removable quotient to manufacture the entire function
      the estimate applies to.

  + HOWEVER:
      Bounded Liouville is often the wrong instrument. For sublinear polynomial
      growth it does not apply at all, and the right tool is Cauchy's derivative
      estimate at an expanding radius — the derivative, not the function, is what
      the growth kills.

      Exceptional sets invite induction, and induction is the expensive route. A
      finite set of punctures is excluded all at once by taking the complement of
      `F.erase z` and intersecting with the punctured neighbourhood filter
      `𝓝[≠] z`; the induction that the classical proof implies is avoidable set
      algebra.

      Branch loci break uniform treatment. Descending an even analytic function
      through the squaring map is one proof away from the branch locus and a
      different proof on it: reindex the invariant Taylor germ where the
      derivative vanishes, and use the analytic inverse-function theorem
      everywhere else.

      Pole geometry decides which theorem applies. For a rational integral over
      the unit circle, classify each pole as interior or exterior *before* doing
      algebra — the split determines whether Cauchy's formula or Cauchy–Goursat
      supplies that term, and algebra performed first hides the classification.

  + THEN:
      Say explicitly which entire function you are building and what its decay
      will be, then build it: zero-fill the reciprocal and remove the
      singularities, or divide by the escaping coordinate and take the induced
      decay, finishing by uniqueness of limits.

      Match the instrument to the growth: bounded → Liouville, sublinear →
      Cauchy's estimate at expanding radius, two-pole normalized ML bound →
      arrange a zero second pole so the bound reads `M/(R - ‖a‖)`.

      Exclude finite exceptional sets by filter algebra, split at branch loci, and
      classify poles before manipulating the integrand. Reuse a compiled
      partial-fraction / Cauchy-kernel contour skeleton rather than rebuilding it.

  + BECAUSE:
      The classical statements in this area — "bounded entire functions are
      constant", "isolated singularities of bounded functions are removable" —
      are conclusions about functions that do not appear in the problem. The
      entire work of the formal proof is producing the function they apply to,
      and that production is where the choices live: which translate, which
      quotient, which coordinate to divide by. Writing the target function down
      first turns an appeal to a famous theorem into a construction with a
      checkable shape, and makes the growth bookkeeping — sublinear versus
      bounded, at which radius — an explicit decision rather than a hope.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Name the entire function you are constructing and the decay it must have.]
    next[Zero-fill a reciprocal or divide by the escaping coordinate to produce it.]
    next[Match the instrument to the growth: bounded Liouville vs Cauchy estimate at expanding radius.]
    next[Exclude finite punctures with F.erase and 𝓝[≠] z rather than by induction.]
    next[Split the proof at the branch locus when descending through a branched map.]
    next[Classify poles as interior or exterior before doing any algebra on the integrand.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CV/frontier-bound-from-arc-hypotheses
@title Close a Frontier Bound From Arc Hypotheses by a Continuity Limit at the Missing Points
@keywords frontier, sphere, arc, semicircle, boundary, continuity, dense, limit, le_of_tendsto, maximum modulus
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, complex-analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-formalization-CV/holomorphic-disk-api
@see-also math-formalization-CV/holomorphic-disk-api

! conclusion:
  When a maximum-modulus or Phragmén-type argument needs a norm bound on the
  whole frontier but the hypotheses only cover it on arcs (an open condition
  like strict sign of the imaginary part), the uncovered frontier points are
  closed by continuity: approach each missing point by a sequence inside a
  covered arc and transfer the bound with `le_of_tendsto`.

  + context: Boundary estimates on the unit circle or the frontier of a ball,
    where hypotheses are stated per-arc rather than per-frontier, and the
    target theorem consumes the bound uniformly over the frontier.

  + IF:
      The covered set is dense in the frontier minus finitely many points —
      e.g. upper and lower open semicircles leaving only the equator points
      where the sign condition degenerates — then case-split the frontier by
      trichotomy on the sign, dispose of the covered arcs directly, and for
      each leftover point z₀ build an explicit sequence uₙ on the circle with
      uₙ → z₀ and uₙ in the covered arc: `Complex.exp (θₙ * I)` with θₙ = 1/(n+1)
      for approach angles, its imaginary part handled by
      `Complex.exp_ofReal_mul_I_im` and `Real.sin_pos_of_pos_of_lt_pi`, its
      unit-norm membership by `Complex.norm_exp`. Compose the continuous-on
      hypothesis with `tendsto_nhdsWithin_iff` to keep the sequence in the
      closed ball, take norms, and conclude `‖g z₀‖ ≤ M` by `le_of_tendsto`.

  + HOWEVER:
      Do not try to strengthen the hypothesis to the whole frontier or search
      for a theorem that accepts semicircle bounds — the continuity transfer
      is short, elementary, and exactly what the boundary regularity is for.
      The sequence must stay inside the covered arc for every n, not merely
      tend into it, or the per-point bound has nothing to attach to.

@flexiarg math-formalization-CV/holomorphic-disk-api
@title Assemble Disk Theorems From the Library's Interfaces, Not From Their Names
@keywords disk, holomorphic, Schwarz, Rouche, Hurwitz, circle-average, DiffContOnCl, divisor, branch-cut, radius
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, complex-analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-informal/reduce-to-known-result
@see-also math-formalization-CA/measure-integration-api math-formalization-CV/complex-polynomial-bound

! conclusion:
  A classical disk theorem is rarely in the library under its classical name.
  Decompose it into the interfaces the library does offer, adapt the hypotheses
  to their exact shape, and carry branch and radius information as explicit
  invariants rather than as understood context.

  + context: Complex analysis on a disk or closed ball — Schwarz, Rouché,
    Hurwitz, the argument principle, zero counting, conformal images — being
    formalized against a library that packages this material by interface rather
    than by theorem name.

  + IF:
      The named theorem decomposes into available pieces, then naming those
      pieces is the whole job. Hurwitz zero persistence is a compact boundary
      margin plus quantitative open mapping, and searching for a monolithic
      Hurwitz wastes the search. A disk zero count is the existing meromorphic-
      divisor API. Local non-injectivity is `analyticOrderAt ≥ 2`. The equality
      case of Schwarz is affine `dslope` equality specialized at the center. Once
      the decomposition is named, each piece is ordinary work.

  + HOWEVER:
      The hypotheses will not be in the shape the library wants. A closed-ball
      differentiability hypothesis has to be separated into its three interfaces
      — differentiability on the open ball, continuity on the closure, a
      sphere-local bound — before a `DiffContOnCl`-shaped theorem will accept it.
      When a construction is blocked on a deep invariance theorem, package every
      elementary hypothesis in that theorem's intended quantifier shape first, or
      the frontier stays entangled with routine boundary estimates and you cannot
      tell which part is actually missing.

      Radius and parameter are where the proof is bought. A weak disk-map bound
      becomes strict Rouché domination only after choosing `t < r < 1`; strict
      radial-contraction fixed points reach `t = 1` only through compact
      subsequences; a hypothesis local on disks globalizes only one smaller
      concentric disk at a time.

      Branch information does not survive being left implicit. A pointwise
      zero-product identity is not a globally coherent branch choice — use
      continuity of the nonzero factor to get an open zero set, then analytic
      connectedness to propagate it. Through a composition of elementary
      conformal maps, prove image control stage by stage and carry the branch cut
      as its own invariant. To exclude an interval from a principal-root image,
      push membership back through the exact power identity; real and imaginary
      projections expose the contradiction more cleanly than argument
      inequalities.

      Finally, check whether the heavy machinery is needed at all. For `az + h z`
      on a convex domain, a Lipschitz constant for `h` strictly below `|a|`
      settles injectivity without the argument principle.

  + THEN:
      Write the target as a composition of library interfaces before searching
      for it by name, and state each interface as its own lemma with its own
      hypotheses.

      Adapt hypotheses explicitly — split a closed-ball assumption into open-ball
      differentiability, boundary continuity and a sphere bound; package
      homotopy slices in the intended quantifier shape.

      Route through the circle-average identity where one exists: rewrite by the
      identity and then apply the norm-of-integral bound, rather than proving the
      inequality directly. It often removes global geometric hypotheses outright.

      Choose the radius deliberately and say why, keep the branch cut as a named
      invariant through every stage, and test the elementary bound before
      reaching for Rouché.

  + BECAUSE:
      Disk theory is old enough that its classical statements have been
      refactored several times on the way into a formal library, and the
      refactoring is by interface — divisors, orders, `dslope`, `DiffContOnCl`,
      open mapping — not by the names in a textbook chapter. Searching by name
      therefore under-reports what is present, and rebuilding by hand reproduces
      material that exists in a shape you did not recognize. The information the
      classical statement suppresses — which radius, which branch, which
      quantifier order — is exactly the information the formal proof needs, so
      the decomposition is not overhead: it is the content.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Write the classical theorem as a composition of library interfaces before searching by name.]
    next[Separate a closed-ball hypothesis into open-ball differentiability, boundary continuity, sphere bound.]
    next[Package elementary hypotheses in the deep theorem's quantifier shape before attacking the frontier.]
    next[Rewrite by the circle-average identity before proving a norm inequality directly.]
    next[Choose the radius explicitly and record why that choice makes the bound strict.]
    next[Carry the branch cut as a named invariant through every stage of a composition.]
    next[Test the elementary Lipschitz bound before invoking Rouché or the argument principle.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-FA/inner-product-space-api
@title Get Uniform Boundedness First, Then Extend From a Dense Span
@keywords inner-product, Banach-Steinhaus, uniform-boundedness, dense-span, weak-convergence, cobounded, projection
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-informal/local-to-global
@see-also math-formalization-FA/weak-convergence-hilbert math-formalization-CA/hilbert-projection-properties

! conclusion:
  Weak-convergence arguments in an inner-product space rest on a uniform norm
  bound: obtain it from Banach–Steinhaus first, then extend convergence from a
  dense span, and let the bound also discharge the `liminf` side conditions.

  + context: A Hilbert-space obligation about a weakly convergent sequence —
    lower semicontinuity of the norm, convergence tested against every vector, a
    uniform constant claimed from pairwise estimates.

  + IF:
      A uniform norm bound is available, then the argument decomposes cleanly:
      prove convergence on the generators, close under finite linear
      combinations, extend to the closed span using the uniform bound, and remove
      the orthogonal complement by projection. Each stage is small, and the
      uniform bound is what licenses the passage from the span to its closure.

  + HOWEVER:
      The uniform bound is also what the `liminf` machinery quietly needs, and
      the two requirements are easily confused into a circle. `le_liminf_of_le`
      demands an `IsCoboundedUnder` premise; deriving that premise from the
      conclusion being proved is circular, and deriving it from Banach–Steinhaus
      is not. Prove actual uniform norm boundedness by uniform boundedness first,
      and the side condition follows without the circle.

      A real-valued sequence that may be unbounded above needs its own treatment:
      `c ≤ liminf u atTop` from an eventual lower bound is a different lemma from
      the bounded case, and picking the wrong one leaves a side condition that
      cannot be discharged.

      Uniform-constant claims derived from pairwise bounds deserve a refutation
      attempt before a proof attempt. Build a triangular family whose support
      grows with the index and compare the pairwise scale against the
      square-summed aggregate scale — pairwise smallness does not survive
      aggregation, and finding this out by attempting the proof is the expensive
      route.

  + THEN:
      Establish the uniform norm bound by Banach–Steinhaus as the first step, and
      use it for both the extension and the `liminf` side conditions.

      Extend in the stated order: generators, finite linear combinations, closed
      span by the uniform bound, orthogonal complement by projection.

      Select the `liminf` variant that matches whether the real sequence may be
      unbounded above, and say which one you chose.

      Before proving a uniform constant from pairwise bounds, try to refute it
      with a growing-support triangular family.

  + BECAUSE:
      Weak convergence is a statement about every test vector, and no argument
      can check every test vector — so every proof in this area is an extension
      argument from a small set, and every extension argument needs the uniform
      bound that makes the closure step legal. That the same bound discharges the
      filter-level side conditions is not a coincidence but the same fact used
      twice, and seeing it as one fact is what keeps the proof out of a circle.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Prove the uniform norm bound by Banach–Steinhaus before anything else.]
    next[Extend convergence: generators, finite combinations, closed span, orthogonal complement.]
    next[Discharge IsCoboundedUnder from the uniform bound, never from the conclusion.]
    next[Pick the liminf variant that matches unbounded-above versus bounded real sequences.]
    next[Try to refute a pairwise-derived uniform constant with a growing-support triangular family.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-FA/lf-map-continuity-via-fixed-support-stages
@title Prove LF Test-Function Operator Continuity Stage by Stage
@keywords TestFunction, LF-topology, continuous-linear-map, compact-support, seminorm, limitCLM
@audience lean-provers, functional-analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@subjects applied
@how own mechanism: Replace a global LF-continuity obligation by compact-stage factorization, prove finite seminorm bounds on each Fréchet stage, and reassemble the global operator with the TestFunction final-topology API.

! conclusion:
  Prove continuity of an operator on compactly supported smooth test functions
  by factoring its restriction to every fixed compact-support stage through a
  controlled target stage, establishing seminorm bounds there, and invoking
  the LF-space final-topology criterion.

  + IF:
      An algebraic linear operator on `TestFunction` is mathematically
      continuous, but no packaged global continuous linear operator exists and
      direct continuity on the LF topology is opaque.

  + HOWEVER:
      The input support varies globally, while the available derivative and
      integral estimates have constants and output supports that depend on a
      fixed input compact. A single global norm estimate is therefore the wrong
      obligation.

  + THEN:
      For each compact `K`, choose a compact `K'` containing the output support
      of every input supported in `K`. Define the induced linear map from
      `ContDiffMapSupportedIn ... K` to `ContDiffMapSupportedIn ... K'`. Prove
      its continuity with `WithSeminorms.continuous_of_isBounded`, supplying for
      each target seminorm a finite set of source seminorms and a nonnegative
      constant. Finally use `TestFunction.continuous_iff_continuous_comp` to
      reduce global continuity to these stage maps and compose each with
      `TestFunction.ofSupportedInCLM`.

  + BECAUSE:
      The test-function topology is an inductive-limit topology. Its continuity
      API is designed to consume compatible continuous maps on fixed-support
      Fréchet stages, exactly where support-dependent seminorm estimates are
      meaningful.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Prove a uniform output-support bound for each fixed input compact.]
    next[Separate the order-zero seminorm estimate from successor derivative estimates.]
    next[Package each stage map continuously, then apply the TestFunction final-topology criterion.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-FA/weak-convergence-hilbert
@title Weak Plus Norm Convergence Is an API Chain With Side Conditions
@keywords weak-convergence, Hilbert, Kadec-Klee, Radon-Riesz, liminf, cobounded, Fatou, side-condition
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA]
@why math-informal/reduce-to-known-result
@see-also math-formalization-CA/lp-norm-comparison math-formalization-CA/hilbert-projection-properties

! conclusion:
  Upgrading weak convergence to strong convergence is a chain of library steps
  through `‖xₙ - x‖²`, and the classical proof suppresses exactly the side
  conditions — coboundedness of the `liminf` — that the chain will demand.

  + context: A Hilbert- or `Lᵖ`-space obligation of Kadec–Klee / Radon–Riesz
    shape: weak convergence plus convergence of norms implies norm convergence,
    or a `liminf` inequality obtained from Fatou has to be turned into a limit.

  + IF:
      The route is taken through the squared norm, then each step is already in
      the library and the proof is assembly: expand `‖xₙ - x‖²` into norms and
      inner products, pass the inner-product term to its weak limit, cancel
      against the norm hypothesis, and take the square root at the end. The
      analogous `Lᵖ` route runs through Fatou to an a.e. limit and then along the
      same chain.

  + HOWEVER:
      The `liminf` steps carry hypotheses the classical argument never states. A
      `liminf` bound in Mathlib is conditional on the sequence being cobounded
      under the relevant filter — the theorem is false without it, because an
      unbounded-above gap makes `liminf` degenerate — and these side conditions
      surface only when the rewrite fails, at which point they look like a tooling
      obstruction rather than the mathematics they are.

      They also do not all discharge the same way. An eventual lower bound, a
      `liminf ≤` from a `≤ 0` bound, and a `le_liminf` under an unbounded-above
      gap each want a different witness, so a single "handle the side conditions"
      step is not a plan.

      The square root is not free either: the chain proves a statement about
      `‖xₙ - x‖²`, and the target is about `‖xₙ - x‖`. Keep the two apart and make
      the passage explicit rather than letting a norm power drift through the
      argument. Where norm powers were used only to establish scalar facts,
      return to the original functions before applying the final convergence
      theorem.

  + THEN:
      Write the chain out as named steps before proving any of them —
      `norm_sub_sq` expansion, weak limit of the inner product, cancellation,
      square root — and treat each side condition as its own obligation with its
      own witness.

      Establish coboundedness where the `liminf` step needs it, and say which
      variant of the `liminf` API you are using and why that one.

      Use norm powers only for the scalar facts, and return to the original
      objects before the last step.

  + BECAUSE:
      This is the standard case of a proof whose informal difficulty and formal
      difficulty sit in different places. Informally the content is the expansion
      of the squared norm; formally that step is a rewrite and the work is in the
      filter hypotheses that make the limit manipulations legal. An agent that
      plans from the informal proof will budget for the wrong half and read the
      side conditions as friction — so naming them in advance is what turns a
      stalled rewrite into a list of small, closable obligations.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Write the chain as named steps: expand, pass to the weak limit, cancel, take the root.]
    next[List each liminf/limsup step's side condition as its own obligation.]
    next[Establish coboundedness explicitly rather than treating its absence as a tooling problem.]
    next[Say which liminf API variant is being used and why that one fits the bound in hand.]
    next[Return from norm powers to the original objects before the final convergence step.]

@title Expose Component Openness Before Reasoning About Frontiers
@keywords connected-component, locally-connected, openness, interior, frontier, counting, unbounded-exterior

  + context: A topological obligation about `connectedComponentIn U x` for an

    frontiers, or separating bounded from unbounded ones.

      themselves open, and that single fact is what makes the rest mechanical:
      `interior_eq` converts component membership into exactly the form frontier
      reasoning consumes, and the frontier of a component can then be placed
      inside the ambient frontier of `U`.

      classically it is obvious. Skipped, every subsequent frontier manipulation
      is off by the difference between a set and its interior, and the failure
      surfaces several lemmas later as an unprovable membership rather than as a
      missing hypothesis.

      own. The complement of a compact set has one unbounded component and
      finitely many bounded ones, and these are counted by different means:
      inject the bounded interior components into algebraic witnesses — roots, in
      the lemniscate case — and reserve a single marker for the common unbounded
      exterior. Counting them uniformly produces an off-by-one that is easy to
      misattribute to the injection.

      unbounded exterior one, inject the bounded family into whatever algebraic
      witnesses the problem supplies, and add the exterior back as a marker.

      pieces rather than like arbitrary closed subsets, and openness is the form

      said so — which is free in prose and unavailable to a proof assistant. The

      component count into an injection plus a constant.

! conclusion:
  When you must subtract finitely many simple principal parts from a
  meromorphic function and Mathlib's divisor machinery only factorizes,
  build each principal part locally from the order germ and prove the
  remainder has nonnegative order; no global additive decomposition
  theorem is needed.

  + IF: Every boundary pole has order exactly `-1`, the pole set is
    finite, and the goal is `f = g + ∑ ζ ∈ P, c ζ / (z - ζ)` with `g`
    holomorphic on a larger disk (e.g. to bound Taylor coefficients).

  + HOWEVER: Searches of `CanonicalDecomposition`, `FactorizedRational`,
    and `MeromorphicOn.extract_zeros_poles` find only multiplicative
    factorizations; the additive form is absent from the library.

  + THEN: (1) At a pole, `(meromorphicOrderAt_eq_int_iff hF).1 horder`
    gives `q` analytic with `q ζ ≠ 0` and `F =ᶠ (z - ζ)^(-1) • q`; shift
    with `comp_sub` and apply `AnalyticAt.exists_eq_sum_add_pow_mul 1` to
    write `q z = q ζ + (z - ζ) * H z`, so `F =ᶠ[𝓝[≠] ζ] H + q ζ / (z - ζ)`.
    (2) `choose c hc` over all poles. (3) The finite sum `S` of principal
    parts is `AnalyticAt` off `P` (`Finset.analyticAt_fun_sum`,
    `AnalyticAt.div`), so at `z ∉ P` use `meromorphicOrderAt_add` and at
    `z ∈ P` use `meromorphicOrderAt_congr` with `Finset.sum_erase_add`
    to see `F - S` has nonnegative order. (4) Normalize and thicken the
    remainder. (5) Coefficients of `c / (z - ζ)` for `‖ζ‖ = 1` come from
    `Complex.one_div_sub_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero` and all have norm `‖c‖`.

      api[Complex.one_div_sub_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero]

@how own mechanism: When two expressions differ only in how a bound variable is written, let the elaborator identify them rather than rewriting under the binder by hand. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  When two expressions differ only in how a bound variable is written, let the
  elaborator identify them rather than rewriting under the binder by hand.

  + context: A goal and a library lemma that state the same integral — or the
    same sum, or the same `∀` — but whose bodies are written with differently
    shaped binders, so the rewrite does not fire.

  + IF:
      The two forms are definitionally equal up to the binder's presentation,
      then the elaborator will accept one where the other is expected, and the
      apparent mismatch costs nothing. Applying the lemma directly, or stating
      the intermediate equality and letting unification close it, is the whole
      repair.

  + HOWEVER:
      The instinct is to rewrite under the binder to force the shapes to match,
      and that is where the cost appears. Rewriting under a binder needs a
      motive, and the motive that a tactic infers is frequently not the one that
      typechecks — the resulting motive error is opaque and describes the
      elaborator's difficulty rather than the mathematical mismatch. The
      hand-written congruence lemma that follows is real work in service of a
      difference that was never mathematical.

  + THEN:
      Try applying the lemma to the goal as it stands before adjusting either
      side. If an intermediate step is needed, state the equality of the two
      whole expressions and let elaboration discharge the binder difference,
      rather than rewriting inside the body.

      Reserve explicit congruence for cases where the bodies genuinely differ,
      not where their binders are merely written differently.

  + BECAUSE:
      Binder presentation is syntax, and syntax differences are what the
      elaborator exists to absorb. Treating them as mathematical differences
      converts a no-op into a motive problem — and the motive problem's error
      message points at the tactic, not at the syntax, so the time is spent in
      the wrong place entirely.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Apply the lemma to the goal unchanged before adjusting either side.]
    next[State the equality of whole expressions rather than rewriting inside a binder.]
    next[Read a motive error as a signal that the rewrite was under a binder, not as a mathematical obstruction.]
    next[Reserve explicit congruence for genuinely different bodies.]

  For a faithful action of a finite group on exactly `p` points, where
  `p` is prime and divides the group order, prove every Sylow
  `p`-subgroup has cardinality `p` by bounding the group order through
  the permutation representation and comparing prime factorizations.

  + IF: `MulAction.toPermHom G X` is injective, `Nat.card X = p`, and a
    transitive action or another argument supplies `p ∣ Nat.card G`.

  + HOWEVER: A direct orbit analysis of the Sylow subgroup may require
    fixed-point congruences and nontriviality arguments that are not
    already packaged in the needed cardinality form.

    rewriting with `Nat.card_perm`. Convert divisibility to an inequality

    via `Nat.factorization_factorial`; divisibility of `Nat.card G` by `p`
    gives the reverse lower bound. Rewrite a Sylow subgroup's cardinality
    with `Sylow.card_eq_multiplicity` and simplify the resulting
    factorization value.

      api[Nat.factorization_factorial] api[Prime.dvd_iff_one_le_factorization]
      api[Sylow.card_eq_multiplicity]

  + BECAUSE: Faithfulness embeds the group into the symmetric group, and
    the prime `p` occurs exactly once in `p!`; once existence supplies one

@how own mechanism: Push casts to the leaves before applying a projection: a real or imaginary part taken through an un-normalized coercion tower will not simplify. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  Push casts to the leaves before applying a projection: a real or imaginary part
  taken through an un-normalized coercion tower will not simplify.

  + context: An expression mixing integer or natural literals with complex
    values, where the goal is about the real or imaginary part of the result.

  + IF:
      The casts are normalized first — pushed inward to the leaves so that each
      coercion sits on an atom — then the projection lemmas apply directly: the
      real part of a cast integer is the cast integer, its imaginary part is
      zero, and the arithmetic simplifies without further help.

  + HOWEVER:
      Applied to a term whose coercions still sit around compound
      subexpressions, the projection lemmas do not fire, because the shape they
      match is a cast of an atom and what is present is a cast of a sum or a
      product. The goal then looks like a mathematical obstruction — the
      projection "does not simplify" — when it is a normalization that has not
      been run.

      The order is not symmetric. Normalizing after projecting leaves the
      projection stuck around a compound cast, and the usual recovery is to undo
      the projection step.

  + THEN:
      Normalize the casts first, pushing them to the leaves, and only then take
      real or imaginary parts and finish the arithmetic.

  + BECAUSE:
      Cast normalization is a syntactic prerequisite of the projection lemmas
      rather than a cleanup step, so doing it late means doing it twice. The
      failure it causes is also mislabelled — nothing reports "the cast is in the
      wrong place", only that a simp set made no progress — which is why the
      ordering is worth stating rather than rediscovering.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Push casts to the leaves before applying any projection.]
    next[Check that each coercion sits on an atom, not on a sum or product.]
    next[Then take real/imaginary parts and finish the arithmetic.]

! conclusion:

  operates in another (ℝ≥0∞), wire through the directed coercion chain
  rather than trying to isomorphism-transport.

  + context: You have proved a key lemma in ℝ (e.g., a limit, an inequality).
    The theorem you need to close operates on eLpNorm, which lives in ℝ≥0∞.
    There is a canonical coercion chain ℝ → ℝ≥0 → ℝ≥0∞ but it is NOT an
    isomorphism — it loses information at each step (negativity at ℝ→ℝ≥0,
    finiteness at ℝ≥0→ℝ≥0∞).

  + IF:
      The informal pattern (transport-across-isomorphism) says "prove in the
      easy setting and transport." But the coercion chain is not an isomorphism,
      so transport is not free. The tension: mathematical convenience (work in ℝ)
      vs API reality (goal is in ℝ≥0∞). The amelioration: make the bridge a
      named, reusable tactic sequence, not a per-proof ad-hoc construction.

  + IF:
      Your real-valued result needs to be used in an ENNReal/NNReal context,
      and the coercion chain applies (the quantities are nonneg and finite).

  + HOWEVER:

  + HOWEVER:
      Unlike transport-across-isomorphism, you cannot freely move results
      back and forth. The coercion is directed. ENNReal.toReal loses ⊤ → 0.
      NNReal.coe is injective but NNReal.mk requires a proof of nonnegativity.
      Each step requires an explicit compatibility hypothesis.

  + THEN:
      (a) Prove the core mathematical content in ℝ where the API is richest.
      (b) Identify the coercion path: which coe/toReal/ofReal lemmas connect
          your ℝ result to the ℝ≥0∞ goal?
      (c) For each coercion step, discharge the compatibility side-condition
          (nonnegativity, finiteness, ne_top).
      (d) If the bridge is >5 steps, consider whether the lemma can be proved
          directly in ℝ≥0∞ instead. Sometimes the Mathlib API has a parallel
          version (e.g., ENNReal.rpow vs Real.rpow) that avoids the bridge.

    + LEAN:
      api[ENNReal.ofReal] api[ENNReal.toReal] api[NNReal.coe_le_coe]
      api[ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal] api[ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal]
      tactic[rw [ENNReal.ofReal...] → exact ... → simp [ne_top_of_lt]]

  + BECAUSE:
      Lean's type system enforces the distinction between ℝ, ℝ≥0, and ℝ≥0∞
      that informal mathematics elides. The coercion bridge is the price of
      rigour. But the bridge is mechanical — once you know the path, each
      step is a named lemma (ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal, NNReal.coe_le_coe,
      ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal). The mathematical insight is in ℝ; the
      engineering is in the bridge.

! conclusion:
  When a finite group acts faithfully and transitively on a prime number
  of points and a Sylow subgroup of that prime order is self-normalizing,
  use Burnside transfer and primitivity to show the Sylow subgroup is the
  whole group; do not count order-prime elements across all Sylow subgroups.

  + IF: `G` acts faithfully and pretransitively on finite `X`,
    `Nat.card X = p` for prime `p`, a Sylow `p`-subgroup `P` has
    `Nat.card P = p`, and `normalizer (P : Subgroup G) = P`.

  + HOWEVER: Partitioning elements of order `p` among Sylow subgroups
    requires an explicit uniqueness and disjoint-union argument that is
    not packaged by the local Sylow API and does not directly exploit the
    prime-degree action.

  + THEN: Give `P` its cyclic structure from its prime cardinality. The
    self-normalizer equality makes `normalizer P ≤ centralizer P`; apply
    `MonoidHom.transferSylow` and let `N` be its kernel. The transfer
    theorem gives `N.IsComplement' P` and normality of `N`. Prime
    cardinality upgrades the ambient transitive action to primitive. If
    `N ≠ ⊥`, faithfulness rules out all points being fixed by `N`, while
    quasi-primitivity makes the normal subgroup action transitive. The
    stabilizer-index formula then forces `p ∣ Nat.card N`, contradicting
    `MonoidHom.not_dvd_card_ker_transferSylow`. Hence `N = ⊥`, and the
    complement's `sup_eq_top` reduces to `P = ⊤`.
    + LEAN:
      api[MonoidHom.transferSylow] api[MonoidHom.ker_transferSylow_isComplement']
      api[MulAction.IsPreprimitive.of_prime_card]
      api[MulAction.IsQuasiPreprimitive.isPretransitive_of_normal]
      api[MulAction.index_stabilizer_of_transitive]
      api[MonoidHom.not_dvd_card_ker_transferSylow]

  + BECAUSE: Transfer converts the self-normalizer hypothesis into a
    normal complement, and a faithful primitive action of prime degree
    leaves no room for a nontrivial normal complement whose cardinality is
    prime to `p`.

    fixes an intermediate field K pointwise, and need to show that every

    elements may be unavailable.

    parameterization is bijective onto the full automorphism type, and compute

! conclusion:
  Linear arithmetic cannot see inside `min` and `max`: split the cases or rewrite
  them away first, and only then call the tactic.

  + context: An inequality goal in which a threshold, a truncation, or a
    `δ = min ε b / 2` choice has introduced `min` or `max`, and linear arithmetic
    is the intended finisher.

  + IF:
      The `min`/`max` are eliminated first — by case split on which branch is
      active, or by rewriting to the branch the hypotheses already determine —
      then what remains is a linear problem and the tactic closes it immediately.

  + HOWEVER:
      Called on the goal as it stands, the tactic treats `min a b` as an opaque
      atom about which it knows nothing, so a goal that is arithmetically
      trivial in each branch is unprovable as stated. The failure carries no
      indication that the obstacle is the `min`, which invites strengthening the
      hypotheses or hunting for a missing lemma.

      Splitting is cheap and the branches are usually near-identical, so the
      instinct to avoid a case split here is a false economy.

  + THEN:
      Case-split on the `min`/`max`, or rewrite it to the branch the hypotheses
      already force, before invoking linear arithmetic. Where the same threshold
      appears repeatedly, do the normalization once as a named step rather than
      inside each goal.

  + BECAUSE:
      Linear arithmetic is complete for linear real arithmetic and blind to
      everything else, so anything that is not a linear atom is an opaque
      constant to it. `min` and `max` are the most common such term in analysis
      goals precisely because threshold choices produce them — which makes this
      the failure most likely to be misread as a mathematical gap rather than a
      normalization that was skipped.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Identify every min/max in the goal before calling linear arithmetic.]
    next[Case-split, or rewrite to the branch the hypotheses already determine.]
    next[Normalize a repeated threshold once as a named step rather than per goal.]
