The agent writes code but no institutional learning accumulates. The developer uses Stack Overflow and gets a working function but no understanding of why it works. What doesn't happen in the absorbed case is the creation of new institutions (Ostrom). The trainer doesn't create a community of practice at their institution. The agent doesn't produce evidence that improves the proof peripheral. The developer doesn't contribute a pattern back to the library. The individual transacts with the system but the system does not change. This is the "programming by Stack Exchange" failure mode applied universally. An interaction that produces output without producing capability is an interaction that has been *absorbed* rather than *institutionalised*. The output is real — the code works, the training was delivered, the problem was solved — but it is non-generative. Nothing was learned at the system level. No new institution was created. No peripheral evolved. The pattern-to-peripheral bridge is what converts absorbed input into institutional creation. When a pattern becomes a peripheral: 1. The envelope defines a positive action space (not a prohibition). 2. The surface earns entry (not commands it). 3. Inhabitation generates data (not just output). 4. The data feeds back into the peripheral's design (Baldwin loop). 5. The improved peripheral earns further inhabitation (virtuous cycle). At step 5, something new exists that didn't exist before: an institution in Ostrom's sense — a set of rules-in-use that govern a shared resource (the action space) and that evolve through the participation of their inhabitants. This is what the absorbed-input mode fails to produce, and it is what the pattern-to-peripheral transition is for. The Spinozan frame is the deepest one: the question is not "did the agent obey the pattern?" but "did the agent's power to act increase?" If it did, the pattern has become a peripheral. `-RA`, `-LO`, `-CV`, `-GN` would each hold **one file**. A one-file directory
buys nothing for retrieval and adds a glob to maintain — and directory globs
are exactly what broke the pattern channel this morning.

**Recommendation: directories only where there is mass** (`-CA` informal 6,
`-CA` formalization 8, `-CT` 7, `-CO` 2), and carry the fine-grained arXiv
code in the **`@subjects` metadata field**, which already exists, flows
into the pattern entity, and can scope retrieval as a store predicate rather
than a path glob. That is the lesson of this morning applied: scope by
queryable attribute, not by directory.

Consider the first-order differential equation $u'(t)+u(t)=\cos(u(t))$
posed as an initial value problem for $t>0$ with initial condition
$u(0)=u_0$
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\begin{alist}
%------------------------------------------------------------------*
\item Use the contraction mapping theorem to show that there is
exactly one solution $u$ satisfying these conditions that corresponds
to any given $u_0\in \R$.
%------------------------------------------------------------------*
\item Prove that there is a number $\xi$ such that $\lim_{t\rightarrow
\infty}u(t)=\xi$ for any solution $u$ of the differential equation,
independent of the value $u_0$.
%------------------------------------------------------------------*
\end{alist}

import Mathlib

/-!
# APM m00A05: A globally attracting scalar ODE equilibrium

## Statement repairs

None.

## Encoding questions

None. Solutions are global real-function representatives whose required
regularity and equation are restricted to `[0,∞)`. Uniqueness is consequently
stated with `Set.EqOn` on that interval, so irrelevant negative-time values are
not accidentally constrained.
-/

open Set Filter
open scoped Topology

noncomputable section

def apm_m00A05_isSolution (u₀ : ℝ) (u : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ContinuousOn u (Ici 0) ∧
  DifferentiableOn ℝ u (Ioi 0) ∧
  u 0 = u₀ ∧
  ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → deriv u t + u t = Real.cos (u t)

/-- The autonomous vector field in the equation is globally Lipschitz. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_lipschitz_vectorField :
    LipschitzWith 2 (fun x : ℝ => Real.cos x - x) := by
  convert Real.lipschitzWith_cos.sub LipschitzWith.id using 1 <;> norm_num

/-- A solution in the frozen weak-regularity encoding satisfies the standard
`HasDerivAt` ODE on the interior of the half-line. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_hasDerivAt_of_isSolution {u₀ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 < t) :
    HasDerivAt u (Real.cos (u t) - u t) t := by
  have hd : DifferentiableAt ℝ u t :=
    (hu.2.1 t ht).differentiableAt (Ioi_mem_nhds ht)
  convert hd.hasDerivAt using 1
  linarith [hu.2.2.2 t ht]

/-- The apparently weak endpoint regularity in `apm_m00A05_isSolution` is
enough to recover the right derivative at zero.  This is the key interface to
Mathlib's closed-interval Gronwall theorem. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_hasDerivWithinAt_zero_of_isSolution {u₀ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) :
    HasDerivWithinAt u (Real.cos (u 0) - u 0) (Ici 0) 0 := by
  apply hasDerivWithinAt_Ici_of_tendsto_deriv
  · exact hu.2.1
  · exact (hu.1 0 (by simp)).mono (Ioi_subset_Ici le_rfl)
  · exact self_mem_nhdsWithin
  · have hcont : Tendsto (fun t : ℝ => Real.cos (u t) - u t)
        (nhdsWithin 0 (Ioi 0)) (nhds (Real.cos (u 0) - u 0)) := by
      exact ((Real.continuous_cos.tendsto _).comp
        ((hu.1 0 (by simp)).mono (Ioi_subset_Ici le_rfl))).sub
        ((hu.1 0 (by simp)).mono (Ioi_subset_Ici le_rfl))
    apply hcont.congr'
    filter_upwards [self_mem_nhdsWithin] with t ht
    have heq := hu.2.2.2 t ht
    linarith

/-- Endpoint-safe global uniqueness for the frozen half-line encoding. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_solution_unique {u₀ : ℝ} {u v : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u)
    (hv : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ v) : EqOn u v (Ici 0) := by
  intro t ht
  have huniq := ODE_solution_unique (K := 2) (v := fun _ x : ℝ => Real.cos x - x)
      (a := 0) (b := t) (f := u) (g := v)
      (fun _ => apm_m00A05_lipschitz_vectorField)
      (hu.1.mono Icc_subset_Ici_self) (by
        intro s hs
        rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hs.1 with rfl | hs0
        · exact apm_m00A05_hasDerivWithinAt_zero_of_isSolution hu
        · exact (apm_m00A05_hasDerivAt_of_isSolution hu hs0).hasDerivWithinAt)
      (hv.1.mono Icc_subset_Ici_self) (by
        intro s hs
        rcases eq_or_lt_of_le hs.1 with rfl | hs0
        · exact apm_m00A05_hasDerivWithinAt_zero_of_isSolution hv
        · exact (apm_m00A05_hasDerivAt_of_isSolution hv hs0).hasDerivWithinAt)
      (hu.2.2.1.trans hv.2.2.1.symm)
  exact huniq ⟨ht, le_rfl⟩

/-- Every fixed point of cosine gives the stationary comparison trajectory. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_const_isSolution {ξ : ℝ} (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ) :
    apm_m00A05_isSolution ξ (fun _ => ξ) := by
  refine ⟨continuous_const.continuousOn, differentiableOn_const ξ, rfl, ?_⟩
  intro t ht
  simp [hξ]

/-- An existing half-line solution can be restarted at any nonnegative time. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_shift_isSolution {u₀ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) :
    apm_m00A05_isSolution (u t) (fun s => u (s + t)) := by
  have hmaps : MapsTo (fun s : ℝ => s + t) (Ici 0) (Ici 0) := by
    intro s hs
    exact add_nonneg hs ht
  refine ⟨hu.1.comp (continuous_id.add continuous_const).continuousOn hmaps, ?_, by simp, ?_⟩
  · intro s hs
    have hst : 0 < s + t := add_pos_of_pos_of_nonneg hs ht
    exact (apm_m00A05_hasDerivAt_of_isSolution hu hst).comp_add_const s t
      |>.differentiableAt.differentiableWithinAt
  · intro s hs
    have hst : 0 < s + t := add_pos_of_pos_of_nonneg hs ht
    have hd := (apm_m00A05_hasDerivAt_of_isSolution hu hst).comp_add_const s t
    rw [hd.deriv]
    ring

/-- If a trajectory reaches an equilibrium, uniqueness forces it to remain
there forever. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_eq_of_eq_equilibrium {u₀ ξ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ)
    {t s : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) (hs : 0 ≤ s) (hut : u t = ξ) : u (s + t) = ξ := by
  have hshift := apm_m00A05_shift_isSolution hu ht
  rw [hut] at hshift
  have heq := apm_m00A05_solution_unique hshift (apm_m00A05_const_isSolution hξ)
  exact heq hs

/-- The vector field points weakly toward every cosine fixed point from the
right.  The proof uses only the global `1`-Lipschitz estimate for cosine. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_vectorField_nonpos_of_fixed_le {ξ x : ℝ}
    (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ) (hξx : ξ ≤ x) : Real.cos x - x ≤ 0 := by
  have h := Real.abs_cos_sub_cos_le x ξ
  have hcos : Real.cos x - Real.cos ξ ≤ x - ξ := by
    calc
      Real.cos x - Real.cos ξ ≤ |Real.cos x - Real.cos ξ| := le_abs_self _
      _ ≤ |x - ξ| := h
      _ = x - ξ := abs_of_nonneg (sub_nonneg.mpr hξx)
  linarith

/-- The symmetric inward-pointing estimate on the left of a fixed point. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_vectorField_nonneg_of_le_fixed {ξ x : ℝ}
    (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ) (hxξ : x ≤ ξ) : 0 ≤ Real.cos x - x := by
  have h := Real.abs_cos_sub_cos_le ξ x
  have hcos : Real.cos ξ - Real.cos x ≤ ξ - x := by
    calc
      Real.cos ξ - Real.cos x ≤ |Real.cos ξ - Real.cos x| := le_abs_self _
      _ ≤ |ξ - x| := h
      _ = ξ - x := abs_of_nonneg (sub_nonneg.mpr hxξ)
  linarith

/-- A solution starting above an equilibrium never crosses it. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_fixed_le_solution {u₀ ξ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ)
    (hinit : ξ ≤ u₀) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) : ξ ≤ u t := by
  by_contra hnot
  have hut : u t < ξ := lt_of_not_ge hnot
  have hcont : ContinuousOn u (Icc 0 t) := hu.1.mono Icc_subset_Ici_self
  have hmem : ξ ∈ Icc (u t) (u 0) := by
    exact ⟨hut.le, hu.2.2.1.symm ▸ hinit⟩
  obtain ⟨r, hr, hur⟩ := intermediate_value_Icc' ht hcont hmem
  have hstay := apm_m00A05_eq_of_eq_equilibrium hu hξ hr.1
      (sub_nonneg.mpr hr.2) hur
  have : u t = ξ := by simpa [sub_add_cancel] using hstay
  linarith

/-- A solution starting below an equilibrium never crosses it. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_solution_le_fixed {u₀ ξ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ)
    (hinit : u₀ ≤ ξ) {t : ℝ} (ht : 0 ≤ t) : u t ≤ ξ := by
  by_contra hnot
  have hut : ξ < u t := lt_of_not_ge hnot
  have hcont : ContinuousOn u (Icc 0 t) := hu.1.mono Icc_subset_Ici_self
  have hmem : ξ ∈ Icc (u 0) (u t) := by
    exact ⟨hu.2.2.1.symm ▸ hinit, hut.le⟩
  obtain ⟨r, hr, hur⟩ := intermediate_value_Icc ht hcont hmem
  have hstay := apm_m00A05_eq_of_eq_equilibrium hu hξ hr.1
      (sub_nonneg.mpr hr.2) hur
  have : u t = ξ := by simpa [sub_add_cancel] using hstay
  linarith

/-- Above an equilibrium, the trapped trajectory is antitone. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_antitoneOn_of_fixed_le_initial {u₀ ξ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ)
    (hinit : ξ ≤ u₀) : AntitoneOn u (Ici 0) := by
  apply antitoneOn_of_deriv_nonpos (convex_Ici 0) hu.1
  · simpa only [interior_Ici] using hu.2.1
  · intro t ht
    rw [interior_Ici] at ht
    have htrap := apm_m00A05_fixed_le_solution hu hξ hinit ht.le
    rw [show deriv u t = Real.cos (u t) - u t by
      linarith [hu.2.2.2 t ht]]
    exact apm_m00A05_vectorField_nonpos_of_fixed_le hξ htrap

/-- Below an equilibrium, the trapped trajectory is monotone. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_monotoneOn_of_initial_le_fixed {u₀ ξ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ)
    (hinit : u₀ ≤ ξ) : MonotoneOn u (Ici 0) := by
  apply monotoneOn_of_deriv_nonneg (convex_Ici 0) hu.1
  · simpa only [interior_Ici] using hu.2.1
  · intro t ht
    rw [interior_Ici] at ht
    have htrap := apm_m00A05_solution_le_fixed hu hξ hinit ht.le
    rw [show deriv u t = Real.cos (u t) - u t by
      linarith [hu.2.2.2 t ht]]
    exact apm_m00A05_vectorField_nonneg_of_le_fixed hξ htrap

/-- Trapping and monotonicity already imply convergence to some finite real
limit; identifying that limit with the equilibrium is handled separately. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_exists_limit {u₀ ξ : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) (hξ : Real.cos ξ = ξ) :
    ∃ L : ℝ, Tendsto u atTop (nhds L) := by
  by_cases hinit : u₀ ≤ ξ
  · let w : ℝ → ℝ := fun t => u (max 0 t)
    have hwmono : Monotone w := by
      intro a b hab
      exact apm_m00A05_monotoneOn_of_initial_le_fixed hu hξ hinit
        (le_max_left 0 a) (le_max_left 0 b) (max_le_max le_rfl hab)
    have hw_bdd : BddAbove (range w) := by
      refine ⟨ξ, ?_⟩
      rintro _ ⟨t, rfl⟩
      exact apm_m00A05_solution_le_fixed hu hξ hinit (le_max_left 0 t)
    refine ⟨⨆ t, w t, ?_⟩
    apply (tendsto_atTop_ciSup hwmono hw_bdd).congr'
    filter_upwards [eventually_ge_atTop (0 : ℝ)] with t ht
    simp [w, max_eq_right ht]
  · have hinit' : ξ ≤ u₀ := le_of_not_ge hinit
    let w : ℝ → ℝ := fun t => u (max 0 t)
    have hwanti : Antitone w := by
      intro a b hab
      exact apm_m00A05_antitoneOn_of_fixed_le_initial hu hξ hinit'
        (le_max_left 0 a) (le_max_left 0 b) (max_le_max le_rfl hab)
    have hw_bdd : BddBelow (range w) := by
      refine ⟨ξ, ?_⟩
      rintro _ ⟨t, rfl⟩
      exact apm_m00A05_fixed_le_solution hu hξ hinit' (le_max_left 0 t)
    refine ⟨⨅ t, w t, ?_⟩
    apply (tendsto_atTop_ciInf hwanti hw_bdd).congr'
    filter_upwards [eventually_ge_atTop (0 : ℝ)] with t ht
    simp [w, max_eq_right ht]

/-- A finite limiting trajectory must limit at a zero of its autonomous vector
field.  Mean-value points on `[n,n+1]` make the derivative converge both to the
vector-field value at the limit and to zero. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_limit_is_fixed {u₀ L : ℝ} {u : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hu : apm_m00A05_isSolution u₀ u) (hL : Tendsto u atTop (nhds L)) :
    Real.cos L = L := by
  have hderiv : Tendsto (deriv u) atTop (nhds (Real.cos L - L)) := by
    have hfield : Tendsto (fun t => Real.cos (u t) - u t) atTop
        (nhds (Real.cos L - L)) :=
      ((Real.continuous_cos.tendsto L).comp hL).sub hL
    apply hfield.congr'
    filter_upwards [eventually_gt_atTop (0 : ℝ)] with t ht
    linarith [hu.2.2.2 t ht]
  have hmvt : ∀ n : ℕ, ∃ c : ℝ, c ∈ Ioo (n : ℝ) ((n : ℝ) + 1) ∧
      deriv u c = u ((n : ℝ) + 1) - u (n : ℝ) := by
    intro n
    have hcont : ContinuousOn u (Icc (n : ℝ) ((n : ℝ) + 1)) :=
      hu.1.mono (by intro x hx; exact le_trans (Nat.cast_nonneg n) hx.1)
    obtain ⟨c, hc, hdc⟩ := exists_deriv_eq_slope u (by linarith)
      hcont (hu.2.1.mono <| by
        intro x hx
        exact lt_of_le_of_lt (Nat.cast_nonneg n) hx.1)
    refine ⟨c, hc, ?_⟩
    simpa using hdc
  choose c hc hdc using hmvt
  have hc_top : Tendsto c atTop atTop := by
    refine tendsto_atTop.2 ?_
    intro b
    filter_upwards [(tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop (R := ℝ)).eventually
      (Ici_mem_atTop b)] with n hn
    exact hn.trans (hc n).1.le
  have hderiv_c : Tendsto (fun n => deriv u (c n)) atTop
      (nhds (Real.cos L - L)) := hderiv.comp hc_top
  have hn : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => u (n : ℝ)) atTop (nhds L) :=
    hL.comp tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop
  have hn1 : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => u ((n : ℝ) + 1)) atTop (nhds L) :=
    hL.comp (tendsto_atTop_add_const_right atTop 1 tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop)
  have hzero : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => deriv u (c n)) atTop (nhds 0) := by
    convert (hn1.sub hn).congr'
      (Filter.Eventually.of_forall fun n => (hdc n).symm) using 1 <;> simp
  have : Real.cos L - L = 0 := tendsto_nhds_unique hderiv_c hzero
  exact sub_eq_zero.mp this

/-- Cosine has at most one real fixed point. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_fixed_unique {x y : ℝ}
    (hx : Real.cos x = x) (hy : Real.cos y = y) : x = y := by
  have hxI : x ∈ Icc 0 Real.pi := by
    have hxm : -1 ≤ x := by rw [← hx]; exact Real.neg_one_le_cos x
    have hxp : x ≤ 1 := by rw [← hx]; exact Real.cos_le_one x
    have hx0 : 0 ≤ x := by
      by_contra hn
      have hxneg : x < 0 := lt_of_not_ge hn
      have hcpos : 0 < Real.cos x := Real.cos_pos_of_mem_Ioo ⟨by
        nlinarith [Real.pi_gt_three], by nlinarith [Real.pi_gt_three]⟩
      linarith
    exact ⟨hx0, hxp.trans (by nlinarith [Real.pi_gt_three])⟩
  have hyI : y ∈ Icc 0 Real.pi := by
    have hym : -1 ≤ y := by rw [← hy]; exact Real.neg_one_le_cos y
    have hyp : y ≤ 1 := by rw [← hy]; exact Real.cos_le_one y
    have hy0 : 0 ≤ y := by
      by_contra hn
      have hyneg : y < 0 := lt_of_not_ge hn
      have hcpos : 0 < Real.cos y := Real.cos_pos_of_mem_Ioo ⟨by
        nlinarith [Real.pi_gt_three], by nlinarith [Real.pi_gt_three]⟩
      linarith
    exact ⟨hy0, hyp.trans (by nlinarith [Real.pi_gt_three])⟩
  rcases lt_trichotomy x y with hxy | hxy | hyx
  · have := Real.strictAntiOn_cos hxI hyI hxy
    linarith
  · exact hxy
  · have := Real.strictAntiOn_cos hyI hxI hyx
    linarith

/-- A uniform-duration Picard step from an arbitrary state.  Although the
vector field is unbounded, a ball whose radius grows with the centre gives the
same quarter-unit lifespan at every state; this is the non-Zeno input for
global continuation. -/
lemma apm_m00A05_uniform_picard_step_at (t₀ x₀ : ℝ) :
    ∃ u : ℝ → ℝ, u t₀ = x₀ ∧
      ∀ t ∈ Icc t₀ (t₀ + 1 / 4),
        HasDerivWithinAt u (Real.cos (u t) - u t) (Icc t₀ (t₀ + 1 / 4)) t := by
  let a : NNReal := ⟨|x₀| + 2, by positivity⟩
  let L : NNReal := ⟨2 * |x₀| + 3, by positivity⟩
  have hb : ∀ x ∈ Metric.closedBall x₀ (a : ℝ), ‖Real.cos x - x‖ ≤ (L : ℝ) := by
    intro x hx
    have hdist : |x - x₀| ≤ |x₀| + 2 := by
      simpa [a, Real.dist_eq] using hx
    have hxabs : |x| ≤ 2 * |x₀| + 2 := by
      calc
        |x| ≤ |x - x₀| + |x₀| := by
          simpa [sub_add_cancel] using abs_add_le (x - x₀) x₀
        _ ≤ 2 * |x₀| + 2 := by linarith
    calc
      ‖Real.cos x - x‖ ≤ ‖Real.cos x‖ + ‖x‖ := norm_sub_le _ _
      _ ≤ 1 + |x| := by simpa using add_le_add_right (Real.abs_cos_le_one x) |x|
      _ ≤ (L : ℝ) := by simp [L]; linarith
  have hpl : IsPicardLindelof (fun _ : ℝ => fun x : ℝ => Real.cos x - x)
      (⟨t₀, by norm_num⟩ : Icc t₀ (t₀ + 1 / 4)) x₀ a 0 L 2 := by
    apply IsPicardLindelof.of_time_independent hb
      (apm_m00A05_lipschitz_vectorField.lipschitzOnWith)
    norm_num [a, L]
    nlinarith [abs_nonneg x₀]
  exact hpl.exists_eq_forall_mem_Icc_hasDerivWithinAt₀

lemma apm_m00A05_uniform_picard_step (x₀ : ℝ) :
    ∃ u : ℝ → ℝ, u 0 = x₀ ∧
      ∀ t ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) (1 / 4 : ℝ),
        HasDerivWithinAt u (Real.cos (u t) - u t) (Icc 0 (1 / 4)) t := by
  simpa using apm_m00A05_uniform_picard_step_at 0 x₀

/-- A deterministic choice of the uniform Picard segment. -/
noncomputable def apm_m00A05_picardStep (t₀ x₀ : ℝ) : ℝ → ℝ :=
  Classical.choose (apm_m00A05_uniform_picard_step_at t₀ x₀)

lemma apm_m00A05_picardStep_start (t₀ x₀ : ℝ) :
    apm_m00A05_picardStep t₀ x₀ t₀ = x₀ :=
  (Classical.choose_spec (apm_m00A05_uniform_picard_step_at t₀ x₀)).1

lemma apm_m00A05_picardStep_hasDerivWithinAt (t₀ x₀ : ℝ) {t : ℝ}
    (ht : t ∈ Icc t₀ (t₀ + 1 / 4)) :
    HasDerivWithinAt (apm_m00A05_picardStep t₀ x₀)
      (Real.cos (apm_m00A05_picardStep t₀ x₀ t) -
        apm_m00A05_picardStep t₀ x₀ t)
      (Icc t₀ (t₀ + 1 / 4)) t :=
  (Classical.choose_spec (apm_m00A05_uniform_picard_step_at t₀ x₀)).2 t ht

/-- Quarter-unit time mesh used for the non-Zeno continuation. -/
def apm_m00A05_mesh (n : ℕ) : ℝ := n / 4

@[simp] lemma apm_m00A05_mesh_zero : apm_m00A05_mesh 0 = 0 := by
  simp [apm_m00A05_mesh]

lemma apm_m00A05_mesh_succ (n : ℕ) :
    apm_m00A05_mesh (n + 1) = apm_m00A05_mesh n + 1 / 4 := by
  norm_num [apm_m00A05_mesh]
  ring

lemma apm_m00A05_mesh_strictMono_step (n : ℕ) :
    apm_m00A05_mesh n < apm_m00A05_mesh (n + 1) := by
  rw [apm_m00A05_mesh_succ]
  norm_num

/-- States obtained by recursively taking the endpoint of each chosen Picard
segment. -/
noncomputable def apm_m00A05_picardState (u₀ : ℝ) : ℕ → ℝ
  | 0 => u₀
  | n + 1 => apm_m00A05_picardStep (apm_m00A05_mesh n)
      (apm_m00A05_picardState u₀ n) (apm_m00A05_mesh (n + 1))

@[simp] lemma apm_m00A05_picardState_zero (u₀ : ℝ) :
    apm_m00A05_picardState u₀ 0 = u₀ := rfl

lemma apm_m00A05_picardState_succ (u₀ : ℝ) (n : ℕ) :

/-
! # APM a93A03: Weak convergence in Hilbert space

Prove:
(a) If hₙ ⇀ h and ‖hₙ‖ → ‖h‖, then ‖hₙ - h‖ → 0 (Kadec-Klee).
(b) If hₙ ⇀ h, then ‖h‖ ≤ liminf ‖hₙ‖ (weak lsc of norm).

import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Basic
import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.LinearMap
import Mathlib.Analysis.Normed.Operator.BanachSteinhaus
import Mathlib.Order.LiminfLimsup
import Mathlib.Topology.Order.LiminfLimsup
import Mathlib.Data.Real.Sqrt

open Filter Topology InnerProductSpace

noncomputable section

variable {H : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H]

/-- Weak convergence: hₙ ⇀ h iff ⟨hₙ, k⟩ → ⟨h, k⟩ for all k. -/
def WeakTendsto (h : ℕ → H) (x : H) : Prop :=
  ∀ k : H, Tendsto (fun n => ⟪h n, k⟫_ℝ) atTop (𝓝 ⟪x, k⟫_ℝ)

/-- **Part (a):** Weak convergence + norm convergence ⟹ strong convergence.

    Uses the identity ‖hₙ - h‖² = ‖hₙ‖² - 2⟨hₙ,h⟩ + ‖h‖² (Mathlib's
    `norm_sub_sq_real`). Weak convergence gives ⟨hₙ,h⟩ → ‖h‖²;
    norm convergence gives ‖hₙ‖² → ‖h‖². So ‖hₙ-h‖² → 0. -/
theorem norm_sub_tendsto_zero_of_weak_and_norm
    {h : ℕ → H} {x : H}
    (hweak : WeakTendsto h x)
    (hnorm : Tendsto (fun n => ‖h n‖) atTop (𝓝 ‖x‖)) :
    Tendsto (fun n => ‖h n - x‖) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
  have h_inner : Tendsto (fun n => ⟪h n, x⟫_ℝ) atTop (𝓝 (‖x‖ ^ 2)) := by
    have := hweak x
    rwa [real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq] at this
  have h_norm_sq : Tendsto (fun n => ‖h n‖ ^ 2) atTop (𝓝 (‖x‖ ^ 2)) :=
    hnorm.pow 2
  have h_rhs : Tendsto (fun n => ‖h n‖ ^ 2 - 2 * ⟪h n, x⟫_ℝ + ‖x‖ ^ 2) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
    have h2 : Tendsto (fun n => 2 * ⟪h n, x⟫_ℝ) atTop (𝓝 (2 * ‖x‖ ^ 2)) :=
      tendsto_const_nhds.mul h_inner
    have h_sub : Tendsto (fun n => ‖h n‖ ^ 2 - 2 * ⟪h n, x⟫_ℝ) atTop
        (𝓝 (‖x‖ ^ 2 - 2 * ‖x‖ ^ 2)) := Tendsto.sub h_norm_sq h2
    have h0 : ‖x‖ ^ 2 - 2 * ‖x‖ ^ 2 + ‖x‖ ^ 2 = (0 : ℝ) := by ring
    rw [← h0]
    exact Tendsto.add h_sub tendsto_const_nhds
  have h_sq : Tendsto (fun n => ‖h n - x‖ ^ 2) atTop (𝓝 0) :=
    Tendsto.congr (fun n => (norm_sub_sq_real _ _).symm) h_rhs
  have h_sqrt : Tendsto (fun n => Real.sqrt (‖h n - x‖ ^ 2)) atTop (𝓝 (Real.sqrt 0)) :=
    Real.continuous_sqrt.tendsto 0 |>.comp h_sq
  rw [Real.sqrt_zero] at h_sqrt
  exact h_sqrt.congr (fun n => Real.sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _))

/-- Helper: for any a < ‖x‖, eventually a ≤ ‖h n‖.

    From ‖hₙ-x‖² ≥ 0: ‖h n‖² ≥ 2⟨hₙ,x⟩ - ‖x‖².
    Since ⟨hₙ,x⟩ → ‖x‖² and a < ‖x‖: eventually 2⟨hₙ,x⟩ - ‖x‖² > a²,
    so ‖h n‖² ≥ a², hence ‖h n‖ ≥ a (both nonneg). -/
private lemma eventually_le_norm_of_weak
    {h : ℕ → H} {x : H} (hweak : WeakTendsto h x) :
    ∀ a : ℝ, a < ‖x‖ → ∀ᶠ n in atTop, a ≤ ‖h n‖ := by
  have h_inner : Tendsto (fun n => ⟪h n, x⟫_ℝ) atTop (𝓝 (‖x‖ ^ 2)) := by
    have := hweak x
    rwa [real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq] at this

  by_cases ha_neg : a < 0
  · exact Eventually.of_forall fun _ => le_trans ha_neg.le (norm_nonneg _)
  push_neg at ha_neg
  have ha_sq : a ^ 2 < ‖x‖ ^ 2 := sq_lt_sq' (by linarith [norm_nonneg x]) ha
  have h_thresh : (a ^ 2 + ‖x‖ ^ 2) / 2 < ‖x‖ ^ 2 := by linarith
  have h_inner_ev : ∀ᶠ n in atTop, (a ^ 2 + ‖x‖ ^ 2) / 2 < ⟪h n, x⟫_ℝ :=
    h_inner.eventually (Ioi_mem_nhds h_thresh)
  filter_upwards [h_inner_ev] with n hn
  have h_id : ‖h n - x‖ ^ 2 = ‖h n‖ ^ 2 - 2 * ⟪h n, x⟫_ℝ + ‖x‖ ^ 2 :=
    norm_sub_sq_real _ _
  have h_nn : 0 ≤ ‖h n - x‖ ^ 2 := pow_nonneg (norm_nonneg _) 2
  have h_sq : a ^ 2 ≤ ‖h n‖ ^ 2 := by linarith

    in the pre-Hilbert space `c₀₀` of finitely supported real sequences, fix a

    norms tend to infinity. Mathlib's real-valued `liminf` is defined using
    `sSup`; for a sequence with unbounded eventual lower bounds this is
    `sSup ∅ = 0`. Thus the conclusion would assert `‖x‖ ≤ 0`.

    of `‖h n‖`; `eventually_le_norm_of_weak` and `le_liminf_of_le` then prove
    the result. -/

-- weak lower semicontinuity of the norm needs `[CompleteSpace H]`, because the
-- standard proof routes through Banach-Steinhaus, whose Mathlib form requires
-- completeness. Counterexample found by codex-7 on durée run 12: in the
-- INCOMPLETE space c00, take h n = x + n * e n. Then h n converges weakly to x
-- while the norms are unbounded, and Mathlib's real liminf collapses to
-- sSup (unbounded set) = sSup empty = 0, so the conclusion fails outright.
-- That collapse is machine-checked: csSup_of_not_bddAbove then Real.sSup_empty.
-- FOURTH instance of the Lean junk-value family, after ENNReal.toReal top = 0,
-- integral of a non-integrable function = 0, and ContDiff top meaning analytic.
theorem norm_le_liminf_of_weak [CompleteSpace H]
    {h : ℕ → H} {x : H}
    (hweak : WeakTendsto h x) :
    ‖x‖ ≤ liminf (fun n => (‖h n‖ : ℝ)) atTop := by
  have h_uniform : ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ n, ‖innerSL ℝ (h n)‖ ≤ C := by
    apply banach_steinhaus
    intro k
    obtain ⟨C, hC⟩ := isBounded_iff_forall_norm_le.mp
      (Metric.isBounded_range_of_tendsto
        (fun n => innerSL ℝ (h n) k)
        (by simpa only [innerSL_apply_apply] using hweak k))
    exact ⟨C, Set.forall_mem_range.mp hC⟩
  obtain ⟨C, hC⟩ := h_uniform
  have h_norm_le : ∀ n, ‖h n‖ ≤ C := fun n => by
    simpa only [innerSL_apply_norm] using hC n
  have h_cobounded :
      IsCoboundedUnder (· ≥ ·) atTop (fun n => (‖h n‖ : ℝ)) :=
    isCoboundedUnder_ge_of_eventually_le atTop (Eventually.of_forall h_norm_le)
  apply le_of_forall_lt
  intro a ha
  let b := (a + ‖x‖) / 2
  have hab : a < b := by dsimp [b]; linarith
  have hbx : b < ‖x‖ := by dsimp [b]; linarith
  exact hab.trans_le
    (le_liminf_of_le h_cobounded (eventually_le_norm_of_weak hweak b hbx))

end

/-
! # APM a93A01: Uniform continuity ⟺ difference quotient condition

Let f : (0,1) → ℝ. Prove equivalence of:
(a) f is uniformly continuous on (0,1).
(b) ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N > 0, ∀ x,y ∈ (0,1) with x ≠ y,
    |(f(x)-f(y))/(x-y)| > N ⟹ |f(x)-f(y)| < ε.
-/

import Mathlib.Analysis.Normed.Group.Basic
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Cauchy
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Bounded

open Set Metric Filter

noncomputable section

abbrev I01 : Set ℝ := Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1

/-- Condition (b). -/
def DiffQuotientCondition (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
    ∃ N : ℝ, 0 < N ∧
      ∀ x ∈ I01, ∀ y ∈ I01, x ≠ y →
        N < |f x - f y| / |x - y| → |f x - f y| < ε

/-- Uniform continuity of f on (0,1). -/
def UnifContOn01 (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
    ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧
      ∀ x ∈ I01, ∀ y ∈ I01,
        |x - y| < δ → |f x - f y| < ε

/-- Bridge: UnifContOn01 ⟹ UniformContinuousOn. -/
lemma unifContOn01_imp (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : UnifContOn01 f) :
    UniformContinuousOn f I01 := by
  rw [Metric.uniformContinuousOn_iff]
  intro ε hε
  obtain ⟨δ, hδ_pos, hδ⟩ := hf ε hε
  refine ⟨δ, hδ_pos, ?_⟩
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  exact hδ x hx y hy (by simpa using hxy)

/-- UC on (0,1) implies f is bounded on (0,1).

    (0,1) is totally bounded ⟹ f's range on (0,1) is totally bounded
    (via restriction + TotallyBounded.image) ⟹ bounded. -/
lemma unifContOn01_bounded {f : ℝ → ℝ} (hf : UnifContOn01 f) :
    ∃ B : ℝ, 0 ≤ B ∧ ∀ x ∈ I01, |f x| ≤ B := by
  have h_uc : UniformContinuousOn f I01 := unifContOn01_imp f hf
  have h_uc_restrict : UniformContinuous (I01.restrict f) := h_uc.restrict
  -- (0,1) is totally bounded
  have h_tb_I01 : TotallyBounded (I01 : Set ℝ) := totallyBounded_Ioo 0 1
  -- Transfer to subtype: TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01)
  have h_tb_univ : TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01) := by
    have h_emb := isUniformEmbedding_subtype_val (p := fun x => x ∈ I01)
    have h_iff : TotallyBounded (Subtype.val '' (Set.univ : Set I01)) ↔
        TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01) :=
      totallyBounded_image_iff h_emb.isUniformInducing
    -- h_iff : ∀ s, TotallyBounded (Subtype.val '' s) ↔ TotallyBounded s
    -- We need: TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01)
    -- Subtype.val '' Set.univ = range Subtype.val = I01
    have h_img : Subtype.val '' (Set.univ : Set I01) = (I01 : Set ℝ) := by
      ext x
      constructor
      · rintro ⟨⟨x', hx'⟩, _, rfl⟩
        exact hx'
      · intro hx
        exact ⟨⟨x, hx⟩, Set.mem_univ _, rfl⟩
    rw [← h_img] at h_tb_I01
    exact h_iff.mp h_tb_I01
  -- Image of Set.univ under restrict f is totally bounded
  have h_tb_img : TotallyBounded ((I01.restrict f) '' Set.univ) :=
    h_tb_univ.image h_uc_restrict
  -- (I01.restrict f) '' Set.univ = f '' I01
  have h_eq : (I01.restrict f) '' Set.univ = f '' I01 := by
    ext y
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨x, _, rfl⟩
      exact ⟨x.1, x.2, rfl⟩
    · rintro ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      exact ⟨⟨x, hx⟩, Set.mem_univ _, rfl⟩
  rw [h_eq] at h_tb_img
  -- Totally bounded ⟹ bounded
  have h_bdd : Bornology.IsBounded (f '' I01) := h_tb_img.isBounded
  -- Extract bound using isBounded_iff_subset_closedBall
  obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ := (Metric.isBounded_iff_subset_closedBall 0).mp h_bdd
  refine ⟨max r 0, le_max_right r 0, ?_⟩
  intro x hx
  have h_in : f x ∈ f '' I01 := ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
  have h_sub : f x ∈ Metric.closedBall (0 : ℝ) r := hr h_in
  simp only [Metric.mem_closedBall, Real.dist_eq, sub_zero] at h_sub
  exact le_trans h_sub (le_max_left r 0)

/-- **(b) ⟹ (a)**. -/
theorem diffQuot_implies_unifCont {f : ℝ → ℝ} (hf : DiffQuotientCondition f) :
    UnifContOn01 f := by
  intro ε hε
  obtain ⟨N, hN_pos, hN⟩ := hf ε hε
  refine ⟨ε / N, by positivity, ?_⟩
  intro x hx y hy hxy_lt
  by_contra hcontra
  push_neg at hcontra
  have hxy_ne : x ≠ y := by
    intro heq
    rw [heq] at hcontra
    simp [sub_self, abs_zero] at hcontra
    linarith
  have hxy_pos : 0 < |x - y| := abs_pos.mpr (sub_ne_zero.mpr hxy_ne)
  have hquot : N < |f x - f y| / |x - y| := by
    rw [lt_div_iff₀ hxy_pos]
    have key : N * (ε / N) = ε := mul_div_cancel₀ ε hN_pos.ne'
    nlinarith [hxy_lt, hcontra, hN_pos, key]
  exact absurd (hN x hx y hy hxy_ne hquot) (not_lt_of_ge hcontra)

/-- **(a) ⟹ (b)**. -/
theorem unifCont_implies_diffQuot {f : ℝ → ℝ} (hf : UnifContOn01 f) :
    DiffQuotientCondition f := by
  intro ε hε
  obtain ⟨B, hB_nonneg, hB_bound⟩ := unifContOn01_bounded hf
  obtain ⟨δ, hδ_pos, hδ⟩ := hf ε hε
  -- B' = max B 1 ensures B' > 0
  set B' := max B 1
  have hB'_pos : 0 < B' := lt_max_iff.mpr (Or.inr (by norm_num))
  have hB'_bound : ∀ x ∈ I01, |f x| ≤ B' := fun x hx =>
    (hB_bound x hx).trans (le_max_left B 1)
  -- N = B' + B' / δ... actually just use 2*B'/δ to bound |f x - f y| ≤ 2*B'
  -- |f x - f y| ≤ |f x| + |f y| ≤ 2 * B'
  set N := (2 * B') / δ
  have hN_pos : 0 < N := div_pos (mul_pos (by norm_num) hB'_pos) hδ_pos
  refine ⟨N, hN_pos, ?_⟩
  intro x hx y hy hxy_ne hquot
  have hxy_pos : 0 < |x - y| := abs_pos.mpr (sub_ne_zero.mpr hxy_ne)
  -- From quotient > N: |x - y| < |f x - f y| / N ≤ 2*B' / N = 2*B' / (2*B'/δ) = δ
  have hxy_lt_δ : |x - y| < δ := by
    have h1 : |x - y| < |f x - f y| / N := by
      have h2 := (lt_div_iff₀ hxy_pos).mp hquot
      -- h2 : N * |x - y| < |f x - f y|
      rwa [lt_div_iff₀ hN_pos, mul_comm]
    have h_fdiff : |f x - f y| ≤ 2 * B' := by
      have hx' : |f x| ≤ B' := hB'_bound x hx
      have hy' : |f y| ≤ B' := hB'_bound y hy
      calc |f x - f y| ≤ |f x| + |f y| := abs_sub _ _
        _ ≤ B' + B' := by gcongr
        _ = 2 * B' := by ring
    calc |x - y| < |f x - f y| / N := h1
      _ ≤ (2 * B') / N := by gcongr
      _ = δ := by
        rw [div_div_eq_mul_div]
        field_simp
  exact hδ x hx y hy hxy_lt_δ

/-- **Main theorem**. -/
theorem unifCont_iff_diffQuot (f : ℝ → ℝ) :
    UnifContOn01 f ↔ DiffQuotientCondition f :=
  ⟨fun hf => unifCont_implies_diffQuot hf,
   fun hf => diffQuot_implies_unifCont hf⟩

end

Suppose that $X$ and $Y$ are complete metric spaces, that $A$ is dense
in $X$ and $f:A\rightarrow Y$ is uniformly continuous. Prove that $f$

import Mathlib

/-!
# APM m99A04 — extending a uniformly continuous map from a dense subset

The subset is represented by its subtype, so the extension equation is
pointwise and type-correct.  Both spaces retain the completeness assumptions
from the source.

## Statement repairs

None.

## Encoding questions

None.
-/

theorem apm_m99a04
    {X Y : Type*} [MetricSpace X] [MetricSpace Y]
    [CompleteSpace X] [CompleteSpace Y]
    {A : Set X} (hA : Dense A) {f : A → Y}
    (hf : UniformContinuous f) :
    ∃! F : X → Y,
      Continuous F ∧ ∀ ⦃x : X⦄ (hx : x ∈ A), F x = f ⟨x, hx⟩ := by
  refine ⟨hA.extend f, ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact ⟨(hA.uniformContinuous_extend hf).continuous,
      fun {x} hx ↦ hA.extend_of_ind hf ⟨x, hx⟩⟩
  · intro G hG
    symm
    apply hA.extend_unique (g := G) _ hG.1
    exact fun x ↦ hG.2 x.property

theorem endpoint_unique_on_unit {u v : ℝ → ℝ} {K : NNReal}
    {F : ℝ → ℝ → ℝ} (hF : ∀ t, LipschitzWith K (F t))
    (hu : ContinuousOn u (Icc 0 1)) (hv : ContinuousOn v (Icc 0 1))
    (hdu : ∀ s ∈ Ioo 0 1, HasDerivAt u (F s (u s)) s)
    (hdv : ∀ s ∈ Ioo 0 1, HasDerivAt v (F s (v s)) s)
    (huv : u 0 = v 0) : EqOn u v (Icc 0 1) := by
  intro t ht
  by_cases h0 : t = 0
  · subst h0
    exact huv
  · have htp : 0 < t := lt_of_le_of_ne (ht.1) (Ne.symm h0)
    have key : ∀ δ ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) t,
        dist (u t) (v t) ≤ dist (u δ) (v δ) * Real.exp ((K : ℝ) * (t - δ)) := by
      intro δ hδ
      have hstep := dist_le_of_trajectories_ODE (K := K) (v := F) hF
        (hu.mono (fun x hx => ⟨le_trans hδ.1.le hx.1, le_trans hx.2 ht.2⟩))
        (fun s hs => (hdu s ⟨lt_of_lt_of_le hδ.1 hs.1, lt_of_lt_of_le hs.2 ht.2⟩).hasDerivWithinAt)
        (hv.mono (fun x hx => ⟨le_trans hδ.1.le hx.1, le_trans hx.2 ht.2⟩))
        (fun s hs => (hdv s ⟨lt_of_lt_of_le hδ.1 hs.1, lt_of_lt_of_le hs.2 ht.2⟩).hasDerivWithinAt)
        (le_refl _) t (right_mem_Icc.2 hδ.2.le)
      exact hstep
    have hcont : ContinuousOn (fun s => dist (u s) (v s)) (Icc 0 1) :=
      ((hu.sub hv).abs).congr
        (fun s _ => (Real.dist_eq (u s) (v s)).symm)
    have hc0 := hcont.continuousWithinAt (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ∈ Icc 0 1)
    have h1 : Tendsto (fun δ => dist (u δ) (v δ)) (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 0) := by
      have hc := ContinuousWithinAt.tendsto hc0
      rw [nhdsWithin_Icc_eq_nhdsGE (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) < 1)] at hc
      have h1' := hc.mono_left (nhdsWithin_mono _ Ioi_subset_Ici_self)
      rw [show dist (u 0) (v 0) = 0 by
        rw [huv]; exact dist_self _] at h1'
      simpa using h1'
    have h2 : Tendsto (fun δ : ℝ => Real.exp ((K : ℝ) * (t - δ))) (𝓝[>] 0)
        (𝓝 (Real.exp ((K : ℝ) * t))) := by
      have h2' := (Continuous.tendsto
        (by continuity : Continuous fun δ : ℝ => Real.exp ((K : ℝ) * (t - δ))) 0).mono_left
        (nhdsWithin_le_nhds (s := Ioi 0) (a := (0:ℝ)) : 𝓝[>] (0:ℝ) ≤ 𝓝 (0:ℝ))
      simpa using h2'
    have hg : Tendsto (fun δ => dist (u δ) (v δ) * Real.exp ((K : ℝ) * (t - δ)))
        (𝓝[>] 0) (𝓝 0) := by simpa using h1.mul h2
    have hmem : Ioo (0 : ℝ) t ∈ 𝓝[>] (0 : ℝ) := by
      have h := inter_mem (mem_nhdsWithin_of_mem_nhds (Iio_mem_nhds htp))
        (self_mem_nhdsWithin (s := Ioi (0:ℝ)))
      rwa [show Iio t ∩ Ioi (0:ℝ) = Ioo 0 t by
        ext x
        show x ∈ Iio t ∩ Ioi 0 ↔ x ∈ Ioo 0 t
        simp only [Set.mem_inter_iff, Set.mem_Iio, Set.mem_Ioi, Set.mem_Ioo]
        exact ⟨fun h => ⟨h.2, h.1⟩, fun h => ⟨h.2, h.1⟩⟩] at h
    have hle : dist (u t) (v t) ≤ 0 :=
      le_of_tendsto_of_tendsto
        (tendsto_const_nhds : Tendsto (fun _ : ℝ => dist (u t) (v t)) (𝓝[>] 0)
          (𝓝 (dist (u t) (v t)))) hg
        (eventually_of_mem hmem (fun δ hδ => key δ hδ))
    exact dist_eq_zero.mp (le_antisymm hle dist_nonneg)

/-- The scalar ODE seam required by the Volterra example, after FTC has
produced the interior derivative. No derivative at zero is assumed. -/
theorem scalar_ode_zero {u : ℝ → ℝ} (c : ℝ)
    (hu : ContinuousOn u (Icc 0 1))
    (hdu : ∀ s ∈ Ioo 0 1, HasDerivAt u (c * u s) s)
    (hu0 : u 0 = 0) : EqOn u (fun _ => 0) (Icc 0 1) := by
  have hF : ∀ _t : ℝ, LipschitzWith (⟨|c|, abs_nonneg c⟩ : NNReal)
      (fun x : ℝ => c * x) := by
    intro t
    apply LipschitzWith.of_dist_le_mul
    intro x y
    simp [Real.dist_eq, ← mul_sub, abs_mul]
  exact endpoint_unique_on_unit hF hu continuousOn_const hdu
    (fun s _ => by simpa using hasDerivAt_const s (0 : ℝ)) hu0

/-- Refuting control: equal ODE derivatives without equal initial values
must not establish equal trajectories. -/
example : ¬ EqOn (fun _ : ℝ => (1 : ℝ)) (fun _ => 0) (Icc 0 1) := by
  intro h
  have hz := h (by norm_num : (0 : ℝ) ∈ Icc 0 1)
  norm_num at hz

    ∃ A : apm_m96j04_H →L[ℝ] apm_m96j04_H,

      ∀ n : ℕ, 2 ≤ n → IsCompactOperator (A ^ n) := by
  let A : apm_m96j04_H →L[ℝ] apm_m96j04_H :=
    (ContinuousLinearMap.inl ℝ ℓ²(ℕ, ℝ) ℓ²(ℕ, ℝ)).comp
      (ContinuousLinearMap.snd ℝ ℓ²(ℕ, ℝ) ℓ²(ℕ, ℝ))

  · intro x y
    simp [A]
  · intro n hn

    compact disk.

    regardless of the leading coefficient; monicity only ever entered

fields.title: Close Real Oscillatory Integrals by Fourier Inversion, Not Residues
fields.keywords: fourier, inversion, oscillatory-integral, residue, contour, cosine-transform, poisson-kernel, exp-decay, transform-pair
fields.why: math-strategy/proof-architecture
fields.how: own mechanism: When a real oscillatory integral (cosine/sine transform of a rational or exponentially decaying kernel) would classically be evaluated by residues and the library has no residue or contour-deformation machinery, dualise: compute the Fourier transform of the *symmetric decaying* kernel directly from the library's one-sided exponential lemmas, then apply Fourier inversion and take the real part. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A target like ∫ cos(tx)/(x² + a²) dx over ℝ or a half-line, where
    the informal proof is a semicircle contour and the residue theorem, and
    searches for `residue`, `circleIntegral`-based deformation, or a packaged
    transform of 1/(x²+a²) come back empty.

IF.text:
The kernel is even and absolutely integrable, then the transform pair
      runs through elementary API: 𝓕(e^{-c|x|}) is two one-sided complex
      exponential integrals (upper half-line for Re a < 0, lower for
      Re b > 0, stitched with `intervalIntegral.integral_Iic_add_Ioi`),
      and inversion `hf.fourierInv_fourier_eq` at the frequency of interest
      recovers the kernel value. The cosine integral is the real part of the
      inversion integral; the half-line integral folds out of the full-line
      one by evenness (`integral_comp_abs`).

HOWEVER.text:
The seam is convention-heavy: Mathlib's Fourier transform is 2π-normalized
      (`Real.fourier_real_eq_integral_exp_smul`, `Real.fourierInv_eq'`), so the
      frequency must be rescaled (s / (2π)) and the phase identity verified at
      each point — plan a `field_simp`-heavy closing block. Inversion also
      demands integrability of the *transform* as an explicit hypothesis, and a
      continuity hypothesis at the evaluation point; both must be discharged by
      hand. Do not expect the ODE route as a cheaper alternative: the second
      derivative of the cosine kernel produces a ∫cos(tx) term that has no
      Bochner-integral meaning, so the ODE argument is structurally unavailable,
      not merely long.

THEN.text:
Split the closure into named lemmas: (1) integrability of the kernel;
      (2) the explicit transform of the decaying kernel; (3) inversion to the
      full-line cosine integral; (4) the evenness fold to the half-line and a
      scaling lemma to move from the problem's kernel to the standard one.
      Each is independently checkable and reusable by sibling problems with the
      same bridge.

BECAUSE.text:
The library's Fourier folder is deep enough to carry the whole argument,
      while its complex-analysis folder has no residue theorem at all; the
      honest cost comparison is "adapt Fourier API and conventions" versus
      "build contour integration from scratch", and it is not close. The
      informal route's difficulty is a property of pen-and-paper infrastructure,
      not of the statement.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[State the full-line integral first; the half-line is a corollary by evenness.]
    next[Compute 𝓕 of the symmetric decaying kernel from one-sided exp lemmas before touching inversion.]
    next[Rescale the frequency by 1/(2π) and verify the phase identity pointwise.]
    next[Discharge integrability of 𝓕 f and continuity at the point explicitly; inversion needs both.]
    next[Take real parts at the end, after the complex inversion equality is established.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When the object is a finite Laurent sum over Icc (-N) N evaluated on the unit circle, multiply through by w ^ N to clear the negative powers and work with an ordinary Polynomial of degree at most 2N, where the whole root-multiplicity API (roots, rootMultiplicity, card_roots) applies. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
The goal speaks about a trigonometric/Laurent expression
    sum over Icc (-N) N of a n * w ^ n with w on Metric.sphere 0 1, and
    Mathlib has no direct integer-valued winding/index API for it.

HOWEVER.text:
Polynomial lemmas (degree bounds, root counts, divisor sums)
    do not apply to Laurent monomials with negative exponents.

THEN.text:
Define the cleared polynomial sum over Finset.range (2 * N + 1)
    with coefficients a (k - N); prove eval w = w ^ N * Laurent-sum via
    Finset.sum_bij (k ↦ k - N) between range (2N+1) and Icc (-N) N,
    using zpow_natCast / zpow_add₀ to relate natural and integer powers at
    w ≠ 0. Nonvanishing of the Laurent sum - z on the circle transfers
    exactly to nonvanishing of the cleared polynomial on the sphere, since
    w ^ N never vanishes there.
    + LEAN:
      api[Finset.sum_bij] api[zpow_add₀] api[zpow_natCast]
      api[Polynomial.card_roots'] api[Polynomial.natDegree_sum_le_of_forall_le]

BECAUSE.text:
The factor w ^ N is a unit on the unit circle, so zeros,
    logarithmic derivatives, and winding contributions shift only by the
    explicit constant N, which the caller can subtract by hand.

fields.title: Find the Library's Measure-Theoretic Statement Before Rebuilding It
fields.keywords: measure, integration, Bochner, lintegral, Haar, normalization, junk-value, instance-diamond, adapter, specialization
fields.why: math-informal/reduce-to-known-result
fields.how: own mechanism: Measure-theoretic results usually exist in the library under a more general statement, a different normalization, or a restricted variant — so treat the work as locating and adapting that statement, and audit the totalized integral's premises before believing the result. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A formalization whose remaining obligation is measure-theoretic —
    an integrability side condition, a convergence theorem, a change of
    coordinates, a norm comparison — and where writing the classical proof
    directly into the problem file looks like the shortest route.

IF.text:
The library already contains the mathematical content, then the residual
      work is an adapter and should be named as one: specialize the general
      statement to the case at hand, compose with an explicit scaling to move
      between conventions, or select the restricted variant that matches the set
      being integrated over. A Fourier limit theorem under another phase
      convention becomes the target composed with a nonzero frequency scaling
      plus a separate character identity; a one-dimensional statement that looks
      absent is often the fixed-dimensional or Jacobian formulation at `n = 1`;
      the radial coefficient in dimension three is the general Haar coefficient
      normalized to `4π`.

HOWEVER.text:
Three things make this harder than a search.

      The library's generality is where the instances hide. Chaining a
      specialization can expose a measurable-space diamond; the repair is to
      return to the general theorem and instantiate its measure and function
      explicitly at the use site rather than to fight the chain. Elaboration will
      also decline to synthesize witnesses that look obvious — a constant on
      `Icc` may need its finite-measure witness supplied by hand.

      Restricted and unrestricted variants are not interchangeable. When the
      comparison holds only on the set being integrated over, the `_on`
      monotonicity theorem is the correct one; strengthening a local bound into
      a global one to fit the unrestricted statement proves something you do not
      have. The same discrimination applies at the Bochner/`lintegral` seam and
      at the compact-support/full-support interface: concentration and tail
      decay do not discharge a compact-support hypothesis, and an approximate-
      identity instantiation that ignores the kernel-support interface is
      unsound rather than merely stuck.

      Most dangerous, the integral is *totalized*. A non-integrable integrand
      does not fail — it returns a junk value, and a missing integrability
      premise becomes a theorem that is false but elaborates. Jensen applied to
      `log ∘ g` without integrability of the transformed function is the standard
      instance; a transform theorem that omits measurability is another, and may
      genuinely need an integrable/non-integrable split rather than an inferred
      hypothesis.

THEN.text:
Search the general form first — fixed-dimensional, Jacobian, Haar, another
      normalization — and specialize, before building the named classical proof.
      When you do adapt, isolate the adaptation: the scaling, the character
      identity, the parity-specific identity, each as its own lemma.

      Instantiate at the use site when a specialization chain produces a
      diamond, and supply concrete measure witnesses rather than waiting for
      elaboration to find them.

      Choose the restricted variant when the hypothesis is restricted, and check
      the support interface before instantiating anything that assumes compact
      support.

      Audit every integrability premise explicitly. Before applying a theorem
      through a totalized integral, state what must be integrable and prove it —
      a junk value will not tell you it was missing.

BECAUSE.text:
Measure theory is the part of a formalization where the library is deepest
      and the local proof is longest, so the ratio between finding and rebuilding
      is at its most extreme here; and it is simultaneously the part where the
      type system's totality is most willing to accept a statement that means
      nothing. Both failures are invisible at the point of writing — the
      rebuilt proof looks like progress, and the junk-valued theorem looks like
      a result. Naming the adapter and auditing the premises is what makes them
      visible while they are still cheap.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Search the general/fixed-dimensional/Haar form and specialize before building.]
    next[Name the adapter — scaling, normalization, character identity — as its own lemma.]
    next[Instantiate the general theorem at the use site when a chain exposes an instance diamond.]
    next[Pick the restricted (`_on`) variant when the hypothesis is restricted.]
    next[Check the kernel-support interface before instantiating a compact-support theorem.]
    next[State and prove every integrability premise; the totalized integral will not.]

fields.title: Prove ODE Flow Stability Through Mathlib's Grönwall APIs
fields.keywords: Lean, Mathlib, ODE, Gronwall, flow, stability, Lipschitz, exponential-bound, reversed-time
fields.why: math-informal/reduce-to-known-result
fields.how: own mechanism: For exponential stability of two ODE trajectories, first search Mathlib's Grönwall layer for a theorem matching either the norm of their difference or their distance; then isolate negative time by applying the same theorem to a reversed field and reversed trajectories. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A Lean goal asks for a bound of the form
    `|phi t a - phi t b| <= exp (L * |t|) * |a - b|` from a state-Lipschitz
    vector field and a flow or trajectory predicate.

IF.text:
The goal is already expressed as distance between two trajectories, use
      `dist_le_of_trajectories_ODE`. If it is expressed as the norm of their
      difference and derivative bounds are readily available, use
      `norm_le_gronwallBound_of_norm_deriv_right_le` and simplify the resulting
      zero-error bound with `gronwallBound_ε0`.

HOWEVER.text:
These theorems are naturally forward-time statements. Applying them
      directly when `t < 0` creates endpoint-order and sign obligations that
      obscure the estimate. Rewriting absolute values alone does not turn a
      backward trajectory into the forward trajectory expected by the API.

THEN.text:
Split on the sign of `t`. For nonnegative time, apply the matching
      Grönwall theorem to `s ↦ phi s a - phi s b`, or directly to the pair of
      trajectories. For negative time define the reversed field
      `(s,y) ↦ -f (-s) y` and reversed trajectories `s ↦ phi (-s) a` and
      `s ↦ phi (-s) b`; prove the same Lipschitz and derivative hypotheses, and
      apply the forward theorem at `-t`. Normalize distance, norm and absolute
      value only after the analytic estimate is obtained.

BECAUSE.text:
Mathlib already contains both a trajectory-distance Grönwall theorem and
      a norm-of-function theorem. Choosing the interface closest to the local
      hypotheses removes most proof plumbing. Time reversal converts the other
      half-line into the same forward theorem instead of requiring a second
      inequality argument.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Choose the distance API or norm-difference API according to the goal's current representation.]
    next[Prove the forward estimate before normalizing norm, distance and absolute value.]
    next[Handle negative time with the reversed field and trajectories.]
    next[Simplify the zero-error Grönwall bound with gronwallBound_ε0.]

fields.title: Bridge Interval Integrals to Contour Integrals by a Pointwise logDeriv Identity
fields.keywords: circleIntegral, logDeriv, circleMap, intervalIntegral, winding, contour integral
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: To convert a contour integral ∮ in C(0, 1) of logDeriv into a real interval integral of a parametrized curve's derivative quotient, prove ONE pointwise identity along circleMap and then integrate it; do not search for a packaged conversion theorem that may not exist. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
The goal holds a normalized contour integral of logDeriv of an
    analytic function (e.g. a polynomial evaluation) and the other side is
    an interval integral ∫ t in 0..2π of fderiv γ t 1 / (γ t - z).

HOWEVER.text:
The library may have no compiled rule converting between the
    two representations for your particular γ; rewriting the contour
    integral via circleIntegral only yields deriv (circleMap) • logDeriv
    (circleMap), still in the wrong terms.

THEN.text:
Prove deriv (circleMap 0 1) t * logDeriv f (circleMap 0 1 t) =
    γ' t / (γ t - z) + c * I pointwise (the clearing factor contributes a
    constant c * I term), by matching HasDerivAt statements for the
    composite polynomial evaluation and the factored curve, then
    integral_congr + integral_add + integral_const to split off the
    constant. Finish the arithmetic with field_simp, push_cast and
    linear_combination on the assembled equation.
    + LEAN:
      api[circleIntegral] api[Polynomial.hasDerivAt] api[hasDerivAt_circleMap]
      api[intervalIntegral.integral_congr] tactic[field_simp → linear_combination]

BECAUSE.text:
Contour-versus-interval is exactly a parametrization
    statement: one pointwise identity carries the whole conversion, and
    the constant term from any monomial factor integrates to an explicit
    multiple of 2πI that cancels in the normalized winding integral.

fields.title: Bridge Darboux Sums to the Lebesgue Integral by Telescoping the Cells
fields.keywords: Darboux, Riemann, Lebesgue, partition, cells, telescoping, bridge, bounded-measurable
fields.why: math-formalization-CA/measure-integration-api
fields.how: own mechanism: The comparison between Darboux sums and the Lebesgue integral is not in the library as a single theorem: prove it cell by cell and telescope, keeping the lower and upper halves as separate statements. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A bounded measurable function on a closed interval where the target
    relates the classical Riemann–Darboux integral to the Lebesgue integral —
    typically that the lower Darboux integral is at most the Lebesgue integral,
    which is at most the upper one.

IF.text:
The comparison is made on a single partition cell, then it is elementary:
      on each cell the infimum bounds the function pointwise from below and the
      supremum from above, and the Lebesgue integral over that cell is between
      the two products with the cell's measure. Summing over the partition
      telescopes to the required inequality.

HOWEVER.text:
The two halves are not one argument. The lower bound and the upper bound
      have different witnesses on each cell, and attempting them together
      produces a proof in which the direction of each inequality has to be
      tracked through the sum — which is where the sign errors are. Keep them as
      two statements.

      The cells themselves need attention rather than assumption. Their measures
      must sum to the interval's measure, and shared endpoints must be shown to
      be almost-everywhere disjoint rather than genuinely disjoint — closed cells
      overlap at endpoints, and a proof that assumes strict disjointness is
      proving something about a partition it does not have.

      Do not expect a packaged bridge. This is the seam between two definitions
      of integral, and libraries generally develop each side thoroughly and leave
      the comparison to the user.

THEN.text:
State the lower and the upper comparison separately. Prove each on a single
      cell first, then sum, showing that the cell measures add up and that
      endpoint overlaps are null.

      Keep the bounded-measurable hypotheses explicit at the cell level, where
      they are used, rather than carrying them as ambient assumptions.

BECAUSE.text:
This comparison is a convention bridge rather than a theorem about
      functions — it reconciles two constructions of the same quantity — and
      bridges of that kind are exactly what a library omits, because neither side
      needs it internally. Recognizing it as a bridge sets the right expectation:
      no search will find it, the work is elementary, and the only difficulty is
      the bookkeeping that the classical statement suppresses.

    next[Show the cell measures sum to the interval's measure.]

fields.title: Evaluate a Series Through Ordered Partial Sums and a Boundary Limit
fields.keywords: series, tsum, conditional-convergence, partial-sums, Abel, index-shift, uniform-continuity, boundary-limit
fields.why: math-strategy/proof-architecture
fields.how: own mechanism: Evaluating a classical series formally means choosing the right notion of sum first — ordered partial sums for anything conditionally convergent — and then separating convergence, transport to the boundary, and evaluation into three independent obligations. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A named series to be evaluated in closed form — a zeta value, a
    Leibniz-type alternating sum, a boundary value of a power series — where the
    textbook derivation is a few lines of manipulation.

IF.text:
The series converges absolutely, then the library's unordered sum is the
      right object and the manipulations are direct: index shifts, term
      regrouping, and interchange all have API and none of them need an ordering
      argument.

HOWEVER.text:
Unordered summation is not what a conditionally convergent series has. A
      classical alternating series is *not* summable in the unordered sense, so
      stating it with `∑'` either fails to elaborate or, worse, states something
      other than what was meant. Conditionally convergent series must be
      expressed as a limit of ordered partial sums, and every later step has to
      respect that ordering.

      The three jobs in a boundary evaluation are genuinely independent and get
      conflated. Establishing that the series converges at the boundary does not
      require knowing its value; Abel's theorem moves the unknown sum to a radial
      limit; evaluating that radial limit is an interior computation with a
      closed form. Attempting them together produces an argument that is circular
      in exactly one place and hard to see.

      Small mechanical steps have their own API and are worth locating rather
      than reproving: an index shift for a two-index zeta rearrangement,
      `integral_comp_add_right` for translating an interval integral, a uniform
      continuity statement for a series of functions. Each is a one-line lookup
      and a half-page reconstruction.

THEN.text:
Decide the notion of sum before writing the statement, and use ordered
      partial sums whenever convergence is conditional.

      Split a boundary evaluation into three named lemmas — convergence at the
      boundary, Abel transport to a radial limit, evaluation of the interior
      closed form — and prove them separately.

      Look up the mechanical steps (index shift, integral translation, uniform
      series continuity) instead of rebuilding them, and reuse a template that
      already worked for a series of the same shape.

BECAUSE.text:
The gap between the classical and the formal treatment of series is almost
      entirely about which sum is meant. Classical notation leaves the ordering
      implicit and lets rearrangement pass unremarked, while the library's
      default is the unordered sum precisely because it is the one that is
      rearrangement-invariant. A conditionally convergent series formalized with
      the default is not a harder proof of the same theorem — it is a different
      statement, and the divergence is silent until something will not close.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Decide absolute vs conditional convergence before writing the statement.]
    next[Use ordered partial sums for conditional convergence and keep the ordering through every step.]
    next[Prove boundary convergence without reference to the value.]
    next[Move the unknown sum to a radial limit by Abel, as its own lemma.]
    next[Evaluate the interior closed form separately.]
    next[Look up index shifts, integral translations and uniform series continuity rather than reproving them.]

fields.title: Bound the Image Before Controlling the Quotient
fields.keywords: uniform-continuity, boundedness, image, quotient, denominator, api-chain
fields.why: math-informal-CA/estimate-by-bounding
fields.how: own mechanism: When an estimate involves a quotient of uniformly continuous functions, get the boundedness of the image first as its own lemma; the quotient control depends on it and cannot be obtained alongside it. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
An analysis obligation where a uniformly continuous function's
    values appear in a denominator or in a ratio, and the target estimate mixes
    the continuity modulus with the size of the values.

IF.text:
The domain is bounded — or totally bounded — then uniform continuity gives
      a bounded image through a short chain of library steps, and that bound is
      the constant every subsequent quotient estimate needs.

HOWEVER.text:
Attempting the quotient bound directly entangles two independent facts: how
      fast the function varies, and how large it gets. The modulus of continuity
      says nothing about the latter, so an argument that needs both and has
      proved neither separately will stall at a point where it is unclear which
      is missing. The order matters more than the difficulty: the boundedness
      step is short, and having it in hand makes the quotient step routine.

THEN.text:
State and prove the boundedness of the image as its own lemma, via the
      uniform-continuity-to-bounded-image chain.

      Only then estimate the quotient, using that bound for the denominator and
      the modulus for the variation, keeping the two roles visibly distinct.

BECAUSE.text:
Uniform continuity is a hypothesis about differences and boundedness is a
      conclusion about values, and the step between them is exactly where the
      domain's boundedness enters. Proving them in one motion hides that entry
      point, so a proof that fails gives no signal about whether the domain
      hypothesis was too weak or the estimate was arranged badly. Separated, the
      failure names itself.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Prove the image is bounded as a standalone lemma from uniform continuity.]
    next[Identify where the domain's boundedness enters and state it explicitly.]
    next[Estimate the quotient using the value bound for the denominator and the modulus for the variation.]

fields.title: Reduce a Lattice-Periodic Entire Function to Its Fundamental Domain
fields.keywords: Liouville, periodicity, lattice, fundamental-domain, compactness, entire, boundedness
fields.why: math-formalization-CV/entire-and-singularity-api

context.text:
An entire function invariant under a lattice of translations, where
    the classical conclusion — that it is constant — is immediate and the formal
    obligation is to produce the boundedness hypothesis Liouville wants.

IF.text:
The periods generate a lattice, then the function's whole range is already
      attained on one fundamental domain, and a fundamental domain can be taken
      compact. Continuity on a compact set gives a bound, periodicity transports
      that bound to the plane, and `Liouville` in its bounded-entire-implies-
      constant form closes the goal.

HOWEVER.text:
The reduction is the content, and it is easy to state as if it were free.
      Two obligations have to be discharged explicitly: that every point of the
      plane is a lattice translate of a point of the chosen domain, and that the
      chosen domain is compact. Neither follows from writing down a
      parallelogram; both are ordinary but real work, and the transport of the
      bound is a separate step from the bound itself.

THEN.text:
Choose the fundamental domain and prove it compact. Prove that every point
      is a lattice translate of one of its points. Bound the function on the
      domain by continuity, transport the bound by periodicity, then apply the
      bounded-entire-implies-constant API.

BECAUSE.text:
Liouville is stated as an implication whose hypothesis is global
      boundedness, and periodicity is a hypothesis about symmetry — the whole
      proof is the bridge between them. Writing that bridge as a compactness
      argument on a named domain turns "obviously bounded" into three checkable
      steps, which is exactly where a formal proof of this shape either closes or
      reveals that the domain was never shown to cover the plane.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Choose a fundamental domain and prove it compact.]
    next[Prove every point of the plane is a lattice translate of a point in it.]
    next[Bound the function on the domain by continuity on a compact set.]
    next[Transport the bound to the plane by periodicity, as its own step.]
    next[Apply the bounded-entire-implies-constant form of Liouville.]

  + HOWEVER:
      The reduction is the content, and it is easy to state as if it were free.
      Two obligations have to be discharged explicitly: that every point of the
      plane is a lattice translate of a point of the chosen domain, and that the
      chosen domain is compact. Neither follows from writing down a
      parallelogram; both are ordinary but real work, and the transport of the
      bound is a separate step from the bound itself.

  + THEN:
      Choose the fundamental domain and prove it compact. Prove that every point
      is a lattice translate of one of its points. Bound the function on the
      domain by continuity, transport the bound by periodicity, then apply the
      bounded-entire-implies-constant API.

  + BECAUSE:
      Liouville is stated as an implication whose hypothesis is global
      boundedness, and periodicity is a hypothesis about symmetry — the whole
      proof is the bridge between them. Writing that bridge as a compactness
      argument on a named domain turns "obviously bounded" into three checkable
      steps, which is exactly where a formal proof of this shape either closes or
      reveals that the domain was never shown to cover the plane.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Choose a fundamental domain and prove it compact.]
    next[Prove every point of the plane is a lattice translate of a point in it.]
    next[Bound the function on the domain by continuity on a compact set.]
    next[Transport the bound to the plane by periodicity, as its own step.]
    next[Apply the bounded-entire-implies-constant form of Liouville.]

fields.title: Bound the Derivative, Then Integrate Back to the Function
fields.keywords: derivative-bound, Schwarz, Cauchy-estimate, radial-integration, Lipschitz, domination, injectivity
fields.why: math-strategy/isolate-computational-kernel-before-transport

context.text:
A quantitative complex-analysis goal — a sharper Schwarz-type bound,
    a constancy result, an injectivity claim — where the direct estimate on the
    function does not follow from the hypotheses in hand.

IF.text:
The hypotheses vanish to higher order than the standard theorem assumes,
      then the standard theorem applies to the derivative. A holomorphic function
      whose value and first derivative both vanish at the origin gets its
      second-order bound by applying first-order Schwarz rigidity to the
      derivative and recovering the function bound by radial integration. The
      same move converts sublinear polynomial growth, where bounded Liouville is
      unavailable, into Cauchy's derivative estimate at an expanding radius.

HOWEVER.text:
The machinery is often unnecessary, and reaching for it first costs the most
      when it succeeds — because then nobody checks. For `az + h z` on a convex
      domain, injectivity follows from a Lipschitz constant for `h` strictly
      below `|a|`; testing that takes a line, while the argument principle or
      Rouché takes a page and yields the same conclusion under a stronger
      hypothesis than the problem needed.

      Integrating back is not free either. The radial integration that recovers
      the function bound from the derivative bound has to be set up over an
      explicit path with an explicit parameterization, and the sharpness of the
      final constant depends on that setup. A bound obtained by an unstated
      integration is a bound nobody can check for sharpness.

THEN.text:
Before invoking global machinery, test the elementary domination: is there
      a Lipschitz constant, a linear term that dominates, a direct comparison?
      Record the test even when it fails, so the machinery is justified rather
      than assumed.

      When the function-level bound is unavailable, state the derivative-level
      theorem you intend to apply, apply it, and write the integration back to
      the function as an explicit step with its path and parameterization.

      Match the estimate to the growth: bounded to Liouville, sublinear to
      Cauchy's derivative estimate at an expanding radius, higher-order vanishing
      to Schwarz on the derivative.

BECAUSE.text:
Derivative bounds are the currency of this subject because the library's
      rigidity theorems are stated at first order, while problems are routinely
      posed at second order or under growth conditions no first-order theorem
      accepts. Moving down to the derivative and integrating back is the standard
      adapter between the two, and it is cheap. What is expensive is skipping the
      elementary test on the way — the machinery will close the goal from a
      hypothesis stronger than the problem gave you, and the resulting proof is
      correct, opaque, and unnecessarily strong.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Test the elementary Lipschitz or domination bound first, and record the test.]
    next[If the function bound is unavailable, name the first-order theorem that applies to the derivative.]
    next[Write the radial integration back to the function as an explicit step with its parameterization.]
    next[Match the instrument to the growth: bounded, sublinear, or higher-order vanishing.]
    next[Check the resulting constant for sharpness against the integration you actually performed.]

fields.title: Prove an Entire Function Is Affine by Making a Divided Difference Constant
fields.keywords: Liouville, entire, affine, divided-difference, dslope, slope, cocompact, limit-at-infinity, one-point-compactification
fields.why: math-formalization-CV/entire-and-singularity-api

context.text:
A rigidity goal stating that an entire function is affine —
    typically reached after a singularity-at-infinity normal form `f(z) - a`
    behaves like the reciprocal of a polynomial in `1/z` of degree exactly one —
    where the classical proof passes through polynomial classification or
    Picard-class theorems the library may lack.

IF.text:
The behaviour at infinity can be stated as `Filter.Tendsto` along
      `cocompact ℂ` of the divided difference `dslope f 0` (Mathlib's
      `Complex.dslope`, i.e. `slope f 0` with the removable value at 0 filled),
      then the goal factors into two library-shaped obligations:
      differentiability of `dslope f 0` on all of ℂ via
      `Complex.differentiableOn_dslope`, and constancy via
      `Differentiable.apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact`, the Liouville form that
      only needs a finite limit at infinity — one point of the
      one-point compactification, not a global bound.

HOWEVER.text:
`apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact` is easy to miss because Liouville is
      usually reached through its bounded-entire form; search for
      `tendsto_cocompact` rather than `Liouville` to find it. The limit along
      `cocompact ℂ` must be transported from a punctured-germ eventual
      equality at 0: compose with `tendsto_inv₀_cobounded'` (inversion maps
      cocompact ℂ into the punctured germ at 0) and rewrite
      `Metric.cobounded_eq_cocompact` to change filter vocabulary. Recovering
      `f z = f 0 + a₁ * z` from a constant divided difference needs an
      explicit `z ≠ 0` case split and multiplication by `z`; `dslope_of_ne`
      unfolds the filled value away from 0.

THEN.text:
Establish the normal form at infinity (degree-one reciprocal pole of the
      inverted translate). Derive `Tendsto (dslope f 0) (cocompact ℂ) (𝓝 L)`
      from it by filter algebra: inverse along cocompact, continuity at the
      germ, `Tendsto.congr'` for the eventual-equality correction term
      `(a - f 0) * z⁻¹ → 0`. Prove `Differentiable ℂ (dslope f 0)` from
      entireness of `f`. Apply `apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact` pointwise to get
      `dslope f 0 = L` everywhere, split on `z = 0`, and multiply out.

BECAUSE.text:
The divided difference converts a two-coefficient existential into a
      constancy statement, which is the shape Liouville-type lemmas discharge;
      every other route (polynomial classification, Picard, coefficient
      killing by Cauchy estimates) needs growth hypotheses or missing
      theorems, while this route needs only a first-order normal form at
      infinity that the earlier singularity work already provides.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[State the goal as constancy of the divided difference, not as a coefficient existential.]
    next[Get differentiability of the filled divided difference from Complex.differentiableOn_dslope.]
    next[Transport the limit along cocompact ℂ from the punctured germ via tendsto_inv₀_cobounded'.]
    next[Apply Differentiable.apply_eq_of_tendsto_cocompact pointwise.]
    next[Split on z = 0 and multiply the constant slope equation by z to finish.]

fields.title: Manufacture the Entire Function Whose Decay Contradicts
fields.keywords: Liouville, entire, removable-singularity, puncture, reciprocal, Cauchy-estimate, growth, branch-locus, pole-classification
fields.why: math-informal/argue-by-contradiction

context.text:
A complex-analysis obligation about global behaviour — an entire
    function's rigidity, a singularity's removability, the non-existence of an
    entire extension — where the classical proof is a sentence and the formal
    proof is a construction.

IF.text:
The growth hypothesis can be turned into decay of some derived entire
      function, then the argument closes by Liouville. The derivations are few and
      reusable: invert an omitted-value translate and zero-fill the reciprocal;
      divide by the escaping coordinate when eventual agreement at infinity is
      the hypothesis; take a removable quotient to manufacture the entire function
      the estimate applies to.

HOWEVER.text:
Bounded Liouville is often the wrong instrument. For sublinear polynomial
      growth it does not apply at all, and the right tool is Cauchy's derivative
      estimate at an expanding radius — the derivative, not the function, is what
      the growth kills.

      Exceptional sets invite induction, and induction is the expensive route. A
      finite set of punctures is excluded all at once by taking the complement of
      `F.erase z` and intersecting with the punctured neighbourhood filter
      `𝓝[≠] z`; the induction that the classical proof implies is avoidable set
      algebra.

      Branch loci break uniform treatment. Descending an even analytic function
      through the squaring map is one proof away from the branch locus and a
      different proof on it: reindex the invariant Taylor germ where the
      derivative vanishes, and use the analytic inverse-function theorem
      everywhere else.

      Pole geometry decides which theorem applies. For a rational integral over
      the unit circle, classify each pole as interior or exterior *before* doing
      algebra — the split determines whether Cauchy's formula or Cauchy–Goursat
      supplies that term, and algebra performed first hides the classification.

THEN.text:
Say explicitly which entire function you are building and what its decay
      will be, then build it: zero-fill the reciprocal and remove the
      singularities, or divide by the escaping coordinate and take the induced
      decay, finishing by uniqueness of limits.

      Match the instrument to the growth: bounded → Liouville, sublinear →
      Cauchy's estimate at expanding radius, two-pole normalized ML bound →
      arrange a zero second pole so the bound reads `M/(R - ‖a‖)`.

      Exclude finite exceptional sets by filter algebra, split at branch loci, and
      classify poles before manipulating the integrand. Reuse a compiled
      partial-fraction / Cauchy-kernel contour skeleton rather than rebuilding it.

BECAUSE.text:
The classical statements in this area — "bounded entire functions are
      constant", "isolated singularities of bounded functions are removable" —
      are conclusions about functions that do not appear in the problem. The
      entire work of the formal proof is producing the function they apply to,
      and that production is where the choices live: which translate, which
      quotient, which coordinate to divide by. Writing the target function down
      first turns an appeal to a famous theorem into a construction with a
      checkable shape, and makes the growth bookkeeping — sublinear versus
      bounded, at which radius — an explicit decision rather than a hope.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Name the entire function you are constructing and the decay it must have.]
    next[Zero-fill a reciprocal or divide by the escaping coordinate to produce it.]
    next[Match the instrument to the growth: bounded Liouville vs Cauchy estimate at expanding radius.]
    next[Exclude finite punctures with F.erase and 𝓝[≠] z rather than by induction.]
    next[Split the proof at the branch locus when descending through a branched map.]
    next[Classify poles as interior or exterior before doing any algebra on the integrand.]

fields.title: Close a Frontier Bound From Arc Hypotheses by a Continuity Limit at the Missing Points
fields.keywords: frontier, sphere, arc, semicircle, boundary, continuity, dense, limit, le_of_tendsto, maximum modulus
fields.why: math-formalization-CV/holomorphic-disk-api

context.text:
Boundary estimates on the unit circle or the frontier of a ball,
    where hypotheses are stated per-arc rather than per-frontier, and the
    target theorem consumes the bound uniformly over the frontier.

IF.text:
The covered set is dense in the frontier minus finitely many points —
      e.g. upper and lower open semicircles leaving only the equator points
      where the sign condition degenerates — then case-split the frontier by
      trichotomy on the sign, dispose of the covered arcs directly, and for
      each leftover point z₀ build an explicit sequence uₙ on the circle with
      uₙ → z₀ and uₙ in the covered arc: `Complex.exp (θₙ * I)` with θₙ = 1/(n+1)
      for approach angles, its imaginary part handled by
      `Complex.exp_ofReal_mul_I_im` and `Real.sin_pos_of_pos_of_lt_pi`, its
      unit-norm membership by `Complex.norm_exp`. Compose the continuous-on
      hypothesis with `tendsto_nhdsWithin_iff` to keep the sequence in the
      closed ball, take norms, and conclude `‖g z₀‖ ≤ M` by `le_of_tendsto`.

HOWEVER.text:
Do not try to strengthen the hypothesis to the whole frontier or search
      for a theorem that accepts semicircle bounds — the continuity transfer
      is short, elementary, and exactly what the boundary regularity is for.
      The sequence must stay inside the covered arc for every n, not merely
      tend into it, or the per-point bound has nothing to attach to.

fields.title: Assemble Disk Theorems From the Library's Interfaces, Not From Their Names
fields.keywords: disk, holomorphic, Schwarz, Rouche, Hurwitz, circle-average, DiffContOnCl, divisor, branch-cut, radius
fields.why: math-informal/reduce-to-known-result

context.text:
Complex analysis on a disk or closed ball — Schwarz, Rouché,
    Hurwitz, the argument principle, zero counting, conformal images — being
    formalized against a library that packages this material by interface rather
    than by theorem name.
