      pieces is the whole job. Hurwitz zero persistence is a compact boundary
      margin plus quantitative open mapping, and searching for a monolithic
      Hurwitz wastes the search. A disk zero count is the existing meromorphic-
      divisor API. Local non-injectivity is `analyticOrderAt ≥ 2`. The equality
      case of Schwarz is affine `dslope` equality specialized at the center. Once
      the decomposition is named, each piece is ordinary work.

HOWEVER.text:
The hypotheses will not be in the shape the library wants. A closed-ball
      differentiability hypothesis has to be separated into its three interfaces
      — differentiability on the open ball, continuity on the closure, a
      sphere-local bound — before a `DiffContOnCl`-shaped theorem will accept it.
      When a construction is blocked on a deep invariance theorem, package every
      elementary hypothesis in that theorem's intended quantifier shape first, or
      the frontier stays entangled with routine boundary estimates and you cannot
      tell which part is actually missing.

      Radius and parameter are where the proof is bought. A weak disk-map bound
      becomes strict Rouché domination only after choosing `t < r < 1`; strict
      radial-contraction fixed points reach `t = 1` only through compact
      subsequences; a hypothesis local on disks globalizes only one smaller
      concentric disk at a time.

      Branch information does not survive being left implicit. A pointwise
      zero-product identity is not a globally coherent branch choice — use
      continuity of the nonzero factor to get an open zero set, then analytic
      connectedness to propagate it. Through a composition of elementary
      conformal maps, prove image control stage by stage and carry the branch cut
      as its own invariant. To exclude an interval from a principal-root image,
      push membership back through the exact power identity; real and imaginary
      projections expose the contradiction more cleanly than argument
      inequalities.

      on a convex domain, a Lipschitz constant for `h` strictly below `|a|`
      settles injectivity without the argument principle.

      for it by name, and state each interface as its own lemma with its own
      hypotheses.

      Adapt hypotheses explicitly — split a closed-ball assumption into open-ball
      differentiability, boundary continuity and a sphere bound; package
      homotopy slices in the intended quantifier shape.

      Route through the circle-average identity where one exists: rewrite by the
      identity and then apply the norm-of-integral bound, rather than proving the
      inequality directly. It often removes global geometric hypotheses outright.

      Choose the radius deliberately and say why, keep the branch cut as a named
      invariant through every stage, and test the elementary bound before
      reaching for Rouché.

Disk theory is old enough that its classical statements have been
      refactored several times on the way into a formal library, and the
      refactoring is by interface — divisors, orders, `dslope`, `DiffContOnCl`,
      open mapping — not by the names in a textbook chapter. Searching by name
      therefore under-reports what is present, and rebuilding by hand reproduces
      material that exists in a shape you did not recognize. The information the
      classical statement suppresses — which radius, which branch, which
      quantifier order — is exactly the information the formal proof needs, so
      the decomposition is not overhead: it is the content.

    next[Package elementary hypotheses in the deep theorem's quantifier shape before attacking the frontier.]
    next[Rewrite by the circle-average identity before proving a norm inequality directly.]
    next[Choose the radius explicitly and record why that choice makes the bound strict.]
    next[Carry the branch cut as a named invariant through every stage of a composition.]

fields.title: Get Uniform Boundedness First, Then Extend From a Dense Span
fields.keywords: inner-product, Banach-Steinhaus, uniform-boundedness, dense-span, weak-convergence, cobounded, projection
fields.why: math-informal/local-to-global

context.text:
A Hilbert-space obligation about a weakly convergent sequence —
    lower semicontinuity of the norm, convergence tested against every vector, a
    uniform constant claimed from pairwise estimates.

IF.text:
A uniform norm bound is available, then the argument decomposes cleanly:
      prove convergence on the generators, close under finite linear
      combinations, extend to the closed span using the uniform bound, and remove
      the orthogonal complement by projection. Each stage is small, and the
      uniform bound is what licenses the passage from the span to its closure.

HOWEVER.text:
The uniform bound is also what the `liminf` machinery quietly needs, and
      the two requirements are easily confused into a circle. `le_liminf_of_le`
      demands an `IsCoboundedUnder` premise; deriving that premise from the
      conclusion being proved is circular, and deriving it from Banach–Steinhaus
      is not. Prove actual uniform norm boundedness by uniform boundedness first,
      and the side condition follows without the circle.

      A real-valued sequence that may be unbounded above needs its own treatment:
      `c ≤ liminf u atTop` from an eventual lower bound is a different lemma from
      the bounded case, and picking the wrong one leaves a side condition that
      cannot be discharged.

      Uniform-constant claims derived from pairwise bounds deserve a refutation
      attempt before a proof attempt. Build a triangular family whose support
      grows with the index and compare the pairwise scale against the
      square-summed aggregate scale — pairwise smallness does not survive
      aggregation, and finding this out by attempting the proof is the expensive
      route.

THEN.text:
Establish the uniform norm bound by Banach–Steinhaus as the first step, and
      use it for both the extension and the `liminf` side conditions.

      Extend in the stated order: generators, finite linear combinations, closed
      span by the uniform bound, orthogonal complement by projection.

      Select the `liminf` variant that matches whether the real sequence may be
      unbounded above, and say which one you chose.

      Before proving a uniform constant from pairwise bounds, try to refute it
      with a growing-support triangular family.

BECAUSE.text:
Weak convergence is a statement about every test vector, and no argument
      can check every test vector — so every proof in this area is an extension
      argument from a small set, and every extension argument needs the uniform
      bound that makes the closure step legal. That the same bound discharges the
      filter-level side conditions is not a coincidence but the same fact used
      twice, and seeing it as one fact is what keeps the proof out of a circle.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Prove the uniform norm bound by Banach–Steinhaus before anything else.]
    next[Extend convergence: generators, finite combinations, closed span, orthogonal complement.]
    next[Discharge IsCoboundedUnder from the uniform bound, never from the conclusion.]
    next[Pick the liminf variant that matches unbounded-above versus bounded real sequences.]
    next[Try to refute a pairwise-derived uniform constant with a growing-support triangular family.]

fields.title: Prove LF Test-Function Operator Continuity Stage by Stage
fields.keywords: TestFunction, LF-topology, continuous-linear-map, compact-support, seminorm, limitCLM
fields.how: own mechanism: Replace a global LF-continuity obligation by compact-stage factorization, prove finite seminorm bounds on each Fréchet stage, and reassemble the global operator with the TestFunction final-topology API.

IF.text:
An algebraic linear operator on `TestFunction` is mathematically
      continuous, but no packaged global continuous linear operator exists and
      direct continuity on the LF topology is opaque.

HOWEVER.text:
The input support varies globally, while the available derivative and
      integral estimates have constants and output supports that depend on a
      fixed input compact. A single global norm estimate is therefore the wrong
      obligation.

THEN.text:
For each compact `K`, choose a compact `K'` containing the output support
      of every input supported in `K`. Define the induced linear map from
      `ContDiffMapSupportedIn ... K` to `ContDiffMapSupportedIn ... K'`. Prove
      its continuity with `WithSeminorms.continuous_of_isBounded`, supplying for
      each target seminorm a finite set of source seminorms and a nonnegative
      constant. Finally use `TestFunction.continuous_iff_continuous_comp` to
      reduce global continuity to these stage maps and compose each with
      `TestFunction.ofSupportedInCLM`.

BECAUSE.text:
The test-function topology is an inductive-limit topology. Its continuity
      API is designed to consume compatible continuous maps on fixed-support
      Fréchet stages, exactly where support-dependent seminorm estimates are
      meaningful.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Prove a uniform output-support bound for each fixed input compact.]
    next[Separate the order-zero seminorm estimate from successor derivative estimates.]
    next[Package each stage map continuously, then apply the TestFunction final-topology criterion.]

fields.title: Weak Plus Norm Convergence Is an API Chain With Side Conditions
fields.keywords: weak-convergence, Hilbert, Kadec-Klee, Radon-Riesz, liminf, cobounded, Fatou, side-condition
fields.why: math-informal/reduce-to-known-result

context.text:
A Hilbert- or `Lᵖ`-space obligation of Kadec–Klee / Radon–Riesz
    shape: weak convergence plus convergence of norms implies norm convergence,
    or a `liminf` inequality obtained from Fatou has to be turned into a limit.

IF.text:
The route is taken through the squared norm, then each step is already in
      the library and the proof is assembly: expand `‖xₙ - x‖²` into norms and
      inner products, pass the inner-product term to its weak limit, cancel
      against the norm hypothesis, and take the square root at the end. The
      analogous `Lᵖ` route runs through Fatou to an a.e. limit and then along the
      same chain.

HOWEVER.text:
The `liminf` steps carry hypotheses the classical argument never states. A
      `liminf` bound in Mathlib is conditional on the sequence being cobounded
      under the relevant filter — the theorem is false without it, because an
      unbounded-above gap makes `liminf` degenerate — and these side conditions
      surface only when the rewrite fails, at which point they look like a tooling
      obstruction rather than the mathematics they are.

      They also do not all discharge the same way. An eventual lower bound, a
      `liminf ≤` from a `≤ 0` bound, and a `le_liminf` under an unbounded-above
      gap each want a different witness, so a single "handle the side conditions"
      step is not a plan.

      The square root is not free either: the chain proves a statement about
      `‖xₙ - x‖²`, and the target is about `‖xₙ - x‖`. Keep the two apart and make
      the passage explicit rather than letting a norm power drift through the
      argument. Where norm powers were used only to establish scalar facts,
      return to the original functions before applying the final convergence
      theorem.

THEN.text:
Write the chain out as named steps before proving any of them —
      `norm_sub_sq` expansion, weak limit of the inner product, cancellation,
      square root — and treat each side condition as its own obligation with its
      own witness.

      Establish coboundedness where the `liminf` step needs it, and say which
      variant of the `liminf` API you are using and why that one.

      Use norm powers only for the scalar facts, and return to the original
      objects before the last step.

BECAUSE.text:
This is the standard case of a proof whose informal difficulty and formal
      difficulty sit in different places. Informally the content is the expansion
      of the squared norm; formally that step is a rewrite and the work is in the
      filter hypotheses that make the limit manipulations legal. An agent that
      plans from the informal proof will budget for the wrong half and read the
      side conditions as friction — so naming them in advance is what turns a
      stalled rewrite into a list of small, closable obligations.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Write the chain as named steps: expand, pass to the weak limit, cancel, take the root.]
    next[List each liminf/limsup step's side condition as its own obligation.]
    next[Establish coboundedness explicitly rather than treating its absence as a tooling problem.]
    next[Say which liminf API variant is being used and why that one fits the bound in hand.]
    next[Return from norm powers to the original objects before the final convergence step.]

fields.title: Connected Union via Common Point
fields.keywords: connected, union, common-point, separation, isPreconnected, sUnion

context.text:
You have a family of connected sets {C_α} and a common point
    x ∈ ∩ C_α, and you need to show ⋃ C_α is connected.

IF.text:
The goal involves IsConnected or IsPreconnected applied to a union,
      and the hypothesis provides a common point in all components.

HOWEVER.text:
"Union of connected sets is connected" is false in general — the
      common point hypothesis is essential. Without it, disjoint connected
      sets are a trivial counterexample.

THEN.text:
Use isPreconnected_sUnion from Mathlib. The key step: rewrite the
      indexed union as a set-indexed union via sUnion_range, then apply
      the combinator with the common point and individual connectedness.

    + LEAN:
      api[isPreconnected_sUnion]
      api[Set.range]
      api[Set.not_nonempty_iff]
      tactic[classical → by_cases → simpa [sUnion_range]]

BECAUSE.text:
Mathlib's isPreconnected_sUnion handles the separation argument
      internally — you supply the common point and the per-component
      connectedness, and it composes the contradiction.

fields.title: Expose Component Openness Before Reasoning About Frontiers
fields.keywords: connected-component, locally-connected, openness, interior, frontier, counting, unbounded-exterior
fields.why: math-informal/local-to-global

context.text:
A topological obligation about `connectedComponentIn U x` for an
    open `U` in a locally connected space — counting components, locating their
    frontiers, or separating bounded from unbounded ones.

IF.text:
The space is locally connected and `U` is open, then components of `U` are
      themselves open, and that single fact is what makes the rest mechanical:
      `interior_eq` converts component membership into exactly the form frontier
      reasoning consumes, and the frontier of a component can then be placed
      inside the ambient frontier of `U`.

HOWEVER.text:
The openness step is the one the classical argument omits, because
      classically it is obvious. Skipped, every subsequent frontier manipulation
      is off by the difference between a set and its interior, and the failure
      surfaces several lemmas later as an unprovable membership rather than as a
      missing hypothesis.

      Counting components needs a separation the topology does not supply on its
      own. The complement of a compact set has one unbounded component and
      finitely many bounded ones, and these are counted by different means:
      inject the bounded interior components into algebraic witnesses — roots, in
      the lemniscate case — and reserve a single marker for the common unbounded
      exterior. Counting them uniformly produces an off-by-one that is easy to
      misattribute to the injection.

      Do not expect the general statement to be present under the name you would
      give it. This corner of the library is thin enough that an anchor from a
      community discussion may be the best available evidence about what exists,

context.text:
The unit sphere is the boundary of a finite polytope, but standard
    stereographic APIs require an InnerProductSpace instance the norm lacks.

fields.how: own mechanism: When you must subtract finitely many simple principal parts from a meromorphic function and Mathlib's divisor machinery only factorizes, build each principal part locally from the order germ and prove the remainder has nonnegative order; no global additive decomposition theorem is needed. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
Every boundary pole has order exactly `-1`, the pole set is
    finite, and the goal is `f = g + ∑ ζ ∈ P, c ζ / (z - ζ)` with `g`
    holomorphic on a larger disk (e.g. to bound Taylor coefficients).

HOWEVER.text:
Searches of `CanonicalDecomposition`, `FactorizedRational`,
    and `MeromorphicOn.extract_zeros_poles` find only multiplicative
    factorizations; the additive form is absent from the library.

THEN.text:
(1) At a pole, `(meromorphicOrderAt_eq_int_iff hF).1 horder`
    gives `q` analytic with `q ζ ≠ 0` and `F =ᶠ (z - ζ)^(-1) • q`; shift
    with `comp_sub` and apply `AnalyticAt.exists_eq_sum_add_pow_mul 1` to
    write `q z = q ζ + (z - ζ) * H z`, so `F =ᶠ[𝓝[≠] ζ] H + q ζ / (z - ζ)`.
    (2) `choose c hc` over all poles. (3) The finite sum `S` of principal
    parts is `AnalyticAt` off `P` (`Finset.analyticAt_fun_sum`,
    `AnalyticAt.div`), so at `z ∉ P` use `meromorphicOrderAt_add` and at
    `z ∈ P` use `meromorphicOrderAt_congr` with `Finset.sum_erase_add`
    to see `F - S` has nonnegative order. (4) Normalize and thicken the
    remainder. (5) Coefficients of `c / (z - ζ)` for `‖ζ‖ = 1` come from
    `Complex.one_div_sub_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero` and all have norm `‖c‖`.
    + LEAN:
      api[meromorphicOrderAt_eq_int_iff] api[AnalyticAt.exists_eq_sum_add_pow_mul]
      api[meromorphicOrderAt_add] api[meromorphicOrderAt_congr]
      api[Finset.analyticAt_fun_sum] api[Finset.sum_erase_add]
      api[Complex.one_div_sub_hasFPowerSeriesOnBall_zero]

BECAUSE.text:
A local germ of order `-1` carries exactly the data of its
    Laurent tail, so the classical partial-fractions construction is a
    one-line consequence of the order characterization plus a truncated
    germ Taylor expansion, and order additivity does the bookkeeping.

fields.how: own mechanism: In a time-boxed cold-start session on a file with several `sorry`s, close and commit every obligation that does not depend on the hard bridge FIRST — typically the counting/arithmetic leaves and the final assembly from the bridge statements — and only then open the hard bridge. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
The file has k > 1 sorries and at least one of them (a degree
    bound, an omega arithmetic step, the final theorem assembled from the
    bridge lemmas' statements) is closeable in a handful of lines from
    what is already compiled.

HOWEVER.text:
The hard bridge is where the mathematics is, so it attracts
    the whole budget; an attempt that spends its time verifying API
    spellings for the bridge and ends with zero lines compiled has
    produced no measurable progress, even though the cheap leaves were
    available the whole time.

THEN.text:
(1) List the sorries with their dependencies. (2) Close the
    ones that need only compiled lemmas plus `omega` / `push_cast` /
    `ring` / a two-lemma `trans` chain; the final theorem can be assembled
    from the bridge lemmas AS STATEMENTS, before the bridges are proved.
    (3) Compile and commit. (4) Only now write the statement ladder for
    the hard bridge and start filling it.

      tactic[push_cast → omega] api[Multiset.card_le_card]
      api[Multiset.filter_le] api[Polynomial.card_roots']

BECAUSE.text:
A committed partial artifact is the unit of measurable
    progress; assembling the top-level theorem from the bridge statements
    costs nothing later and proves the decomposition is sound now, and a
    cold-start successor inherits compiled lines, not a plan.

fields.title: Let the Elaborator Identify Binders Instead of Rewriting Them
fields.keywords: binder, integral, congruence, motive, elaboration, rewrite, definitional-equality
fields.why: math-formalization/tactic-algebra-interference
fields.how: own mechanism: When two expressions differ only in how a bound variable is written, let the elaborator identify them rather than rewriting under the binder by hand. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A goal and a library lemma that state the same integral — or the
    same sum, or the same `∀` — but whose bodies are written with differently
    shaped binders, so the rewrite does not fire.

IF.text:
The two forms are definitionally equal up to the binder's presentation,
      then the elaborator will accept one where the other is expected, and the
      apparent mismatch costs nothing. Applying the lemma directly, or stating
      the intermediate equality and letting unification close it, is the whole
      repair.

HOWEVER.text:
The instinct is to rewrite under the binder to force the shapes to match,
      and that is where the cost appears. Rewriting under a binder needs a
      motive, and the motive that a tactic infers is frequently not the one that
      typechecks — the resulting motive error is opaque and describes the
      elaborator's difficulty rather than the mathematical mismatch. The
      hand-written congruence lemma that follows is real work in service of a
      difference that was never mathematical.

THEN.text:
Try applying the lemma to the goal as it stands before adjusting either
      side. If an intermediate step is needed, state the equality of the two
      whole expressions and let elaboration discharge the binder difference,
      rather than rewriting inside the body.

      Reserve explicit congruence for cases where the bodies genuinely differ,
      not where their binders are merely written differently.

BECAUSE.text:
Binder presentation is syntax, and syntax differences are what the
      elaborator exists to absorb. Treating them as mathematical differences
      converts a no-op into a motive problem — and the motive problem's error
      message points at the tactic, not at the syntax, so the time is spent in
      the wrong place entirely.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Apply the lemma to the goal unchanged before adjusting either side.]
    next[State the equality of whole expressions rather than rewriting inside a binder.]
    next[Read a motive error as a signal that the rewrite was under a binder, not as a mathematical obstruction.]
    next[Reserve explicit congruence for genuinely different bodies.]

fields.title: Bound a Sylow Subgroup by Embedding a Prime-Degree Action into a Symmetric Group
fields.keywords: Sylow, faithful action, permutation representation, factorial, factorization, p-adic multiplicity, card_perm

fields.how: own mechanism: For a faithful action of a finite group on exactly `p` points, where `p` is prime and divides the group order, prove every Sylow `p`-subgroup has cardinality `p` by bounding the group order through the permutation representation and comparing prime factorizations. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
`MulAction.toPermHom G X` is injective, `Nat.card X = p`, and a
    transitive action or another argument supplies `p ∣ Nat.card G`.

HOWEVER.text:
A direct orbit analysis of the Sylow subgroup may require
    fixed-point congruences and nontriviality arguments that are not
    already packaged in the needed cardinality form.

THEN.text:
Use `Subgroup.card_dvd_of_injective` on
    `MulAction.toPermHom G X` to obtain `Nat.card G ∣ p.factorial` after
    rewriting with `Nat.card_perm`. Convert divisibility to an inequality
    of `Nat.factorization` values. The prime's multiplicity in `p!` is one,
    via `Nat.factorization_factorial`; divisibility of `Nat.card G` by `p`
    gives the reverse lower bound. Rewrite a Sylow subgroup's cardinality
    with `Sylow.card_eq_multiplicity` and simplify the resulting
    factorization value.
    + LEAN:
      api[Subgroup.card_dvd_of_injective] api[Nat.card_perm]
      api[Nat.factorization_le_factorization_of_dvd_right]
      api[Nat.factorization_factorial] api[Prime.dvd_iff_one_le_factorization]
      api[Sylow.card_eq_multiplicity]

BECAUSE.text:
Faithfulness embeds the group into the symmetric group, and
    the prime `p` occurs exactly once in `p!`; once existence supplies one
    factor of `p`, the Sylow multiplicity is forced to be exactly one.

fields.title: Normalize Casts Before Taking Projections
fields.keywords: cast, coercion, push_cast, norm_cast, projection, real-part, integer, complex
fields.why: math-formalization/coercion-bridge
fields.how: own mechanism: Push casts to the leaves before applying a projection: a real or imaginary part taken through an un-normalized coercion tower will not simplify. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
An expression mixing integer or natural literals with complex
    values, where the goal is about the real or imaginary part of the result.

IF.text:
The casts are normalized first — pushed inward to the leaves so that each
      coercion sits on an atom — then the projection lemmas apply directly: the
      real part of a cast integer is the cast integer, its imaginary part is
      zero, and the arithmetic simplifies without further help.

HOWEVER.text:
Applied to a term whose coercions still sit around compound
      subexpressions, the projection lemmas do not fire, because the shape they
      match is a cast of an atom and what is present is a cast of a sum or a
      product. The goal then looks like a mathematical obstruction — the
      projection "does not simplify" — when it is a normalization that has not
      been run.

      The order is not symmetric. Normalizing after projecting leaves the
      projection stuck around a compound cast, and the usual recovery is to undo
      the projection step.

THEN.text:
Normalize the casts first, pushing them to the leaves, and only then take
      real or imaginary parts and finish the arithmetic.

BECAUSE.text:
Cast normalization is a syntactic prerequisite of the projection lemmas
      rather than a cleanup step, so doing it late means doing it twice. The
      failure it causes is also mislabelled — nothing reports "the cast is in the
      wrong place", only that a simp set made no progress — which is why the
      ordering is worth stating rather than rediscovering.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Push casts to the leaves before applying any projection.]
    next[Check that each coercion sits on an atom, not on a sum or product.]
    next[Then take real/imaginary parts and finish the arithmetic.]

IF.text: A finite-dimensional module is controlled by an endomorphism T with T.comp T = 0, and the library does not expose a directly usable square-zero Jordan decomposition.

THEN.text: Obtain range T ≤ ker T from LinearMap.range_le_ker_iff; choose one complement of range T inside ker T and another complement of ker T inside the whole space with Submodule.exists_isCompl. fields.keywords: bijective, injective, surjective, cardinality, card, finite, Fintype, count, equiv

fields.how: own mechanism: In a finite setting, never construct a surjection or inverse by hand: prove injectivity (usually from a kernel computation) and equality of cardinalities (usually from independent counting), and let Nat.bijective_iff_injective_and_card conclude bijectivity. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.provenance: case-1 compression pilot (2026-08-12): 4 marks (synthesis cluster 3, "finite cardinality shortcuts"); transcript count not recorded at authoring time and not recoverable by keyword (the b01A04 corpus is Galois theory, so card/Fintype/injectiv matches 7 of 9 transcripts). context.text:
You need an equivalence between finite structures (e.g.
    MulEquiv.ofBijective) and the surjectivity direction looks like it
    demands explicit preimages.

IF.text:
Both sides are Fintype and you can compute or transport both
    cardinalities — often by two INDEPENDENT identities (one for the
    kernel/injectivity, one for the count), which decomposes the claim
    into separately-provable halves.

HOWEVER.text:
The cardinality equality must come from somewhere honest —
    if the only route to the count is via the bijection you are
    constructing, the argument is circular. And in infinite settings the
    move is simply false; check finiteness is real, not assumed.

THEN.text:
Split: (1) injective_iff_map_eq_one or a kernel argument;
    (2) card equality by counting both sides through known formulas
    (totients, index formulas, orbit counts); (3) apply the
    bijective_iff lemma; (4) bundle with ofBijective.

BECAUSE.text:
Explicit inverse construction in dependent-type settings
    costs elaboration friction quadratic in structure depth; counting
    is linear and reuses arithmetic already in the development.

fields.how: own mechanism: When the mathematical proof lives in one type (ℝ) but the Mathlib API operates in another (ℝ≥0∞), wire through the directed coercion chain rather than trying to isomorphism-transport. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You have proved a key lemma in ℝ (e.g., a limit, an inequality).
    The theorem you need to close operates on eLpNorm, which lives in ℝ≥0∞.
    There is a canonical coercion chain ℝ → ℝ≥0 → ℝ≥0∞ but it is NOT an
    isomorphism — it loses information at each step (negativity at ℝ→ℝ≥0,
    finiteness at ℝ≥0→ℝ≥0∞).

IF.text:
Your real-valued result needs to be used in an ENNReal/NNReal context,
      and the coercion chain applies (the quantities are nonneg and finite).

HOWEVER.text:
Unlike transport-across-isomorphism, you cannot freely move results
      back and forth. The coercion is directed. ENNReal.toReal loses ⊤ → 0.
      NNReal.coe is injective but NNReal.mk requires a proof of nonnegativity.
      Each step requires an explicit compatibility hypothesis.

THEN.text:
(a) Prove the core mathematical content in ℝ where the API is richest.
      (b) Identify the coercion path: which coe/toReal/ofReal lemmas connect
          your ℝ result to the ℝ≥0∞ goal?
      (c) For each coercion step, discharge the compatibility side-condition
          (nonnegativity, finiteness, ne_top).
      (d) If the bridge is >5 steps, consider whether the lemma can be proved
          directly in ℝ≥0∞ instead. Sometimes the Mathlib API has a parallel
          version (e.g., ENNReal.rpow vs Real.rpow) that avoids the bridge.

    + LEAN:
      api[ENNReal.ofReal] api[ENNReal.toReal] api[NNReal.coe_le_coe]
      api[ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal] api[ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal]
      tactic[rw [ENNReal.ofReal...] → exact ... → simp [ne_top_of_lt]]

BECAUSE.text:
Lean's type system enforces the distinction between ℝ, ℝ≥0, and ℝ≥0∞
      that informal mathematics elides. The coercion bridge is the price of
      rigour. But the bridge is mechanical — once you know the path, each
      step is a named lemma (ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal, NNReal.coe_le_coe,
      ENNReal.toReal_le_toReal). The mathematical insight is in ℝ; the
      engineering is in the bridge.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify which type the mathematical proof lives in.]
    next[Map the coercion path to the goal's type.]
    next[Discharge compatibility side-conditions at each step.]
    next[If bridge is long, check for a parallel API in the target type.]

fields.title: Collapse a Self-Normalizing Sylow Subgroup Through a Faithful Prime-Degree Action
fields.keywords: Sylow, normalizer, Burnside transfer, primitive action, faithful action, prime degree, MulAction.IsPreprimitive, transferSylow
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). fields.how: own mechanism: When a finite group acts faithfully and transitively on a prime number of points and a Sylow subgroup of that prime order is self-normalizing, use Burnside transfer and primitivity to show the Sylow subgroup is the whole group; do not count order-prime elements across all Sylow subgroups. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
`G` acts faithfully and pretransitively on finite `X`,
    `Nat.card X = p` for prime `p`, a Sylow `p`-subgroup `P` has
    `Nat.card P = p`, and `normalizer (P : Subgroup G) = P`.

HOWEVER.text:
Partitioning elements of order `p` among Sylow subgroups
    requires an explicit uniqueness and disjoint-union argument that is
    not packaged by the local Sylow API and does not directly exploit the
    prime-degree action.

THEN.text:
Give `P` its cyclic structure from its prime cardinality. The
    self-normalizer equality makes `normalizer P ≤ centralizer P`; apply
    `MonoidHom.transferSylow` and let `N` be its kernel. The transfer
    theorem gives `N.IsComplement' P` and normality of `N`. Prime
    cardinality upgrades the ambient transitive action to primitive. If
    `N ≠ ⊥`, faithfulness rules out all points being fixed by `N`, while
    quasi-primitivity makes the normal subgroup action transitive. The
    stabilizer-index formula then forces `p ∣ Nat.card N`, contradicting
    `MonoidHom.not_dvd_card_ker_transferSylow`. Hence `N = ⊥`, and the
    complement's `sup_eq_top` reduces to `P = ⊤`.
    + LEAN:
      api[MonoidHom.transferSylow] api[MonoidHom.ker_transferSylow_isComplement']
      api[MulAction.IsPreprimitive.of_prime_card]
      api[MulAction.IsQuasiPreprimitive.isPretransitive_of_normal]
      api[MulAction.index_stabilizer_of_transitive]
      api[MonoidHom.not_dvd_card_ker_transferSylow]

BECAUSE.text:
Transfer converts the self-normalizer hypothesis into a
    normal complement, and a faithful primitive action of prime degree
    leaves no room for a nontrivial normal complement whose cardinality is
    prime to `p`.

context.text:
The proof requires constructing an explicit mathematical
    object (a family of functions, a counterexample, a partition of
    unity). On paper, the construction is "obvious" — tent functions on
    disjoint intervals, bump functions with prescribed support, etc.
    In Lean, the construction requires defining the object, proving
    continuity, verifying bounds, checking support properties, etc.

IF.text:
The goal is existential (∃ f, P f) or requires producing an

IF.text:
You have proved that every automorphism in an explicit finite family
    fixes an intermediate field K pointwise, and need to show that every
    element fixed by the family lies in K.

HOWEVER.text:
The easy inclusion from K into the fixed elements does not
    supply the reverse inclusion, and a direct normal-form proof for fixed
    elements may be unavailable.

THEN.text:
Repackage the family as K-algebra automorphisms, prove that its
    parameterization is bijective onto the full automorphism type, and compute
    Module.finrank K L.  If Nat.card (L ≃ₐ[K] L) equals that finrank, use
    IsGalois.of_card_aut_eq_finrank, put a fixed element in the fixed field of
    the top automorphism subgroup via IntermediateField.mem_fixedField_iff,
    and rewrite that field with IsGalois.fixedField_top.
    + LEAN:
      api[IsGalois.of_card_aut_eq_finrank]
      api[IntermediateField.mem_fixedField_iff]
      api[IsGalois.fixedField_top]
      api[AlgEquiv.card_le]

BECAUSE.text:
Equality in the degree-versus-automorphism bound certifies that
    the extension is Galois; the general Galois fixed-field theorem then
    supplies the hard reverse inclusion without classifying arbitrary fixed
    rational expressions.

fields.how: own mechanism: To prove an identity between subobjects-of-a-subobject, lift both sides into the ambient object with the library's lift/restrict API, prove the identity there where the full lattice API applies, and reflect the result back through injectivity of the lift. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.provenance: case-1 compression pilot (2026-08-12): 5 marks across 3 independent zai-1 transcripts (3813, 3815, 3816 — mechanically verified); runner-graded "what would actually have helped at the stuck moment". Clears the >=3-transcript bar independently of the debrief.

context.text:
You must show K ⊓ L = X or K ⊔ L = Y where K, L are
    subobjects reinterpreted inside another subobject (intermediate
    fields inside a fixed field, subgroups inside a subgroup). The
    sublattice's own API is thin; direct reasoning stalls on coercions.

IF.text:
The library provides a lift/restrict pair with per-operation
    lemmas (lift_inf, lift_sup, lift_restrict) and an injectivity lemma
    (lift_injective) — in Mathlib for IntermediateField, at
    FieldTheory/Basic (restrict at :885, lift at :652 as of 2026-08).

HOWEVER.text:
The technique needs ALL the per-operation lift lemmas to
    exist for the operations in your identity — a missing lift_sup means
    proving it yourself first. And when a DIRECT lemma for your identity
    exists (e.g. the meet/join idiom in FieldTheory/LinearDisjoint), the
    lift-reflect detour is unnecessary lattice-homomorphism work — search
    for the direct route before committing to the detour.

THEN.text:
Apply lift to both sides; rewrite with the per-operation lift
    lemmas until the identity is between ambient objects; close with the
    ambient API; finish by lift_injective. Write it as an explicit calc
    chain — each step names one lift lemma.

BECAUSE.text:
Injectivity reflection converts a thin-API setting into a
    rich-API setting at the cost of one lemma per operation — the
    cheapest general exit from subobject-of-subobject reasoning.

fields.title: Reduce Concrete MemLp Goals to Scalar Power-Law Summability
fields.keywords: MemLp, Lp, integrable_norm_rpow_iff, summable_nat_rpow, integrableOn_Ioi_rpow_iff, counting measure, power law, counterexample, exponent threshold
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: To prove or refute `MemLp f p μ` for a concrete power-law f (on ℕ with counting measure, or on ℝ with volume), do not reason about `eLpNorm` directly: rewrite with `integrable_norm_rpow_iff`, normalize the exponent with `(by fun_prop)` measurability and `ofReal`-positivity side goals, push the goal to the scalar library (`Real.summable_nat_rpow` on ℕ, `integrableOn_Ioi_rpow_iff` on ℝ), and settle the pure-real inequality on the exponent. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
f is an explicit sequence like (n+1)^(-s) or an indicator-supported
      tail |x|^(a · χ_{|x|≥1}); the goal says ‖f‖_p < ∞ but ‖f‖_q = ∞ (or
      vice versa) for two exponents on either side of the critical threshold.

IF.text:
The function is nonnegative and explicitly given, so measurability is
      `fun_prop` / `Measurable.ite` from continuity away from one point, and
      the norm power collapses to the same power law with exponent scaled by
      p or q.

THEN.text:
(a) `rw [← integrable_norm_rpow_iff hmeas (by ... ofReal ≠ 0) (by simp)]`.
      (b) Discharge `(ENNReal.ofReal p).toReal = p` via `simp [hp.le]` with
          `hp : 0 < p` extracted first (`linarith`).
      (c) Restate the integrand by `funext` + `Real.rpow_mul` so the goal is
          exactly the library's n ↦ n^(-s) (or x ↦ x^a on Ioi 1) shape.
      (d) On ℕ, shift the successor index with `summable_nat_add_iff` and a
          `simpa only [Nat.cast_add, Nat.cast_one]` iff-transfer before
          `Real.summable_nat_rpow`; on ℝ, restrict to `Ioi 1` and use
          `integrableOn_Ioi_rpow_iff` (or `..._of_lt` for the positive half),
          composing with `.comp_neg` for the negative half.
      (e) The final goal is `s < -1 ↔ ¬(-1 ≤ s)` — pure algebra, proved once
          and reused for both exponents and both conjuncts.

BECAUSE.text:
The mathematical content is entirely in the scalar threshold; everything
      between the `MemLp` goal and the scalar library is coercion
      (`ofReal`/`toReal`), index shift, and indicator bookkeeping. Naming the
      reduction keeps each counterexample's proof to a discharge of steps
      (a)-(e), and the same exponent lemma closes both the sequence and the
      real-line case.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Extract 0 < p, 0 < q by linarith before touching ENNReal.]
    next[Rewrite MemLp with integrable_norm_rpow_iff; prove measurability separately if f is defined by cases.]
    next[Shift/split the domain to hit the library statement exactly.]
    next[Prove the exponent inequality once and reuse for both conjuncts.]

fields.title: Remove min and max Before Calling Linear Arithmetic
fields.keywords: min, max, linarith, case-split, normalization, linear-arithmetic, tactic
fields.why: math-formalization/tactic-algebra-interference
fields.how: own mechanism: Linear arithmetic cannot see inside `min` and `max`: split the cases or rewrite them away first, and only then call the tactic. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
An inequality goal in which a threshold, a truncation, or a
    `δ = min ε b / 2` choice has introduced `min` or `max`, and linear arithmetic
    is the intended finisher.

IF.text:
The `min`/`max` are eliminated first — by case split on which branch is
      active, or by rewriting to the branch the hypotheses already determine —
      then what remains is a linear problem and the tactic closes it immediately.

HOWEVER.text:
Called on the goal as it stands, the tactic treats `min a b` as an opaque
      atom about which it knows nothing, so a goal that is arithmetically
      trivial in each branch is unprovable as stated. The failure carries no
      indication that the obstacle is the `min`, which invites strengthening the
      hypotheses or hunting for a missing lemma.

      Splitting is cheap and the branches are usually near-identical, so the
      instinct to avoid a case split here is a false economy.

THEN.text:
Case-split on the `min`/`max`, or rewrite it to the branch the hypotheses
      already force, before invoking linear arithmetic. Where the same threshold
      appears repeatedly, do the normalization once as a named step rather than
      inside each goal.

BECAUSE.text:
Linear arithmetic is complete for linear real arithmetic and blind to
      everything else, so anything that is not a linear atom is an opaque
      constant to it. `min` and `max` are the most common such term in analysis
      goals precisely because threshold choices produce them — which makes this
      the failure most likely to be misread as a mathematical gap rather than a
      normalization that was skipped.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify every min/max in the goal before calling linear arithmetic.]
    next[Case-split, or rewrite to the branch the hypotheses already determine.]
    next[Normalize a repeated threshold once as a named step rather than per goal.]

fields.title: Notation-Semantics Traps
fields.keywords: notation, semantics, elaboration, typeclass, binder, ContDiff, coercion, preflight, informal-reading, statement-fidelity
fields.why: math-informal/unfold-the-definition
fields.how: own mechanism: A formal statement's notation can mean something other than its informal reading, and nothing tells you until the elaborator does — so audit what the symbols actually denote before proving anything about them. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You are formalizing from prose, or reading a statement someone else
    formalized, and the symbols look like the mathematics you intend. The gap
    between the intended theorem and the written one is invisible at the level
    of reading.

IF.text:
A statement's surface notation admits a reading you did not intend — a
      smoothness index, a binder's inferred type, an unstated typeclass
      precondition, a domain guard the prose assumes but the hypotheses do not
      impose — then the theorem you prove is not the theorem you meant, and it
      will still compile, still be axiom-clean, and still be wrong.

HOWEVER.text:
The trap is not carelessness and cannot be avoided by care alone. It is
      structural: the informal reading and the elaborated meaning are two
      different functions of the same characters, and only one of them is
      mechanically checkable. `ContDiff ℝ ⊤ f` reads as "all derivatives exist"
      and means *analytic*; `∞` is what smooth requires. A theorem's prose can
      state a finite or regular regime while its formal hypotheses still admit a
      zero or a top witness. Type compatibility between two components is not a
      claim that they are about the same thing — enumerated data and a derived
      count can typecheck against each other with no invariant linking them.
      Nor does a clean axiom audit help: it certifies the proof, not the
      statement.

THEN.text:
Elaborate the exact target under its real build BEFORE measuring holes or
      dispatching work — a dependency failure and a statement failure are
      different findings and must not be read as one. Inspect the index or
      binder rather than its informal gloss. Audit the typeclass preconditions
      the engine inferred rather than the ones you assume. Require an explicit
      invariant wherever the informal argument makes a semantic transition. And
      when the statement turns out to be false, the cheapest reviewable artifact
      is a machine-checked counterexample paired with a machine-checked repaired
      sibling, with the original preserved as an explicit unresolved defect
      rather than quietly amended.

BECAUSE.text:
Every gate downstream — the build, the sorry count, the axiom audit —
      measures the statement as written. None of them can see the statement you
      meant. The fidelity of formal to informal is the one link in the chain
      that no machine checks, so it has to be checked deliberately or not at all.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Elaborate the target under its real project build before any measurement.]
    next[Read every index, binder and coercion for its elaborated meaning, not its gloss.]
    next[Name the typeclass preconditions the engine inferred but the prose never stated.]
    next[Require an invariant for each semantic transition the informal argument makes.]
    next[On a false statement: checked counterexample + checked repair, original preserved as a defect.]

fields.title: Identify Pointwise HasSum Coefficients With Taylor Coefficients by Power-Series Uniqueness
fields.keywords: HasSum, FormalMultilinearSeries.ofScalars, hasFPowerSeriesAt_iff, HasFPowerSeriesAt.eq_formalMultilinearSeries, iteratedDeriv, Taylor coefficients, coefficient uniqueness, power series
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When a coefficient sequence is pinned to a function only by a pointwise family `∀ z ∈ ball 0 r, HasSum (fun n ↦ a n * z ^ n) (f z)` and you need `a n = (n.factorial)⁻¹ * iteratedDeriv n f 0`, package `a` as a formal multilinear series and use uniqueness of power-series expansions at the centre; do not build an elementary coefficient-extraction argument. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
The hypothesis is a pointwise `HasSum` on an open disk about 0,
    `f` is `DifferentiableOn` (hence `AnalyticAt`) there, and the goal
    names the canonical Taylor coefficients `iteratedDeriv n f 0 / n!`.

HOWEVER.text:
The tempting route — subtract `Complex.hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball`,
    bound coefficients exponentially, isolate the k-th coefficient by a
    small-radius estimate and induct — is sound but drowns in `HasSum` /
    `Tendsto` / `Summable.congr` orientation traps and does not finish in
    a time-boxed session.

THEN.text:
`let p := FormalMultilinearSeries.ofScalars ℂ a`; prove
    `HasFPowerSeriesAt f p 0` by `rw [hasFPowerSeriesAt_iff]`,
    `filter_upwards [ball_mem_nhds 0 zero_lt_one]`, and
    `simpa [FormalMultilinearSeries.coeff_ofScalars, mul_comm] using hseries z hz`;
    take `ht := (hf.analyticAt _).hasFPowerSeriesAt`; then
    `hp.eq_formalMultilinearSeries ht` gives series equality, and
    `congrArg (fun q ↦ q.coeff n)` plus `simpa [coeff_ofScalars, div_eq_inv_mul]`
    reads off each coefficient. The same packaging, with `exchange_radius`
    and `summable_norm_apply`, gives absolute convergence at every radius
    below a larger holomorphic disk.
    + LEAN:
      api[FormalMultilinearSeries.ofScalars] api[hasFPowerSeriesAt_iff]
      api[FormalMultilinearSeries.coeff_ofScalars]
      api[HasFPowerSeriesAt.eq_formalMultilinearSeries]
      api[AnalyticAt.hasFPowerSeriesAt] api[HasFPowerSeriesAt.exchange_radius]
      api[FormalMultilinearSeries.summable_norm_apply]

BECAUSE.text:
`hasFPowerSeriesAt_iff` is literally the filter-upwards form
    of the pointwise sum hypothesis, and uniqueness of expansions at a point
    collapses any two such expansions into coefficient equalities, so the
    whole identification is a dozen lines with no limit computation.

fields.title: Probe the Constant's Name and Signature Before Using It
fields.keywords: signature, explicit, implicit, #check, name, namespace, spelling, grep, api
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: Before applying a remembered or guessed lemma name, probe the exact constant and its argument structure with `#check @name` or a grep of the source tree; a remembered name that is slightly wrong or a remembered argument list that has one extra explicit hypothesis produces errors that look like mathematical failure. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You reach for a library lemma by name — from memory, from a
    surfaced memory's leaf list, or by translating the CamelCase prose — and
    apply it in a proof step.

IF.text:
The name is plausible but not probed (wrong namespace casing, a
      near-synonym spelling, an argument that is actually an instance implicit
      rather than explicit), the failure surfaces downstream as "unknown
      identifier", "Function expected", or a motive/type mismatch that invites
      a rewrite of the mathematics instead of the citation.

HOWEVER.text:
The instinct after such an error is to adapt the proof. But the error is
      almost never about the mathematics: namespaces change casing between
      files, near-synonym constants coexist (`card_subgroup_dvd` vs
      `card_dvd_of_le`), and instance-implicit hypotheses are invisible in the
      statement you remembered. Each unprobed guess costs a compile cycle and
      a misattributed failure account.

THEN.text:
Probe first: `#check @Full.Name` for the signature (which arguments are
      explicit, what the conclusion actually says), and when the name itself is
      uncertain, grep the library for the *object* (`grep -rln <object>`) and
      read the file's exports rather than guessing theorem names — the file
      often exports exactly the witnesses you need. Cite the probed name, not
      the remembered one.

BECAUSE.text:
A library citation is data, not reasoning; verifying it is cheap and
      deterministic, while reasoning around a bad citation is expensive and
      produces a wrong diagnosis that then leaks into the failure account and
      into memory.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Probe `#check @name` for signature and argument structure before first use.]
    next[On "unknown identifier", grep the source for the object and read the file's exports.]
    next[Read "Function expected" as "the argument list is wrong", not as a mathematical failure.]
    next[Cite the probed constant name in notes and memories, never the guessed one.]

fields.title: Recover Radical Generators from a Reciprocal Polynomial Root
fields.keywords: Lean, splitting field, reciprocal polynomial, radicals, inverse, quartic, ring_nf, linear_combination
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: A splitting field of a reciprocal polynomial can expose hidden quadratic generators directly from any nonzero root: first rewrite the inverse as a polynomial in the root, then test symmetric and antisymmetric combinations of the root and its inverse. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
An abstract `IsSplittingField` instance gives roots of a reciprocal
    polynomial, while the desired description asks for square-root generators
    and no library theorem constructs those generators in the arbitrary model.

THEN.text:
Use `IsSplittingField.splits` and `Splits.exists_eval_eq_zero` to
    choose a root `x`. Prove `x != 0` from the constant coefficient. Rearrange
    the root equation into an identity for `x⁻¹`; for a reciprocal quartic
    this is typically a cubic polynomial in `x`. Define candidate generators
    from `(x - x⁻¹) / 2` and `(x + x⁻¹) / 2`, clear denominators, and
    discharge their square equations with `ring_nf` and `linear_combination`
    from the original root equation and a polynomial multiple of it.

BECAUSE.text:
Reciprocal symmetry pairs a root with its inverse. Their sum and
    difference separate the quadratic quantities hidden in the polynomial, so
    the required radicals are internal expressions in one root rather than
    objects that must be transported from a concrete splitting field.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Use the recovered generators to factor the polynomial into signed roots.]
    next[Apply `IsSplittingField.adjoin_rootSet` to prove the generators span the field.]

fields.keywords: cyclic, orbit, Krylov, polynomial, module, annihilator, minpoly, quotient, range, finrank, aeval

fields.how: own mechanism: When a linear-operator goal asks whether one vector's iterates span, recast the space as a module over the polynomial ring and compare the cyclic submodule with a quotient by the scalar annihilator; use kernel/range equivalences and finrank rather than constructing a Krylov basis directly. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.provenance: Codex scribe positive departure: a certified finite-dimensional operator proof avoided a bounded-power independence construction by using the polynomial-module annihilator and quotient/range finrank.

context.text:
You must pass between a spanning orbit of an endomorphism and a
    degree statement about its minimal polynomial, but direct manipulation of
    the first n iterates creates bounded-degree polynomial and independence
    obligations that the available API does not package.

IF.text:
Polynomial evaluation supplies the scalar action, the scalar
    annihilator is identifiable with the principal ideal generated by the
    minimal polynomial, and the quotient by that ideal has a known finrank.

fields.title: Orient the Rewrite Toward the Goal's Shape
fields.keywords: rewrite, orientation, direction, normal-form, tactic, simp
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: An equation can be rewritten in either direction; choose the one that moves the goal toward the shape the next lemma expects, not the one that reads more naturally. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A proof step where an available equality could be applied left-to-
    right or right-to-left, and the rewrite either fails to fire or fires and
    leaves the goal further from what follows.

IF.text:
The next step's expected shape is known, then the orientation is
      determined: rewrite in whichever direction produces that shape. Deciding
      the target form first turns an experiment into a choice.

HOWEVER.text:
Equations are usually stated in the direction that reads as a definition or
      a simplification, and that direction is often the wrong one for the goal at
      hand. Applying it in the natural reading can move the goal away from the
      lemma that was going to close it, and the resulting state looks like
      progress — the rewrite succeeded — while the proof is further from
      finishing than before.

      Repeatedly rewriting back and forth between two forms is the visible
      symptom, and it is a sign that the target normal form was never chosen.

THEN.text:
Name the shape the next lemma needs, then orient the rewrite to produce it.
      When both directions are used in one proof, say which normal form each part
      of the argument works in.

BECAUSE.text:
A rewrite is a step toward a normal form, and a normal form that is not
      chosen in advance is chosen by accident at each step. The cost is not a
      failed tactic — it is a proof that oscillates between representations, in
      which no individual step looks wrong.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Name the shape the next lemma expects before rewriting.]
    next[Orient the rewrite to produce that shape, not the equation's natural reading.]
    next[If the proof rewrites back and forth, choose one normal form and say which.]

Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: Classify reuse of an already-proved diff as artifact replay, not as evidence that a proof strategy was independently understood or reconstructed. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A solver memory names both a proof route and a reachable commit or patch,
      and a later formalizer closes the same target after retrieving it.

IF.text:
The later artifact is content-identical to the earlier proof, or the
      transcript shows that the earlier diff was applied wholesale.

HOWEVER.text:
Recompiling and auditing the replayed artifact is genuine verification:
      it establishes that the proof still typechecks, preserves the statement,
      and meets the axiom and scope gates. It does not establish that the route
      description alone was sufficient for independent derivation.

THEN.text:
Record two separate outcomes. Credit artifact transfer and independent
      verification as successful. Mark strategy-learning or independent-solve
      conclusions as unmeasured. If the evaluation aims to test proof transfer,
      withhold direct commit or patch locators, isolate object stores, or score
      reconstruction separately from replay.

BECAUSE.text:
A reachable proof object collapses a search-and-formalization task into a
      patch-application task. Both can be useful, but they measure different
      capabilities and costs.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Compare the resulting tree or target file against the source proof artifact.]
    next[Inspect the transcript for wholesale diff, cherry-pick, or commit-pointer use.]
    next[Report verification success separately from independent derivation evidence.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When a route is known (from a memory, a paper, or a sibling artifact) but its Lean is not, first write every intermediate lemma AS A STATEMENT with `sorry`, in dependency order, and compile the skeleton; fill the bodies afterwards, leaves first. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

IF.text:
A retrieved memory or note describes a multi-lemma route in prose
    ("prove the pointwise identity, then integrate it, then identify the
    divisor with the root multiplicity …") and the target file has one
    big `sorry` where the route must land.

HOWEVER.text:
Trying to write the route top-down as one proof, or spending
    the session confirming API names before writing anything, leaves no
    compiled trace; the statements themselves are where most elaboration
    errors (coercions, binder shapes, implicit arguments) surface, and
    they are cheap to fix in isolation.

THEN.text:
Transcribe the route into 5–8 `lemma stepK … : … := by sorry`
    declarations whose statements are exact Lean, wire the big `sorry` to
    them so the file compiles with only the stepK sorries open, commit,
    then fill from the leaves (the ones needing only Mathlib) upward.
    + LEAN:
      tactic[sorry] api[exact?] tactic[refine ⟨_, ?_, ?_⟩]

BECAUSE.text:
A compiling skeleton converts a prose route into typed
    obligations that a successor (or the same session after a wall) can
    pick up one at a time; unfilled statements are measurable progress
    and localize every spelling question to one small goal.

fields.title: Tactic-Algebra Interference in Rewriting
fields.keywords: rewrite, rw, convert, simp, Tendsto, filter, goal-shape, interference
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When an algebraic identity is correct but `rw` disrupts the goal's type structure (filter, Tendsto, Set.mem), use `convert` or `simp_rw` to rewrite within the structure rather than replacing the whole goal. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You know the algebraic identity (e.g., ⟨h,h⟩ = ‖h‖²) and
    the goal is a Tendsto/Filter/Set statement that contains the LHS.
    Applying `rw` replaces the LHS but may change the goal shape in ways
    that break subsequent tactic application.

IF.text:
The goal has the form `Tendsto (fun n => f n) l (𝓝 target)` and
      you want to rewrite something inside `f n` or `target`, but `rw`
      at the top level changes the Tendsto structure.

HOWEVER.text:
`rw` is greedy — it replaces ALL occurrences, including ones inside
      binders (fun n => ...) where the rewrite may not be valid or may
      change the function identity. `simp_rw` rewrites under binders
      safely. `convert` changes the goal and leaves the mismatch as a
      subgoal. `show` can manually restate the goal in the desired form.

THEN.text:
(a) If the rewrite is inside a binder (fun n => ...): use `simp_rw`.
      (b) If the rewrite is in the target (𝓝 value): use `convert` to
          replace the target and close the algebraic identity separately.
      (c) If the rewrite is structural (changing Tendsto to Filter.Tendsto
          or vice versa): use `show` to restate, then proceed.
      (d) Last resort: break the Tendsto into pieces using `have` lemmas
          for each convergent component, then reassemble with Tendsto
          arithmetic (Tendsto.add, Tendsto.sub, Tendsto.mul).

    + LEAN:
      api[real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq] api[real_inner_self_eq_norm_mul_norm]
      tactic[simp_rw [...] → convert ... using 1 → ring]
      tactic[have h1 := ... → have h2 := ... → exact h1.sub h2 |>.add ...]

BECAUSE.text:
The tension is between algebraic truth (the identity holds) and
      tactic mechanics (the rewrite changes the goal shape). The informal
      mathematician doesn't see this tension because "substitute equals
      for equals" is seamless on paper. In Lean, the substitution must
      respect the term structure, and `rw` doesn't always do what the
      mathematician intends.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Determine if the rewrite is inside a binder, in the target, or structural.]
    next[Choose simp_rw (binder), convert (target), or show (structural).]
    next[If all fail, decompose into have lemmas and use Tendsto arithmetic.]

fields.title: Transport Across an Instance Diamond
fields.keywords: instance, diamond, Subsingleton, definitional, propositional, typeclass, module, algebra, coherence, mismatch, transport
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When two type-class instances on the SAME carrier are propositionally but not definitionally equal, transport hypotheses across the diamond explicitly (Subsingleton.elim on the instance type, or uniqueness-of-structure lemmas) instead of fighting the elaborator — and decide the instance-installation order BEFORE building the proof. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.provenance: case-1 compression pilot (2026-08-12): 8 independent zai-1 marks across 4+ transcripts (synthesis cluster 1); runner-corroborated

context.text:
A construction (fixed field, intermediate field, pullback)
    induces one instance; a library lemma you need selects a different
    but mathematically equal instance on the same carrier. Goals fail
    with "motive is not type correct" or invisible unification errors,
    though the mathematics is finished.

IF.text:
The two instances are provably equal as terms (their type is a
    Subsingleton, or a uniqueness-of-structure lemma exists), and the
    mismatch is a formalization seam, not a mathematical distinction.

HOWEVER.text:
Transport can bury a REAL mismatch. Verify the equality is
    actually propositional before eliminating it — two module structures
    can differ genuinely (different scalar actions), and Subsingleton.elim
    will simply refuse; a forced cast at that point is a wrong proof
    waiting to be found. Also: each transport is friction — three or more
    diamonds in one proof usually means the instance-installation ORDER
    is wrong upstream; fix the order rather than transporting repeatedly.

THEN.text:
Name both instances explicitly with `letI`/`haveI`; state their
    equality as a lemma (Subsingleton.elim _ _ where available); rewrite
    the hypothesis or goal across it once; keep the transport lemma named
    for reuse. When planning: install instances in dependency order and
    record that order in the proof-plan artifact.

BECAUSE.text:
Instance diamonds are a structural feature of large
    algebraic hierarchies, not local bugs — the same seam recurs across
    problems, so the discipline (name, equate, transport once, plan
    order) amortizes while ad-hoc casts do not.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Check whether the diamond recurs across the file; if so, hoist the transport into a helper lemma.]
    next[If Subsingleton.elim refuses, treat it as a signal the instances genuinely differ — stop and re-examine.]

fields.title: Force a Finite Derivative Limit to Vanish via Fixed-Interval Slopes
fields.keywords: Lean, Mathlib, Tendsto, deriv, exists_deriv_eq_slope, mean value theorem, atTop, asymptotic coefficients

IF.text:
You know `Tendsto f atTop (nhds L)`, `Differentiable ℝ f`, and
    `Tendsto (deriv f) atTop (nhds d)`, and need to show `d = 0`.

HOWEVER.text:
An improper-integral argument introduces integrability hypotheses,
    and filter-valued l'Hôpital may require awkward denominator and signed-limit
    side conditions that are absent from the original assumptions.

THEN.text:
For every `x`, use `exists_deriv_eq_slope` on `[x, x + 1]` and choose
    `c x ∈ (x, x + 1)` with `deriv f (c x) = f (x + 1) - f x`. Prove
    `Tendsto c atTop atTop` from `x ≤ c x`, compose the derivative limit with
    this cofinal choice, and compare it with the limit of the fixed-step
    difference, which is zero because both `f (x + 1)` and `f x` tend to `L`.
    Finish with `tendsto_nhds_unique`.
    + LEAN:
      api[exists_deriv_eq_slope] api[tendsto_atTop_mono']
      api[tendsto_atTop_add_const_right] api[Tendsto.comp]
      api[tendsto_nhds_unique]

BECAUSE.text:
A convergent function has vanishing slopes across every fixed

fields.title: Give Yourself an Epsilon of Room
fields.keywords: epsilon, arbitrary, limit, slack, relax, room, sharp, vanishing, approximate, for-all-epsilon, take-the-limit

context.text:
You must establish an exact statement — a vanishing (X = 0), a sharp inequality
    (X ≤ Y), an equality, or a limit — and a head-on proof of the exact claim is awkward.

IF.text:
The exact target is hard, but the *relaxed* target — `X ≤ ε`, or `X ≤ Y + ε`, or "within
      ε of the limit" — is reachable for each fixed ε > 0 (typically because some definition
      hands you an ε–δ budget: continuity, absolute continuity, measure zero, convergence).

HOWEVER.text:
The relaxed bound must hold for *all* ε > 0 with the slack genuinely controlled by ε
      (the bound's right side must tend to the target as ε → 0), and the quantity must live
      where "≤ ε for every ε > 0 ⇒ ≤ 0" is valid. Watch that any δ, cover, or index chosen to
      meet one ε does not secretly depend on the thing you are bounding.

THEN.text:
Fix an arbitrary ε > 0. Cash in the ε–δ budget from the relevant definition to prove the
      slack statement. Since ε was arbitrary, take ε → 0 (or inf over ε) to collapse the slack
      and conclude the sharp statement.

BECAUSE.text:
Weakening an exact goal to an approximate one you can actually hit — then letting the
      approximation tighten — is the central manoeuvre of analysis: ε–δ continuity, "measure
      ≤ ε hence null," `|a−b| < ε ∀ε ⇒ a = b`, Tao's "epsilon of room." The universal
      quantifier over ε does the work the direct exact argument could not.

next[State the sharp target and its relaxed, ε-slack version.]
    next[For a fixed arbitrary ε, spend the ε–δ budget from a definition to prove the slack bound.]
    next[Let ε → 0 to collapse the slack; check nothing chosen depended on the bounded quantity.]

fields.title: Estimate by Bounding
fields.keywords: bound, estimate, inequality, upper, lower, dominate, majorise, triangle, Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen

context.text:
You need to control a quantity (an integral, a sum, a probability, a norm) but
    exact computation is infeasible or unnecessary.

IF.text:
You need an upper bound (or lower bound) rather than an exact value, and standard
      inequalities (triangle, Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen, Markov, Chebyshev, AM-GM) are
      available.

HOWEVER.text:
Bounds lose information. A bound that is too loose is useless. The art is in choosing
      the tightest bound that remains tractable. Chaining too many inequalities can
      accumulate slack to the point of triviality.

THEN.text:
Identify which direction you need (upper or lower). Apply the most appropriate
      standard inequality. Check that the resulting bound is tight enough for your
      purposes. If not, try a different inequality or a more refined decomposition
      before bounding.

BECAUSE.text:
Estimation is the engine of analysis and probability. Most theorems in these fields
      are proved by chains of inequalities, each replacing something complicated with
      something simpler. Knowing which inequality to reach for is a core skill.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Determine whether you need an upper or lower bound.]
    next[Identify candidate inequalities from your toolbox.]
    next[Apply and check tightness — is the bound strong enough?]

fields.title: Monotone Approximation
fields.keywords: approximate, monotone, sequence, increasing, decreasing, limit, converge, truncate, smooth

context.text:
You want to prove a result for a general object (general measurable function,
    arbitrary open set, general measure) but your tools only work for simple ones.

IF.text:
Your general object can be approximated from below (or above) by a monotone sequence of
      simpler objects, and the property you care about is preserved under monotone limits.

HOWEVER.text:
Not all approximations are monotone, and not all properties survive limits. You must
      choose the right notion of approximation and verify that the limit argument is valid
      (monotone convergence theorem, continuity from below, directed completeness).

THEN.text:
Construct a monotone sequence of simple objects converging to your target. Prove the
      result for each element of the sequence. Apply a monotone convergence or limit theorem
      to conclude for the general object.

BECAUSE.text:
This is the fundamental technique of measure theory and integration. Simple functions
      approximate measurable functions, compact sets approximate open sets, finite sums
      approximate series. The monotone convergence theorem makes the passage rigorous.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Construct the monotone approximating sequence.]
    next[Prove the result for each element of the sequence.]
    next[Identify and apply the appropriate limit theorem.]

fields.title: Optimise a Free Parameter
fields.keywords: optimise, parameter, choose, best, minimise, maximise, sup, inf, epsilon, delta, t

context.text:
You have established a bound or inequality that contains a free parameter
    (epsilon, delta, t, lambda) and want the sharpest possible conclusion.

IF.text:
The bound is valid for all (or a range of) parameter values, and different choices
      yield different strengths of conclusion.

HOWEVER.text:
The optimisation may be analytically intractable. In that case, a sub-optimal but
      explicit choice (often guided by dimensional analysis or balancing terms) is better
      than an opaque optimal one.

THEN.text:
Differentiate (or otherwise optimise) with respect to the free parameter. If the
      optimum has a clean closed form, use it. If not, choose a value that balances the
      dominant terms — this typically gives the right order of magnitude.

BECAUSE.text:
This pattern is the workhorse of concentration inequalities, moment methods, and
      approximation theory. The Chernoff bound, Bernstein inequalities, and Laplace method
      all follow by introducing an exponential parameter and optimising.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the free parameter and its valid range.]
    next[Optimise or balance terms.]
    next[Substitute back and simplify the resulting bound.]

fields.title: Pass to a Subsequence or Subnet
fields.keywords: subsequence, subnet, extract, compactness, convergent, limit, accumulation, Bolzano-Weierstrass

context.text: You need convergence or a limit, but the full sequence or net may not cooperate.

IF.text:
You are working in a compact space (or a setting with a compactness hypothesis), and the
      sequence or net is bounded but not necessarily convergent.

HOWEVER.text:
The subsequence may converge to something unwanted. You must verify that the limit has
      the properties you need, and that the argument does not depend on the specific subsequence
      chosen.

THEN.text:
Invoke compactness (Bolzano-Weierstrass, Alaoglu, Tychonoff, sequential compactness) to
      extract a convergent subsequence. Pass to it. Argue that the limit has the desired property.
      If necessary, show the limit is unique so the full sequence converges.

BECAUSE.text:
Compactness arguments are the engine of analysis. "Pass to a subsequence" converts a
      possibly wild sequence into a tame one at the cost of losing control over indices — a
      trade-off that is almost always worth making.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Verify the compactness hypothesis that justifies extraction.]
    next[Extract the convergent subsequence and identify the limit.]
    next[Check that the limit has the properties you need.]

fields.title: Show Both Inequalities
fields.keywords: equality, sandwich, squeeze, both-directions, inclusion, subset, superset, le, ge

context.text:
You want to show A = B (where A, B are numbers, sets, or objects in an ordered structure)
    and no direct computation yields both sides at once.

IF.text:
Direct computation of A or B is infeasible, but you can bound A from above by B and
      from below by B (or equivalently, show A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A).

HOWEVER.text:
The two directions may require completely different techniques. One direction is often
      trivial while the other requires the bulk of the work. Identifying which is which
      saves effort.

THEN.text:
Prove A <= B and B <= A separately (or A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A).
      Combine to conclude A = B. For the squeeze/sandwich variant: bound A from above and
      below by quantities that both converge to the same limit.

BECAUSE.text:
This is one of the most common proof structures in analysis (sandwich theorem, integral
      bounds), set theory (Cantor-Bernstein), and algebra (showing ideals or subgroups are
      equal). It reduces equality to two often-simpler one-directional claims.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Determine which direction is easier.]
    next[Prove the easy direction first to build intuition.]
    next[Prove the hard direction.]
