fields.title: Count over a Decomposition
fields.keywords: counting, class-equation, orbit, Burnside, divisibility, congruence, partition, remainder, fixed-points, pigeonhole, double-counting

context.text:
You want to determine (or bound, or prove nonzero) a quantity — a cardinality, a
    sum, a measure, a dimension — that is hard to compute directly.

IF.text:
The quantity decomposes additively over a partition (orbits, conjugacy classes, cosets,
      cases, a cover), and you control all-but-one of the parts via a uniform property — each
      shares a divisibility, a congruence, a bound, or simply vanishes — so the distinguished
      part is forced.

HOWEVER.text:
The decomposition must be **exhaustive and disjoint** (no part double-counted, none missed),
      and the shared constraint must genuinely hold on *every* part you are not solving for — one
      uncounted orbit or one exception breaks the conclusion.

THEN.text:
Choose the decomposition that isolates the term you want (the center as the singleton
      classes; the fixed points as the size-1 orbits). Establish the uniform constraint on the
      other parts. Subtract / take congruences to force the distinguished term.

BECAUSE.text:
This is the counting principle behind the class equation, Burnside's lemma, Cauchy's and
      the Sylow theorems, inclusion–exclusion remainders, and pigeonhole: when the parts you can
      control cover all but a little, the little is determined by what is left over. The art is
      choosing the decomposition so the thing you want lands in the residual term.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Find the decomposition whose residual term is the quantity you want.]
    next[Check the decomposition is exhaustive and disjoint.]
    next[Establish the shared constraint on every other part, then isolate the residual.]

fields.title: The Probabilistic Method
fields.keywords: probabilistic, random, expectation, counting, existence, Erdos, random-variable, expected-value

context.text:
You want to show that an object with certain combinatorial properties exists, but
    explicit construction seems intractable.

IF.text:
The desired property can be expressed as an event in a probability space on the set of
      candidate objects, and you can estimate the probability of failure.

HOWEVER.text:
The probabilistic method typically does not produce an explicit object. It proves existence
      without construction. For applications requiring an actual witness, derandomisation
      techniques may be needed.

THEN.text:
Define a probability distribution on candidate objects. Show that the probability of
      having the desired property is positive (by union bound, expectation argument, Lovász
      local lemma, or second moment method). Conclude existence.

BECAUSE.text:
Erdős's probabilistic method revolutionised combinatorics by proving the existence of
      objects (Ramsey graphs, codes, expanders) that no one could construct explicitly. The
      expected value alone often suffices: if the expected number of bad events is less than 1,
      a good object exists.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Define the probability space on candidate objects.]
    next[Estimate the probability of failure.]
    next[Apply the appropriate probabilistic tool (union bound, expectation, LLL).]

fields.title: Chase the Diagram
fields.keywords: chase, chasing, pasting, snake-lemma, five-lemma, diagrammatically

context.text:
You must show two composites agree — a naturality square, a
    universal map's uniqueness, or a lemma of five-lemma type — and the objects
    themselves are opaque or have no elements to compute with.

IF.text:
The claim is an equation between composites, every square you need is
      already known to commute or is a hypothesis, and the diagram can be pasted
      from those known-commuting pieces. Then the equation follows from the
      pasting alone, with no information about the objects required.

HOWEVER.text:

fields.title: Check It on Generators
fields.keywords: suffices, enough, generators, generating, dense, densely, subcategory, representables, objectwise, reduce-to-the-case

context.text:
You must verify something for all objects of a category, and the
    category is large or its objects are not concretely described — but every
    object is built from a small family by colimits.

IF.text:
There is a dense (or strongly generating) subcategory, the property in
      question is stable under the colimits that rebuild arbitrary objects from
      it, and each generator can be checked directly. Then checking the
      generators checks everything, and the reduction is not an approximation —
      it is exact.

HOWEVER.text:
The reduction is only valid for properties the rebuilding colimits
      preserve, and this is where it fails silently. A functor that preserves
      colimits transports the property; one that merely preserves the *objects*
      does not. "Suffices to check" is often written when the author means
      "suffices to check, given a preservation lemma proved three sections
      earlier" — and sometimes when no such lemma exists. Beware also the
      generator that is dense in the wrong sense: dense, strongly generating,
      and separating are different conditions, and only density licenses the
      colimit reconstruction. If you cannot name the colimit that rebuilds a
      general object, you have not made a reduction, you have made a wish.

THEN.text:
Name the generating family and the sense in which it generates. State the
      colimit that reconstructs an arbitrary object from it, and the lemma saying
      the property survives that colimit. Check the generators. Then extend, and
      say explicitly where the extension step is justified.

BECAUSE.text:
Categories are usually presented by generators and relations even when the
      presentation is not written down; a dense subcategory is that presentation.
      Working there replaces a quantifier over a proper class with a check on a
      set.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Name the generating family and whether it is dense, strongly generating, or separating.]
    next[State the colimit that rebuilds a general object from it.]
    next[Cite or prove that the property is preserved by that colimit.]
    next[Check the generators, then extend.]

fields.title: Identify Two Constructions by Comparing Their Universal Properties
fields.keywords: coincide, corepresentable, weighted-limit, Kan-extension, up-to-unique-isomorphism, characterises

context.text:
Two constructions built by different routes (a homotopy limit and a
    weighted limit, a Kan extension and a coend, a Kleisli category and a
    category of free algebras) are claimed to coincide.

IF.text:
Each construction is characterised by a universal property, and the two
      properties can be shown to be the same problem — the same representing
      functor, or the same weight after a change of shape. Then the objects are
      canonically isomorphic, and the isomorphism is unique compatibly with the
      structure maps, which is more than a bare isomorphism gives you.

HOWEVER.text:
Two universal properties can be stated in nearly identical language and
      characterise different things. Watch the variance (a limit weighted by W is
      not the limit weighted by W's opposite); the *shape* of the indexing
      diagram, which a change-of-base along a functor silently alters; and
      whether the property is required to hold up to isomorphism, up to *unique*
      isomorphism, or strictly — the three give different objects, and only the
      middle one gives canonicity. Conversely two properties may look different
      and coincide, so a failure to match the words is not a proof that the
      constructions differ. If you cannot exhibit the comparison map, you have
      matched sentences rather than objects.

THEN.text:
State both universal properties in the same form — as representations of
      the same functor where possible. Exhibit the comparison morphism the
      properties induce, and show it is invertible by giving the inverse from the
      other property. Record what the identification preserves: canonicity, the
      structure maps, and any 2-cells.

BECAUSE.text:
A universal property determines its object up to unique isomorphism, so an
      identification made this way carries the structure with it, where an
      ad-hoc isomorphism has to be checked compatible with everything separately.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Write both universal properties as representations of one functor.]
    next[Check variance and diagram shape agree before comparing.]
    next[Exhibit the induced comparison map and its inverse.]
    next[Say whether the identification is up to unique isomorphism or merely isomorphism.]

fields.title: Factor the Map, Then Lift Against It
fields.keywords: factorization, factorisation, right-lifting, left-lifting, anodyne, awfs

context.text:
A single map is too coarse to argue about, but the ambient category
    has a factorization system whose two classes have complementary behaviour.

IF.text:
Every map factors as one from the left class followed by one from the right
      class, and the classes are orthogonal — every left map lifts against every
      right map, uniquely or not. Then a property that holds for both halves and
      is closed under composition holds for the map, and a lifting problem posed
      against the map can be solved half at a time.

HOWEVER.text:
Orthogonal and weak factorization systems differ exactly where it matters:
      in the orthogonal case the lift is *unique*, in the weak case it merely
      exists, and an argument that silently uses uniqueness in a weak system is
      wrong. Factorizations may or may not be functorial, and an argument that
      factors inside a colimit needs functoriality it should state. The two
      classes determine each other by lifting, so "the left class" is not a free
      choice — check that the class you named is the one orthogonality gives you,
      not a convenient subclass. And the retract argument that recovers a map
      from its factorization needs the class to be retract-closed, which is a
      hypothesis rather than a formality.

THEN.text:
Name the factorization system and whether it is orthogonal or weak. Factor
      the map explicitly and say which half carries the difficulty. Pose the
      lifting problem, solve it against the appropriate class, and if you need
      uniqueness say where it comes from. Where functoriality is used, cite it.

BECAUSE.text:
A factorization system is the categorical form of "surjective part and
      injective part" — it turns one intractable map into two tractable ones
      whose interaction is governed by a single lifting condition rather than by
      ad-hoc analysis.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Name the system and say whether it is orthogonal or weak.]
    next[Factor the map and identify which half is hard.]
    next[Pose the lifting problem and solve it against the right class.]
    next[If uniqueness or functoriality is used, cite where it comes from.]

fields.title: Strictify via Coherence
fields.keywords: strictify, strictification, coherence, pentagon, associator, unitor, biequivalent, up-to-isomorphism, pseudofunctor, bicategory

context.text:
The associativity or unit laws you need hold only up to specified
    isomorphism, and carrying those isomorphisms through the argument would bury
    it in bookkeeping.

IF.text:
A coherence theorem applies — every diagram built from the structural
      isomorphisms commutes — and the strictification is an equivalence, not
      merely a comparison. Then any statement invariant under that equivalence
      may be proved in the strict setting and transported back.

HOWEVER.text:
Coherence is not a licence to ignore the isomorphisms; it is a theorem that
      they compose predictably, and it has hypotheses. Three failures recur.
      Not every weak structure strictifies: tricategories are not triequivalent
      to strict 3-categories, and the analogous hope fails higher up. The
      property you transport must be invariant under the equivalence — a claim
      about *strict* limits or about equality of objects is not, and will be
      false or meaningless after transport. And coherence for the structure does
      not extend to the *morphisms* between such structures: pseudo, lax and
      colax maps have their own coherence questions, and a strictification of
      objects can leave the 1-cells weak.

THEN.text:
Name the coherence theorem and check its hypotheses. Say what strictifies
      — objects, 1-cells, or both. State the property being transported and why
      it is invariant under the equivalence. Then argue strictly, and note at the
      end what the weak statement is.

BECAUSE.text:
The content of a weak structure is almost never in its structural
      isomorphisms; it is in what the structure does. Coherence is the theorem
      that lets you say so rigorously instead of by apology.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Name the coherence/strictification theorem and check its hypotheses.]
    next[Say whether objects, 1-cells, or both are strictified.]
    next[Check the transported property is invariant under the equivalence.]
    next[State the weak form of the conclusion at the end.]

fields.title: Transpose Across an Adjunction
fields.keywords: adjoint, adjunction, adjunct, transpose, mate, unit, counit, left-adjoint, right-adjoint, Kleisli, Eilenberg-Moore, free-forgetful, hom-set-bijection

context.text:
You must prove something about a map out of a free object, into a
    limit, or between categories linked by a free–forgetful pair — and the
    structure obstructing you lives on only one side.

IF.text:
You have an adjunction F ⊣ G, and the claim concerns a morphism
      F(A) → B (or A → G(B)). The hom-set bijection Hom(F A, B) ≅ Hom(A, G B) is
      natural in both variables, so the two formulations carry exactly the same
      information — but rarely the same difficulty. The same move transposes a
      *diagram* rather than a map: a square commutes if and only if its mate
      under the adjunction does.

HOWEVER.text:
Transposing is only faithful if the naturality you rely on is the
      naturality you have. Three ways this goes wrong: the bijection is natural
      in one variable but you used it in the other; the adjunction is only a
      *lax* or *relative* one, so the unit and counit are not isomorphisms and
      the transpose is weaker than the original; or the mate correspondence
      reverses 2-cells, turning a lax morphism into a colax one, so a condition
      that looked preserved has silently dualised. Check which of unit and
      counit you actually invoked — a proof that needs both is usually asserting
      an equivalence, not an adjunction.

THEN.text:
Name the adjunction and its unit η and counit ε explicitly. Transpose the
      statement, prove it on the easier side, and transport the conclusion back
      through the same bijection. For a diagram, take mates throughout and
      verify the transposed diagram instead. Where the argument passes through
      Kleisli or Eilenberg–Moore categories, say which, since the two present
      the same monad with different morphisms.

BECAUSE.text:
Adjunctions are the principal way category theory moves a problem to where
      it is easy without losing information. The hom-set bijection is an
      isomorphism, so nothing is given up; what changes is which structure is
      free and therefore which side admits a construction by generators.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Name the adjunction, its unit, and its counit.]
    next[State the transposed claim and check the naturality you rely on holds in the variable you used.]
    next[Prove the transposed claim, then transport the conclusion back.]
    next[If the adjunction is lax or relative, say what the transpose loses.]

fields.title: Verify the Universal Property
fields.keywords: universal, property, unique, morphism, initial, terminal, adjoint, representable, Yoneda

context.text:
You want to prove that an explicit construction actually gives the correct
    categorical object (product, coproduct, limit, free algebra, tensor product, adjoint).

IF.text:
The object you have constructed should be characterised by a universal mapping property:
      for every object of a certain kind, there exists a unique morphism through yours.

HOWEVER.text:
Universal properties require checking both existence and uniqueness of the mediating
      morphism. Existence is usually the construction; uniqueness is often the harder part
      and is where most proof errors occur.

THEN.text:
State the universal property precisely. For existence: given an arbitrary test object
      and compatible data, construct the required morphism. For uniqueness: assume two
      morphisms work and show they are equal, typically by checking on generators or using
      a cancellation argument.

BECAUSE.text:
Universal properties are the categorical way of saying "this is the canonical

fields.title: Complexity Classification
fields.keywords: complexity, NP-complete, hardness, reduction, computability, classification

context.text:
A computational problem P has been defined, and its complexity
    is unknown or only roughly known. The paper's contribution is to classify
    P at a known level of the complexity hierarchy: P, NP-complete, PSPACE,
    decidable, undecidable, ETH-hard, and so on.

IF.text:
You can construct a polynomial-time (or appropriate) reduction from a
      complexity-class-complete problem to P, or vice versa, establishing
      membership / hardness with a sharp boundary.

HOWEVER.text:
Complexity-classification is *one specific subtype* of
      `characterization-result` — its analogue in non-computational settings
      is `classification-result` (e.g., classifying KMS states or AFD outer
      actions). The reasoning shape is "list-the-cases-and-show-exhaustion"
      but the deliverable is "the problem belongs to class C" rather than
      "the structure has these instances." Use this leaf only when the result
      is genuinely complexity-theoretic.

THEN.text:
1. Construct the reduction (typically polynomial-time many-one or
         Turing) from a complexity-class-complete problem to P (for
         hardness) or from P to a problem already in C (for membership).
      2. Verify the reduction is correct and within the resource bounds for
         the target class.
      3. State the classification theorem: P is C-complete (or C-hard, or
         in C, as appropriate).

      that places a problem at a precise location in a known hierarchy. It
      depends on the existence of a complete problem for the target class
      (Cook-Levin, etc.); reductions are the workhorse construction. The
      family parent is characterization-result; this leaf is the
      complexity-theoretic specialisation.

      next[Construct the reduction; verify resource bounds.]
      next[State the classification with the appropriate complete / hard / member language.]

fields.title: Hybrid Certification
fields.keywords: hybrid, numerical, exact, certification, roots, sign, Sturm, interval, rigorous, fast

context.text:
You need a rigorous result about a polynomial or algebraic system (root count,
    sign determination, bound verification) but the standard exact methods (Sturm sequences,
    Groebner bases, cylindrical algebraic decomposition) are computationally infeasible for
    the problem size, while purely numerical methods lack rigour.

IF.text:
The exact method's bottleneck is a specific subroutine (polynomial GCD, resultant,
      matrix factorization) that scales badly with coefficient size or degree, but the
      qualitative structure of the answer (number of roots, sign pattern) can be determined
      cheaply by approximate computation.

HOWEVER.text:
The hybrid method must be provably correct. The numerical step identifies candidates;
      the exact step certifies them. If the certification step fails (e.g., the approximate
      root is too far from the true root for sign determination), the method must detect this
      and fall back rather than produce a wrong answer.

    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - Double roots: if two roots are very close, the numerical step may merge them and the
          sign-change count will be wrong. Mitigation: compare numerical root count with exact
          Sturm count on a COARSE interval first.
        - Coefficient explosion: the exact evaluation at a rational test point may involve very
          large integers. Mitigation: choose simple test points (small-denominator rationals).
        - False separation: numerical noise places a test point on the wrong side of a root.
          Mitigation: use exact arithmetic for the test point evaluation, not floating-point.

THEN.text:
1. Use fast numerical computation (numpy, LAPACK, floating-point) to compute approximate
         answers: root locations, eigenvalues, sign patterns.
      2. Design an exact verification step that checks the numerical answer: evaluate the
         polynomial at rational test points, verify sign conditions, count roots by IVT.
      3. The exact step should be O(n) in the problem size (not O(n³) like the numerical step),
         since it's certifying known answers, not discovering them.
      4. If the exact step disagrees with the numerical step, investigate rather than trust either.

BECAUSE.text:
Exact symbolic computation has enormous constant factors (arbitrary-precision integer
      arithmetic, polynomial GCD over Z[x] with 100+ digit coefficients). Numerical computation
      is fast but approximate. The hybrid avoids the worst of both: fast location + cheap
      certification = rigorous result at numerical speed.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P4 n=4 Case 2 (futon6, Feb 2026): Sturm's theorem on a degree-70 polynomial with
        100+ digit integer coefficients ran for 4 hours without completing (polynomial GCD
        bottleneck). The hybrid method: numpy.roots for approximate root locations (O(n³),
        milliseconds), then exact sympy.Rational evaluation at midpoints between consecutive
        roots (O(n) evaluations, 0.2s total). Same rigour as Sturm. 72,000x speedup.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the bottleneck in the exact method.]
    next[Design a numerical locator + exact certifier pipeline.]
    next[Validate: compare hybrid result with exact method on a smaller instance.]

fields.title: Numerical Scout
fields.keywords: numerical, landscape, critical-point, search, scout, map, verify, grid, Monte-Carlo, domain

context.text:
You want to prove a statement about a continuous or polynomial function on a
    domain (e.g., positivity, uniqueness of extrema, critical point enumeration). The
    function has enough variables that the proof strategy is not obvious.

IF.text:
The domain is bounded, the function is computable, and there are multiple plausible
      proof strategies (SOS, interval arithmetic, elimination, Groebner, etc.), but you
      don't know which will work.

HOWEVER.text:
Numerical evidence does not constitute proof. Floating-point computation can miss
      critical points near boundaries, produce false precision, and confirm true conjectures
      whose proofs require entirely different techniques. The scout must inform the proof
      strategy, not replace it.

    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - Scout finds zero violations → prover assumes the "obvious" approach works → but
          the proof technique fails for structural reasons unrelated to the landscape
          (e.g., SOS blocked by interior zeros). The scout informs WHAT to prove, not HOW.
        - Scout misses a critical point in a thin region → prover claims exhaustive enumeration
          → proof is incomplete. Mitigate: multiple independent searches, boundary-focused
          sampling, increase start count.

THEN.text:
1. Grid evaluation: compute the function on a uniform grid over the domain. Record the
         minimum, maximum, and any near-zero values.
      2. Critical point search: run multiple independent local optimization searches (L-BFGS,
         differential evolution) from random starting points. Use at least 3 independent
         searches with 1000+ starts each.
      3. Domain boundary survey: evaluate on constraint boundaries (where disc=0, f=0, etc.).
      4. Symmetry detection: check whether critical points cluster along symmetry subspaces.
      5. Case structure identification: from the critical point map, identify natural
         subcases ordered by symmetry/difficulty.

BECAUSE.text:
The scout reveals what the proof must handle: how many critical points, where they
      are, what the minimum margin is, which subspaces are trivial and which are hard. This
      guides the choice of proof technique. A proof strategy designed without scouting is
      guessing; one designed after scouting is engineering.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P4 n=4 Stam inequality proof (futon6, Feb 2026): 4 numerical scripts with 11,000+
        optimization starts mapped 12 critical points in 4D. This map identified the 5-case
        decomposition (Cases 1, 2, 3a, 3b, 3c by symmetry subspace) that led to algebraic
        proofs for Cases 1-3b. Without scouting, the case decomposition would have been
        unmotivated.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Run grid evaluation + critical point search on the domain.]
    next[Identify symmetry subspaces from the critical point map.]
    next[Design the proof strategy based on the landscape, not the other way around.]

fields.title: Construct Through a Finite Correspondence
fields.keywords: existence, construct, witness, Galois, correspondence, finite, subgroup, lattice, transport, concrete
fields.provenance: case-1 compression pilot (2026-08-12): runner's self-graded PRINCIPLE (debrief-corroborated) + 3 marks across 2 independent zai-1 transcripts (3814 marks 1-2; 3809 mark 1). Meets the >=2-transcripts+debrief bar EXACTLY; 3809 mark 1 (correspondence-transport of a lattice-join condition to a fixing-subgroup characterisation) is the swing vote — excluding it drops this to n=1. Transcript 3816 mark 6 (ambient abelian-ness => automatic normality) was considered and EXCLUDED as hypothesis-leverage, not this move.

context.text:
"Exhibit E/ℚ of degree 9 with two cyclic cubic subfields
    meeting trivially and joining to everything" — the object carries
    lattice constraints that are hard to verify directly on fields.

IF.text:
A correspondence theorem (Galois, Pontryagin, Stone) maps your
    target's constraint lattice anti-isomorphically onto a FINITE,
    computable side (subgroups of (ZMod n)ˣ), and a concrete realization
    (cyclotomic field, product group) makes the finite side explicit.

HOWEVER.text:
The finite-side work "by itself does not resolve the
    implementation blockage" (the runner's own verdict): the transport
    step — reinterpreting fixed fields, matching instances, reindexing —
    is where formalization time actually goes, and it needs its own
    techniques (instance-diamond transport, lift/reflect). Budget the
    transport as the major cost, not an afterthought.

THEN.text:
(1) realize the ambient object concretely; (2) state and prove
    every lattice fact on the finite side as standalone lemmas — meet,
    join, orders, indices; (3) transport through the correspondence one
    named lemma at a time; (4) read degrees/dimensions off indices via
    the correspondence's numerology.

BECAUSE.text:
Finite-side facts are decidable-adjacent and independently
    checkable; the correspondence converts each into a field-side fact
    that would be a research-grade verification directly.

fields.title: Encode as Algebra
fields.keywords: algebra, encode, translate, homomorphism, representation, structure, ring, module, group-ring

context.text: You have a problem in geometry, combinatorics, topology, or analysis that resists direct methods.

IF.text:
The objects in your problem carry algebraic structure (composition, addition, multiplication)
      that direct methods are not exploiting, or there is a known algebraic invariant that
      captures the property you care about.

HOWEVER.text:
The algebraic translation may lose geometric or combinatorial information. The algebra may
      be harder to compute with than the original objects. Not every problem benefits from
      algebraisation.

THEN.text:
Assign algebraic objects to your problem's ingredients: groups to symmetries, rings to
      coordinate systems, modules to representations, homology groups to topological spaces.
      Reformulate the problem as an algebraic question. Solve using algebraic tools (exact
      sequences, spectral sequences, Groebner bases, character theory).

BECAUSE.text:
Algebraic encoding has been one of the most successful strategies in mathematics:
      Galois theory encodes field extensions as groups, algebraic topology encodes spaces as
      groups, algebraic geometry encodes varieties as rings. The algebra often reveals structure
      that was invisible in the original setting.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify what algebraic structure your objects carry.]
    next[Choose the right algebraic invariant or encoding.]
    next[Translate the problem and solve algebraically.]

context.text: You want to prove a statement P and no direct construction or chain of implications is apparent.

IF.text:
The conclusion P is existential ("there exists..."), uniqueness ("at most one..."), or
      impossibility ("no X satisfies..."), and direct proof routes are blocked.

HOWEVER.text:
Proofs by contradiction can obscure the constructive content of a result, making it harder to
      extract algorithms or explicit witnesses. Some mathematical communities prefer direct proofs
      when available.

THEN.text:
Assume not-P. Use the assumed structure to build or derive objects, then show these objects
      violate a known fact. The contradiction forces P.

BECAUSE.text:
Contradiction proofs gain traction by giving you an extra hypothesis (not-P) to work with.
      Many fundamental results (irrationality of sqrt(2), uncountability of the reals, infinitude
      of primes) were first proved this way.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Write down the precise negation of P.]
    next[Identify what new objects or properties not-P gives you.]
    next[Find the known fact that these objects violate.]

context.text: You have a general statement and want to know if it is plausible before investing in a proof.

IF.text:
The statement involves a parameter, a set, or a structure that can take degenerate or
      extreme values.

HOWEVER.text:
Extreme cases can be vacuously true or pathologically special, giving false confidence.
      Passing extreme-case checks is necessary but not sufficient.

THEN.text:
Instantiate the statement at every extreme: n=0, n=1, the empty set, the one-point space,
      the trivial group, infinite dimension, the identity morphism. Check whether the statement
      is true, vacuously true, or false. A failure at an extreme case is a cheap disproof.

BECAUSE.text:
Extreme cases are the cheapest tests available. Many false conjectures die at n=0. Many
      correct theorems reveal their essential content at the boundary.

next[List all parameters and identify their extreme values.]

    next[Record which extremes are informative vs vacuous.]

context.text: You need to show that an object with certain properties exists.

IF.text:
The existence statement is concrete enough that you can describe what the object would look
      like, and abstract existence arguments (Zorn's lemma, compactness, probabilistic method)
      either do not apply or would leave you without a usable object.

HOWEVER.text:
Explicit constructions can be intricate and may obscure *why* the object exists. Sometimes
      a non-constructive proof reveals more about the landscape than a single explicit example.

THEN.text:
Build the object step by step. Define it concretely. Verify each required property. If the
      construction is complex, build intermediate objects and compose them.

BECAUSE.text:
An explicit witness is the gold standard of existence proofs: it gives you something to
      compute with, to test, and to modify. Many of mathematics' most valued results are
      constructions (Cantor's diagonal, Weierstrass's nowhere-differentiable function, Vitali sets).

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[List the properties the witness must satisfy.]
    next[Attempt to build an object satisfying them one at a time.]
    next[If stuck, relax a property and see what you can build.]

context.text: You have a hypothesis and a conclusion, but no direct path between them.

IF.text:
The gap between hypothesis and conclusion is structural: you need an intermediate
      object (a function, a sequence, a set, a morphism) that does not appear in the
      problem statement but whose existence would bridge the gap.

HOWEVER.text:
Auxiliary objects can feel like magic when encountered for the first time. The skill
      is in recognising which construction is needed: truncation, mollification, partition
      of unity, Hahn-Banach extension, free object on generators, approximating sequence.

THEN.text:
Identify the gap. Ask: what kind of object would connect my hypothesis to my
      conclusion? Construct it explicitly. Verify it has the properties needed on both
      sides. Common auxiliary objects include: truncated random variables, bump functions,
      test morphisms, approximating sequences, and free resolutions.

BECAUSE.text:
Many of the most important proofs in mathematics turn on a single clever auxiliary
      construction. The Radon-Nikodym derivative, the partition of unity, the resolvent
      operator — these are all auxiliary objects that became standard tools precisely
      because they bridge common structural gaps.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the structural gap between hypothesis and conclusion.]
    next[Survey known auxiliary constructions in your domain.]
    next[Build the object and verify it bridges the gap.]

fields.how: own mechanism: Turn a polynomial growth bound for points in balls into convergence of a decaying sum by partitioning the points into geometric shells. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You need to prove that a sum of decreasing radial weights converges, but
      your available quantitative information controls only the number of
      points in balls (or a weighted counting function).

IF.text:
The counting function satisfies N(R) <= C * R^d for large R, and the
      summand is bounded by a negative power comparable to R^(-alpha).

HOWEVER.text:
A ball count does not directly bound the whole infinite sum, and a
      logarithmically weighted count may not give an ordinary count at the
      same radius.

THEN.text:
First convert any weighted count to an ordinary count by enlarging the
      radius by a fixed factor so every point in the smaller ball has weight
      bounded below by a positive constant. Partition the indices into shells
      b^j <= radius < b^(j+1), with b > 1. Bound the cardinality of shell j by
      N(b^(j+1)) and each summand there by b^(-alpha*j). The shell total is
      therefore bounded by a constant times (b^(d-alpha))^j, so comparison
      with a geometric series proves convergence when alpha > d.

BECAUSE.text:
Geometric shells put the growth of the number of terms and the decay of
      each term on the same exponential scale. Their exponents subtract, and
      the convergence threshold becomes the transparent inequality alpha > d.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Prove a usable ordinary ball-count bound, dilating the radius if the available count is weighted.]
    next[Define geometric shells and prove they form a unique partition of the indices.]
    next[Bound each finite shell total and compare the outer sum with a geometric series.]

context.text: You have a problem stated in terms of maps, sets, or conditions, and direct approaches are stuck.

IF.text:
The problem has a natural duality: a categorical opposite, a vector space dual, a Boolean
      complement, a Fourier transform, a Lagrangian dual, or simply the contrapositive of a
      logical statement.

HOWEVER.text:
Not every problem dualises cleanly. Some dualities lose structure (the double dual may not
      be isomorphic to the original). You must verify that the dual problem actually helps.

THEN.text:
Reformulate the problem in the dual setting. Solve it there if easier. Translate the
      solution back. For logical statements, try the contrapositive before attempting direct proof.

BECAUSE.text:
Duality is pervasive: Pontryagin duality, Stone duality, linear programming duality,
      Poincare duality, Serre duality. A problem that is opaque in one setting can become
      transparent in its dual.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify which duality applies to your setting.]
    next[Reformulate the problem in the dual language.]
    next[Solve and translate back.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When a problem has symmetry, use it to reduce the work. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text: You are working on a problem where some transformation preserves the relevant structure.

IF.text:
The problem is invariant under a group action, permutation, rotation, translation, or
      relabelling, and you are doing redundant work on equivalent configurations.

HOWEVER.text:
Not all apparent symmetries are real: a function may look symmetric but have hidden asymmetries.
      And exploiting symmetry requires proving the symmetry exists, which itself may be non-trivial.

THEN.text:
Identify the symmetry group. Use it to reduce to a canonical representative ("without loss of
      generality"). Count orbits instead of elements. Decompose representations into irreducibles.
      Apply fixed-point theorems when the action has no escape.

BECAUSE.text:
Symmetry arguments can reduce exponential case analysis to a single case. The "WLOG" move
      is one of the most powerful sentence fragments in mathematics.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify what transformations preserve the problem.]
    next[Choose a canonical representative for each orbit.]
    next[Reformulate the problem in terms of orbits or invariants.]

fields.how: own mechanism: Characterize the regime where a known result FAILS, rather than only characterizing where it holds. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A theorem T is known under hypotheses H. It is natural to ask
    whether T extends to a broader class. Rather than producing yet another
    sufficient condition, the paper instead pins down the *boundary of
    applicability*: it identifies exactly the regime where T is no longer
    valid, often with quantitative or structural sharpness.

IF.text:
You have a theorem T with hypotheses H and you want to articulate the
      *failure regime* — typically (a) examples that violate T outside H,
      (b) a structural reason the failure occurs, (c) a sharp boundary
      between holds-here and fails-here.

HOWEVER.text:
Failure-mode characterization is structurally distinct from a *negative
      result* (T is false in this case). A negative result asserts something
      doesn't hold; failure-mode-characterization specifies the *regime* where
      it doesn't hold and the *structural reason* it doesn't. The latter is
      stronger — it tells the reader where the theorem still works, where it
      fails, and *why*.

THEN.text:
1. Construct an explicit counterexample or family of counterexamples
         that lie just outside H.
      2. Identify the structural feature of the counterexamples that makes
         T fail — the "failure mechanism."
      3. State the boundary as a theorem: "T fails iff [structural
         condition]."
      4. Optional: re-prove T with a refined hypothesis H' that excludes
         the failure regime.

BECAUSE.text:
Failure-mode characterization is information-dense: it tells the
      community both where to apply T and where to stop. It also exposes
      the structural feature that drives validity, which often illuminates
      analogous theorems in adjacent settings. This pattern is closely
      related to `structural-obstruction-as-theorem` but distinct: that
      pattern is about a *method* failing on a problem, this pattern is
      about a *theorem* failing in a regime.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Construct an explicit counterexample and verify it fails T.]
      next[Identify the structural feature that drives the failure.]
      next[State the boundary theorem precisely; check it is sharp.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When a proof is ugly or a pattern recurs, seek a higher-level framework where it becomes natural. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text: You have a proof that works but feels ad hoc, or you see the same argument repeated in several settings.

IF.text:
The proof involves case splits, coordinate choices, or auxiliary constructions that seem to
      serve no conceptual purpose, or the same lemma keeps reappearing in different guises across
      different domains.

HOWEVER.text:
Premature abstraction obscures rather than clarifies: abstracting before you have enough
      examples risks building a framework that fits nothing well. The right abstraction is found,
      not prescribed.

THEN.text:
Identify the minimal structural assumptions your argument actually uses. Reformulate in terms
      of those assumptions alone. If a known framework (group, category, topological space, measure
      space) fits, use it; if not, you may have discovered a new one.

BECAUSE.text:
The right abstraction turns a difficult proof into a trivial one. Much of 20th-century
      mathematics consisted of finding the right level of generality (e.g., Grothendieck's schemes,
      Eilenberg-Mac Lane's categories).

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[List the properties your proof actually uses.]
    next[Search for existing frameworks that axiomatise those properties.]
    next[Reformulate and check whether the proof simplifies.]

context.text:
You want to prove a statement P(n) for all n in some well-ordered domain
    (natural numbers, ordinals, well-founded trees).

IF.text:
The statement involves a natural number, a finite structure with a size parameter, or more
      generally any well-ordered or well-founded index.

HOWEVER.text:
The inductive step can be harder than it looks — it requires proving P(n+1) from P(n)
      (or from all P(k) with k<n for strong induction). Choosing the wrong induction variable
      makes the step impossible even when the theorem is true.

THEN.text:
Choose the right quantity to induct on. Verify the base case. For the inductive step,
      assume P holds for smaller values and show it holds for the current value. Consider strong
      induction if simple induction is too weak.

BECAUSE.text:
Induction is the fundamental proof method for discrete mathematics and much of algebra.
      Choosing the right induction variable is often the key creative step.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the right quantity to induct on.]
    next[Verify the base case.]
    next[Prove the inductive step, being explicit about where the hypothesis is used.]

fields.how: own mechanism: Prove something locally (on small pieces) and then assemble the local results into a global one. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text: You want to establish a property of a large or complicated object.

IF.text:
The object admits a decomposition into simpler pieces (open cover, partition, filtration,
      localisation at primes), and the property you want can be checked on pieces.

HOWEVER.text:
Not every property is local. You must verify that local data can be patched: the pieces
      must be compatible on overlaps, and the patching procedure must not introduce new problems.

THEN.text:
Cover the object with pieces where the property is manageable. Prove it on each piece.
      Check compatibility on overlaps. Glue the local results into a global one, using
      partitions of unity, sheaf conditions, or patching lemmas as appropriate.

BECAUSE.text:
Local-to-global is one of the deepest recurring themes in mathematics: sheaf theory,
      Mayer-Vietoris, local-global principles in number theory, partitions of unity in
      differential geometry. The power comes from reducing a hard global problem to many
      easy local ones.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Decompose the object into local pieces.]
    next[Verify the property on each piece.]
    next[Check compatibility and assemble the global result.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When two parts of a proof have conflicting requirements on a parameter, recognize the tension as a structural constraint and seek a construction that dissolves it by changing the underlying geometric or algebraic setup. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Your proof has two logically independent obligations. Each constrains a shared
    parameter (dimension, degree, codimension, rank, etc.) in conflicting directions. The
    natural construction satisfies one obligation perfectly but creates headwinds for the
    other.

IF.text:
Obligation A requires parameter p to have property X (e.g., n even), while
      obligation B benefits from property Y (e.g., n odd), and X and Y are incompatible.
      The conflict is not a matter of insufficient technique but of the parameter itself.

HOWEVER.text:
Not every difficulty is a tension. If obligation B merely "prefers" Y but can be
      completed with X, the tension is aesthetic, not structural. Only apply this pattern
      when the conflict genuinely blocks or severely impedes completion. Also: the
      alternative construction that dissolves the tension must exist — don't assume it does
      without checking.

    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - The alternative construction may not exist (the tension may be intrinsic to the
          problem, not just the approach).
        - The alternative may dissolve one tension but create another. Map all obligations
          before committing.

THEN.text:
1. State the tension precisely: which obligations conflict on which parameter.
      2. Ask: is there a different construction where both obligations want the same
         parameter value? This often means replacing the initial geometric or algebraic
         object (reflection → rotation, codim-1 → codim-2, etc.).
      3. Check that the new construction still satisfies both obligations (it may make
         the previously-easy obligation slightly harder).
      4. If the tension dissolves, record the resolution as a structural insight.

BECAUSE.text:
Parametric tensions are theorems about the approach, not the problem. They reveal that
      the initial construction, however natural, is suboptimal for the full proof. Dissolving
      the tension often simplifies the entire proof architecture by removing structural
      headwinds that would otherwise require heavy machinery to overcome.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): E2 obligation (place Γ in FH(Q))
        requires even n (so fixed set has odd dimension and χ = 0 by topology). S obligation
        (upgrade to manifold) benefits from odd n (favorable L-theory parity, equivariant
        surgery available). Tension is structural for the reflection construction. Resolution:
        replace codimension-1 reflection with codimension-2 rotation in odd dimension. Both
        obligations then want odd n. The rotation route dissolves the tension and opens two
        parallel S-branch options (Wall surgery with favorable parity, or equivariant surgery
        with satisfied gap hypothesis).

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify which obligations conflict on which parameters.]
    next[Search for alternative constructions where the conflict dissolves.]
    next[Verify the alternative satisfies all obligations, even if less cleanly.]

context.text: You are working with objects that carry more structure than your problem needs.

IF.text:
Different-looking objects behave identically for your purposes, and keeping track of the
      differences creates bookkeeping overhead or case splits.

HOWEVER.text:
Quotienting loses information. You must verify that the operations and properties you care
      about are well-defined on equivalence classes, not just on representatives.

THEN.text:
Define an equivalence relation that identifies objects agreeing on what matters. Pass to the
      quotient. Verify well-definedness. Work in the quotient where the irrelevant distinctions
      are gone.

BECAUSE.text:
Quotient constructions are one of the most universal moves in mathematics: integers from
      naturals, rationals from integers, homology from chains, projective space from vector space.
      Recognising when to quotient is recognising what the problem is really about.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify which distinctions between your objects are irrelevant.]
    next[Define the equivalence relation precisely.]
    next[Check that your operations respect the equivalence.]

fields.how: own mechanism: Transform your problem until it matches the hypothesis of a known theorem, then invoke it. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text: You want to prove a result and suspect it follows from something already established.

IF.text:
The conclusion you need resembles the conclusion of a known theorem, but the hypotheses
      do not quite match your setup.

HOWEVER.text:
Forcing a reduction to the wrong theorem produces fragile, unenlightening proofs. The
      reduction step must be natural, not a contortion.

THEN.text:
Identify the candidate theorem. Compare its hypotheses to your situation. Bridge the gap:
      verify missing hypotheses, apply a change of variables, restrict to a subcase, or
      reformulate to match. Then invoke the theorem.

BECAUSE.text:
Mathematics is cumulative. The power of a proof is proportional to the depth of the results
      it can invoke. "By Theorem X" is the most efficient move in mathematics when X genuinely
      applies.

next[Identify which known result has the conclusion you need.]
    next[Compare hypotheses: what is missing or different?]
    next[Bridge the gap or choose a different target theorem.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When you must control an aggregate of many pieces, engineer the pieces so their supports are disjoint (or independent) — then the cross-terms vanish and the global property collapses to a per-piece one. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You are building or analysing a sum, union, product, or family of objects, and the
    difficulty is that the pieces could interact (overlap, interfere, correlate).

IF.text:
You have freedom in how to construct the pieces (you are exhibiting a witness, or you may
      choose the decomposition), and a hard global property (uniform convergence, a norm bound, a
      probability, an independence) would become trivial if the pieces did not overlap or correlate.

HOWEVER.text:
Independence must be *earned*, not assumed. You must verify the supports really are disjoint
      (or the events really are independent), and that disjointness actually delivers the aggregate
      property you need — e.g. that at most one piece is active at each point, so the aggregate
      reduces to a supremum/sum over single pieces with no cross-terms.

THEN.text:
Arrange the construction so the pieces occupy disjoint regions (separated intervals, orthogonal
      subspaces, independent coordinates, disjoint cycles). Reduce the global quantity to a per-piece
      quantity using disjointness, then bound or compute piece by piece.

BECAUSE.text:
This is the constructive dual of local-to-global: rather than patch overlapping pieces and pay
      for the overlaps, you design the overlaps away so no patching is needed. It recurs everywhere —
      disjointly-supported bump functions, orthogonal vectors, independent random variables, disjoint
      cycles in a permutation, almost-disjoint families — because non-interference turns an aggregate
      problem into a pointwise one.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the freedom you have in choosing the pieces.]
    next[Make the supports disjoint (or the components independent) by construction.]
    next[Verify the disjointness, and that it reduces the global property to a per-piece one.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When a single argument cannot handle all situations, partition into cases and handle each one. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You are trying to prove a statement that behaves differently depending on some
    condition or parameter value.

IF.text:
The objects or hypotheses fall into a finite number of qualitatively different types,
      and the proof technique that works for one type fails for another.

HOWEVER.text:
Too many cases make a proof unreadable and suggest you are missing a unifying idea.
      If you find yourself with more than 3-4 cases, consider whether a different approach
      (symmetry, abstraction, contradiction) would eliminate the case split entirely.

THEN.text:
Identify the exhaustive partition. Prove the result separately for each case. Verify
      the cases are exhaustive (no gaps) and handle any overlap. Common splits: positive/
      negative/zero, finite/infinite, convergent/divergent, trivial/non-trivial.

BECAUSE.text:
Case analysis is often the simplest proof strategy available, even if not the most
      elegant. Many results in combinatorics, number theory, and real analysis require it
      because the underlying structure genuinely behaves differently in different regimes.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the natural partition of your domain or hypothesis.]
    next[Verify the cases are exhaustive.]
    next[Prove each case, noting where the proof differs.]

fields.how: own mechanism: Give a complete intrinsic description of an object — what it is, in terms of simpler structures or invariants — rather than asserting properties about it. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
An object (an algebra, a representation, a measure, a group
    action, a category) has been defined or is the focus of attention. The
    paper's contribution is to *say what the object is* in a complete sense:
    as a quotient, as a fibration, as a tensor product, as a module over a
    smaller object, etc. — typically with a uniqueness or universality
    statement.

IF.text:
You have an object X about which existing results give partial
      information (some properties, some bounds, some examples), and you can
      identify a description of X that is *complete*: another object Y plus a
      construction such that X is exactly built from Y by that construction.

HOWEVER.text:
Structural characterization differs from `find-the-right-abstraction` in
      direction: that pattern abstracts from many examples to a unifying
      framework; this pattern starts with one object and resolves it into
      simpler components. It also differs from `exhaustion-as-theorem`: that
      lists all instances of a type, this describes one instance fully. Choose
      this leaf when the deliverable is *one* full description, not a list.

THEN.text:
1. Identify the simpler components from which X can be built (Y plus a
         construction).
      2. Establish the construction rigorously, with whatever
         uniqueness / universality clauses are appropriate.
      3. Verify the structural identification by re-deriving known
         properties of X from the new description.

BECAUSE.text:
A complete structural description of an object is the strongest
      possible characterization: it lets every property of X be derived from
      properties of Y plus the construction. When such a description exists,
      it is essentially always more useful than a list of properties, because
      it tells you why the properties hold.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the simpler structure Y and the construction that yields X.]
      next[State the structural identity precisely (with uniqueness / universal property).]
      next[Re-derive known properties of X from the identification.]

fields.how: own mechanism: Establish that two structures are structurally identical at the level of the relevant invariants — typically by exhibiting a bidirectional map (an isomorphism, an equivalence of categories, or a biduality) and verifying that the relevant operations transport across. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Two structures X and Y are in view, often arising from
    different definitions or different settings (e.g., a cohomology
    constructed combinatorially and one constructed algebraically; a
    representation-theoretic invariant and a topological invariant). The
    paper's contribution is to show *they are the same thing*, in a
    structural sense.

IF.text:
You can construct maps X → Y and Y → X and verify they are mutually
      inverse, *and* both maps preserve the operations / morphisms / metrics
      that the equivalence is supposed to preserve.

HOWEVER.text:
Structural equivalence is symmetric. It differs from
      `transport-across-isomorphism`: that pattern *uses* a known
      isomorphism to transfer a result; this pattern *establishes* a new
      structural identity. It also differs from `structural-inclusion`:
      that is directional; this is bidirectional. Use this leaf when the
      paper's contribution is a new equivalence.

THEN.text:
1. Construct both directions of the equivalence.
      2. Verify they are mutually inverse (or mutually quasi-inverse, in the
         categorical case).
      3. Verify preservation of the structural features of interest.
      4. State the equivalence as a theorem; identify what consequences

fields.how: own mechanism: Show that one structure contains, embeds into, or is dominated by another — with directional preservation of the relevant invariants. Strictly weaker than equivalence; strictly stronger than mere correlation. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Two structures X and Y are in view, and the paper's contribution
    is to establish that X is contained in Y (in some structural sense), or
    that an invariant on X is dominated by the analogous invariant on Y, or
    that X embeds as a sub-object of Y.

IF.text:
You can construct an order-preserving / structure-preserving map
      X → Y, or argue that the unit ball / minimal class / norm of X is
      contained in that of Y, with directional rather than symmetric
      content.

HOWEVER.text:
Structural inclusion differs from `transport-across-isomorphism`: that
      pattern is symmetric (X ≅ Y); this pattern is directional (X ⊆ Y but
      not necessarily Y ⊆ X). Inclusion alone is weaker but often more
      useful in practice — many monotonicity results carry strict inclusion
      that no equivalence can replicate. Use this leaf when the relation is
      genuinely one-way.

THEN.text:
1. Identify the inclusion / embedding / domination map and verify it
         preserves the structural feature of interest.
      2. Verify that the inclusion is strict (or note explicitly when it is
         tight / non-strict).
      3. Identify the consequence: what holds for X because it holds for Y,
         or what fails to hold because the reverse inclusion does not.

BECAUSE.text:
Inclusion / monotonicity statements are the workhorses of comparison:
      they let one transfer results from a well-understood object to a less-
      understood one, or rule out behaviour by appeal to a containing
      structure. Cobordism, norm-domination, lattice-embedding, and
      sub-representation arguments all live here.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Construct the structural map and verify directional preservation.]
      next[Determine whether the inclusion is strict or tight.]
      next[Identify the property of X that this inclusion gives access to.]

fields.keywords: diagonal, diagonalise, enumerate, surjection, cardinality, self-reference, Cantor, Goedel, fixed-point
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). fields.how: own mechanism: Defeat any purported enumeration by constructing an object that differs from every item on the list. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You want to show that a collection is too large to be listed, or that a certain
    map cannot be surjective.

IF.text:
Someone claims a surjection or enumeration exists from a countable (or smaller) set onto
      a larger one, and the objects in the target can be defined pointwise.

HOWEVER.text:
The diagonal construction requires the ability to "flip" or modify the diagonal entry. Not
      all settings admit this. The argument also only gives non-existence; it does not say how
      much larger the target is.

THEN.text:
Given the purported list f(1), f(2), ..., construct an object d that differs from f(n) at
      position n for every n. Since d differs from every listed item, d is not on the list,
      contradicting surjectivity.

BECAUSE.text:
Cantor's diagonal argument is one of the most fertile ideas in mathematics, spawning
      Goedel's incompleteness theorems, Turing's halting problem, Russell's paradox, and the
      Lawvere fixed-point theorem. The same pattern recurs whenever self-reference meets totality.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the purported enumeration or surjection.]
    next[Construct the diagonal object.]
    next[Verify it genuinely differs from every listed item.]

fields.keywords: isomorphism, transport, transfer, equivalent, identify, same, canonical, natural

fields.how: own mechanism: Prove something in one setting, then transport the result to an isomorphic setting for free. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You need to prove a property of an object X, and there is an isomorphic object Y
    where the property is already known or easier to establish.

IF.text:
X and Y are connected by an isomorphism (or equivalence) in the relevant category, and
      the property you care about is invariant under isomorphism.

HOWEVER.text:
You must verify that the property is indeed isomorphism-invariant. Not all properties
      transfer: a specific element, an embedding into a particular ambient space, or a
      computational representation may not survive transport.

THEN.text:
Establish the isomorphism between X and Y. Prove the property for whichever side is
      easier. Invoke isomorphism-invariance to conclude for the other side. For structured
      settings, use the naturality of the isomorphism.

BECAUSE.text:
"Isomorphic objects are the same for all mathematical purposes" is the fundamental
      principle of abstract mathematics. Transport lets you work in whichever representation
      is most convenient.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Establish the isomorphism or equivalence.]
    next[Verify the property is invariant under it.]
    next[Prove in the easier setting and transport.]

fields.how: own mechanism: When a problem resists direct attack, try a simpler or smaller version first. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text: You are stuck on a problem whose generality or size makes it hard to see what is going on.

IF.text:
The problem involves parameters (dimension, cardinality, degree, number of variables) and no
      direct approach is working.

HOWEVER.text:
Jumping to the simplest case can miss structure that only appears at intermediate complexity,
      and results for small cases do not always generalise.

THEN.text:
Reduce one or more parameters to the smallest non-trivial value. Solve that case. Examine what
      made it work and what would break if the parameter grew. Use the insight to guide the general
      argument.

BECAUSE.text:
Simpler cases reveal the essential mechanism while hiding accidental complexity. Most successful
      general proofs were found by someone who first understood n=2 or dimension 1.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify which parameter to reduce.]
    next[Solve the reduced case completely.]
    next[Articulate what generalises and what does not.]

context.text: You need to prove or use a property of an object, and the path forward is not clear.

IF.text:
The statement involves a defined concept (compact, continuous, exact, measurable, adjoint)
      and you are treating it as a black box instead of engaging with its content.

HOWEVER.text:
Definitions can unfold into multiple equivalent characterisations, and not all unfoldings
      are equally useful. Choosing the wrong characterisation can make the problem harder.

THEN.text:
Write out the definition of every technical term in the statement. Replace defined terms
      with their meanings. The proof obligation often becomes clear once the definitions are
      fully expanded. If multiple equivalent definitions exist, try each one.

BECAUSE.text:
Most proofs at the textbook level consist of nothing more than carefully unfolding
      definitions. "I don't see how to start" almost always means "I haven't written out
      what the words mean."

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify which terms in the statement are defined concepts.]
    next[Write out each definition fully.]
    next[See which unfolding makes the proof obligation match your tools.]

context.text: You have a conjecture or a definition and want to understand what it really says.

IF.text:
The statement is abstract or involves multiple quantifiers, and you cannot yet see why it
      should be true (or false).

HOWEVER.text:
Examples alone do not prove theorems, and poorly chosen examples can mislead by being too
      special or too symmetric.

THEN.text:
Compute several concrete instances. Choose examples that are generic (not too symmetric),
      that test boundary conditions, and that span different regimes of the parameters. Record
      what each example teaches you about the conjecture.

BECAUSE.text:
Examples are the empirical base of mathematics. A conjecture you cannot verify on a single
      instance is a conjecture you do not understand.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Pick 3-5 examples spanning different regimes.]
    next[Compute each one explicitly.]
    next[Record which features of the examples matter for the conjecture.]

fields.how: own mechanism: Your paper describes what some object or class of objects *is* — not whether one exists, not how it relates to another, but its intrinsic structure. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
An object or class has been singled out, and the question is
    "what does it look like?" — exhaustively (full structural description),
    partially (where it fails some property), in cases (classification), or in
    a sharp regime split (dichotomy).

IF.text:
The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "we describe completely
      the structure of X", or "we classify all instances of X", or "we exhibit
      the regime where X fails property P", or "we show X belongs to one of
      two regimes".

HOWEVER.text:
Characterization is the most populous family in mathematical literature
      (≈ 33 % of papers in our pilot — see
      `futon3/holes/excursions/E-math-prototype-pilot.md` Phase 2). Within it,
      the leaves diverge sharply: full-characterization is positive structural
      content; failure-mode is "where this fails"; classification lists cases;
      dichotomy is the special case of classification with two regimes. The
      analytic moves needed for each leaf are different.

THEN.text:
1. Decide whether the paper aims at full description, partial / failure
         description, an enumeration of cases, or a binary regime split.
      2. Pick the matching leaf member-pattern.
      3. Identify the *witness* of the characterization: what theorem,
         equivalence, or list constitutes the description?

    + EXEMPLAR-PAPERS:
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20815v1]   # Zarankiewicz sharp dichotomy
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20827v1]   # Entropic OT failure-mode
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20787v1]   # Exchange-number complexity
        exemplar[arxiv-math/0603592v1] # KMS classification
        exemplar[arxiv-math/0603593v1] # AFD outer-actions classification

    + MEMBER-PATTERNS:
        member[math-strategy/exhaustion-as-theorem]                 # full / classification
        member[math-strategy/structural-obstruction-as-theorem]     # failure-mode
        member[math-informal/split-into-cases]                      # dichotomy / classification
        member[math-informal/structural-characterization]           # full description (new leaf)
        member[math-informal/failure-mode-characterization]         # failure-regime (new leaf)
        member[math-informal-LO/complexity-classification]             # specific subtype (new leaf)

BECAUSE.text:
Characterization papers do "describing-work" rather than "proving-X-exists"
      or "showing-X-relates-to-Y" work. The family parent serves as a coarse
      classifier; the leaves carry the analytic differences (e.g. dichotomy
      proofs almost always need a phase-transition argument; classification
      proofs need exhaustion).

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Decide whether the characterization is full, partial / failure-mode, classification, or dichotomy.]
      next[Identify the witness — list, theorem, equivalence — that constitutes the description.]
      next[Cross-check: does the paper *prove the characterization is exhaustive*, or only *exhibit examples*?]

context.text:
Your main result follows from several sub-results that can be
    proved independently. The conclusion is a logical composition (conjunction,
    chain of implications, or substitution) of the pieces.

IF.text:
The sub-results address different concerns (existence, uniqueness,
      nontriviality, notation compatibility, etc.) and no sub-result's proof
      depends on another sub-result being true.

HOWEVER.text:
Independence must be genuine, not assumed. If lemma B uses lemma A as
      a hypothesis, they are not independent — B depends on A. The composition
      step must also be checked: it is tempting to wave hands at "combining"
      results when the combination itself requires a non-trivial argument
      (e.g., that two constructions refer to the same object, or that
      hypotheses of one result are satisfied by another).

THEN.text:
(a) Identify the independent pieces. Draw the dependency graph.
      (b) For each piece, verify it is self-contained: its proof uses only its
          own hypotheses and prior results, not sibling lemmas.
      (c) Write the composition step as a separate, explicit argument. It
          should be short — if it is long, one of the pieces is incomplete.
      (d) Check that the composition step does not silently introduce new
          claims. Every assertion in the composition must trace to a piece.

BECAUSE.text:
Modular proofs are easier to review, easier to repair, and easier to
      generalize. When a reviewer finds a gap, modular structure localizes
      the damage: you know which piece is broken and which are unaffected.
      A monolithic proof hides dependencies and makes gaps contagious.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[List the pieces and draw the dependency graph.]
    next[Verify each piece is self-contained.]
    next[Write the composition step. Keep it short.]
    next[Trace every assertion in the composition to its source piece.]

fields.keywords: constraint, tension, conflict, parameter, parity, dimension, resolution, dissolve, construction, obligation, trade-off, structural, incompatible

fields.how: own mechanism: When two parts of a proof impose conflicting requirements on a shared parameter, recognize the conflict as a first-class structural constraint and search for a construction that satisfies both requirements simultaneously — typically by changing the underlying geometric or algebraic object rather than trying to force compatibility within the existing setup. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Your proof decomposes into two or more obligations that share a
    parameter (dimension, codimension, degree, rank, characteristic, etc.). You
    have found a construction that cleanly discharges one obligation but discover
    that the parameter choice it forces creates genuine obstacles for the other.
    The obstacles are not failures of technique but consequences of the parameter
    value itself.

HOWEVER.text:
The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure).
    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - The tension is intrinsic: every construction that satisfies A forces X.
          This is a structural impossibility result — record it.
        - The alternative construction dissolves the original tension but
          introduces a new one. Iterate: apply the pattern again to the new
          tension, or recognize that the problem may require a fundamentally
          different decomposition.
        - The alternative construction exists in principle but no concrete instance
          is known (e.g., "a lattice with an order-2 rotation in Isom(H^n)"
          exists if and only if a number-theoretic condition holds). The pattern
          has done its job — it has reduced the proof to a well-posed existence
          question — but the question remains open.

THEN.text:
1. State the tension precisely: name both obligations, the shared parameter,
         and the conflicting requirements. Write it as a proposition: "For
         construction C, obligations A and B cannot both be satisfied because
         A needs p in X and B needs p in Y."
      2. Determine whether the tension is intrinsic to the problem or specific
         to the construction. Ask: does every construction that satisfies A
         necessarily impose X on p? Or is X an artifact of this particular
         approach?
      3. Search for an alternative construction C' where both obligations are
         compatible — where they both want the same parameter value, or where
         the parameter is no longer constrained. This typically means replacing
         the underlying geometric/algebraic object (e.g., reflection with
         rotation, codimension-1 with codimension-2).
      4. Verify that C' actually satisfies both obligations. The new construction
         may make the previously-easy obligation harder (a legitimate trade-off)
         or may introduce new constraints. Map all obligations against C' before
         committing.
      5. If the tension is intrinsic (no C' exists), record this as a structural
         impossibility result — it constrains the solution space and may redirect
         the entire proof strategy.

    + QUALITY-CRITERIA:
        Well-applied:
          - The tension is stated as a precise proposition with named obligations,
            named parameter, and named conflicting requirements.
          - The investigation distinguishes intrinsic tensions (problem-level) from
            approach-specific tensions (construction-level).
          - The alternative construction is verified against ALL obligations, not
            just the two that were in tension.
          - The resolution is recorded as a structural insight that informs future
            proof design.
        Badly-applied:
          - Declaring tension when the conflict is merely inconvenient, not
            blocking. If obligation B can still be completed with property X
            (just with more work), the tension is a preference, not a structural
            constraint. Do not pivot constructions for preferences.
          - Replacing the construction without checking that the new one actually
            satisfies the previously-easy obligation. The trade-off must be mapped.
          - Tunnel vision: finding an alternative construction that dissolves one
            tension but creates a worse one elsewhere.
          - Treating the tension as a dead end rather than information. Even if no
            resolution exists, the tension statement constrains the solution space
            and is worth recording.

    + WHEN:
        Obligation A requires parameter p to have property X (e.g., n even for
        Euler characteristic vanishing), while obligation B requires property Y
        (e.g., n odd for favorable L-theory parity or equivariant surgery
        availability), and X and Y are incompatible for the current construction.
        The conflict is not aesthetic preference but a genuine blockage: at least
        one obligation cannot be completed with the wrong parity/value.

BECAUSE.text:
Parametric tensions are theorems about the approach, not the problem. When
      an initial construction discharges one obligation "too perfectly" by locking
      in a parameter value, the resulting structural headwinds for other
      obligations are predictable consequences, not bad luck. Recognizing the
      tension early — before investing in heavy machinery to overcome the
      headwinds — saves effort and often reveals a simpler proof architecture.
      The alternative construction that dissolves the tension frequently simplifies
      the entire proof by removing the need for workarounds.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): The proof splits into two
        obligations — E2 (place Gamma in FH(Q) via a finite CW complex with
        rationally acyclic universal cover) and S (upgrade the finite CW complex
        to a closed manifold). The reflection construction in even dimension n
        discharges E2 perfectly: the codimension-1 fixed set has odd dimension,
        so its Euler characteristic vanishes (required by Fowler's criterion).
        But this forces n even, which creates three headwinds for S:
          (a) Equivariant surgery is BLOCKED (Costenoble-Waner gap hypothesis
              fails for codimension-1 fixed sets).
          (b) Wall surgery faces unfavorable even-dimensional L-theory parity.
          (c) No orbifold resolution technique is known.
        The tension statement: "For the reflection construction, E2 needs n even
        and S needs n odd; these are incompatible."
        Resolution: replace the codimension-1 reflection with a codimension-2
        rotation in odd dimension n. The fixed set now has codimension 2 (so the
        equivariant surgery gap hypothesis is satisfied) and odd dimension (so
        L-theory parity is favorable). Both E2 and S want odd n. The tension
        dissolves entirely, and the problem reduces to a single lattice-existence
        question in number theory.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[State the tension as a precise proposition.]
    next[Determine if the tension is intrinsic or construction-specific.]
    next[Search for alternative constructions where conflicting requirements align.]
    next[Verify the alternative against all obligations before committing.]
