fields.title: Finish Defining the Object Before Estimating It
fields.keywords: construction, definition, piecewise, well-definedness, estimates, ordering, totality
fields.why: math-strategy/proof-architecture
fields.how: own mechanism: When a proof needs an object assembled from infinitely many pieces, define the whole object — and prove it well defined — before proving anything about its size. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A construction given by cases over an infinite family: a piecewise
    function on a countable decomposition, a series of bumps, a limit of
    successive approximations, whose purpose is to satisfy an estimate.

IF.text:
The object exists as a total, well-defined thing before any estimate is
      attempted, then the estimate is a statement about a fixed object and can be
      proved by ordinary means — the cases are already reconciled, the overlaps
      already settled, and the estimate quantifies over something that does not
      move.

HOWEVER.text:
The tempting order is the opposite one, because the estimate is what the
      construction is *for*: define the first few pieces, check the bound, and
      let the remaining pieces be whatever makes the bound work. That leaves the
      definition depending on the estimate and the estimate depending on the
      definition, and every subsequent adjustment to one invalidates the other.

      It also hides the real obligations. An infinite piecewise object needs its
      overlaps reconciled and its totality established, and those obligations are
      easy to leave implicit while attention is on the bound. In a formal
      setting they cannot be left implicit at all — a partially specified object
      is not an object — so the interleaved order stalls at a definition that
      will not elaborate, at a point where the estimate is also incomplete and
      neither can be worked on independently.

THEN.text:
Write down the whole construction first, including the behaviour on every
      case and at the boundaries between them. Prove it well defined. Only then
      state and prove the estimate, treating the object as fixed.

      If the estimate then fails, change the construction deliberately and
      re-establish well-definedness — rather than patching the definition inside
      the estimate's proof.

BECAUSE.text:
An estimate is a statement about an object, so it has no content until the
      object exists. Interleaving the two produces an argument in which neither
      half can be checked alone, and the failure mode is not a wrong bound but an
      unfalsifiable one: whatever the estimate needs, the definition can be made
      to supply, and nothing in the proof records that this happened.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Write the construction for every case, including boundaries and overlaps.]
    next[Prove it is well defined and total before stating any estimate.]
    next[State the estimate about the fixed object.]
    next[If the estimate fails, change the construction deliberately and re-prove well-definedness.]

fields.keywords: notation, convention, normalization, starred, unstarred, identify, bridge, factor, cancel, ratio

fields.how: own mechanism: When two notational conventions refer to the same mathematical object (or differ by a known factor), make the identification explicit and prove it. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Your argument needs to connect results stated in different notational
    conventions — e.g., starred vs unstarred polynomials, different normalization
    choices, author-specific definitions of the same concept.

IF.text:
Two sources use different notation for what you believe is the same object,
      and your conclusion depends on equating them (or showing their ratio cancels).

HOWEVER.text:
Convention differences are a common source of silent errors. What looks like
      "the same thing with different notation" may hide a genuine mathematical
      difference — a constant factor, a domain restriction, or an implicit
      specialization that does not always hold. Asserting equivalence without proof
      is precisely where reviewers find gaps.

THEN.text:
(a) State both conventions precisely, with citations.
      (b) Write the explicit relationship: A* = c · A, or A* = f(A), giving the
          transformation.
      (c) Prove the relationship holds in your parameter regime (e.g., q=1, x_i>0).
      (d) If the relationship is well-known, cite the specific proposition — do not
          write "it is well known that."
      (e) If only cancellation in a ratio matters, prove that the bridging factor
          is state-independent.

BECAUSE.text:
Notation bridges that seem trivial to the author are the #1 source of
      reviewer objections in proofs that invoke external results. The five minutes
      spent making the bridge explicit saves weeks of back-and-forth. The bridge
      itself may reveal constraints you missed.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Write both conventions side by side.]
    next[Identify the bridging factor or transformation.]
    next[Prove or cite the relationship in your parameter regime.]
    next[Check that the bridge holds at boundary cases (t→0, t→1, n=2).]

  When two notational conventions refer to the same mathematical object (or differ
  by a known factor), make the identification explicit and prove it.

  + context: Your argument needs to connect results stated in different notational
    conventions — e.g., starred vs unstarred polynomials, different normalization
    choices, author-specific definitions of the same concept.

  + IF:
      Two sources use different notation for what you believe is the same object,
      and your conclusion depends on equating them (or showing their ratio cancels).

  + HOWEVER:
      Convention differences are a common source of silent errors. What looks like
      "the same thing with different notation" may hide a genuine mathematical
      difference — a constant factor, a domain restriction, or an implicit
      specialization that does not always hold. Asserting equivalence without proof
      is precisely where reviewers find gaps.

  + THEN:
      (a) State both conventions precisely, with citations.
      (b) Write the explicit relationship: A* = c · A, or A* = f(A), giving the
          transformation.
      (c) Prove the relationship holds in your parameter regime (e.g., q=1, x_i>0).
      (d) If the relationship is well-known, cite the specific proposition — do not
          write "it is well known that."
      (e) If only cancellation in a ratio matters, prove that the bridging factor
          is state-independent.

  + BECAUSE:
      Notation bridges that seem trivial to the author are the #1 source of
      reviewer objections in proofs that invoke external results. The five minutes
      spent making the bridge explicit saves weeks of back-and-forth. The bridge
      itself may reveal constraints you missed.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Write both conventions side by side.]
    next[Identify the bridging factor or transformation.]
    next[Prove or cite the relationship in your parameter regime.]
    next[Check that the bridge holds at boundary cases (t→0, t→1, n=2).]

fields.title: Trust the Corpus Per Artifact, and Record What You Consulted
fields.keywords: corpus, trust, vacuity, domain-guard, stale-label, attribution, consultation, non-use, invariant, provenance
fields.why: math-strategy/non-circularity-check
fields.how: own mechanism: A statement, a label, or a prior result is trustworthy only as far as it has been checked — so audit the artifact you are about to build on, and record what you consulted and what you did with it, including what you discarded. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Work that stands on a corpus someone else produced — problem
    statements, compiled neighbours, "blocked" labels, surfaced memories, prior
    agents' claims about what they used — where the corpus is large enough that
    re-deriving everything is impossible and taking it on faith is how false
    results propagate.

IF.text:
The artifact has been checked at the level you are relying on it, then it
      is a foundation and re-deriving it is waste. Compiled neighbours are the
      cheapest source of formal machinery, and searching them before rebuilding
      is almost always the shorter route.

HOWEVER.text:
A formal statement can be false or vacuous while its prose is correct. The
      prose states the intended finite or regular regime; the formal hypotheses
      still admit a zero or top witness, and the theorem then proves nothing at
      the cost of looking proved. Audit operation domains and inferred binder
      types before attempting the advertised analysis.

      Type compatibility is not semantic connection. Over a bundled problem
      structure, enumerated data and derived counts can typecheck against each
      other with no invariant linking them, and axiom-clean helper proofs will
      not supply one. Every semantic transition in the informal argument needs a
      formal invariant, or the theorem is about two unrelated fields that happen
      to fit.

      Labels decay. A "blocked" marker records the library as it was at some
      revision; verify it against the current library before treating it as a
      fact about the present. The same applies to `-- not in Mathlib` comments
      and to any hole accounting taken from a file that has not been elaborated
      under its real build.

      Attribution decays fastest of all, because nothing forces it. An agent that
      reports its work without per-memory USED/IGNORED verdicts leaves no way to
      tell a memory that helped from one that merely surfaced — and the repeated
      correction of exactly this omission is what this pattern is largely made of.

THEN.text:
Audit before building: check domain guards and inferred binder types, and
      look for the invariant that links each pair of fields the informal argument
      moves between.

      When a statement is false, do not silently fix it. Pair a machine-checked
      counterexample with a machine-checked repaired sibling and preserve the
      original target as an explicit unresolved defect — that triple is the
      cheapest artifact a reviewer can act on.

      Search solved neighbours before building machinery, and repeat bounded
      reconnaissance after selecting a route, this time with the obstacle
      vocabulary the route exposed.

      Record every consultation with its outcome and its reason: what the
      resource returned, and why it was used or discarded. Give per-memory
      USED/IGNORED verdicts. Reasoned non-use is a first-class result; an
      unrecorded consultation is indistinguishable from one that never happened.

BECAUSE.text:
A corpus is only worth building on if its claims degrade gracefully, and
      claims degrade gracefully only when their basis is recorded. A vacuous
      theorem, a stale label, and an unattributed use all fail the same way: they
      look like evidence, they cost nothing to produce, and the next reader
      cannot distinguish them from the real thing without redoing the work. The
      protocol is cheap precisely where the failure is expensive — at the moment
      of consultation, when you still know what you looked at and why.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Audit domain guards and binder types before relying on a formal statement.]
    next[Find the invariant linking each pair of fields the informal argument moves between.]
    next[For a false statement, ship counterexample + repaired sibling + the original as an open defect.]
    next[Verify stale blocked/absent labels against the current library.]
    next[Search compiled neighbours before rebuilding machinery.]
    next[Repeat reconnaissance after route selection, with the obstacle vocabulary.]
    next[Record each consultation's outcome and reason; give per-memory USED/IGNORED verdicts.]

fields.title: Exhaustion as Theorem
fields.keywords: exhaust, technique, class, wall, barrier, fundamental, ceiling, quadratic, linear, scaling, sublinear, impossible, family
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When multiple approaches to the same proof step all fail at the same quantitative barrier, prove that the barrier is fundamental to the technique class, not an artifact of any individual approach. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You have tried several methods for a proof step (concentration inequalities,
    subsampling arguments, spectral bounds, etc.) and each gives a bound that is too weak
    by the same qualitative amount. The failure pattern is suspiciously consistent.

IF.text:
Three or more techniques from the same family (e.g., "subsample and concentrate,"
      "bound trace then convert to operator norm," "linearize the quadratic term") all
      fail at the same quantitative step, producing bounds with the same scaling deficiency.

HOWEVER.text:
Consistent failure might be coincidence rather than structure. Before declaring the
      barrier fundamental, verify that the techniques genuinely span the family — not just
      three variants of the same idea. Also check whether a technique outside the family
      avoids the barrier entirely.

    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - Premature exhaustion claim: the family is not actually exhausted. Check that new
          techniques outside the family avoid the barrier.
        - Overgeneralization: "no concentration argument can work" when the ceiling only
          applies to trace-based certification. Scope the barrier precisely.

THEN.text:
1. Identify the common quantitative step where all techniques fail.
      2. Formulate the barrier as a theorem: "any technique in class C that proceeds via
         step X produces a bound of at most f(n)" where f(n) is weaker than the target.
      3. Prove the ceiling theorem (often by exhibiting a worst case for step X).
      4. Record the ceiling as a lemma. It eliminates the technique class and redirects
         effort toward techniques outside the class.

BECAUSE.text:
A proved ceiling theorem is qualitatively different from "we tried 6 things and they
      didn't work." It converts empirical failure into structural understanding: the barrier
      is not a failure of ingenuity but a consequence of the technique class's structure.
      This prevents future revisitation ("maybe if we try the 7th variant...") and focuses
      effort on genuinely different approaches.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P6 epsilon-light subsets (futon6, Feb 2026): 6 subsample-and-concentrate techniques
        (trace/Markov, star domination, decoupling+MSS 1-shot, decoupling+MSS recursive,
        greedy/chromatic, rank spreading) all hit the quadratic-vs-linear scaling wall:
        spectral contribution scales as q² while set size scales as q. The trace-only ceiling
        was proved as a lemma (Step 1), eliminating the entire technique class and redirecting
        toward operator-norm-aware barrier greedy (a technique outside the class).

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[List all techniques tried and their failure points.]
    next[Identify the common quantitative step.]
    next[Prove the ceiling theorem for the technique class.]
    next[Search for techniques outside the class that avoid the ceiling.]

fields.title: Existence-Result Family
fields.keywords: existence, exhibit, construction, realisation, demonstration, witness, family-parent
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: Your paper shows that an object of a desired class exists. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A class of objects has been defined or implied; whether the class
    is non-empty (or contains an instance with specified properties) is the
    salient question of the paper.

IF.text:
The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "we show there is an
      X satisfying Y", or "we construct an X satisfying Y", or "for every
      precondition P there is an X with property Q".

HOWEVER.text:
"Existence" admits many depths: pure-classical (object exists by an
      abstract argument), constructive (an explicit witness is exhibited),
      with-error-bounds (a witness is exhibited with quantitative tolerance),
      via-cross-domain-bridge (existence transferred from a different domain).
      The depth determines downstream usefulness — a theorem prover wants a
      constructive witness, an applied mathematician may need error bounds, a
      structuralist may accept abstract existence. Pick the leaf that matches
      the depth your paper actually reaches.

THEN.text:
1. Identify the depth: pure-classical / constructive / with-error-bounds /
         via-bridge.
      2. Locate the leaf member-pattern that matches the depth.
      3. Identify the witness that the paper exhibits (or argues exists).
      4. State explicitly what the witness shows and which preconditions
         determine it.

    + EXEMPLAR-PAPERS:
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.21888v1]   # Kneser graph Hamilton cycle exists
        exemplar[arxiv-math/0603597v1] # Gevrey ultardistribution algebras (constructive)
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20840v1]   # Z/2-harmonic forms via 4-polytopes (constructive)

    + MEMBER-PATTERNS:
        member[math-informal/construct-an-explicit-witness]      # constructive
        member[math-informal/construct-auxiliary-object]         # constructive (indirect)
        member[math-informal-CO/use-probabilistic-method]           # pure-classical / non-constructive
        member[math-informal-NA/numerical-scout]                    # with-error-bounds (hint of construction)

BECAUSE.text:
Existence claims are the load-bearing skeleton of much of mathematical
      research, but they vary enormously in their constructive content. Putting
      the family parent above its members lets pattern-classification (manual
      or automated) recognise an existence-paper at family granularity even
      when the leaf depth is uncertain, then refine to the leaf when more
      detail is available. The family is the *useful coarse classifier*; the
      leaf is the *precise depth*.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Determine the existence depth and pick the matching leaf.]
      next[Identify the witness explicitly (object + precondition for it).]
      next[Cross-check: does the paper *exhibit* the witness, or only *argue* one exists?]

fields.title: Hypothesis Category Check
fields.keywords: category, smooth, PL, topological, algebraic, scheme, variety, hypothesis, mismatch, regularity, bridge
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When invoking a theorem, verify that your objects live in the category (smooth, PL, topological, algebraic, measurable, ...) that the theorem is stated for. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You want to apply a known result to objects in your proof,
    and the result's statement specifies regularity or categorical
    hypotheses on its inputs.

IF.text:
The theorem you want to invoke is stated for objects in category C
      (e.g., smooth manifolds, algebraic varieties, measurable functions),
      and your objects live in a different category C' (e.g., PL complexes,
      schemes, continuous functions).

HOWEVER.text:
Category mismatches are a common source of silent errors in proofs
      that cross domain boundaries. A theorem about smooth Lagrangian
      intersections does not apply to polyhedral creases. A result about
      algebraic varieties may fail for general schemes. The mismatch may
      be bridgeable (via a smoothing lemma, GAGA, regularity bootstrap)
      but the bridge itself requires proof.

THEN.text:
(a) State the category of the theorem's hypotheses explicitly.
      (b) State the category of your objects explicitly.
      (c) If they differ, provide a bridge: a smoothing lemma, a
          regularity result, a comparison theorem, or a specialization
          argument that places your objects in the required category.
      (d) If no bridge exists, the theorem does not apply -- find an
          alternative or prove a new version in your category.

BECAUSE.text:
Cross-category theorem application is one of the most common gaps
      in proofs that invoke external results. The fix is mechanical:
      check the fine print. The cost of checking is minutes; the cost
      of not checking is a critical reviewer finding.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[State the theorem's category explicitly.]
    next[State your objects' category explicitly.]
    next[If they differ: prove a bridge or find an alternative.]
    next[Check boundary cases where category differences bite hardest.]

      (a) State the category of the theorem's hypotheses explicitly.
      (b) State the category of your objects explicitly.
      (c) If they differ, provide a bridge: a smoothing lemma, a

          alternative or prove a new version in your category.

      check the fine print. The cost of checking is minutes; the cost
      of not checking is a critical reviewer finding.

    next[State your objects' category explicitly.]

fields.title: Localize a Missing Dependency, Don't Rebuild Around It
fields.keywords: dependency, gap, sorry, absence-claim, search-scope, adapter, terrain-gap, proof-hole, curriculum-signal
fields.why: math-informal/reduce-to-known-result
fields.how: own mechanism: When a proof stalls because the library appears to lack a theorem, first establish that the gap is real, then localize it at exactly one `sorry` and write beside it what you searched and what is left to build. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Formalizing against a large library, where the argument is
    substantially complete and one bridge is missing — and where the cheap moves
    are to rebuild the missing piece, to spread `sorry`s across the file, or to
    declare "not in Mathlib" on the strength of one failed search.

IF.text:
The gap is real and bounded — the surrounding argument closes and only one
      named bridge is absent — then the missing dependency is a *deliverable*
      rather than a defeat. It can be written as a signature, searched for once
      more with the library's own vocabulary, and either imported from work
      already in flight or built as its own piece of work with its own gate.

HOWEVER.text:
An absence claim is only as strong as the index actually searched. A
      promoted-store fetch plus a single-lane grep cannot establish absence
      across unpromoted drafts in other lanes, and a `-- not in Mathlib` comment
      is a revision-scoped search claim someone once made, not a fact about the
      library. Scope every absence claim to what was searched.

      An empty recall is more often a malformed query than a gap in the terrain.
      Diagnose the query — vocabulary, namespace, the installed source rather
      than the index — before concluding the theorem does not exist. Repeatedly
      the theorem was present under a different interface, and the work needed
      was an adapter, not a construction. Bound that heuristic too: some gaps
      really are construction, and treating every one as an adapter search is the
      mirror failure.

      Once stalled, the tempting work is the easy leaves. Polish spent on leaves
      that depend on a missing assembler is wasted twice — once in the doing, and
      again when the assembler forces the shape to change. Probe the high-risk
      assembly dependency first, and inventory what the assembly needs before
      descending into any leaf.

      A lexical `sorry` count is not a proof-hole count, and a file that does not
      elaborate cannot be measured at all. Relocating a `sorry` to make a file
      read cleaner is honest only when what remains is an axiom-clean partial.

      The cheapest wrong outcome is a theorem that discharges the claim without
      proving it. Placeholder definitions and vacuous hypotheses make hard
      results look inexpensive. When a proof closes far more cheaply than its
      prose, its cited dependencies, or the known library frontier suggest,
      inspect the definitions and the binding structure before believing it.

THEN.text:
Search once more against the installed source with the library's naming
      conventions, and look for an adapter to an existing theorem before
      building. Scope whatever absence you then claim to the index you searched.

      State the missing theorem as a signature. Put exactly one `sorry` at the
      observed gap — not spread, not relocated — and preflight the file's
      elaboration under its real build before counting holes at all, separating
      dependency-build failures from source-statement failures.

      Beside that `sorry`, leave the consultation trail: the bridge that is
      needed, the nearest existing API, the searches that came back empty, and
      the routes still open. Name the residual explicitly so the completed half
      is not rebuilt — "the circle identity is done; what remains is the measure-
      theoretic bridge from circle averages to disk area."

      Record repeated empty recalls as curriculum signal rather than as private
      frustration, record surfaced-but-unrelated memories as honest non-use, and
      stop researching once the misses repeat.

BECAUSE.text:
A missing dependency is the one kind of blocker that is cheap to describe
      and expensive to guess at, so the whole value of the stall is the
      information it carries: precisely which theorem the library lacks, in a
      form someone else can act on. That information survives only if the gap is
      localized and written down where the next reader will stand. A proof spread
      over five `sorry`s under a "not in Mathlib" comment records nothing — the
      next agent repeats the same search, reaches the same wall, and adds a sixth.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Diagnose the query before declaring the terrain: vocabulary, namespace, installed source.]
    next[Look for an adapter to an existing theorem before building a new one.]
    next[State the missing theorem as a signature.]
    next[Put exactly one sorry at the observed gap; preflight elaboration before counting holes.]
    next[Leave the bridge, the nearest API, the empty searches and the open routes beside it.]
    next[Scope every absence claim to the index actually searched.]
    next[Record repeated empty recalls as curriculum signal, and stop after the misses repeat.]

fields.title: Non-Circularity Check
fields.keywords: nontrivial, circular, independence, construction, target, bootstrap, witness
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When you construct an object to witness an existence claim, verify that the construction does not secretly depend on the thing you are trying to prove exists. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You are proving "there exists X with property P" by exhibiting a
    concrete X. The construction uses ingredients (parameters, formulas, prior
    results) that might implicitly assume P already holds.

IF.text:
Your construction involves the same mathematical objects that appear in the
      target property (e.g., building a Markov chain whose stationary distribution
      involves certain polynomials, using transition rates that might depend on
      those same polynomials).

HOWEVER.text:
Not all apparent circularity is real. A construction may use the same
      *notation* as the target without logical dependence — the transition rates
      may be defined purely from combinatorial data, even though the stationary
      distribution involves special functions. The check must be precise about
      what "depends on" means.

THEN.text:
(a) List every ingredient of the construction (parameters, rates, rules).
      (b) For each ingredient, trace its definition: does it reference the
          target property or the objects whose existence you claim?
      (c) If yes: either restructure the construction to remove the dependence,
          or prove that the dependence is only apparent (e.g., the formula
          simplifies to something independent).
      (d) State the non-circularity explicitly in the proof ("note that the
          transition rates depend only on x, t, and the current configuration,
          not on values of F*_μ").

BECAUSE.text:
Circularity in existence proofs is subtle and common. The most dangerous
      form is a construction that "works" only because it smuggles the
      conclusion into the premises. Reviewers trained in constructive mathematics
      will spot this; the rest will be misled. An explicit non-circularity
      statement inoculates the proof.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[List all ingredients of the construction.]
    next[Trace each ingredient to its definition.]
    next[Flag any that reference the target property.]
    next[Resolve or state the independence explicitly.]

context.text:
A difficult proof has enough moving parts that local hints can pull
    the attempt from one obligation to another without preserving an architecture.

HOWEVER.text:
A plan is a working hypothesis, not a contract. Preserve revisions
    in the artifact, and do not defend a step after its assumptions fail.

THEN.text:
State the lemma-sized steps first, record their dependencies, prove in
    that order, and update the written plan whenever compilation or mathematics
    exposes a missing or false step. Guidance should address the process and the
    plan's gaps rather than silently supplying mathematical content.

BECAUSE.text:
A visible, revisable plan makes progress and failed assumptions
    inspectable while preventing guidance from replacing the solver's architecture.

next[Write the numbered lemma plan.]
    next[Mark dependencies and the first executable step.]
    next[Revise the plan in place when an assumption fails.]

fields.title: Preemptive Objection Clearance
fields.keywords: objection, anti-obstruction, defensive, Smith-theory, clearance, preemptive, does-not-apply, non-obstruction, challenge, dismiss, ground-clearing
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When a natural objection or potential obstruction exists against your construction, include an explicit defensive section showing that the objection does NOT apply — and clearly distinguish this "ground-clearing" move from a constructive contribution to the proof. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You have a proof architecture with constructive steps that build
    toward a conclusion. A knowledgeable reader would naturally ask: "But
    doesn't X obstruct this?" where X is a well-known theorem, phenomenon, or
    structural concern in the relevant domain. If you leave this question
    unanswered, the reader (or reviewer) will either (a) assume you overlooked
    it, or (b) spend effort checking it themselves. Either outcome weakens the
    proof's persuasive force.

HOWEVER.text:
The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure).
    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - The objection DOES apply, and the defensive section is wrong. This is
          worse than not including it — it signals overconfidence. Before writing
          the section, verify the non-applicability rigorously.
        - The objection is partially applicable: it constrains the construction
          in ways that are compatible with the conclusion but impose additional
          conditions. In this case, state the partial constraint honestly rather
          than dismissing the objection entirely.
        - The objection is well-known enough that addressing it feels patronizing
          to expert readers. Judgment call: if the proof is written for a broad
          audience or a review process, include it. If for a specialist seminar,
          a brief remark may suffice.

THEN.text:
1. Identify the natural objection explicitly: name the theorem, phenomenon,
         or structural concern. State what it would imply if it applied.
      2. Show precisely why it does not apply to your setting. This typically
         involves identifying a hypothesis of the obstructing result that fails
         in your context, or showing that the obstruction operates over a
         different coefficient ring / category / parameter regime.
      3. Mark the section clearly as defensive (anti-obstruction, ground-clearing,
         challenge-and-dismiss) rather than constructive. In a wiring diagram,
         this is a "challenge" edge, not an "assert" or "clarify" edge.
      4. State the conclusion of the defensive section precisely: "X does not
         obstruct our construction because hypothesis H fails in our setting"
         — not "X is not a problem" (too vague) and not "X actually helps us"
         (overclaiming, unless it genuinely does).

    + QUALITY-CRITERIA:
        Well-applied:
          - The objection is named explicitly (not "some might worry that...").
          - The non-applicability argument is precise: it identifies the specific
            hypothesis or condition that fails, not just a general sense that
            the objection is irrelevant.
          - The section is clearly marked as defensive / ground-clearing, distinct
            from constructive proof steps.
          - The conclusion states what the objection does NOT do, without
            overclaiming that it provides positive support.
          - In a wiring diagram, the section appears as a "challenge" edge (not
            "assert" or "clarify").
        Badly-applied:
          - Conflating anti-obstruction with construction: claiming that the
            absence of obstruction is evidence FOR the conclusion. "Smith theory
            doesn't obstruct" is not the same as "Smith theory supports."
          - Vague dismissal: "this is not a problem" without explaining why the
            objection fails. This invites the very reviewer finding the pattern
            is meant to prevent.
          - Addressing phantom objections: including defensive sections for
            objections that no competent reader would raise. This wastes space
            and suggests insecurity about the argument.
          - Missing the real objection: including a defensive section for one
            concern while overlooking a more serious natural objection. Survey
            the likely objections before choosing which to address.
          - Burying the defensive section: placing it inline within constructive
            steps so that its ground-clearing role is invisible. Give it its own
            section or clearly delimited subsection.

    + WHEN:
        There exists a well-known result, technique, or structural phenomenon that
        a competent reader would reasonably expect to obstruct your construction or
        conclusion. The objection is natural enough that NOT addressing it would be
        a gap in the argument. Importantly, the objection turns out to be
        inapplicable — it does not actually obstruct — but this non-applicability
        is not obvious and requires argument.

BECAUSE.text:
Proofs operate on two levels: logical validity (does the argument hold?)
      and rhetorical completeness (are foreseeable objections addressed?). A
      proof that is logically valid but leaves obvious objections unaddressed
      invites reviewer findings and erodes confidence. The defensive section
      costs little to include but removes a predictable source of doubt.
      Moreover, the act of checking the objection often yields structural
      insight — understanding WHY the obstruction fails clarifies the
      construction's strengths and limitations.

      Critically, the defensive section must be honest about its role. It does
      not contribute constructive content to the proof — it clears ground. If
      it is conflated with constructive steps, readers may mistakenly believe
      the anti-obstruction result provides positive evidence for the conclusion,
      when it only removes a potential counterargument.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): Section 5 of the proof
        addresses Smith theory — a well-known tool that constrains fixed-point
        sets of group actions on manifolds. A reader familiar with the area would
        naturally ask: "Doesn't Smith theory obstruct a manifold with the
        claimed properties?" The answer is no: Smith theory operates over F_p
        (finite field coefficients) and constrains mod-p homology, while the
        construction only claims rational acyclicity (Q-coefficients). The
        Smith-theoretic constraints on mod-p Betti numbers are compatible with
        rational acyclicity.
        This section appears as a "challenge" edge (s5 -> problem) in the wiring
        diagram — the only non-constructive edge in the 9-edge graph. Reviewer
        Finding 4 (medium severity) noted that this section's role as
        anti-obstruction-only needed to be clearer: the original draft risked
        being read as if Smith theory positively supported the construction,
        when it merely does not obstruct it. A well-applied instance of this
        pattern would have prevented Finding 4 by explicitly marking the section
        as defensive and stating "Smith theory does not obstruct (but does not
        help construct)" rather than leaving the reader to infer the distinction.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[List natural objections a competent reader would raise against the construction.]
    next[For each, determine: does it apply? If not, identify the failing hypothesis.]
    next[Write a clearly-marked defensive section for each non-trivial non-applicability.]
    next[Verify the defensive argument is correct before including it.]

      2. Show precisely why it does not apply to your setting. This typically
         involves identifying a hypothesis of the obstructing result that fails
         in your context, or showing that the obstruction operates over a
         different coefficient ring / category / parameter regime.
      3. Mark the section clearly as defensive (anti-obstruction, ground-clearing,
         challenge-and-dismiss) rather than constructive. In a wiring diagram,
         this is a "challenge" edge, not an "assert" or "clarify" edge.
      4. State the conclusion of the defensive section precisely: "X does not
         obstruct our construction because hypothesis H fails in our setting"
         — not "X is not a problem" (too vague) and not "X actually helps us"
         (overclaiming, unless it genuinely does).

    + QUALITY-CRITERIA:
        Well-applied:
          - The objection is named explicitly (not "some might worry that...").
          - The non-applicability argument is precise: it identifies the specific
            hypothesis or condition that fails, not just a general sense that
            the objection is irrelevant.
          - The section is clearly marked as defensive / ground-clearing, distinct
            from constructive proof steps.
          - The conclusion states what the objection does NOT do, without
            overclaiming that it provides positive support.
          - In a wiring diagram, the section appears as a "challenge" edge (not
            "assert" or "clarify").
        Badly-applied:
          - Conflating anti-obstruction with construction: claiming that the
            absence of obstruction is evidence FOR the conclusion. "Smith theory
            doesn't obstruct" is not the same as "Smith theory supports."
          - Vague dismissal: "this is not a problem" without explaining why the
            objection fails. This invites the very reviewer finding the pattern
            is meant to prevent.
          - Addressing phantom objections: including defensive sections for
            objections that no competent reader would raise. This wastes space
            and suggests insecurity about the argument.
          - Missing the real objection: including a defensive section for one
            concern while overlooking a more serious natural objection. Survey
            the likely objections before choosing which to address.
          - Burying the defensive section: placing it inline within constructive
            steps so that its ground-clearing role is invisible. Give it its own
            section or clearly delimited subsection.

    + WHEN:
        There exists a well-known result, technique, or structural phenomenon that
        a competent reader would reasonably expect to obstruct your construction or
        conclusion. The objection is natural enough that NOT addressing it would be
        a gap in the argument. Importantly, the objection turns out to be
        inapplicable — it does not actually obstruct — but this non-applicability
        is not obvious and requires argument.

  + BECAUSE:
      Proofs operate on two levels: logical validity (does the argument hold?)
      and rhetorical completeness (are foreseeable objections addressed?). A
      proof that is logically valid but leaves obvious objections unaddressed
      invites reviewer findings and erodes confidence. The defensive section
      costs little to include but removes a predictable source of doubt.
      Moreover, the act of checking the objection often yields structural
      insight — understanding WHY the obstruction fails clarifies the
      construction's strengths and limitations.

      Critically, the defensive section must be honest about its role. It does
      not contribute constructive content to the proof — it clears ground. If
      it is conflated with constructive steps, readers may mistakenly believe
      the anti-obstruction result provides positive evidence for the conclusion,
      when it only removes a potential counterargument.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): Section 5 of the proof
        addresses Smith theory — a well-known tool that constrains fixed-point
        sets of group actions on manifolds. A reader familiar with the area would
        naturally ask: "Doesn't Smith theory obstruct a manifold with the
        claimed properties?" The answer is no: Smith theory operates over F_p
        (finite field coefficients) and constrains mod-p homology, while the
        construction only claims rational acyclicity (Q-coefficients). The
        Smith-theoretic constraints on mod-p Betti numbers are compatible with
        rational acyclicity.
        This section appears as a "challenge" edge (s5 -> problem) in the wiring
        diagram — the only non-constructive edge in the 9-edge graph. Reviewer
        Finding 4 (medium severity) noted that this section's role as
        anti-obstruction-only needed to be clearer: the original draft risked
        being read as if Smith theory positively supported the construction,
        when it merely does not obstruct it. A well-applied instance of this
        pattern would have prevented Finding 4 by explicitly marking the section
        as defensive and stating "Smith theory does not obstruct (but does not
        help construct)" rather than leaving the reader to infer the distinction.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[List natural objections a competent reader would raise against the construction.]
    next[For each, determine: does it apply? If not, identify the failing hypothesis.]
    next[Write a clearly-marked defensive section for each non-trivial non-applicability.]
    next[Verify the defensive argument is correct before including it.]

fields.title: Decide the Proof's Architecture Before Proving Any of It
fields.keywords: architecture, layers, reduction, decomposition, bridge, convention, problem-faithful, proof-shape, api-location
fields.why: math-informal/separate-into-independent-pieces
fields.how: own mechanism: Before proving anything, name the layers the proof will have and the reduction between each pair — including the layer that reconciles the problem's own statement with the library's conventions. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
A theorem that mixes several kinds of work — a decomposition, an
    estimate, a transport between two notions, a library API whose definitions
    differ from the problem's — and where it is tempting to start at the first
    line and see where it goes.

IF.text:
The proof decomposes into layers each of which can be stated and closed
      independently — regularity inside a disk and singular behaviour on its
      boundary; a strictly monotone subsequence extracted before an almost-
      everywhere argument; a contraction reduced to an inequality the library
      already has — then naming the layers first turns one intractable proof
      into several tractable ones, and the reductions between them become the
      things to look up rather than to invent.

HOWEVER.text:
The layer that gets skipped is the one nobody counts as mathematics: the
      bridge between the problem's statement and the library's. A problem
      phrased with strict bad sets `{x | ε < |fₙ x - g x|}` meets an API phrased
      with closed ones `{x | ε ≤ dist (fₙ x) (g x)}`, and the cheap move is to
      silently replace `>` by `≤` and carry on. That is not a reduction, it is a
      change of theorem. The same applies to tail conventions (`N₀ < n` versus
      `N₀ + 1 ≤ n`) and to threshold choices that look like bookkeeping. Skipping
      the bridge does not remove the work; it relocates it to a place where no
      gate will look at it.

      The opposite failure is building machinery before checking whether the
      general case needs it. Verify the degenerate or equality case first: it is
      cheap, and it sometimes closes the problem or shows the heavy route is the
      wrong one.

THEN.text:
Write the layers down as named statements before proving any. For each
      adjacent pair, say which reduction connects them and whether it exists in
      the library or must be proved. Keep a problem-faithful statement of the
      goal alongside the library-shaped one and make the translation an explicit
      lemma with its own proof — including the threshold arithmetic
      (`δ = min ε b.toReal / 2` and the `b = ⊤` case) rather than eliding it.
      Check the degenerate case before building for the general one.

BECAUSE.text:
A proof's difficulty is rarely uniform across its layers, and the layer
      that fails is seldom the one that looked hard. Naming the layers first
      makes the hard one visible while it is still cheap to change route, and
      makes the translation layer — the one that silently changes what is being
      proved — an object with a name, a statement and a proof instead of a step
      nobody wrote down.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[List the layers as named statements before proving any of them.]
    next[For each adjacent pair, name the reduction and say whether the library has it.]
    next[State the problem-faithful goal and the library-shaped goal separately; prove the bridge.]
    next[Do the threshold arithmetic explicitly, including the infinite/degenerate cases.]
    next[Check the degenerate or equality case before building general machinery.]

fields.title: Property-of-Object-Result Family
fields.keywords: property, regularity, rigidity, bound, asymptotic, family-parent, domain-specific
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: Your paper establishes a property of a *fixed* object — its regularity, its rigidity, an asymptotic, a bound, a stability estimate — rather than asserting the object exists or relating it to another. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
An object is given (a PDE solution, a measure, a representation,
    a numerical scheme, a physical state); the question is what it does. The
    object's existence is taken for granted (or established earlier); the
    paper's contribution is properties that follow.

IF.text:
The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "the solution has
      such-and-such regularity", or "any solution with property P must vanish",
      or "the asymptotic behaviour is X", or "we bound this quantity by Y".

HOWEVER.text:
Property-of-object is the *smaller and more domain-specific family* in
      our pilot (≈ 8 % of papers — see
      `futon3/holes/excursions/E-math-prototype-pilot.md` Phase 2). Many of its
      leaves are domain-tied (PDE regularity, measure-theoretic decay, group-
      action rigidity). The family parent serves as the umbrella; the
      domain-specific leaves accrete as we tag more papers.

THEN.text:
1. Identify the property class — regularity / asymptotic / rigidity /
         bound / decay / stability.
      2. Locate or note the absence of a domain-specific leaf for that class.
         (If absent, this is the seed for a new leaf flexiarg.)
      3. Identify the *witness* of the property — explicit estimate, decay
         rate, regularity exponent, vanishing condition.

    + EXEMPLAR-PAPERS:
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20798v1]   # PDE solution regularity + edge singularity
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20794v1]   # Hardy-uncertainty / rigidity
        # The pilot only saw 2 papers in this family; the leaves are placeholder
        # until the next ≈ 25-paper extension expands the tail.

    + MEMBER-PATTERNS:
        member[math-informal-CA/estimate-by-bounding]              # general bounds
        member[math-informal-CA/monotone-approximation]            # asymptotic
        member[math-informal-CA/pass-to-a-subsequence]             # convergence / asymptotic
        # Domain-specific leaves (to be authored as the corpus grows):
        # math-informal/regularity-and-asymptotics (PDE-flavoured)
        # math-informal/rigidity-from-decay-conditions  (analytic-rigidity-flavoured)

BECAUSE.text:
Property-of-object papers do "what-it-does work" rather than asserting
      existence or relating structures. They are heavily domain-shaped — a
      PDE-regularity result and a measure-theoretic-rigidity result share the
      family form but almost no analytic technique. The family parent gives
      the coarse classifier; *domain-specific leaves are expected to grow over
      time*, and their accretion is itself a signal of corpus coverage.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Identify the property class and check for a domain-specific leaf.]
      next[If no leaf fits, note the gap as a candidate new flexiarg.]
      next[Cross-check: is the property quantitative (with a number / rate) or qualitative (with / without)?]

fields.title: Route Exploration and Pivot
fields.keywords: route, approach, pivot, abandon, blocked, obstruction, triage, architecture, exploration, multi-approach, proof-path, backtrack, strategy, wiring
fields.why: no problem-corpus source matched (@holds-at absent; holds-token and id-text searches over every node in [problems futon-theory] found no match). Negative claim per the committed check futon2 holes labs library-loop runs l6_no_source_check.py, receipt runs/L8-no-source-check.edn. Rationale not invented (L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)
fields.how: own mechanism: When a proof admits multiple candidate approaches, explore them as lightweight wiring diagrams with explicit status (solid/open/blocked) before investing deeply. Abandon blocked routes promptly, record why they fail, and pivot to the most structurally favorable surviving route. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You face a proof obligation that could plausibly be discharged by
    several distinct approaches (different machinery, different constructions,
    different reduction targets). The natural impulse is to pursue the "obvious"
    first approach until it either works or exhausts your patience — but this
    ignores structural information that a quick survey would reveal.

HOWEVER.text:
The structural tension above manifests in the following concrete shapes (see substructure).
    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - All approaches are blocked. This is a legitimate outcome — the pattern
          then outputs "no known approach works" as a structural result (see
          exhaustion-as-theorem).
        - The surviving approach is only marginally better than the others. In
          this case, the triage has low signal; consider whether a fundamentally
          different construction is needed rather than choosing among mediocre
          options.
        - The "best" approach has an open node that turns out to be as hard as
          the original problem (reduction to an equally hard problem). Set
          checkpoints to detect this early.

THEN.text:
1. Sketch each candidate approach as a lightweight proof architecture: list
         the intermediate steps, mark each as solid (proved), open (plausible but
         unproved), or blocked (known obstruction).
      2. Triage immediately: kill any approach with a blocked node unless the
         blockage can be circumvented cheaply. Deprioritize approaches with
         multiple sequential open nodes (each is a conjunctive risk).
      3. Among surviving approaches, prefer the one with the fewest open nodes
         and the most independent sub-goals (parallel risk, not serial).
      4. Record the abandoned approaches and their specific failure points. These
         are not wasted work — they constrain the search space and may inform
         future attempts.
      5. When investing in the chosen approach, set a checkpoint: if a specific
         open node proves harder than expected, re-evaluate the triage rather
         than sinking further.

    + QUALITY-CRITERIA:
        Well-applied:
          - Each candidate approach is sketched with explicit node status, not just
            named ("try surgery" is insufficient; "Wall surgery: need normal map
            [open], need obstruction vanishing [open], need L-theory parity
            [unfavorable]" is correct).
          - Abandoned approaches have specific, documented failure points.
          - The pivot rationale is structural, not just "this one looks easier."
          - A checkpoint is set for re-evaluating the chosen approach.
        Badly-applied:
          - Premature abandonment: killing an approach because one step is hard,
            when the step is actually routine. Verify blockages before triaging.
          - Sunk-cost pursuit: refusing to abandon an approach after investing
            effort, despite blocked nodes.
          - Phantom triage: listing approaches without assessing node status,
            then "choosing" based on familiarity rather than structure.
          - Failure to record: abandoning an approach without documenting why,
            losing the constraint information for future work.

    + WHEN:
        A proof step has two or more candidate approaches, and at least one approach
        has non-trivial obstacles (unverified hypotheses, unfavorable parameter
        regimes, missing intermediate results). The obligation is significant enough
        that choosing the wrong approach wastes substantial effort.

BECAUSE.text:
Multi-approach proof problems have a branching search structure. Investing
      deeply in the first approach encountered is a depth-first strategy that
      ignores breadth information. A brief survey (often 30 minutes to sketch
      4-5 architectures) can eliminate entire branches and redirect effort to
      structurally favorable paths. The abandoned approaches are Lakatosian
      "refuted lemmas" — they don't prove the theorem, but they prove something
      about the problem's structure.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): the manifold-upgrade
        obligation (S) admitted four candidate approaches:
          I.   Wall surgery (reflection route) — 3 sequential open obstacles,
               unfavorable even-dimensional L-theory parity.
          II.  Equivariant surgery — BLOCKED (Costenoble-Waner codimension-2 gap
               hypothesis fails for codimension-1 fixed sets of reflections).
          III. Orbifold resolution — UNEXPLORED, no known technique applies.
          IV.  Rotation route (codimension-2, odd dimension) — dissolves the
               dimension-parity tension, equivariant surgery becomes available,
               reduces to a single lattice-existence question.
        Triage killed Approach II immediately, deprioritized I and III, and
        identified IV as most promising — despite IV not being the "obvious"
        continuation of the reflection construction that had discharged E2.
        Without the survey, the default path would have been Approach I (3
        sequential obstacles, structural headwinds). The triage took one sketch
        session; pursuing Approach I would have consumed days before hitting the
        parity wall.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Sketch all candidate approaches with explicit node status.]
    next[Triage: kill blocked, deprioritize serial-open, focus on best survivor.]
    next[Record abandoned approaches with specific failure points.]
    next[Set a checkpoint for re-evaluation of the chosen approach.]

          - Phantom triage: listing approaches without assessing node status,
            then "choosing" based on familiarity rather than structure.
          - Failure to record: abandoning an approach without documenting why,
            losing the constraint information for future work.

    + WHEN:
        A proof step has two or more candidate approaches, and at least one approach
        has non-trivial obstacles (unverified hypotheses, unfavorable parameter
        regimes, missing intermediate results). The obligation is significant enough
        that choosing the wrong approach wastes substantial effort.

  + BECAUSE:
      Multi-approach proof problems have a branching search structure. Investing
      deeply in the first approach encountered is a depth-first strategy that
      ignores breadth information. A brief survey (often 30 minutes to sketch
      4-5 architectures) can eliminate entire branches and redirect effort to
      structurally favorable paths. The abandoned approaches are Lakatosian
      "refuted lemmas" — they don't prove the theorem, but they prove something
      about the problem's structure.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P7 lattices with 2-torsion (futon6, Feb 2026): the manifold-upgrade
        obligation (S) admitted four candidate approaches:
          I.   Wall surgery (reflection route) — 3 sequential open obstacles,
               unfavorable even-dimensional L-theory parity.
          II.  Equivariant surgery — BLOCKED (Costenoble-Waner codimension-2 gap
               hypothesis fails for codimension-1 fixed sets of reflections).
          III. Orbifold resolution — UNEXPLORED, no known technique applies.
          IV.  Rotation route (codimension-2, odd dimension) — dissolves the
               dimension-parity tension, equivariant surgery becomes available,
               reduces to a single lattice-existence question.
        Triage killed Approach II immediately, deprioritized I and III, and
        identified IV as most promising — despite IV not being the "obvious"
        continuation of the reflection construction that had discharged E2.
        Without the survey, the default path would have been Approach I (3
        sequential obstacles, structural headwinds). The triage took one sketch
        session; pursuing Approach I would have consumed days before hitting the
        parity wall.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Sketch all candidate approaches with explicit node status.]
    next[Triage: kill blocked, deprioritize serial-open, focus on best survivor.]
    next[Record abandoned approaches with specific failure points.]
    next[Set a checkpoint for re-evaluation of the chosen approach.]

fields.keywords: obstruction, infeasible, impossible, structural, failure, blocked, certificate, SOS, barrier

fields.how: own mechanism: When a proof method fails, characterize the failure as a theorem about the problem's structure rather than discarding the approach silently. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You have tried a standard proof technique (SOS certificate, Groebner basis,
    spectral method, induction scheme, etc.) and it has failed — not due to insufficient
    computation, but apparently due to a structural feature of the problem.

IF.text:
The failure is reproducible across multiple parameter settings (different degrees,
      different multiplier sets, different starting points) and the failure pattern
      suggests a structural reason rather than a computational limitation.

HOWEVER.text:
Not every failure is structural. Computational failures (memory, time, numerical
      instability) look like structural failures when resources are insufficient. Before
      claiming a structural obstruction, verify that increasing resources (degree, precision,
      time) does not help, or identify the algebraic reason for the failure.

    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - Premature declaration: calling a failure "structural" when it's actually computational.
          One failed SOS attempt doesn't prove structural infeasibility — but infeasibility at
          degrees 10, 12, AND 14 with multiple solver backends, plus an algebraic explanation,
          does.
        - Overgeneralization: concluding "no algebraic certificate exists" when only Putinar-type
          certificates are blocked. The obstruction is specific to the method, not to all methods.

THEN.text:
1. State the obstruction precisely: what property of the problem blocks what method.
      2. Prove the obstruction (even informally): show that the method CANNOT work, not
         just that it HASN'T worked.
      3. Record the obstruction as a theorem or remark in the proof status document.
      4. Use the obstruction to redirect: if method A is blocked, what does the obstruction
         tell you about which methods might succeed?

BECAUSE.text:
A proved obstruction is as valuable as a successful certificate. It eliminates an
      entire proof strategy from consideration and often reveals structural information
      (interior zeros, indefiniteness, topological obstructions) that constrains the
      space of viable approaches. The alternative — silently trying the next method —
      wastes effort and loses information.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P4 n=4 Stam inequality (futon6, Feb 2026): 7 SOS scripts at degrees 10, 12, 14 all
        infeasible. The obstruction: -N has an interior zero at x₀ where all constraint
        polynomials are strictly positive, forcing σ₀(x₀) = 0 in any Putinar decomposition.
        But σ₀ is SOS and vanishing at a point with positive constraints creates algebraic
        contradictions. This theorem immediately eliminated SOS as a strategy and redirected
        effort toward algebraic elimination, which succeeded.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[State the obstruction precisely.]
    next[Verify it's structural, not computational (try multiple settings).]
    next[Record it and use it to constrain the viable approach space.]

fields.keywords: relation, equivalence, inclusion, transfer, generalization, bridge, family-parent

fields.how: own mechanism: Your paper relates two structures — by equivalence, by inclusion, by theorem-transfer to a new class, or by extending a theory's scope. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
Two structures (or one structure and a theory) are in view; the
    question is how they correspond. The paper does not (primarily) describe a
    single structure or assert existence; it builds a bridge.

IF.text:
The paper's main contribution can be expressed as "X and Y are equivalent",
      or "X is contained in Y" (with a directional structural argument), or
      "the theorem T holds for the new class C", or "we extend theory T to a
      broader setting".

HOWEVER.text:
Structural-relation papers are the second-most-populous family in our
      pilot (≈ 25 % — see `futon3/holes/excursions/E-math-prototype-pilot.md`
      Phase 2). The leaves diverge: equivalence is symmetric, inclusion is
      directional, transfer is "we re-prove T in setting C", generalization is
      "we extend T's framework to admit new objects". They share a *bridge-
      building* shape but the proof obligations differ.

THEN.text:
1. Decide whether the relation is symmetric (equivalence), directional
         (inclusion / monotonicity), a theorem-transfer (re-proving in a new
         class), or a theory-extension (generalising the framework).
      2. Pick the matching leaf member-pattern.
      3. Identify the *witness* of the relation: a map, an embedding, a
         re-proof, a strict containment of a parameter family.

    + EXEMPLAR-PAPERS:
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20808v1]   # Coxeter cohomology equivalence
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20785v1]   # Thurston norm inclusion
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20818v1]   # Coburn → edge-modes bridge
        exemplar[arxiv-2604.20778v1]   # Infinite matroid generalization
        exemplar[arxiv-math/0603598v1] # Noether to fractional control

    + MEMBER-PATTERNS:
        member[math-informal/transport-across-isomorphism]      # equivalence / transfer
        member[math-informal/find-the-right-abstraction]        # generalization
        member[math-informal/reduce-to-known-result]            # cross-domain bridge
        member[math-informal/structural-inclusion]              # inclusion / monotonicity (new leaf)

BECAUSE.text:
Bridge-building is structurally different from describing or asserting
      existence. The "tension" being relieved is the *gap between two formerly
      separate structures*; the "move" is a constructed correspondence; the
      "witness" is the correspondence itself plus its preserved-property
      checks. Per the BHK framing of M-pattern-application-diagnostic, this
      family includes the most structurally rich BHK arrows in the corpus.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Decide whether the relation is equivalence, inclusion, transfer, or generalization.]
      next[Identify the bridge object: map, embedding, re-proof, or framework extension.]
      next[Cross-check: does the relation *preserve* the properties of interest, or only *correspond on a subset*?]

fields.keywords: technique, landscape, library, wiring, method, survey, bridge, gap, decomposition, mechanism, certificate, partial

fields.how: own mechanism: When a problem sits at the intersection of multiple standard techniques, build a typed library of those techniques before attempting the proof. The library reveals the exact structural gap between existing methods and the target. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

context.text:
You have a theorem to prove that resembles results in several papers, but no
    single paper's method directly applies. The temptation is to pick the "closest" method
    and adapt it. But without mapping the full landscape, you may miss that the gap is
    structural rather than parametric.

IF.text:
Multiple published techniques (3+) partially address your problem — they prove related
      results with similar objects but different outputs, or the same output under stronger
      hypotheses.

HOWEVER.text:
Building the library is upfront investment that may feel premature. Not every problem
      needs it — only problems where the mismatch between existing methods and the target
      is non-obvious. If one method clearly applies modulo a minor adaptation, just adapt it.

    + FAILURE-MODES:
        - Over-investment: building an exhaustive library when the problem only needs one
          adaptation. Start with 3-4 methods; expand only if the gap remains unclear.
        - False bridge: classifying a method as "partial" when the gap is actually fundamental.
          Be honest about bridge status — partial means the core technique transfers; none
          means only the vocabulary transfers.

THEN.text:
1. For each related method, construct a typed wiring diagram with nodes:
         Q (objective), D (decomposition), M (mechanism), C (certificate), O (output).
      2. Add a bridge node B assessing the match to your target: direct, partial, or none.
      3. For each B = partial, write down the exact structural mismatch.
      4. Look for patterns across mismatches — they often share a common structural feature.
      5. The common feature is the gap. Target it directly.

BECAUSE.text:
The library converts vague intuition ("these papers are related") into a typed
      structural comparison. The bridge-status classification surfaces whether the gap is
      parametric (same structure, different bounds) or structural (different output type).
      Structural gaps require new ideas; parametric gaps require optimization. Knowing which
      you face changes the approach entirely.

    + EVIDENCE:
        P6 epsilon-light subsets (futon6, Feb 2026): a library of 10 methods (D1-D10) was
        constructed with typed wiring diagrams. All 10 had bridge status partial or none.
        The common mismatch: all methods produce edge-weighted sparsifiers, not vertex-induced
        subsets. This structural gap — not visible from any single paper — directed the proof
        toward leverage-based vertex selection (a new technique) rather than adapting any
        existing method.

NEXT-STEPS.text:
next[Survey 3-5 related methods with typed wiring diagrams.]
    next[Classify bridge status for each: direct, partial, or none.]
    next[Identify the common structural mismatch across partial bridges.]

fields.title: When a Proof Stalls, Ask Whether the Library Is What's Missing
fields.keywords: stalled proof, missing lemma, mathlib, library extension, cross-problem impact, expected information gain, effort allocation

context.text:
Formalization effort is scarce and proofs stall constantly.
    The visible unit of progress is "my proof compiles," which biases
    effort toward local workarounds.

IF.text: A proof stalls at a missing lemma, instance, or tactic.

HOWEVER.text:
Grinding the single proof forward IS possible — an inline lemma, a
      20-line workaround, a weaker statement — and feels like progress,
      while the same gap silently stalls other proofs in the corpus.

THEN.text:
Check the gap against the corpus (the sorry-boundary atlas, or a
      search over other partials): if the missing piece would unblock
      more than this proof, promote it — state it at library generality,
      close it there, and let every blocked proof consume it. Only
      workaround locally when the gap is genuinely proof-local.

BECAUSE.text:
Effort should flow to the highest cross-problem impact: the value
      of a library extension is the expected number of unblocked
      arguments (EIG over the corpus), while a local workaround's value
      is bounded by one. The library is the generative model; local
      workarounds are unshared observations.
      (Kin: [[proof-search/sorry-boundary-clustering]].)

  + canonical-instance:
      The M-diagramprover thesis in one line: rank Mathlib extensions by
      expected impact over the 489-problem prelim corpus rather than
      completing proofs one at a time — the readiness numbers (39
      partials, ~76 of ≥200 problems attempted) exist precisely to make
      this allocation computable. Authored as a proof-search seed
      2026-07-05.

fields.title: Cluster Sorry Boundaries; Extend Where the Clusters Point
fields.keywords: sorry, proof hole, blocker, cluster, boundary atlas, mathlib extension, cross-problem, formalization, lean

context.text:
A corpus of formalization attempts (proofs, exercises, ports)
    accumulates partial proofs, each stopped at one or more sorries. Effort
    naturally flows to grinding individual proofs forward.

IF.text:
You have many partial proofs, each blocked at a sorry (a typed hole
      the proof needs filled).

HOWEVER.text:
The blockers REPEAT: the same missing lemma family, the same absent
      instance, the same tactic gap appears across otherwise-unrelated
      problems — but nobody sees the repetition because each sorry is
      examined only inside its own proof.

THEN.text:
Build the sorry-boundary atlas: extract every sorry's interface (what
      it wants, in what context), cluster by type/shape across the whole
      corpus, and rank clusters by how many problems each would unblock.
      Spend effort on the top cluster's LIBRARY extension, not on the
      hardest single proof.

BECAUSE.text:
Sorry boundaries are not independent — they are samples from the
      library's gap distribution. A targeted extension at a dense cluster
      pays across the corpus (expected information gain over the corpus,

@flexiarg proof-search/sorry-boundary-clustering
@title Cluster Sorry Boundaries; Extend Where the Clusters Point
@sigils [∴/🗺]
@keywords sorry, proof hole, blocker, cluster, boundary atlas, mathlib extension, cross-problem, formalization, lean
@audience anyone driving a formalization corpus with many partial proofs
@tone procedural
@style pattern

! conclusion: When a proof corpus has many partial proofs, do not treat each sorry as a private blocker: CLUSTER the sorry boundaries by type across the corpus, and direct effort at the clusters — one targeted library extension (lemma, tactic, instance) closes many problems at once. The atlas of failures, read as intensities, is the intervention map.

  + context: A corpus of formalization attempts (proofs, exercises, ports)
    accumulates partial proofs, each stopped at one or more sorries. Effort
    naturally flows to grinding individual proofs forward.

  + IF:
      You have many partial proofs, each blocked at a sorry (a typed hole
      the proof needs filled).

  + HOWEVER:
      The blockers REPEAT: the same missing lemma family, the same absent
      instance, the same tactic gap appears across otherwise-unrelated
      problems — but nobody sees the repetition because each sorry is
      examined only inside its own proof.

  + THEN:
      Build the sorry-boundary atlas: extract every sorry's interface (what
      it wants, in what context), cluster by type/shape across the whole
      corpus, and rank clusters by how many problems each would unblock.
      Spend effort on the top cluster's LIBRARY extension, not on the
      hardest single proof.

  + BECAUSE:
      Sorry boundaries are not independent — they are samples from the
      library's gap distribution. A targeted extension at a dense cluster
      pays across the corpus (expected information gain over the corpus,
      not the instance); grinding one proof pays once.

  + canonical-instance:
      M-diagramprover (futon3c): 39 partial Lean proofs over the 489-problem
      prelim corpus, ~30 with diagnosed sorry boundaries, 12 recurring
      formalization patterns identified — the readiness condition for the
      Bayesian model that ranks Mathlib extensions by expected impact.

      a well-formed diagramprover ψ drew a size-1 cascade because no
      proof-search vocabulary existed here).

fields.title: The Frontier Is Enumerable: Represent Incompleteness as Typed Holes
fields.keywords: typed hole, sorry, want-signature, frontier, incompleteness, proof obligation, interface, dispatchable

context.text:
Incomplete formal work accumulates in proofs, specs, and
    ports. The default representations — TODO comments, "mostly done"
    status lines, prose apologies — carry none of the structure the
    incompleteness actually has.

IF.text:
A piece of formal work is incomplete and must be recorded, handed
      off, or prioritized.

HOWEVER.text:
"Incomplete" as prose is unqueryable: nobody can list the gaps,
      rank them, cluster them, or hand one to an agent — the knowledge of
      what's missing lives in heads and scrollback.

THEN.text:
Write the hole with its type: WANT (the signature or codomain of
      what's missing — what would have to be true/constructed), HAVE (the
      endpoints in hand), and the discharge condition. Store holes where
      they can be enumerated (a ledger, a corpus of sorry records), so
      the frontier is a queryable set, not an impression.

BECAUSE.text:
A typed hole is a proof obligation with an interface — it can be
      matched against candidate fillers mechanically (does this lemma's
      conclusion unify with the WANT?), clustered with its kin, and
      dispatched to whoever/whatever can fill it. The type is what makes
      effort allocation computable.
      (This is [[sorry-is-proof-hole]] doctrine at the corpus grain; kin:
      [[proof-search/sorry-boundary-clustering]].)

  + canonical-instance:
      The A-next EMPIRICAL corpus (futon2/holes/labs/): 10 gold-standard
      sorries recovered with :want-signature, :hungry-for, and typed
      endpoints — the sealed test data whose very shape (want/hungry-
      for/have) became the ψ recipe that fixed the cascade lane's
      starvation (E-live-loop-1 S1). Authored as a proof-search seed
      2026-07-05.
