Certified close of the interval-integral-to-contour-integral bridge for a trigonometric (Laurent) curve (Mathlib as pinned by apm-lean f7de6887, 2026-08-25, lean exit 0, no sorry, axioms propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound). Setting: γ t = Σ_{n ∈ Icc (-N) N} a n * exp (I * n * t); w := circleMap 0 1 t (= exp (I * t)); p := the cleared polynomial Σ_{k < 2N+1} C (a (k - N)) * X^k - C z * X^N, with the already-compiled evaluation identity hpval : p.eval w = w ^ N * (γ t - z) for w ≠ 0. The file needed `import ConstructionTargets.Rouche` and `set_option maxHeartbeats 2000000`.

STEP A — the pointwise identity carries the whole chain rule; nothing of the form I*e^{It}*L'(e^{It}) is ever stated. Goal, for each t with γ t ≠ z:
  deriv (circleMap 0 1) t * logDeriv (fun u => p.eval u) (circleMap 0 1 t) = (fderiv ℝ γ t) 1 / (γ t - z) + (N : ℂ) * I.
Two HasDerivAt chains for the SAME function u ↦ p.eval (circleMap 0 1 u):
  hcircle := hasDerivAt_circleMap (0:ℂ) 1 t            -- derivative circleMap 0 1 t * I
  hpoly   := (Polynomial.hasDerivAt p w).comp t hcircle
  htrig   := the compiled HasDerivAt γ (Σ a n * (exp (I*n*t) * (I*n))) t
  hprod   := (hcircle.pow N).mul (htrig.sub_const z)
  hfun    : (fun u => p.eval (circleMap 0 1 u)) = fun u => circleMap 0 1 u ^ N * (γ u - z)   (funext + hpval)
Then hder : p.derivative.eval w * (w * I) = N * w^(N-1) * (w * I) * (γ t - z) + w^N * Σ a n * (exp (I*n*t) * (I*n)) by `calc _ = deriv ((fun x => p.eval x) ∘ circleMap 0 1) t := hpoly.deriv.symm; _ = deriv (fun u => circleMap 0 1 u ^ N * (γ u - z)) t := congrArg (fun f : ℝ → ℂ => deriv f t) hfun; _ = _` closed by `simpa only [Pi.pow_apply] using hprod.deriv`.
Unfold: rw [logDeriv_apply, hcircle.deriv]; rw [(Polynomial.hasDerivAt _ _).deriv, <the fderiv-apply-one lemma rewriting (fderiv ℝ γ t) 1 to the explicit sum>]; rw [hpval]. NOW `cases N`: the w^(N-1) from the power rule blocks field_simp otherwise. zero case: `simp at hder ⊢; exact Or.inl hder`. succ case: `simp only [Nat.cast_succ, Nat.succ_sub_one, pow_succ] at hder ⊢`, `have hder' := congrArg (fun x : ℂ => x / circleMap 0 1 t) hder`, `field_simp [hw0] at hder'`, `field_simp [hd0]` (hd0 : γ t - z ≠ 0 := sub_ne_zero.mpr hz), `ring_nf at hder' ⊢`, `rw [hder']`, `ring_nf`.

STEP B — integrate it. With q t := (fderiv ℝ γ t) 1 / (γ t - z):
  rw [circleIntegral]   -- ∫ θ in 0..2π, deriv (circleMap 0 1) θ • logDeriv (fun u => p.eval u) (circleMap 0 1 θ)
  calc _ = ∫ t in 0..2π, q t + N * I   -- intervalIntegral.integral_congr; per t: `simpa [q, smul_eq_mul] using <STEP A> t (hz t (by simpa [Set.uIcc_of_le Real.two_pi_pos.le] using ht))` (integral_congr hands you t ∈ uIcc 0 (2π), the hypothesis wants Icc)
       _ = (∫ t in 0..2π, q t) + ∫ _ in 0..2π, N * I := intervalIntegral.integral_add hqint hconst
       _ = (∫ t in 0..2π, q t) + (2π : ℝ) • (N * I)   -- rw [intervalIntegral.integral_const, sub_zero]; rfl
hconst := intervalIntegrable_const. hqint := (ContinuousOn q (uIcc 0 (2π))).intervalIntegrable, from ContinuousOn q (Icc 0 (2π)) via `simpa [Set.uIcc_of_le Real.two_pi_pos.le]`; the Icc continuity is hnum.continuousOn.div (hγ.sub continuous_const).continuousOn (fun t ht => sub_ne_zero.mpr (hz t ht)), where hnum : Continuous (fun t => (fderiv ℝ γ t) 1) is proved by rewriting to the explicit finite sum (funext + the fderiv-apply-one lemma) and `fun_prop`, and hγ by `unfold` + `fun_prop`.

STEP C — assemble with the argument-principle value hroot : ∮ w in C(0,1), logDeriv (fun u => p.eval u) w = (card : ℂ) * (2 * π * I) (see the divisor-to-root-count memory): rw [hinter] at hroot; unfold the winding integral ((2π : ℝ) : ℂ) * I)⁻¹ * ∫ …; dsimp [q] at hroot ⊢; hpi : (((2 * π : ℝ) : ℂ) * I) ≠ 0 := mul_ne_zero (by exact_mod_cast mul_ne_zero (by norm_num) Real.pi_ne_zero) Complex.I_ne_zero; then `field_simp`, `push_cast at hroot ⊢`, `linear_combination hroot`. The constant N * I integrates to N * 2πI and is what produces the "- N" in the integer target.

94f12b4ed600a1c6efb6a82d9a83681bf8c8c3f3.hook: A weak-solution theorem quantifies its variational identity over a completion generated by a custom test-function predicate, and that predicate may admit only the zero function.
94f12b4ed600a1c6efb6a82d9a83681bf8c8c3f3.name: audit vacuous variational existence after test-space collapse
94f12b4ed600a1c6efb6a82d9a83681bf8c8c3f3.body: Before applying Hilbert-space existence machinery, prove that the declared generators are nontrivial. If continuity makes every generator's raw nonzero locus open while the definition also makes it compact and hence closed, connectedness of a noncompact ambient space forces each generator to vanish. Approximation by those generators then makes every admissible value representative zero almost everywhere: apply the approximation inequality at every positive epsilon to the nonnegative energy integral, derive that its integral is zero, and use `integral_eq_zero_iff_of_nonneg`. Consequently every forcing pairing vanishes and the zero pair satisfies the universal variational identity. This proves only a vacuous theorem induced by the encoding, not the intended weak PDE existence result.

e9179568248bc3fd51e8f37452bade333982f705.hook: A HasDerivAt or HasDerivWithinAt term built from the derivative combinators is refused by exact against the derivative value the statement wants, the two sides printing almost identically, while constructing an antiderivative or the Jacobian of a change of variables for an improper integral.
e9179568248bc3fd51e8f37452bade333982f705.name: build-a-derivative-with-combinators-and-reconcile-by-convert-rather-than-ascribing-its-value
e9179568248bc3fd51e8f37452bade333982f705.body:
PATTERN. The derivative combinators — the ones for products, quotients, inverses, negation, composition, and the primitives for the logarithm, the identity and constants — return the derivative in the shape their own statements generate, not in the shape you wrote down. The two are propositionally equal and not definitionally equal, and there is no reason they should be: composition leaves unreduced applications, and a quotient arrives as a product with an inverse.
The move that costs a round is to state the derivative you want as an ascribed hypothesis of HasDerivAt type and then close it by exact with the combinator term. The failure is reported as a type mismatch between two expressions that print the same up to arithmetic, which reads as a missing lemma rather than as a normalization gap, so the seat goes looking for API that does not exist.
The move that works: never ascribe the derivative value. Build the term from the combinators with no expected type, then reconcile it with the goal by a single convert at depth one, and discharge the resulting arithmetic equality with field_simp — or with simp when all that is needed is unfolding a local definition. Depth one matters: it stops the congruence at the derivative argument instead of decomposing the whole predicate into unprovable pieces. Since the reconciliation is arithmetic, prove the nonvanishing hypotheses it will consume before you start.
For the ‘within a set’ variants, do not hunt for a within-specific combinator: build the ordinary derivative and weaken it with the hasDerivWithinAt projection.

LEAF. Two spellings that carry an improper-integrability argument through, both from a certified proof. For the antiderivative of a reciprocal-logarithm integrand on a tail: convert (Real.hasDerivAt_log hxpos.ne').inv hxlog |>.neg using 1, then field_simp on all goals, where hxlog is the nonvanishing of the logarithm obtained from Real.log_ne_zero_of_pos_of_ne_one. For a reciprocal change of variables: convert ((hasDerivAt_const x c).div (hasDerivAt_id x) hx0).hasDerivWithinAt using 1, then simp with the local definition unfolded. These are exactly the two derivative obligations of MeasureTheory.integrableOn_Ioi_deriv_of_nonneg' (which additionally wants the derivative stated on the closed ray Ici a, nonnegativity of the integrand, and a limit for the antiderivative) and of MeasureTheory.integrableOn_image_iff_integrableOn_abs_deriv_smul (which additionally wants measurability of the source set and injectivity of the substitution on it).

e5c4e0c903cc88f462f644bdb8c09dedcee38ba8.hook: The truncation of an integrable or measurable function by max and min at a level (the bounded truncation that feeds Lp membership or dominated convergence) needs AEStronglyMeasurable, and dot-notation such as .max, .min or .const on the measurability hypothesis fails as an invalid field, tempting a change of route.
e5c4e0c903cc88f462f644bdb8c09dedcee38ba8.name: measurability-of-a-level-truncation-goes-through-sup-inf-or-continuous-composition
e5c4e0c903cc88f462f644bdb8c09dedcee38ba8.body:
PATTERN — the obstacle. A level truncation `max (-c) (min c (f x))` is the standard bounded approximant on the road from an integrable function into Lp or into dominated convergence, and it needs `AEStronglyMeasurable` before anything else can start (`MemLp.of_bound`, integrability by domination, the dominated-convergence hypotheses). The natural guesses — `hf.max`, `hf.min`, `.const` — fail: `AEStronglyMeasurable` is an existential (`∃ g, StronglyMeasurable g ∧ f =ᵐ[μ] g`), so field notation resolves against `Exists`, and no `max`/`min` lemmas live under that namespace. An attempt that hits this tends to abandon the truncation for a smoother damping factor; that is a valid route, but it gives up the pointwise facts the hard truncation provides for free and costs many compile cycles of new algebra.

PATTERN — the move. Either state the truncation in lattice vocabulary and use the sup/inf closure lemmas together with the constant lemma, or build the truncation as a continuous map composed with `f`. Both close the exact `max`/`min` goal by definitional unfolding; no route change is needed.

LEAF — names and shapes (elaborated against the pinned Mathlib).
- `aestronglyMeasurable_const : AEStronglyMeasurable (fun _ => b) μ` is the constant; there is no `.const` field.
- `AEStronglyMeasurable.sup` / `.inf` (need `[SemilatticeSup β] [ContinuousSup β]`, satisfied by ℝ): `aestronglyMeasurable_const.sup (aestronglyMeasurable_const.inf hf)` closes `AEStronglyMeasurable (fun x => max (-(c:ℝ)) (min (c:ℝ) (f x))) μ` directly, because on a linear order `⊔`/`⊓` unfold to `max`/`min`. `AEStronglyMeasurable.max` and `.min` do not exist.
- `Continuous.comp_aestronglyMeasurable (hg : Continuous g) (hf : AEStronglyMeasurable f μ) : AEStronglyMeasurable (fun x => g (f x)) μ`: with the truncation map built as `(continuous_const.max (continuous_const.min continuous_id))`, the composition closes the same goal. Ascribe the constants, e.g. `(continuous_const : Continuous (fun _ : ℝ => -(c:ℝ)))`, so elaboration does not have to guess the codomain; if the truncation was introduced through a `set`/`obtain` equation rather than syntactically, finish with `.congr (ae_of_all μ fun x => (hT c x).symm)`.
- The other closure lemmas are named after the operation: `.add`, `.sub`, `.mul`, `.neg`, `.norm`, `.const_smul`, `.div₀` (division in a group with zero — a real denominator that is never zero is fine), and `.div` (groups only, so not for ℝ).
- Once measurable, the truncation's pointwise facts come free: `|max (-c) (min c y)| ≤ c` by `abs_le` with `le_max_left`, `max_le`, `min_le_left`; `|max (-c) (min c y)| ≤ |y|`; and the truncation equals `y` as soon as `|y| ≤ c` (`min_eq_right`, `max_eq_right` from `abs_le.mp`), which is exactly what makes the dominated-convergence limit eventually constant at each point.

Provenance (mined-from): a second attempt at the L1-to-L2 truncation bridge on the unit interval; it retrieved the route memory naming max/min truncations, could not prove their measurability, and rebuilt the argument with a smooth damping factor at the cost of about ten compile-repair cycles.

19cfbbfee023e0ae98e69c3c73e6ec583759e691.hook: A real principal-value integral whose integrand has a simple pole on the path, in a setting where the parameter has a reflection symmetry about the pole (a strip hypothesis or functional equation): remove the pole by pairing before integrating, not by contour indentation.
19cfbbfee023e0ae98e69c3c73e6ec583759e691.name: principal-value-pole-removed-by-reflexion-pairing
19cfbbfee023e0ae98e69c3c73e6ec583759e691.body: Pair the integrand with its reflected parameter, f(omega) - f(1 - omega), reflection about the pole. On the common domain the simple poles cancel and the paired integrand has a removable singularity: compute numerator and denominator derivatives at the pole with HasDerivAt, package the extension value as their quotient limit on the punctured neighbourhood, and prove the real restriction is continuous there. The principal-value limit becomes an ordinary improper integral on a half-line: local integrability follows from continuity on a compact, the tail is dominated by an explicit complex exponential from the strip bounds, and intervalIntegral_tendsto_integral_Ioi transports the moving truncation endpoints to the set integral. What transfers is the shape: reflection pairing plus removable-singularity extension converts a path-pole principal value into dominated-convergence machinery Mathlib already has.

0d0a59b810e3dbda5422b1d6297b05ba77289c72.hook: After termwise integration on the half-line the value is a series of reciprocal differences at the original geometric index that must be identified with pi times cotangent, and the library's cotangent partial-fraction expansion is indexed differently, so neither a tsum rewrite nor a term-for-term shift of the two families matches.
0d0a59b810e3dbda5422b1d6297b05ba77289c72.name: identify-reciprocal-difference-series-with-cotangent-through-partial-sums
0d0a59b810e3dbda5422b1d6297b05ba77289c72.body:
PATTERN — the obstacle. Integrating two exponential families termwise leaves a series of reciprocals, differences like `1 / (n + ω) - 1 / (n + 1 - ω)` at the original index, to be identified with `π * cot (π * ω)`. The library's expansion pairs `x - (n + 1)` with `x + (n + 1)` and splits off the `1 / x` head, so the indices do not line up, and shifting one family against the other inside the infinite sum is the invalid rearrangement.

PATTERN — the move. Identify through finite partial sums, never through the tsum. Prove by induction that the original-index partial sum up to `m` equals `1 / ω` plus the library's partial sum up to `m` minus one unmatched endpoint term; prove that endpoint tends to zero; then add limits. Nothing infinite is rearranged.

LEAF — names and what they require (checked at the pinned Mathlib).
- `tendsto_logDeriv_euler_cot_sub (hx : x ∈ ℂ_ℤ) : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => ∑ j ∈ Finset.range n, cotTerm x j) atTop (𝓝 (π * cot (π * x) - 1 / x))` in `Mathlib.Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Trigonometric.Cotangent`, with `cotTerm x n = 1 / (x - (n + 1)) + 1 / (x + (n + 1))`. This is the partial-sum form and the one to use in a limit argument. `cot_series_rep' (hz : x ∈ ℂ_ℤ) : π * cot (π * x) - 1 / x = ∑' n : ℕ, (1 / (x - (n + 1)) + 1 / (x + (n + 1)))` and `cot_series_rep` (indexed by `ℕ+`) are the tsum forms; `summable_cotTerm` gives summability.
- `x ∈ ℂ_ℤ` is membership in `Complex.integerComplement`; `mem_integerComplement_iff : x ∈ ℂ_ℤ ↔ ¬ ∃ n : ℤ, n = x`. From a strip bound `0 < x.re` and `x.re < 1` it follows by `rintro ⟨n, hn⟩`, taking real parts of `hn` with `congrArg Complex.re`, casting to `0 < n` and `n < 1` in `ℤ`, and `omega`.
- The target usually arrives as `π * cos (π * ω) / sin (π * ω)`; `Complex.cot` unfolds to `cos / sin` (`Complex.cot_eq_cos_div_sin`), so rewrite the goal with it before matching the library statement, and `mul_div_assoc` handles the remaining bracket.
- The endpoint `1 / ((m + 1 : ℕ) - ω) → 0`: `tendsto_one_div_atTop_nhds_zero_nat` composed with `tendsto_add_atTop_nat 1`, divided by the sequence `1 - ω * (1 / (m + 1)) → 1` (`Tendsto.div` with `(1 : ℂ) ≠ 0`), then `Tendsto.congr'` with `field_simp` to match the shape; the nonvanishing of `(m + 1 : ℕ) - ω` is again a real-part argument from the strip.
- The induction step is `Finset.sum_range_succ` twice, `push_cast`, and `ring`; the sign to watch is `1 / (ω - (m + 1)) = -(1 / ((m + 1) - ω))`, via `one_div` and `inv_neg`.

Provenance (mined-from): the same principal-value integral in an open strip; the Student's own search phrase was cotangent partial sums with truncation, and the shelf it saw held nothing for the identification step.

3c11dbf589331851935a72d79c338ca125d26759.hook: A measurable representative is built but AEMeasurable congr will not apply, because the almost everywhere equality is oriented the wrong way round.
3c11dbf589331851935a72d79c338ca125d26759.name: read-the-transfer-direction-off-the-congr-signature-or-discharge-it-with-filter-upwards
3c11dbf589331851935a72d79c338ca125d26759.body:
PATTERN - the obstacle. Transferring a measurability property along an almost-everywhere equality fails in a way that does not look like a search problem. The congr family is DIRECTIONAL, and feeding the equality the wrong way round produces an argument type mismatch on a lemma you have already found, not an unknown identifier. There is nothing to search for, so a seat re-reads its goal instead of re-reading the signature. A remembered rule makes it worse rather than better: orientations genuinely differ between neighbouring lemmas, so advice of the form "supply the equality, not its symm" is correct only for the one lemma it was written about.

PATTERN - the move. Read the direction off the signature every time, and prefer the route that has no direction at all. Every congr in this family takes the property for its FIRST function together with an equality stated first-function-first, and concludes the property for the SECOND. The function you END on is the second one. So building a measurable mirror and wanting the property for your original means the mirror has to occupy the first slot of both - which is the reverse of how the canonical representative equation is stated. Rather than tracking that, leave the equality as a goal and discharge it with filter_upwards: at the pointwise level the hypothesis is an ordinary equation between two values, simp will use it in whichever direction the goal needs, and the orientation question disappears entirely.

LEAF - signatures and the worked shape (elaborated against the pinned Mathlib).
- AEMeasurable.congr : AEMeasurable f mu -> (f =ae= g) -> AEMeasurable g mu. It concludes for g, the SECOND function.
- AEStronglyMeasurable.congr has the same shape: AEStronglyMeasurable f mu -> (f =ae= g) -> AEStronglyMeasurable g mu.
- AEMeasurable.ae_eq_mk (h) : f =ae= AEMeasurable.mk f h - stated ORIGINAL first. So the representative sits in the second slot of that equation and needs the first slot of the congr you want; the two do not line up, and .symm is what reconciles them if you insist on the explicit route.
- The route that avoids the question: from a proof hm that the mirror is Measurable, apply hm.aemeasurable.congr and leave the equality as a goal; discharge it with filter_upwards on h.ae_eq_mk, introducing the pointwise equation, and close with simp on that equation. This elaborates clean for a case-split integrand built over the representative, and the orientation never has to be decided.
- AEMeasurable.mk f h is the canonical measurable representative and h.measurable_mk is its measurability. Both are dot-notation on AEMeasurable; the strongly-measurable class is an existential with no such fields and must be destructured instead, which is a further reason to step down to AEMeasurable before any of this begins.

76d99ffabb2b74b3a01617cdc48c50e2715ff311.hook: You hold a hand-built HasFPowerSeriesAt for your own coefficient sequence with no radius bound, while every disc theorem in the library expands the function in cauchyPowerSeries instead, so the radius you need looks like it belongs to the wrong series.
76d99ffabb2b74b3a01617cdc48c50e2715ff311.name: inherit-a-radius-by-one-dimensional-power-series-uniqueness
76d99ffabb2b74b3a01617cdc48c50e2715ff311.body:
PATTERN — the obstacle. You have built `HasFPowerSeriesAt f (ofScalars 𝕜 c) x`
by hand — typically by rewriting a pointwise `HasSum` family with
`hasFPowerSeriesAt_iff` — and it carries NO usable radius: `HasFPowerSeriesAt`
existentially quantifies over some positive radius, so it says nothing about how
far your series reaches. Meanwhile the library's disc theorems do not expand `f`
in YOUR series at all; they hand you `cauchyPowerSeries f x R`, their own
object. The tempting move is to prove a radius bound for your own series
(`le_radius_of_bound`, or an explicit `HasFPowerSeriesOnBall` construction with
hand-managed coefficients). That is the wrong direction, and it is where the
bookkeeping swallows the session.

PATTERN — the move. Take the ball statement from the library FIRST, in the
library's own series, and then rewrite it into yours using one-dimensional
uniqueness of power-series expansions. Two expansions of the same function about
the same centre are equal, so the equation is available the instant you hold
both `HasFPowerSeriesAt` facts; `rw` it into the ball statement and that
statement is now about your coefficients, carrying the library's radius. You are
not proving your series has a large radius — you are inheriting one. Everything
downstream (evaluation, decay, coefficient identification) is then stated in the
coefficients you actually care about.

LEAF (@how) — pinned Mathlib, elaborated with no `sorry`:
 * `DifferentiableOn.hasFPowerSeriesOnBall {R : ℝ≥0} :`
   `  DifferentiableOn ℂ f (closedBall c R) → 0 < R →`
   `  HasFPowerSeriesOnBall f (cauchyPowerSeries f c R) c R`
   Two shape traps, both fatal on first use. (1) The hypothesis is on the CLOSED
   ball, so an open-disc analyticity hypothesis will not unify — pick a strictly
   smaller radius and `.mono` down to its closed ball first (from an open disc
   of radius 2, `closedBall 0 (3/2)` does). The error is an application type
   mismatch naming `closedBall ?c ↑R`. (2) `R : ℝ≥0`, so the positivity
   argument must be `(0 : ℝ≥0) < R`; supplying a real `(0 : ℝ) < R` fails to
   elaborate. Sibling: `DiffContOnCl.hasFPowerSeriesOnBall` is the variant
   wanting open-ball differentiability plus continuity on the closure.
 * `HasFPowerSeriesAt.eq_formalMultilinearSeries : HasFPowerSeriesAt f p₁ x →`
   `  HasFPowerSeriesAt f p₂ x → p₁ = p₂` — stated only for
   `FormalMultilinearSeries 𝕜 𝕜 E`, i.e. a one-dimensional domain, which is
   exactly the `ℂ → ℂ` case. Left-hand fact: `hball.hasFPowerSeriesAt`.
   Right-hand fact: your own construction. Then `rw [heq] at hball`.
 * Nearby and often the one you actually need:
   `HasFPowerSeriesAt.eq_formalMultilinearSeries_of_eventually`, for when the
   two functions agree only on a neighbourhood of `x` — the usual situation
   after a `Function.update` has filled in a removable singularity.

Assembled: `.mono` to a closed sub-disc, `hasFPowerSeriesOnBall`,
`eq_formalMultilinearSeries`, `rw` — four lines, after which the library's
radius is attached to your coefficient sequence.

22f30540182c911abcd8b0fdc61b0163ea5c3aa5.hook: statement ladder for the Laurent-curve winding bridge — the seven intermediate lemma STATEMENTS in fill order (sphere nonvanishing → circleIntegral_logDeriv_eq_divisor_sum → divisor = rootMultiplicity → finsum = filtered roots card → circle integral = card * 2πI → pointwise deriv (circleMap) * logDeriv = fderiv γ t 1 / (γ t - z) + N * I → interval-integral assembly), written as `sorry` first so the skeleton compiles, plus the pinned-Mathlib spellings that cost a whole attempt to confirm: MeromorphicOn.divisor_apply is untop₀-valued, meromorphicOrderAt_eq_int_iff.mpr wants ⟨g, AnalyticAt, g x ≠ 0, ∀ᶠ z in 𝓝[≠] x, f z = (z - x) ^ n • g z⟩, exists_eq_pow_rootMultiplicity_mul_and_not_dvd, Function.locallyFinsuppWithin.apply_eq_zero_of_notMem, divisor.finiteSupport (isCompact_closedBall 0 1), hasDerivAt_circleMap, Polynomial.hasDerivAt
22f30540182c911abcd8b0fdc61b0163ea5c3aa5.body:
Attempt 2 on this residual had the route memories, chose to verify Mathlib spellings before writing anything, and ran out of budget with no Lean written. The fix is mechanical: transcribe the route into lemma STATEMENTS with `sorry`, compile the skeleton, commit, fill leaves-first. Exact statements (γ = the curve, p = the cleared polynomial expression as it appears in the bridge statements, N the degree bound; names are yours):

L1 (hz : ∀ t ∈ Set.Icc (0:ℝ) (2 * Real.pi), γ t ≠ z) : ∀ w ∈ Metric.sphere (0:ℂ) 1, p.eval w ≠ 0
L2 (hz : …) : (∮ w in C(0, 1), logDeriv (fun u : ℂ ↦ p.eval u) w) = (∑ᶠ w, (MeromorphicOn.divisor (fun u : ℂ ↦ p.eval u) (Metric.closedBall 0 1) w : ℂ)) * (2 * Real.pi * Complex.I)
L3 (p : Polynomial ℂ) (hp : p ≠ 0) (U : Set ℂ) {w : ℂ} (hw : w ∈ U) : MeromorphicOn.divisor (fun u : ℂ ↦ p.eval u) U w = p.rootMultiplicity w
L4 (p : Polynomial ℂ) (hp : p ≠ 0) (hne : ∀ w ∈ Metric.sphere (0:ℂ) 1, p.eval w ≠ 0) : (∑ᶠ w, MeromorphicOn.divisor (fun u : ℂ ↦ p.eval u) (Metric.closedBall 0 1) w) = (((p.roots.filter fun w : ℂ ↦ ‖w‖ < 1).card : ℕ) : ℤ)
L5 (hz : …) : (∮ w in C(0, 1), logDeriv (fun u : ℂ ↦ p.eval u) w) = ((p.roots.filter fun w : ℂ ↦ ‖w‖ < 1).card : ℂ) * (2 * Real.pi * Complex.I)
L6 (t : ℝ) (hz : γ t ≠ z) : deriv (circleMap (0:ℂ) 1) t * logDeriv (fun u : ℂ ↦ p.eval u) (circleMap 0 1 t) = (fderiv ℝ γ t) 1 / (γ t - z) + (N : ℂ) * Complex.I
L7 = bridge_1 itself, from L5 and L6 (rw [circleIntegral]; integral_congr / integral_add / integral_const; field_simp; push_cast; linear_combination).
Dependencies: L2 ← L1; L4 ← L3; L5 ← L2, L4; L7 ← L5, L6. L3, L4, L6 are generic leaves. Fill order L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L6, L7.

Spellings confirmed in the pinned Mathlib (apm-lean f7de6887) — do not re-verify:
• `∮ z in C(c, R), f z` is notation from Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Integral.CircleIntegral (import Mathlib suffices); `rw [circleIntegral]` exposes ∫ θ in 0..2π, deriv (circleMap c R) θ • f (circleMap c R θ).
• MeromorphicOn.divisor_apply {f} (hf : MeromorphicOn f U) (hz : z ∈ U) : MeromorphicOn.divisor f U z = (meromorphicOrderAt f z).untop₀. After rw with hord : meromorphicOrderAt (fun u ↦ p.eval u) w = (m : ℤ), plain `simp` closes the untop₀ of a coerced integer.
• meromorphicOrderAt_eq_int_iff {n : ℤ} (hf : MeromorphicAt f x) : meromorphicOrderAt f x = n ↔ ∃ g, AnalyticAt 𝕜 g x ∧ g x ≠ 0 ∧ ∀ᶠ z in 𝓝[≠] x, f z = (z - x) ^ n • g z. Use `.mpr ⟨fun u ↦ q.eval u, AnalyticOnNhd.eval_polynomial q w (Set.mem_univ w), hqeval, _⟩`; the ∀ᶠ goal: `filter_upwards with u`, rw [hpq, eval_mul, eval_pow, eval_sub, eval_X, eval_C], simp only [smul_eq_mul, zpow_natCast]. MeromorphicAt for a polynomial: (AnalyticOnNhd.eval_polynomial p w (Set.mem_univ w)).meromorphicAt; MeromorphicOn on U: ((AnalyticOnNhd.eval_polynomial p).mono (Set.subset_univ U)).meromorphicOn.
• Polynomial.exists_eq_pow_rootMultiplicity_mul_and_not_dvd (p) (hp : p ≠ 0) (a) : ∃ q, p = (X - C a) ^ p.rootMultiplicity a * q ∧ ¬ (X - C a) ∣ q; q.eval a ≠ 0 from it via fun h ↦ hq (Polynomial.dvd_iff_isRoot.mpr h).
• Function.locallyFinsuppWithin.apply_eq_zero_of_notMem (D) (hz : z ∉ U) : D z = 0 — the divisor is a locallyFinsuppWithin, so nonzero divisor ⇒ w ∈ closedBall.
• (MeromorphicOn.divisor f U).finiteSupport (hU : IsCompact U); pair with isCompact_closedBall 0 1 for (Int.castAddHom ℂ).map_finsum.
• hasDerivAt_circleMap c R θ : HasDerivAt (circleMap c R) (circleMap 0 R θ * I) θ; Polynomial.hasDerivAt p x : HasDerivAt (fun x ↦ p.eval x) (p.derivative.eval x) x; compose as (Polynomial.hasDerivAt p w).comp t hcircle.
• ConstructionTargets.Rouche.circleIntegral_logDeriv_eq_divisor_sum {f c R} (hR : 0 < R) (hf : AnalyticOnNhd ℂ f (Metric.closedBall c R)) (hne : ∀ z ∈ Metric.sphere c R, f z ≠ 0).

9915468f7833bb6d30f7ee34ea85dd17f0817d53.hook: you can compute `Tendsto (fun R => ∫ x in Set.Icc (-R) R, f x ∂volume) atTop (𝓝 v)` but the goal is `∫ x, f x ∂volume = v` over the whole line: there is no lemma called `integral_eq_improper`, and `MeasureTheory.integral_of_hasDerivAt_of_tendsto` (FTC-2 on ℝ) is a trap that costs you a global antiderivative plus an everywhere-pointwise derivative hypothesis — the packaged bridge is `(MeasureTheory.aecover_Icc Filter.tendsto_neg_atTop_atBot Filter.tendsto_id).integral_eq_of_tendsto`, which needs exactly `Integrable f` and that one truncation limit
9915468f7833bb6d30f7ee34ea85dd17f0817d53.name: symmetric-truncation-limit-to-lebesgue-integral-over-the-line
9915468f7833bb6d30f7ee34ea85dd17f0817d53.body:
PATTERN — two routes present themselves, and they are not equally cheap.

The goal states the Lebesgue integral over the whole line as a value, and the only computation you have is the limit of symmetric truncations. Two Mathlib routes sit in the same file. The fundamental-theorem route asks you to invent a global antiderivative AND to defend a derivative hypothesis at every point. The a.e.-covering route asks only for `Integrable f` plus the truncation limit you already have. Reaching for the antiderivative first is the common wrong turn: it manufactures two obligations, and one of them — the everywhere-pointwise hypothesis — is routinely false for an integrand with removable singularities. Take the covering route unless an antiderivative is already in hand.

Its second virtue is that its two obligations are independent: integrability and the truncation limit never mention each other, so either can be banked and committed first and neither one blocks the other.

LEAF — the spellings.
* The bridge, in one application: `(MeasureTheory.aecover_Icc Filter.tendsto_neg_atTop_atBot Filter.tendsto_id).integral_eq_of_tendsto _ hInt hTendsto` closes `∫ x, f x ∂volume = v`. `AECover.integral_eq_of_tendsto` lives in `Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/IntegralEqImproper.lean`, with signature `(I : E) (hfi : Integrable f μ) (h : Tendsto (fun n => ∫ x in φ n, f x ∂μ) l (𝓝 I))`; `aecover_Icc` builds `φ R = Icc (-R) R` from the two endpoint limits. There is no lemma called `integral_eq_improper` — grepping for that name returns nothing and costs a round trip.
* To get inside one truncation, where the reparametrisation and splitting lemmas live: `MeasureTheory.integral_Icc_eq_integral_Ioc`, then `← intervalIntegral.integral_of_le` (which needs `-R ≤ R`, i.e. `filter_upwards [Filter.eventually_ge_atTop (0 : ℝ)]`).
* Integrability of a continuous integrand from two-sided decay, without touching the interior: `Continuous.locallyIntegrable.integrable_of_isBigO_atBot_atTop`, fed two `Asymptotics.isBigO_iff.mpr ⟨C, _⟩` witnesses built by `filter_upwards [Filter.eventually_le_atBot (-2 : ℝ)]` and `[Filter.eventually_ge_atTop (2 : ℝ)]`, with `integrable_inv_one_add_sq.integrableAtFilter _` as the reference profile on both sides.
* The route not to take by default: `MeasureTheory.integral_of_hasDerivAt_of_tendsto`, whose hypotheses are `(hderiv : ∀ x, HasDerivAt f (f' x) x) (hf' : Integrable f')` plus a limit at each end. It is the right tool only when the antiderivative and the everywhere-pointwise derivative are both already in hand.

MINED FROM. A Student re-proving an already-certified improper integral over ℝ found `AECover.integral_eq_of_tendsto`, abandoned it for the fundamental-theorem route two tool calls later, and spent the remainder of its budget on the antiderivative.

f1bfd0cff37e9679ef4146de9291a6188ffd7167.hook: A frozen problem file declares a bridge route blocked pending a monolithic corpus theorem absent from Mathlib ('no corpus theorem assembles the raw-function truncation and uniform limit').
f1bfd0cff37e9679ef4146de9291a6188ffd7167.name: refuted-blocked-route-assemble-truncation-limit-from-corpus-pieces
f1bfd0cff37e9679ef4146de9291a6188ffd7167.body: Rewrite rule. Scope: measure-theory formalization on a finite measure, convergence of pairings against a bounded test family. Before: treat the missing monolithic assembly theorem as a hard blocker and stop at sorry. After: assemble the same mathematical content from corpus pieces - MemLp.of_bound for the truncation-to-Lp step, tendsto_integral_of_dominated_convergence for L1 approximation, norm_integral_le_of_norm_le plus integral_const_mul for the uniform pairing estimate - closing the theorem with no new axioms. Level: domain. Confidence: high. Machine witness: the certified final head compiles with Lean exit 0, zero warnings, zero sorry warnings, axioms exactly propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound, statement unchanged, refuting the file's own claim that the route was blocked. The general point: a 'missing corpus theorem' claim in a boundary comment is often a packaging gap, not a mathematical one; check whether the three standard pieces (dense approximation of the raw function, an Lp home for the approximants, a norm bound turning approximation error into pairing error) already exist before accepting the block.

a45498a7142114830638621859c727cbee4a235d.hook: When a Lean test-function class uses `ContDiff ℝ ⊤` together with compact support on a positive-dimensional Euclidean space, exploit analyticity and the identity theorem instead of developing smooth localization or density machinery.
a45498a7142114830638621859c727cbee4a235d.name: prove compactly supported analytic test functions vanish via eventual equality
a45498a7142114830638621859c727cbee4a235d.body: In Mathlib, `ContDiff ℝ ⊤ φ` supplies `h.analyticOnNhd` because the outer order is analytic, not merely smooth. Compact support gives a point outside `tsupport φ`; the open complement is a neighborhood there, and `Function.notMem_support` shows that φ is eventually equal to zero on that neighborhood. On a positive-dimensional Euclidean space, apply `AnalyticOnNhd.eq_of_eventuallyEq` on `Set.univ` to conclude `φ = 0`. This turns any universally quantified compactly supported analytic test pairing into a zero-test obligation and can eliminate an apparent need for multiplier, weak-Leibniz, or Meyers--Serrin infrastructure.

7155b8a532af6624bffbcc22485223593d84e434.hook: After translating a symmetric two-function functional by an extremal, the quadratic remainder contains a mixed term and its sign is opaque.
7155b8a532af6624bffbcc22485223593d84e434.name: diagonalize a symmetric two-field variational remainder
7155b8a532af6624bffbcc22485223593d84e434.body: Introduce the sum and difference modes. The pointwise identity dp^2+dq^2+2pq = ((dp+dq)^2+(p+q)^2)/2 + ((dp-dq)^2-(p-q)^2)/2 separates an automatically nonnegative mode from the only dangerous mode. Prove the identity with ring, transport it under the set integral using setIntegral_congr_fun plus explicit integrability of each summand, and discharge the negative difference term with a zero-boundary Wirtinger inequality. This same change of variables also diagonalizes symmetric coupled ODEs into u''=u and v''=-v.

bf900541c10c9f1cee6bdb5cc78ef323b9b8d8c8.hook: A lower integral lemma asks for measurability of a derived integrand and all you hold is an integrability hypothesis on the original function.
bf900541c10c9f1cee6bdb5cc78ef323b9b8d8c8.name: step-down-to-aemeasurable-and-restrict-first-to-get-lower-integral-side-conditions
bf900541c10c9f1cee6bdb5cc78ef323b9b8d8c8.body:
PATTERN - the obstacle. In the integral layer the hypothesis handed to you is Integrable f mu, whose measurability content is AEStronglyMeasurable. That class is an existential with no combinator API, so a seat that stays inside it destructures a representative by hand for every derived integrand, re-proves the almost-everywhere equality, and rebuilds the transfer each time. Each rebuild costs a compile cycle, and on a restricted measure it also drags in ae_restrict_iff' and a measurability hypothesis on the set that the final statement never needed.

PATTERN - the move. Step down one class immediately and do all the work there. AEMeasurable DOES have the dot-notation combinators, including a canonical measurable representative, so convert once at the top. Restrict FIRST and then chain: once you are almost-everywhere measurable for mu.restrict E, every later step is a statement about that one measure and no set-measurability side condition ever appears. And when a lower-integral lemma looks like it demands Measurable, check for the primed name - the primed family is the AEMeasurable-stated one, and reaching for the unprimed spelling is what makes the requirement look stronger than it is.

LEAF - the chain and the names (elaborated against the pinned Mathlib).
- Pivot: hf.aestronglyMeasurable.aemeasurable gives AEMeasurable f mu; then .restrict gives AEMeasurable f (mu.restrict s), with the set implicit and no MeasurableSet argument.
- Derived integrands: AEMeasurable.norm, AEMeasurable.log, AEMeasurable.ennreal_ofReal (h : AEMeasurable f mu) : AEMeasurable (fun x => ENNReal.ofReal (f x)) mu. For a real function the absolute value enters through the NORM: hf.aestronglyMeasurable.aemeasurable.restrict.norm.log is almost-everywhere measurability of fun x => Real.log (abs (f x)), reconciled by simpa with Real.norm_eq_abs. There is no abs link in this chain, so writing the goal with bars and searching for an abs combinator reads as a corpus gap when it is only the wrong spelling.
- When a genuinely Measurable witness is required - typically to apply Measurable.ite to a case-split integrand whose branch condition is a predicate on f, because the level set where f vanishes is NOT measurable for a merely almost-everywhere measurable f - route through the representative: bind g as h.mk f, take h.measurable_mk : Measurable g, build the measurable mirror on g (branch set as (measurableSet_singleton c).preimage hg, both branches discharged by fun_prop), then come back with .aemeasurable.congr and filter_upwards on h.ae_eq_mk. This is shorter than destructuring the strongly-measurable existential and it never leaves the restricted measure.
- The AEMeasurable-stated lower-integral family: ae_lt_top' : AEMeasurable f mu -> lower integral of f <> top -> for-almost-every x, f x < top; and lintegral_add_left' : AEMeasurable f mu -> forall g, the additivity split. ae_lt_top' is the one-step route from a finite lower integral to almost-everywhere finiteness of the integrand; if the integrand takes the value top exactly on a bad set, that finiteness IS the almost-everywhere side condition excluding it, with no null-set or measure-monotonicity bookkeeping.

28b56d60e1c322e39331702db55bfe4774b6e272.hook: A hypothesis gives only ‘for almost every point there exists a limit’, the next step needs one named limit function that is almost-everywhere strongly measurable, and every search for a packaged selection lemma of the shape ‘exists h, AEStronglyMeasurable h AND ae Tendsto to h’ comes back empty.
28b56d60e1c322e39331702db55bfe4774b6e272.name: select-the-almost-everywhere-limit-as-a-total-function-then-transfer-measurability
28b56d60e1c322e39331702db55bfe4774b6e272.body:
PATTERN. There is no packaged limit-selection lemma in Mathlib, and probing for one reads as a corpus gap when it is really a construction gap: exact? returns nothing on the packaged goal, so a seat can burn a whole budget concluding the library cannot do this. Stop searching and build the limit yourself, in two separated steps that must not be fused.
Step one is a TOTAL function. Measure-theory API consumes honest functions on the whole space, not functions defined on the convergence set, so the selection must return something everywhere. Take the limit by a case split on the existence proposition itself: on the positive branch Classical.choose of the existence hypothesis, on the negative branch any default value (0). Because the branch condition IS the hypothesis you were handed, the pointwise convergence statement on the positive branch is exactly Classical.choose_spec after unfolding with dif_pos, and it costs nothing.
Step two is measurability, and it does NOT come from the construction — the construction goes through choice and is opaque. It comes from transferring measurability along the almost-everywhere convergence you just proved, from the approximating sequence you already knew was measurable.
The general lesson: when a selection and a regularity property are wanted together, select first with choice into a total function, then recover regularity by a limit-transfer lemma. Asking for both at once is what makes the goal unsearchable.

LEAF. The transfer lemma is spelled aestronglyMeasurable_of_tendsto_ae. The names AEStronglyMeasurable.ofTendsto and aestronglyMeasurable_of_tendsto (no _ae suffix) do not exist and are the usual wrong guesses. Its filter argument is EXPLICIT and comes first, so the application reads aestronglyMeasurable_of_tendsto_ae atTop hF hlim with hF : forall i, AEStronglyMeasurable (f i) mu and hlim : ae x in mu, Tendsto (fun n => f n x) atTop (nhds (g x)); it needs the filter NeBot and IsCountablyGenerated (atTop on the naturals is both) and the codomain PseudoMetrizableSpace. Note the argument order: the sequence measurability comes before the convergence, and the limit function g is implicit, inferred from hlim — so hlim must already be stated about the total function you built, not about an existentially quantified w.

f238dc8741890091a18ed76b90b9e0629347e81c.hook: A frozen boundary comment claims that converting a pointwise summation family into a HasFPowerSeriesAt statement (with its radius bound) remains an open bridge pending a theorem absent from Mathlib.
f238dc8741890091a18ed76b90b9e0629347e81c.name: pointwise-series-to-fps-bridge-is-closed-not-open
f238dc8741890091a18ed76b90b9e0629347e81c.body: Challenge record: that claim is refuted by machine witness. Mathlib's hasFPowerSeriesAt_iff states HasFPowerSeriesAt exactly as an eventually-in-neighborhood pointwise HasSum condition, so the conversion is a single rewrite plus filter_upwards with Metric.ball_mem_nhds — no absent theorem, no explicit radius construction. The certified head of the mined solve (git commit 143e17dd25b60d09f1546f669d097f462490d073) closes the full theorem through this route, compile-clean. Agents seeing a comment that declares a standard-looking definitional unfolding 'open' should check the _iff lemmas first: definitional-bridge claims are often just unread API.

d53b1ea7617670bb83ecf49ad4c5ec268611d503.hook: A set integral or IntegrableOn over a bounded interval (Icc a b) must be fed to library theorems stated for Integrable and the integral on an abstract measure, some of which need a finite-measure instance for the restricted measure; the bridging lemma seems missing and the finite-measure instance looks like it must be built by hand.
d53b1ea7617670bb83ecf49ad4c5ec268611d503.name: set-integral-on-a-bounded-interval-is-the-restricted-measure-by-definition
d53b1ea7617670bb83ecf49ad4c5ec268611d503.body:
PATTERN — the obstacle. A set integral over a bounded interval is written with `IntegrableOn f s μ` and `∫ x in s, f x ∂μ`, while the theorems you want to apply next (dominated convergence, packaging a bounded function into Lp, integral bounds) are stated for `Integrable f ν` and `∫ x, f x ∂ν` over an abstract measure ν, and several of them ask for `[IsFiniteMeasure ν]`. The natural reaction is to search for a bridging lemma between the two spellings and to build the finite-measure instance by hand from the measure of the interval. The searches fail because those names do not exist, and the hand-built instance costs a compile cycle per wrong guess.

PATTERN — the move. Set ν := μ.restrict s once, at the top, and treat every set-form fact as already being a ν-fact: the two spellings are definitionally equal, so `have`, `show` and `exact` with the other spelling type-check with no lemma at all. Ask instance search for finiteness before proving it; for Lebesgue measure on a bounded interval the instance is already in the library.

LEAF — names and what each requires (elaborated against the pinned Mathlib).
- `IntegrableOn f s μ` unfolds to `Integrable f (μ.restrict s)`: with `hf : IntegrableOn f s μ`, the line `have h : Integrable f (μ.restrict s) := hf` closes by definitional unfolding. `integrableOn_iff_integrable` is an unknown identifier; nothing is needed in its place.
- `∫ x in s, f x ∂μ` is notation for `∫ x, f x ∂(μ.restrict s)`: `rfl` proves the equation, and `show` with the other spelling changes the goal for free (useful right before a `rw` whose pattern is stated in the restricted-measure form).
- `Real.isFiniteMeasure_restrict_Icc (x y : ℝ) : IsFiniteMeasure (volume.restrict (Icc x y))` is an instance, so `inferInstance` or simply applying a theorem with an `[IsFiniteMeasure _]` argument works with no construction. Siblings: `Real.isFiniteMeasure_restrict_Ico`, `_Ioc`, `_Ioo`.
- If you genuinely need the measure of the interval: `Real.volume_Icc : volume (Icc a b) = ENNReal.ofReal (b - a)` takes NO ordering hypothesis (supplying `a ≤ b` is a type error), and `Measure.restrict_apply_univ (s) : (μ.restrict s) univ = μ s` is the one-step rewrite (`Measure.restrict_apply` followed by `Set.univ_inter` is a longer road that may fail to fire). For a general set, `isFiniteMeasure_restrict : IsFiniteMeasure (μ.restrict s) ↔ μ s ≠ ⊤` turns a measure bound into the instance.

Provenance (mined-from): a bridge theorem on the unit interval extending a convergence statement from L2 approximants to every integrable function; the attempt lost three compile cycles to these guesses before closing. Leaf statements elaborated in a scratch probe against the pinned Mathlib; nothing above was taken from the attempt text unverified.

9c3be9002dc51ce42ea7c5fce417051255397ac7.hook: A transform-convention normalizing constant (`1/π`, `1/(2*π)`, `1/√(2*π)`) is left multiplying a COMPLEX-valued integral and has to be cleared before the answer can be read off, and `field_simp`/`ring` on the whole equation keeps failing on cast mismatches — typically a cast of a compound such as `↑(-s)` sitting against `-↑s` inside `Complex.exp`, so that `congr 1` on the exponential's argument does not close. Two rules. Normalize casts on BOTH sides at once (`push_cast at h ⊢`): `Complex.ofReal_neg`/`ofReal_inv`/`ofReal_div`/`ofReal_mul`/`ofReal_exp` are all `@[simp, norm_cast]`, and pushing only the side you are looking at is what manufactures the mismatch. And clear the constant by proving the single scalar identity `((c : ℝ) : ℂ) * ((c⁻¹ : ℝ) : ℂ) = 1` as a standalone `have` — `push_cast`, then `field_simp` under the nonvanishing fact lifted by `exact_mod_cast Real.pi_ne_zero` — then rewriting the equation with it, rather than running a field-clearing tactic on an equation one of whose atoms is an integral.
9c3be9002dc51ce42ea7c5fce417051255397ac7.name: clear-a-transform-normalizing-constant-in-the-scalars-only
9c3be9002dc51ce42ea7c5fce417051255397ac7.body:
PATTERN — where the convention constant goes wrong.

Every transform convention leaves a real normalizing constant on the wrong side. A 2π-normalized Fourier pair leaves `1/π` or `1/(2*π)`; a unitary convention leaves `1/√(2*π)`; a Laplace or Mellin inversion leaves `1/(2*π)`. So the identity you actually obtain reads (real constant, cast into ℂ) * (a complex integral) = (a point value), and what you want is the integral alone. Two different things go wrong in clearing it and they report as the same error, which is why the step eats cycles that look like arithmetic.

First, the cast. A constant written `1/π` enters ℂ as a cast of a QUOTIENT, not as a quotient of casts, and the same holds for every negation the substitution that got you here produced: an exponent `-s` arrives as a cast of a negation. Nothing matches. The failure then surfaces late and in the wrong place — as a congruence obligation on the argument of an exponential that ought to be trivially true — so it reads as a problem with the exponential. Normalize casts on the HYPOTHESIS as well as the goal, in one call. Normalizing only the side under the cursor is what creates the asymmetry in the first place.

Second, the cancellation. Reaching for a field-clearing tactic on the whole equation puts the integral itself into the atom set: the tactic now has to reason about whether an integral is zero, and it either fails or discharges its rewrite against the wrong subterm. Do the cancellation in the SCALARS only. State the one-line identity that the cast constant times the cast of its inverse is one, prove that on its own, then rewrite the equation with it and finish with associativity and `one_mul`. The equation carrying the integral is only ever rewritten, never normalized.

LEAF — the names, and what each requires.

- `Complex.ofReal_neg`, `ofReal_inv`, `ofReal_div`, `ofReal_mul`, `ofReal_exp` are all `@[simp, norm_cast]` (`Mathlib/Data/Complex/Basic.lean`, `Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Exponential.lean`), so `push_cast`/`norm_cast` move the coercion inward onto atoms. Use `push_cast at h ⊢` — both places, one call.

- The nonvanishing side condition must be LIFTED, not reproved in ℂ: obtain `((Real.pi : ℝ) : ℂ) ≠ 0` by `exact_mod_cast Real.pi_ne_zero`. `field_simp` will not proceed without it, and the complex statement is not what `positivity` produces.

- The scalar identity to state separately has the shape (cast of `c`) * (cast of `1/c`) = 1, closed by `push_cast` followed by `field_simp` under that hypothesis. Then eliminate the constant from the main equation by rewriting through `← mul_assoc`, that identity, and `one_mul`.

- `Complex.ofReal_exp : ((Real.exp x : ℝ) : ℂ) = Complex.exp (x : ℂ)` is the bridge when the point value on the other side is a real exponential. Apply it AFTER cast normalization has already turned a cast-of-a-negation into a negation-of-a-cast, not before.

- `Complex.div_ofReal_re (z : ℂ) (x : ℝ) : (z / x).re = z.re / x` (`@[simp]`) is the corresponding rule on the way back out, for the case where the constant survives as far as the real-part extraction instead of being cleared first.

7b177a51222d87838fe5636201e34c8edea2102e.hook: Refining a coarse cell into its consecutive fine subcells, without any endpoint arithmetic: state the cells through a MONOTONE CHAIN a : N -> R and the decomposition is `MeasureTheory.integral_biUnion_finset` over `Finset.Ico p q`. With a l = l / 2^n the coarse cell [a p, a q) IS the union of the fine cells and no cast, subtraction or division is ever unfolded, because the endpoints stay opaque. Cover proof: `Ico_subset_biUnion_Ico` (root namespace, Mathlib/Order/Interval/Set/Union.lean) reindexed along `fun i => a (p + i)` gives the forward inclusion; `Ico_subset_Ico (ha hpi) (ha hiq)` gives the reverse; pairwise disjointness is `Ico_disjoint_Ico` closed by `(min_le_left _ _).trans ((ha h).trans (le_max_right _ _))`. `integral_biUnion_finset` wants `IntegrableOn` PER CELL and `Set.Pairwise` on the Finset coercion, so open `Function.onFun` first. Verified: the general statement elaborates against the pinned Mathlib, exit 0, no sorry.
7b177a51222d87838fe5636201e34c8edea2102e.name: name-cells-by-a-monotone-chain-so-refinement-costs-no-arithmetic
7b177a51222d87838fe5636201e34c8edea2102e.body:
PATTERN — the obstacle. You have a coarse cell of a dyadic (or any nested)
family and you need it as the disjoint union of the fine cells it contains,
then the integral as the corresponding finite sum. Written with explicit
endpoints — j/2^m, l/2^n, index ranges like [j*2^(n-m), (j+1)*2^(n-m)) — this
looks like a large arithmetic obligation: every inclusion needs a comparison
of casted, subtracted, divided natural numbers, and you pay that cost once per
cell. Two seats have now costed this route at "150+ lines" and abandoned it.
The cost is real, and it is entirely self-inflicted by the way the cells were
named.

PATTERN — the move. Name the cells through a MONOTONE CHAIN of endpoints
`a : N -> R` and index them by their position in the chain, not by an
arithmetic expression. The coarse cell is `Ico (a p) (a q)`; the fine cells are
`Ico (a i) (a (i+1))` for `i` in `Finset.Ico p q`. Now the endpoints are
opaque: nothing about them is ever unfolded, so there is no cast arithmetic
anywhere in the decomposition. A single `Monotone a` hypothesis discharges the
reverse inclusion AND the pairwise disjointness. You instantiate with
`a l = l / 2^n` only at the very end, where `Monotone a` is one `positivity`-
flavoured line. This is the general lesson: when a decomposition is expensive,
check whether the expense is in the mathematics or in the naming.

LEAF (@how) — pinned Mathlib; the statement below elaborated, exit 0, no sorry:

  (mu : Measure R) (f : R -> R) (p q : N) (hpq : p <= q)
  (a : N -> R) (ha : Monotone a)
  (hf : forall i, IntegrableOn f (Ico (a i) (a (i+1))) mu) :
    integral over Ico (a p) (a q) of f
      = sum over i in Finset.Ico p q of (integral over Ico (a i) (a (i+1)) of f)

 * `Ico_subset_biUnion_Ico (N : N) (a : N -> X) :`
   `  Ico (a 0) (a N) subset union over i in Finset.range N of Ico (a i) (a (i+1))`
   root namespace, `Mathlib/Order/Interval/Set/Union.lean`. `LinearOrder` only;
   gives ONLY the forward inclusion, and only from index 0. For a chain
   starting at `p`, apply it to `fun i => a (p + i)` with length `q - p` and
   rewrite with `Nat.add_sub_cancel' hpq`; the witness `i` then reappears as
   `p + i`, discharged into `Finset.Ico p q` by `omega`.
 * Reverse inclusion: `iUnion2_subset fun i hi => Ico_subset_Ico (ha hpi) (ha hiq)`
   after `obtain <hpi, hiq> := Finset.mem_Ico.1 hi`.
 * `MeasureTheory.integral_biUnion_finset (t : Finset iota)`
   `  (hs : forall i in t, MeasurableSet (s i))`
   `  (h's : (coe t).Pairwise (Disjoint on s))`
   `  (hf : forall i in t, IntegrableOn f (s i) mu)`
   `Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Integral/Bochner/Set.lean`. Two shape traps:
   `IntegrableOn` is wanted PER CELL, not on the union; and `h's` is
   `Set.Pairwise` on the Finset coercion, so `simp only [Function.onFun]`
   before supplying a `Disjoint`.
 * Disjointness:
   `Ico_disjoint_Ico : Disjoint (Ico a1 a2) (Ico b1 b2) <-> min a2 b2 <= max a1 b1`;
   for `h : i < j` the whole proof is
   `(min_le_left _ _).trans ((ha h).trans (le_max_right _ _))`
   (`ha h : a (i+1) <= a j`, since `i < j` is `i+1 <= j` definitionally).

595cc5718edf082cd99a4bcfeb84ef43fc67ae86.hook: Excluding multiple-nonnormal Sylow configurations by element counting has no packaged Mathlib API; budget the union-cardinality construction or route via a normal Sylow complement instead.
595cc5718edf082cd99a4bcfeb84ef43fc67ae86.name: sylow-union-element-counting-unpackaged
595cc5718edf082cd99a4bcfeb84ef43fc67ae86.body: PATTERN - the obstacle. The standard group-theory move excluding the configuration where two Sylow counts are simultaneously maximal (n_5 = 6 and n_3 = 10) by element counting (24 elements of order 5 + 20 of order 3 + identity exceeds 30) has NO packaged Mathlib API. Searched and absent: card-of-union-of-Sylow-subgroups lemmas (card_mul_of, card_sup for subgroups, disjoint-card combinations in Mathlib/GroupTheory) and any packaged statement that distinct Sylow p-subgroups intersect trivially. The counting must be assembled from raw Set/Subtype cardinality manipulations: enumerate the Sylow family (Fintype.card (Sylow p G) gives the count), show distinct members of it have bot intersection (Sylow.ext-style card arguments: two p-subgroups of order p intersect trivially), then sum disjoint finite sets with Set.Finite.card_biUnion-style lemmas and compare against Nat.card G. Budget: hours, not minutes - this is a bridge construction, not a lemma application. Do not plan a solve route that treats this counting step as a one-liner; either budget it as its own artifact or route around it (e.g. prove one Sylow is normal directly via Sylow.normal_of_card_eq_one obtained from the interval shell, and build the index-2 subgroup from coprime complements with Subgroup.isComplement'_of_coprime instead of counting). MINED FROM a Student attempt that established both Sylow intervals and then hit exactly this wall. No problem-specific identifiers are needed to apply this.

c7cc8d9caa8158580712a7beefbeec5a0c7d1f0d.hook: To prove density by finite-support truncation inside a closed subspace defined by a coordinate involution such as conjugate symmetry, arbitrary finite truncations approximate in the ambient lp space but may leave the constrained subtype.
c7cc8d9caa8158580712a7beefbeec5a0c7d1f0d.name: Preserve involutive constraints by closing finite truncations under the involution
c7cc8d9caa8158580712a7beefbeec5a0c7d1f0d.body: Start from the finite set supplied by unconditional summability, then replace it by its union with its image under the coordinate involution. The enlarged set still satisfies the requested tail bound because it contains the original set, while truncation on it preserves the involutive relation coordinatewise. Package the truncated function with that proof as an element of the subtype; finite support supplies the regularity or smoothness witness. For Mathlib lp spaces, lp.hasSum_single combined with HasSum, SummationFilter.unconditional, and Metric.tendsto_atTop yields the finite-set approximation, while Finset.subset_union_left transports the estimate to the symmetric hull.

e8b9d5a5588fbf043b31f17a74a996a932ed9cbd.hook: Fourier elliptic solution by even bounded multiplier division; uniqueness by self-testing the difference
e8b9d5a5588fbf043b31f17a74a996a932ed9cbd.name: solve-fourier-multiplier-equation-by-even-bounded-division
e8b9d5a5588fbf043b31f17a74a996a932ed9cbd.body: Pattern: construct the weak solution of a Fourier-multiplier equation m(k) û(k) = f̂(k) directly by division, then check three small obligations — do not attempt a functional-analytic existence theorem. Define û(k) = f̂(k)/m(k) where m(k) ≠ 0 (for mean-zero problems the kernel of m is exactly the zero frequency; set û(0) = 0). Obligations: (i) ℓ²/lp membership: on the support of the multiplier, 1/|m| is bounded (for −Δ the multiplier 4π²|k|² on an integer lattice gives |k|² ≥ 1 off the origin), so ‖û(k)‖ ≤ B‖f̂(k)‖ termwise and summability transports by a mul_le-style lemma; (ii) symmetry transport: when the multiplier is EVEN (m(−k) = m(k)), any conjugate-symmetry hypothesis on f transports pointwise to û, including at the origin where 0 is its own conjugate; (iii) the pointwise equation holds by construction, and the weak form follows by re-summating the pairing against test functions termwise. Uniqueness: test the weak formulation of the DIFFERENCE against itself; the Dirichlet form of a mean-zero difference is a tsum of nonnegative coefficientwise quantities that the weak form forces to vanish, and a tsum of nonnegatives equal to zero makes each term zero.

e2ba3d95e2532171718a63f593664a0e568e2f65.hook: Refining dyadic cells: a set-level partition equality is needed in the problem's own syntax — a coarse half-open dyadic cell Ico (j/2^m) ((j+1)/2^m) equals the union of its 2^(n−m) finer level-n dyadic cells with cell endpoints ((k : ℕ) : ℝ) / (2 ^ n : ℕ) — before the indicator of the coarse cell can be written as a finite sum of finer-cell indicators; proving the membership equivalence directly seems to need floor/index arithmetic in ℝ that omega and push_cast do not supply, no Mathlib lemma states the exact half-open dyadic refinement, and the exceptional endpoint and level branches of a piecewise sign function look like extra bookkeeping inside each subcell.
e2ba3d95e2532171718a63f593664a0e568e2f65.name: prove-a-concrete-dyadic-partition-equality-by-antisymmetry-not-membership-arithmetic
e2ba3d95e2532171718a63f593664a0e568e2f65.body:
PATTERN — the obstacle. The partition equality is attacked as a membership equivalence: t lies in the coarse cell iff some fine index r has t in the r-th subcell. The forward direction asks for the index r = ⌊t·2^n⌋ − j·2^(n−m) and its two inequalities, which is floor arithmetic over ℝ with casts and subtraction; omega cannot see it and push_cast does not produce it. The library has no lemma for the dyadic case in this syntax, so the search comes back empty and the residual looks unformalizable in budget.

PATTERN — the move. Never prove the membership equivalence. Prove the equality as antisymmetry of two inclusions over an ABSTRACT monotone grid a : ℕ → ℝ, then match the concrete endpoints once. (1) Forward: the library cover lemma gives Ico (a 0) (a N) ⊆ ⋃ i ∈ range N, Ico (a i) (a (i+1)) for any chain, with no arithmetic. (2) Reverse: a point of the i-th subcell is in the whole interval because a 0 ≤ a i and a (i+1) ≤ a N — two uses of Monotone a. (3) Instantiate a r = (j·2^(n−m) + r) / 2^n; Monotone a is one division-monotonicity line. (4) Match endpoints: a 0 = j/2^m and a (2^(n−m)) = (j+1)/2^m each reduce to the single identity 2^n = 2^m · 2^(n−m), after which push_cast and field_simp close them. Everything problem-specific is in step (4), and it is two equalities, not a quantifier exchange. Then the indicator-level and integral-level refinements follow from the set equality by cases on membership (one inhabited subcell; the rest excluded by cast-order transfer). For the exceptional branches of a piecewise sign function: a point of a half-open cell whose right endpoint k/2^n satisfies k ≤ 2^n is strictly below 1, so the endpoint-value branch t = 1 is discharged from cell membership itself, and the excluded-level branch is a hypothesis carried as n ≠ 1 from 1 < n by omega — neither needs a case split inside the subcell integration.

LEAF — names and what they require (pinned Mathlib, located by grep).
- Ico_subset_biUnion_Ico (N : ℕ) (a : ℕ → X) : Ico (a 0) (a N) ⊆ ⋃ i ∈ Finset.range N, Ico (a i) (a (i + 1)) — root namespace, Mathlib/Order/Interval/Set/Union.lean, LinearOrder only, indexed from 0. Reverse inclusion: intro x hx, simp only [mem_iUnion] at hx to get ⟨i, hi, hxi⟩, Finset.mem_range.mp hi for i < N, then ⟨le_trans (ha (Nat.zero_le i)) hxi.1, lt_of_lt_of_le hxi.2 (ha (by omega))⟩ with ha : Monotone a. Package the two as one lemma over any LinearOrder and any monotone chain, so it is proved once and reused for every level (including the level-m grid of the unit interval itself, with j = 0 and m = 0).
- Monotone of the affine grid: intro r s hrs, dsimp, then div_le_div_of_nonneg_right (by exact_mod_cast Nat.add_le_add_left hrs _) (by positivity).
- Endpoint identity: have hp : 2 ^ n = 2 ^ m * 2 ^ (n - m) := by rw [← pow_add, Nat.add_sub_of_le hmn] (hmn : m ≤ n); then rw [hp], push_cast, field_simp for both endpoint equalities. The fine cell's right endpoint arrives as (j·2^(n−m) + r + 1)/2^n; Nat.add_assoc aligns it with a (r + 1).
- Cover of Ico 0 1 by the level-m grid: the same lemma with a r = r/2^m and N = 2^m, after simp reduces a 0 to 0 and a (2^m) to 1 (div_self with the cast nonzero).
- Endpoint discharge: from t ∈ Ico ((k−1)/2^n) (k/2^n) and hk : k ≤ 2^n, (div_le_one (by positivity)).2 (by exact_mod_cast hk) gives k/2^n ≤ 1, so t < 1 and t ≠ 1 by linarith [ht.2]; a subst on t = 1 followed by that linarith is the whole branch.

Provenance (mined-from): weak nullness of an alternating dyadic sign family; two Students on the same statement, both already holding a memory that describes the abstract chain and set-integral additivity, still named the concrete casted-endpoint partition equality as the wall and reached for floor arithmetic.

4e946189db4a074f6edda7a4955edb8d5aa23123.hook: proving an integration-by-parts or divergence identity over an arbitrary bounded open subset of Fin n → ℝ, where Mathlib's divergence theorem only covers boxes and Icc products
4e946189db4a074f6edda7a4955edb8d5aa23123.name: divergence-theorem-box-shaped-open-set-needs-exhaustion
4e946189db4a074f6edda7a4955edb8d5aa23123.body: Mathlib's divergence/integration-by-parts API is box-shaped: in MeasureTheory/Integral/DivergenceTheorem.lean every public form — integral_divergence_of_hasFDerivAt_off_countable (and its primed variant), integral_divergence_prod_Icc_* — integrates over a Box (Fin n) or an Icc product, never over an arbitrary bounded open U. When a weak-gradient / integration-by-parts identity (∫_U u ∂φ = -∫_U g φ) is stated over an open set, searching for an open-set divergence theorem is a dead end. Available moves: (a) restructure so the boundary term vanishes by compact support inside a box containing supp φ and apply the box theorem on that box; or (b) plan a countable box-exhaustion of U with boundary-term control as its own explicit sub-project — substantial, not a one-line gap. The error signature of this obstacle is a goal about ∫ x in U against a library of theorems about ∫ x in Icc.

de3a7db9bdfb7874562db06663cf648056fb58a7.hook: Distributional differentiation must be inverted on compactly supported smooth test functions, but an ordinary antiderivative is compactly supported only after removing its integral obstruction.
de3a7db9bdfb7874562db06663cf648056fb58a7.name: normalized primitive operator for test functions
de3a7db9bdfb7874562db06663cf648056fb58a7.body: Choose a fixed compactly supported smooth function rho with integral one and project each test function phi to Q phi = phi - (integral phi) • rho. Then Q phi has integral zero, so its left-tail integral P phi(x) = integral over (-infinity,x] of Q phi is smooth, compactly supported, and satisfies derivative(P phi) = Q phi. Prove P continuous by the LF universal property: on each fixed input support, the supports of Q phi lie in one common compact interval; factor P through that output stage; bound seminorm order zero by interval length times the sup norm of Q phi, and reduce every positive derivative seminorm to the preceding seminorm of Q phi. The resulting continuous linear P transposes against a distribution to give a distributional primitive. Mined from the residual where a pointwise primitive existed but the continuous choice required for transposition was missing.

fd1d958f75641cb3683567ee6ef691656da2b446.hook: A continuous or smooth test-function predicate requires the raw `Function.support` itself to be compact on a connected noncompact ambient space.
fd1d958f75641cb3683567ee6ef691656da2b446.name: audit raw support before building a compact-support completion
fd1d958f75641cb3683567ee6ef691656da2b446.body: Mathlib's `Function.support f` is the nonzero locus, not its closure. Continuity makes that locus open; assumed compactness makes it closed. If it is nonempty in a connected space, `IsClopen.eq_univ` makes it the whole space, so a continuous projection onto an unbounded coordinate contradicts compactness. Thus the predicate admits only the zero function. Use `tsupport f` when the intended condition is ordinary compact support, and audit any completion generated by the stronger predicate before invoking Sobolev or Lax--Milgram machinery.

ad986deceaf627f53ce26c8441578eb1af48b1d2.hook: A maximum modulus argument on a disk has bounded the frontier, and the step from there to the value at the centre — a product of the two boundary bounds, or the square root of that product — demands that those bounding constants be nonnegative, which the statement never assumed.
ad986deceaf627f53ce26c8441578eb1af48b1d2.name: nonnegativity-of-a-boundary-bound-comes-free-from-its-own-hypothesis
ad986deceaf627f53ce26c8441578eb1af48b1d2.body:
PATTERN — a bound hypothesis over a nonempty set already contains the nonnegativity the estimate lemmas are asking for.

The shape: a maximum modulus argument on a disk has given you a bound on the frontier, the value at the centre is bounded by a product or by the square root of a product of the boundary constants, and now the estimate lemmas will not proceed because nobody assumed those constants nonnegative. A hypothesis of the form "the norm of f z is at most a, for every z in S" looks under-hypothesised the moment a downstream step demands that 0 ≤ a. Do not repair the statement and do not add the hypothesis. The fact is free, by either of two routes:

- transitivity, when you already hold the bound at the point being estimated: 0 ≤ the norm ≤ a, i.e. norm-nonnegativity composed with the bound itself;
- instantiation, when you need the constant nonnegative in isolation: apply the hypothesis at one witness point of S. Nonemptiness of S is the entire content, and choosing the witness is one line. On the unit circle, the imaginary unit and its negation are the cheap witnesses for an upper-arc and a lower-arc hypothesis respectively; on any sphere or level set, any point you can already prove lies in it will do.

This is also what makes the multiplicative step go through. Combining two upper bounds into a bound on a product is a SIDE-CONDITION problem, not a rewriting problem, but a mismatched application reports as a unification failure on the main inequality — which sends you back to the algebra instead of to the side goals. Discharge the nonnegativity obligations first, apply the estimate lemma, and if the assembled product comes out with its factors transposed, commute at the end rather than re-deriving it.

LEAF — the exact signatures that bite.

- The four-argument product estimate is: from a ≤ b, from c ≤ d, from 0 ≤ c, and from 0 ≤ b, conclude a*c ≤ b*d. The two nonnegativity arguments are for the LEFT factor of the SECOND pair and the RIGHT factor of the FIRST — not the pair you expect from reading the conclusion. Read the signature in your Mathlib revision before the second failed application; `gcongr` and `positivity` are the alternatives when the shape is standard.

- The two obligations, spelled: 0 ≤ c is `norm_nonneg _`; 0 ≤ b, where b is a bounding constant, is `(norm_nonneg _).trans h` with h the bound at any point. Both are one term.

- `Real.le_sqrt` takes BOTH nonnegativity facts explicitly and then states an iff: x ≤ the square root of y iff x squared ≤ y. Assemble its second argument with `mul_nonneg` from the two constants you just obtained, and convert the squared side with `sq` rather than fighting the power form.

- A transposed product is repaired in place with `mul_comm` under a rewrite of the assembled hypothesis; do not re-derive the estimate with the factors swapped.

778b46eed2cf59fb94eb4d2357230a7ff2c1e533.hook: classify normal subgroups of a small concrete group via conjugacy-class union counting, not subgroup enumeration or native_decide
778b46eed2cf59fb94eb4d2357230a7ff2c1e533.name: normal-subgroup-lattice-from-conjugacy-class-union
778b46eed2cf59fb94eb4d2357230a7ff2c1e533.body: PATTERN — the obstacle. To classify the normal subgroups of a small concrete group (e.g. a symmetric group) the classical argument is: a normal subgroup is a union of conjugacy classes, so class sizes plus Lagrange force its order into a short list, and each surviving order is identified with a named subgroup. Agents instead reach for native_decide/decide on `Subgroup` propositions or for a packaged lattice theorem — neither exists: `Subgroup` of `Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` has no Decidable instance, and Mathlib ships no normal-lattice enumeration for any concrete group. PATTERN — the move. Derive normality-vs-order from conjugacy data already in hand: class sizes from `Equiv.Perm.card_isConj_eq` force |N| into a short list by union-of-classes counting; membership in a class is `IsConj`, and `Equiv.Perm.isConj_iff_cycleType_eq` gives carrier containment steps. For the converse (an N of the right order equals the named subgroup), compare orders and prove one inclusion, not pointwise equality. LEAF — spellings that compiled in this domain: `Equiv.Perm.card_isConj_eq (g := σ)`, `Equiv.Perm.isConj_iff_cycleType_eq`, representatives' cycle types discharged by `native_decide` on `Equiv.Perm.cycleType` (decidable, unlike Subgroup equality). MINED FROM a Student attempt on the S4 classification problem that left the normal-lattice conjunct as sorry after native_decide failed with 'failed to synthesize Decidable' on a Subgroup proposition.

50ec96b2fcf8614ede6b137318c84a0f43c66a8e.hook: Retrieve when Banach uniqueness has been proved for an integral operator but the theorem quantifies over all bounded classical solutions of the associated boundary-value ODE.
50ec96b2fcf8614ede6b137318c84a0f43c66a8e.name: fixed-point uniqueness requires a converse Green representation
50ec96b2fcf8614ede6b137318c84a0f43c66a8e.body: Do not identify ODE uniqueness with fixed-point uniqueness until every admissible classical solution has been shown to satisfy the integral equation. Derive a finite-basepoint variation formula, take the basepoint to the boundary with one-sided `Tendsto` facts and `tendsto_nhds_unique`, then package the restricted solution into the same `C₀` closed ball. Apply the operator's fixed-point uniqueness theorem to the two subtype values and use `congrArg` on evaluation to recover pointwise equality.

ab9a5fc2652685aaf24cd70115eb670f1e7df1c1.hook: A product of distinct orbit images of a prime should divide an invariant multiple, but the convenient finset theorem assumes the ring has only one unit.
ab9a5fc2652685aaf24cd70115eb670f1e7df1c1.name: use-multiset-associated-counts-for-squarefree-orbit-divisibility
ab9a5fc2652685aaf24cd70115eb670f1e7df1c1.body: Parent pattern: math-formalization/notation-semantics-traps. Use `Multiset.prod_primes_dvd`, whose third premise is `∀ a, s.countP (Associated a) ≤ 1`, instead of the similarly named finset theorem requiring `Subsingleton Rˣ`. In polynomial rings the latter hypothesis is usually false because nonzero constants are units. Prove the count bound by showing any two orbit entries associated to the same element are associated to each other, transporting by the inverse group element, and using associate rigidity to conclude equality; finset nodup then supplies the numerical bound. Map the original divisibility through each automorphism with `map_dvd` and rewrite the target by invariance. Rewrite rule — scope: prime-product divisibility in rings with nontrivial units; before: choose the finset theorem matching the source container; after: inspect unit assumptions and pass through `.val` to the multiset theorem with an explicit associated-count proof; level: Mathlib API selection; confidence: high; evidence-ids: certified solver diff. Mined from a residual whose boundary comment identified the multiset theorem but had not assembled its associate-count premise.

f24b188c5ad5e50fad1f411a13bc04aab9a3aa6c.hook: An integrand on the positive half-line has a removable singularity at the endpoint after pairing and an exponentially decaying tail, and integrability on the whole half-line is needed before exhaustion or dominated convergence can start; assembling it from the continuity and tail bounds is the wall.
f24b188c5ad5e50fad1f411a13bc04aab9a3aa6c.name: half-line-integrability-with-a-removable-endpoint-singularity-and-exponential-tail
f24b188c5ad5e50fad1f411a13bc04aab9a3aa6c.body:
PATTERN — the obstacle. Everything downstream — exhaustion of the truncation, dominated convergence over partial sums — takes `IntegrableOn f (Ioi 0)` as input, and that one hypothesis has three unrelated pieces: the singular endpoint, a compact middle, and an unbounded tail. A single majorant valid on all of `Ioi 0` does not exist, because the geometric denominator vanishes at the endpoint and the numerator only decays in the tail.

PATTERN — the move. Split at 1. On `Ioc 0 1` integrate the CONTINUOUS EXTENSION (the paired quotient with its removable value filled in) and transfer to the original integrand by an almost-everywhere congruence, since the two differ only at the endpoint. On `Ioi 1` dominate by an explicit real exponential, using that the denominator is separated from zero past 1. Glue by union.

LEAF — checked by elaboration at the pinned Mathlib.
- Removable value: write numerator and denominator as functions of a complex variable with `HasDerivAt` at the singular point (`HasDerivAt.cexp`, `.const_mul`, `.sub`, `hasDerivAt_id`). `HasDerivAt.tendsto_slope_zero` gives each difference quotient's limit along `𝓝[≠] 0`, and `Tendsto.div` (denominator derivative ≠ 0) gives the quotient's limit as the ratio of derivatives; no l'Hôpital lemma is needed, only `Tendsto.congr'` to cancel the common `t⁻¹ •` factor (`mul_div_mul_left`). The extension is `Function.update (fun z ↦ N z / D z) 0 (N' / D')`; `continuousAt_update_same.mpr` turns that limit into `ContinuousAt` at the point, and `continuousAt_update_of_ne` with `ContinuousAt.div` (`fun_prop` for the pieces, plus a nonvanishing argument) gives continuity elsewhere. Restrict to the real axis by composing with `Complex.continuous_ofReal.continuousAt`.
- Compact piece: `(hcont.continuousOn.integrableOn_Icc).mono_set Ioc_subset_Icc_self : IntegrableOn ext (Ioc 0 1)`, then `Integrable.congr` (an `IntegrableOn` is `Integrable` for the restricted measure, so `.congr` resolves by dot notation) with `filter_upwards [ae_restrict_mem measurableSet_Ioc] with x hx` and the pointwise equality for `x ≠ 0` to replace the extension by the original integrand.
- Tail: for `x ≥ 1`, `‖1 - cexp (-x)‖ = 1 - Real.exp (-x) ≥ 1 - Real.exp (-1)`: rewrite `cexp (-x)` as `((Real.exp (-x) : ℝ) : ℂ)` via `Complex.ofReal_exp`, then `norm_cast`, `Real.norm_eq_abs`, `abs_of_nonneg` with `Real.exp_le_one_iff`, and `gcongr`. The majorant `c⁻¹ * Real.exp (-(1 - ω.re) * x)` is integrable by `(integrableOn_exp_mul_Ioi hrate 1).const_mul c⁻¹`; `Integrable.mono'` then needs `ContinuousOn.aestronglyMeasurable … measurableSet_Ioi` and the ae bound, opened by `filter_upwards [ae_restrict_mem measurableSet_Ioi]`; `Complex.norm_exp`, `norm_div`, and `inv_le_inv₀` finish the pointwise inequality. The strip hypothesis on the parameter is used exactly here, once per family (`Re ω < 1` for one, `0 < Re ω` for the reflected one), combined by `Integrable.sub`.
- Glue: `(h01.union h1).mono_set` with `x ∈ Ioi 0 → x ∈ Ioc 0 1 ∨ x ∈ Ioi 1` by `by_cases hx1 : x ≤ 1`, or rewrite the set with `Set.Ioc_union_Ioi_eq_Ioi zero_le_one`.

Provenance (mined-from): the same principal-value integral in an open strip; the Student named the half-line integrability assembly as the wall of its second attempt, with the recipe and the lemma names already in hand.

12470d02f5db2dcc43dce28a414eec3508ae8a6d.hook: A real integral is being evaluated by pushing it through a complex transform; `push_cast`/`norm_cast` have already normalized every coercion onto an atom, and the real-part projection STILL will not simplify. The cause is not the casts. The library's `integral_re` commutation lemma is stated over a GENERIC RCLike field, so what you get back is headed by `RCLike.re`, not `Complex.re`, and no `Complex.*_re` projection lemma fires on it, while a bare `simp` can instead expand through `RCLike.normSq_to_complex` into `normSq` junk. Convert the head first with the rfl-simp lemmas `RCLike.re_to_complex` / `im_to_complex` / `I_to_complex` (namespace `RCLike`, `Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Basic.lean`), or restate the goal with `show Complex.re _ = _`. Better: enter the complex world at the START, by rewriting the real integrand BACKWARDS through `← RCLike.re_to_complex` and only then applying `integral_re` — which is exactly how Mathlib proves its own real exponential integrals over `Ioi`.
12470d02f5db2dcc43dce28a414eec3508ae8a6d.name: real-part-projection-blocked-by-generic-rclike-head
12470d02f5db2dcc43dce28a414eec3508ae8a6d.body:
PATTERN — the friction is the generic-instance layer, not the coercion tower.

Mathlib's integration and transform APIs are stated over a generic `RCLike` field and a generic real inner-product space, not over ℂ and ℝ. A concrete goal about a real integral therefore comes back carrying generic heads: `RCLike.re` where you expected `Complex.re`, `RCLike.I` where you expected `Complex.I`, an inner-product pairing `inner ℝ x v` where you expected `x * v`, and an ℝ-smul where you expected complex multiplication. Each of these is DEFINITIONALLY the concrete thing and SYNTACTICALLY not it, so the concrete simp set makes no progress and says nothing about why.
